chapters.title: Book 1
paragraphs: Agamemnon and Achilles quarrel—Achilles withdraws from the war and sends his mother Thetis to ask Zeus to help the Trojans—Zeus and Hera have a scene on Olympus.

Sing, goddess, of the anger of Achilles son of Peleus. It brought countless sufferings on the Achaeans. It sent many brave souls rushing down to Hades, and it left many heroes as prey for dogs and vultures. In this the counsels of Zeus were fulfilled, from the day when the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles first fell out with each other.

Which of the gods set them quarreling? It was the son of Zeus and Leto. He was angry with the king, and he sent a plague on the army that killed the people, because the son of Atreus had dishonored his priest Chryses. Chryses had come to the ships of the Achaeans to free his daughter, and he brought a great ransom with him. In his hand he carried the scepter of Apollo, wrapped in a suppliant’s wreath, and he begged the Achaeans for help, above all the two sons of Atreus, who were their chiefs.

“Sons of Atreus,” he cried, “and all you other Achaeans, may the gods who live on Olympus let you sack the city of Priam and get home safely. But free my daughter and take a ransom for her, out of respect for Apollo, son of Zeus.”

All the other Achaeans cried out together that the priest should be respected and the ransom accepted. Agamemnon did not agree. He spoke harshly to the priest and drove him off with rough words. “Old man,” he said, “do not let me find you loitering by our ships, and do not come back later either. Your scepter of the god and your wreath will do you no good. I will not free her. She will grow old in my house at Argos, far from her own country, working at her loom and sharing my bed. Now go, and do not provoke me, or you will be sorry.”

The old man was afraid and obeyed. He said not a word. He walked along the shore of the roaring sea, and when he was far off he prayed to King Apollo, whom lovely Leto bore. “Hear me,” he cried, “god of the silver bow, you who protect Chryse and holy Cilla and rule Tenedos with your might. Hear me, god of Sminthe. If I ever covered your temple with garlands, or burned the thigh-bones of bulls and goats for you in their fat, then grant my prayer. Make the Danaans pay with your arrows for my tears.”

So he prayed, and Apollo heard him. The god came down furious from the peaks of Olympus, with his bow and quiver on his shoulder. The arrows rattled on his back from the rage shaking him. He sat down apart from the ships with a face as dark as night. Then he shot an arrow among them, and his silver bow rang out with death. He hit the mules and the dogs first. Soon he aimed his shafts at the people themselves, and the pyres of the dead burned all day long.

For nine days he shot his arrows among the people. On the tenth day Achilles called them to an assembly, put up to it by Hera, who saw the Achaeans dying and pitied them. When they had gathered, he stood up and spoke to them.

“Son of Atreus,” he said, “I think we should turn back and go home, if we want to escape destruction, since war and plague together are cutting us down. Let us ask some priest or prophet, or some interpreter of dreams (dreams too come from Zeus), to tell us why Phoebus Apollo is so angry. Let him say whether it is over a vow we broke or a great sacrifice we failed to offer, and whether Apollo will accept the smoke of unblemished lambs and goats and lift the plague from us.”

With that he sat down. Then Calchas son of Thestor stood up to speak. He was the wisest of augurs and knew what was, what is and what is to come. It was he who had led the Achaean fleet to Ilium, using the prophecies Phoebus Apollo had given him. Honestly and kindly, he spoke to them like this.

“Achilles, beloved of heaven, you ask me to explain the anger of King Apollo. I will do so. But first think, and swear that you will stand firmly beside me in word and deed. I know I will offend a man who rules the Argives with great power, and all the Achaeans are subject to him. An ordinary man cannot stand against a king’s anger. Even if the king swallows his displeasure now, he will keep his resentment until he has taken his revenge. So consider whether you will protect me or not.”

Achilles answered, “Do not be afraid. Say whatever heaven puts in your mind. I swear by Apollo, Calchas, the god you pray to and whose oracles you reveal to us, that no Danaan at our ships will lay a hand on you while I am alive and looking at the light of day. That holds even if you name Agamemnon himself, who is by far the greatest of the Achaeans.”

Then the seer spoke with confidence. “The god,” he said, “is not angry over any vow or sacrifice. He is angry for his priest, whom Agamemnon dishonored by refusing to free his daughter or take a ransom for her. That is why Apollo has sent these troubles on us, and he will send more. He will not lift this plague from the Danaans until Agamemnon gives the girl back to her father without payment or ransom, and sends a holy sacrifice to Chryse. Then perhaps we can win him over.”

With that he sat down. Agamemnon rose in anger. His heart was black with rage and his eyes blazed like fire as he glared at Calchas. “Prophet of evil,” he said, “you have never once told me anything pleasant. You always love to foretell trouble. You have never brought me a good word or a good deed. Now you stand among the Danaans and say that Apollo plagues us because I would not accept a ransom for this girl, the daughter of Chryses. I wanted to keep her in my own house. I love her more than my own wife Clytemnestra, and she is Clytemnestra’s equal in looks and figure, in mind and skills. Even so, I will give her up if I must, because I want the people to live, not die. But you must find me another prize, or I alone of the Argives will have none. That is not right. All of you can see that my prize is going somewhere else.”

Achilles answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, greediest of all men, how will the Achaeans find you another prize? We have no common store to take one from. What we took from the cities has already been shared out, and we cannot take back those awards. Give this girl to the god. If Zeus ever lets us sack the city of Troy, we will repay you three and four times over.”

Agamemnon said, “Achilles, brave as you are, you will not trick me like this. You will not get the better of me or persuade me. Are you to keep your own prize while I sit meekly with my loss and hand the girl over because you tell me to? Let the Achaeans find me a prize that suits me, as a fair exchange. If not, I will come and take your prize myself, or the prize of Ajax or of Odysseus, and whoever I come to will regret my visit. But we can think about that later. For now, let us launch a ship into the sea and find a crew for her specially. Let us load a great sacrifice on board, and let us put Chryseis on her too. Let one of our chiefs command the ship, either Ajax, or Idomeneus, or you, son of Peleus, mighty warrior that you are. Then we can offer sacrifice and calm the god’s anger.”

Achilles glared at him and answered, “You are steeped in insolence and greed. How can any Achaean obey you, whether on a raid or in open battle? I did not come here to fight because of any wrong the Trojans did me. I have no quarrel with them. They have never driven off my cattle or my horses, or cut down my crops on the rich soil of Phthia. A great distance lies between them and me, with mountains and the roaring sea. We followed you, Sir Insolence, to please you, not ourselves. We came to win satisfaction from the Trojans for your shameless self and for Menelaus. You forget all this. Now you threaten to rob me of the prize I worked for, which the sons of the Achaeans gave me. When the Achaeans sack some rich Trojan city, I never get a prize as good as yours, even though my hands do the greater part of the fighting. When the sharing comes, your share is by far the biggest. And I, naturally, go back to my ships with whatever I can get, and I must be grateful, once the labor of fighting is over. Now I am going back to Phthia. It is far better for me to sail home with my ships. I will not stay here dishonored, piling up gold and wealth for you.”

Agamemnon answered, “Run away if you want. I will not beg you to stay. I have others here who will honor me, and above all Zeus, the lord of counsel. Of all the kings here, none is so hateful to me as you. You are always quarreling and spiteful. So you are brave? Was it not heaven that made you so? Go home with your ships and your comrades, and lord it over the Myrmidons. I do not care about you or your anger. And this is what I will do. Phoebus Apollo is taking Chryseis from me, so I will send her off with my own ship and my own men. But then I will come to your tent and take your prize Briseis, so that you learn how much stronger I am than you, and so that anyone else will be afraid to set himself up as my equal or compare himself with me.”

The son of Peleus was furious. In his shaggy chest his heart was torn between two choices. He could draw his sword, push the others aside and kill the son of Atreus. Or he could hold himself back and check his anger. While he was in two minds, and was already drawing his mighty sword from its sheath, Athena came down from heaven. Hera had sent her, out of her love for both men. She seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair. Only he could see her, and none of the others. Achilles turned in amazement, and from the fire flashing in her eyes he knew at once that she was Athena. “Why have you come,” he said, “daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus? To see the arrogance of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? Let me tell you—and it will certainly happen—he will pay for this insolence with his life.”

Athena said, “I have come from heaven, if you will listen, to tell you to hold back your anger. Hera sent me, who cares for you both equally. So stop this brawling, and do not draw your sword. Abuse him with words if you like, and your words will not be wasted. I tell you—and it will certainly happen—that for this insult you will one day receive gifts three times as splendid. Hold back, and obey us.”
“Goddess,” Achilles answered, “however angry a man is, he must do what you two command. That is best, for the gods always hear the prayers of the man who has obeyed them.”

He kept his hand on the silver hilt of his sword and pushed the blade back into its sheath, as Athena told him. Then she went back to Olympus, to the other gods and to the house of aegis-bearing Zeus.

But the son of Peleus began abusing the son of Atreus again, for he was still in a rage. “Drunkard,” he cried, “with the face of a dog and the heart of a deer! You never dare to arm and go out to fight with the army, or to join our chosen men in an ambush. You shrink from that as you do from death itself. You would much rather go around and rob any man who speaks against you of his prize. You feed on your people, because you are king over a feeble folk. Otherwise, son of Atreus, this would be the last time you insulted anyone. So I tell you, and I swear it with a great oath. By this scepter of mine—which will never sprout leaf or shoot, nor bud again, from the day it left its stem in the mountains, since the axe stripped it of leaf and bark, and now the sons of the Achaeans carry it as judges and guardians of the laws of heaven—as surely as this, I swear that one day they will long for Achilles and not find him. On the day of your distress, when your men fall dying under the murderous hand of Hector, you will not know how to help them. You will tear your heart with rage that you insulted the bravest of the Achaeans.”

With that the son of Peleus threw his gold-studded scepter on the ground and sat down. On the other side the son of Atreus was starting a furious reply. Then smooth-tongued Nestor got up, the clear speaker of the Pylians, and the words flowed from his lips sweeter than honey. Two generations of men, born and raised in Pylos, had died under his rule, and now he was king over the third. Honestly and kindly, he spoke to them like this.

“Truly,” he said, “a great sorrow has come on the land of the Achaeans. Priam and his sons would surely be delighted, and the Trojans glad at heart, if they could hear of this quarrel between you two, who are so excellent in battle and in counsel. I am older than either of you, so listen to me. Besides, I have been the close friend of men even greater than you, and they did not ignore my advice. I will never see such men again as Pirithous and Dryas, shepherd of his people, or Caeneus, Exadius, godlike Polyphemus, and Theseus son of Aegeus, the equal of the immortals. These were the mightiest men ever born on this earth. They were the mightiest, and when they fought the fiercest tribes of mountain savages, they crushed them completely. I came from far-off Pylos and joined them, because they asked me to come, and I fought as well as I could. No man alive today could stand against them, yet they heard my words and were persuaded. Let it be the same with you, for this is the better way. So, Agamemnon, strong as you are, do not take this girl away, since the sons of the Achaeans have already given her to Achilles. And you, Achilles, do not keep fighting with the king, for no man who holds a scepter by the favor of Zeus has the same honor as Agamemnon. You are strong, and a goddess is your mother. But Agamemnon is stronger than you, because he has more people under him. Son of Atreus, I beg you, check your anger. End this quarrel with Achilles, who on the day of battle is a tower of strength for the Achaeans.”

Agamemnon answered, “Old friend, everything you have said is true. But this man wants to be our lord and master. He wants to be lord of everyone, king of everyone, and captain of everyone, and that will hardly happen. Suppose the gods have made him a great warrior. Have they also given him the right to speak abusively?”

Achilles cut in. “I would be a mean coward,” he cried, “if I gave way to you in everything. Give your orders to other people, not to me, because I will obey you no longer. And I tell you this—take it to heart—I will not fight you or any man over this girl, since those who took her away were the ones who gave her. But of everything else at my ship, you will carry off nothing by force. Try it, so that others can see. If you do, my spear will be red with your blood.”

When they had quarreled like this in anger, they stood up and broke up the assembly at the ships of the Achaeans. The son of Peleus went back to his tents and ships with the son of Menoetius and his company. Agamemnon launched a vessel into the water and chose a crew of twenty oarsmen. He led Chryseis on board and also sent a great sacrifice for the god. Odysseus went as captain.

Those men boarded their ship and set out over the sea. Meanwhile the son of Atreus told the people to purify themselves, and they did so, throwing their filth into the sea. On the sea-shore they made great sacrifices of bulls and goats without blemish, and the smoke of the offering, with its savory smell, curled up toward heaven.

So they busied themselves all through the host. But Agamemnon had not forgotten the threat he had made against Achilles. He called his trusty messengers and squires, Talthybius and Eurybates. “Go to the tent of Achilles, son of Peleus,” he said. “Take Briseis by the hand and bring her here. If he will not give her up, I will come with others and take her myself—and that will press him harder.”

He gave them further strict orders and sent them off. They went sorrowfully along the seaside until they reached the tents and ships of the Myrmidons. There they found Achilles sitting beside his tent and his ships, and he was displeased to see them. They stood before him in fear and reverence and did not say a word. But he knew them and said, “Welcome, heralds, messengers of gods and men. Come closer. My quarrel is not with you but with Agamemnon, who has sent you for the girl Briseis. Patroclus, bring her out and hand her over to them. But let these two be my witnesses before the blessed gods, before mortal men, and before the fierceness of Agamemnon’s anger: if there is ever again a need for me to save the people from ruin, they will seek me and they will not find me. Agamemnon is mad with rage. He does not know how to look both before and after, so that the Achaeans might fight safely by their ships.”

Patroclus did what his dear comrade had told him. He brought Briseis out of the tent and gave her to the heralds, who took her with them to the ships of the Achaeans—and the woman did not want to go. Then Achilles went off alone to the shore of the hoary sea. He wept and looked out over the boundless waste of waters. Raising his hands, he prayed to his immortal mother. “Mother,” he cried, “you bore me doomed to live only a short season. Surely Zeus, who thunders from Olympus, could have made that short life glorious. He has not. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, has dishonored me and taken my prize from me by force.”

He wept aloud as he spoke, and his mother heard him where she sat in the depths of the sea beside her father, the old man. At once she rose out of the waves like a gray mist. She sat down in front of him as he stood weeping, stroked him with her hand, and said, “My son, why are you weeping? What grieves you? Do not hide it from me. Tell me, so that we can know it together.”

Achilles sighed deeply and said, “You know it already. Why should I tell you what you know well? We went to Thebe, the strong city of Eetion, sacked it, and brought the spoil back here. The sons of the Achaeans divided it fairly among themselves, and they chose lovely Chryseis as the prize for Agamemnon. Then Chryses, priest of Apollo, came to the ships of the Achaeans to free his daughter. He brought a great ransom, and in his hand he carried the scepter of Apollo, wreathed with a suppliant’s wreath. He begged the Achaeans, and most of all the two sons of Atreus, who were their chiefs.

“All the rest of the Achaeans, with one voice, wanted to respect the priest and accept the ransom he offered. Agamemnon did not. He spoke fiercely to Chryses and sent him roughly away. So the priest went back in anger, and Apollo, who loved him dearly, heard his prayer. The god sent a deadly dart against the Argives, and the people died in heaps, one on top of another, for the arrows flew everywhere through the wide host of the Achaeans. At last a seer, with full knowledge, explained the oracles of Apollo to us. I was the first to say that we should appease the god. Then the son of Atreus rose in anger and made a threat, and he has since carried it out. The Achaeans are now taking the girl by ship to Chryse and sending sacrificial gifts to the god. But the heralds have only just taken from my tent the daughter of Briseus, whom the Achaeans had awarded to me.

“So help your brave son, if you are able. Go to Olympus, and if you have ever done Zeus a service in word or deed, ask for his help. Often in my father’s house I have heard you boast that you alone of the immortals saved the son of Cronus from ruin, when the others—Hera, Poseidon, and Pallas Athena—would have put him in bonds. It was you, goddess, who freed him, by calling to Olympus the hundred-handed monster whom the gods call Briareus but men call Aegaeon, for he is stronger even than his father. When he took his seat in all his glory beside the son of Cronus, the other gods were afraid and did not bind Zeus. Go to him now, remind him of all this, clasp his knees, and ask him to help the Trojans. Let the Achaeans be hemmed in at the sterns of their ships and die on the sea-shore, so that they may have whatever joy they can get from their king, and so that Agamemnon may regret his blindness in insulting the foremost of the Achaeans.”

Thetis wept and answered, “My son, how unhappy I am that I ever bore you or nursed you. If only you had lived out your span at your ships free from all sorrow, for it is all too short. Alas, that you should be short of life and long of sorrow beyond your peers. It was a cruel hour in which I bore you. Nevertheless I will go to the snowy heights of Olympus and tell this tale to Zeus, if he will hear our prayer. Meanwhile stay where you are with your ships, nurse your anger against the Achaeans, and keep out of the fighting. Zeus went yesterday to Oceanus, to a feast among the Ethiopians, and the other gods went with him. He will return to Olympus in twelve days. Then I will go to his house with its floor of bronze and beg him, and I do not doubt that I can persuade him.”

With that she left him, still furious over the loss of the girl who had been taken from him. Meanwhile Odysseus reached Chryse with the sacrificial animals. When they were inside the harbor, they furled the sails and laid them in the ship’s hold. They slackened the forestays, lowered the mast into its place, and rowed the ship to the spot where they wanted her to lie. There they threw out the mooring-stones and made the hawsers fast. Then they climbed out onto the sea-shore and unloaded the offering for Apollo. Chryseis also left the ship, and Odysseus led her to the altar to put her in her father’s hands. “Chryses,” he said, “King Agamemnon has sent me to bring your child back to you, and to offer sacrifice to Apollo on behalf of the Danaans. We want to win over the god, who has now brought sorrow on the Argives.”

With these words he gave the girl to her father, who received her gladly. They set the holy offering in order around the altar of the god. They washed their hands and took up the barley-meal to sprinkle over the victims, while Chryses lifted up his hands and prayed aloud for them. “Hear me,” he cried, “god of the silver bow, who protect Chryse and holy Cilla and rule Tenedos with your might. You heard me before when I prayed, and you pressed hard on the Achaeans. Hear me again now, and keep this terrible plague away from the Danaans.”

So he prayed, and Apollo heard his prayer. When they had finished praying and sprinkling the barley-meal, they pulled back the heads of the victims, killed them, and flayed them. They cut out the thigh-bones and wrapped them in two layers of fat, with pieces of raw meat on top. Chryses laid these on the wood fire and poured wine over them, while the young men stood near him with five-pronged spits in their hands. When the thigh-bones were burned and they had tasted the inner meats, they cut up the rest small, put the pieces on the spits, and roasted them until done, then drew them off. When the work was finished and the feast was ready, they ate, and every man had his full share, so that all were satisfied. After they had had enough to eat and drink, pages filled the mixing-bowl with wine and water and handed it around, after giving every man his drink-offering.

All day long the young men worshipped the god with song, hymning him and singing the joyful paean, and the god took pleasure in their voices. When the sun went down and darkness came, they lay down to sleep by the stern cables of the ship. When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, they set sail again for the host of the Achaeans. Apollo sent them a fair wind, so they raised their mast and hoisted their white sails. The wind filled the sail, and the ship flew through the deep blue water, with the foam hissing against her bows as she sped on. When they reached the wide-stretching host of the Achaeans, they drew the vessel up onto the sands, high and dry, and set her strong props beneath her. Then they went off to their own tents and ships.
But Achilles stayed at his ships and nursed his anger. He did not go to the honorable assembly, and he did not go out to fight. He gnawed at his own heart, pining for battle and the war cry.

After twelve days the immortal gods came back to Olympus in a body, with Zeus leading the way. Thetis had not forgotten the task her son had given her. She rose from under the sea and went up through great heaven in the early morning to Olympus. There she found the mighty son of Cronus sitting all alone on its topmost ridges. She sat down in front of him, seized his knees with her left hand, and with her right caught him under the chin. Then she begged him, saying:—

“Father Zeus, if I ever did you a service in word or deed among the immortals, hear my prayer and honor my son, whose life is to be cut short so early. King Agamemnon has dishonored him by taking his prize and keeping her. Honor him yourself, then, Olympian lord of counsel, and give victory to the Trojans until the Achaeans give my son his due and load him with riches to make up for it.”

Zeus sat silent for a while and said nothing, but Thetis kept her firm hold of his knees and begged him a second time. “Nod your head,” she said, “and promise me for certain, or else refuse me—you have nothing to fear—so that I may learn how much you scorn me.”

Zeus was deeply troubled at this and answered, “It will bring me trouble if you set me quarreling with Hera, for she will provoke me with her taunting speeches. Even now she is always railing at me in front of the other gods and accusing me of helping the Trojans. Go back now, before she finds out. I will think the matter over and bring it about as you wish. Look, I nod my head so that you may believe me. This is the most solemn promise I can give to any god. When I have nodded my head, I never take back my word, or deceive, or fail to do what I have said.”
As he spoke, the son of Cronus bowed his dark brows. The ambrosial locks swayed on his immortal head, and vast Olympus shook.

Having made their plans, the two parted—Zeus to his house, while the goddess left the splendor of Olympus and plunged into the depths of the sea. The gods rose from their seats at the coming of their father. Not one of them dared to stay sitting, but all stood up as he came among them. So he took his seat there. But Hera saw him and knew that he and the old merman’s daughter, silver-footed Thetis, had been hatching mischief, and she began at once to scold him. “Trickster,” she cried, “which of the gods have you been taking into your counsels now? You are always settling matters in secret behind my back. If you can help it, you have never yet told me a word of your intentions.”

“Hera,” replied the father of gods and men, “do not expect to hear every one of my plans. You are my wife, yet you would struggle to understand them. Whenever it is right for you to know, you will hear it before any other god or man. But if I choose to keep something to myself, you are not to pry or ask me questions.”

“Dread son of Cronus,” answered Hera, “what are you saying? I? Pry and ask questions? Never. I let you have your own way in everything. Still, I strongly suspect that the old merman’s daughter Thetis has talked you over, for she was with you this very morning, holding your knees. I believe you have promised her that you will give glory to Achilles and kill many people at the ships of the Achaeans.”

“Wife,” said Zeus, “I can do nothing without your suspecting me and finding it out. You will gain nothing by it. I will only dislike you the more, and it will go harder with you. Granted that it is as you say, I mean to have it so. Sit down and hold your tongue as I order you. If I once begin to lay my hands on you, it will do you no good, though all heaven were on your side.”

Hera was frightened at this, so she curbed her stubborn will and sat down in silence. But the heavenly beings were uneasy throughout the house of Zeus, until the cunning workman Hephaestus began trying to calm his mother Hera. “It will be intolerable,” he said, “if you two fall to wrangling and set heaven in an uproar over a pack of mortals. If such ill counsels are going to win out, we shall have no pleasure at our banquet. So let me advise my mother—and she must know herself that it will be better—to make friends with my dear father Zeus, so that he does not scold her again and disturb our feast. If the Olympian Thunderer wants to hurl us all from our seats, he can, for he is by far the strongest. So give him fair words, and he will soon be in a good humor with us.”

As he spoke, he took a double cup of nectar and put it in his mother’s hand. “Cheer up, my dear mother,” he said, “and make the best of it. I love you dearly, and I would be very sorry to see you get a thrashing. However grieved I might be, I could not help, for there is no standing against Zeus. Once before, when I was trying to help you, he caught me by the foot and flung me from the heavenly threshold. I fell all day long, from morning until evening. At sunset I landed on the island of Lemnos, and there I lay with very little life left in me, until the Sintians came and tended me.”

This made Hera smile, and smiling, she accepted the cup from her son’s hands. Hephaestus then drew sweet nectar from the mixing-bowl and poured for the other gods, going around from left to right. When the blessed gods saw him bustling through the heavenly mansion, they broke into loud laughter.

So they feasted through the livelong day until the going down of the sun, and every one had his full share, so that all were satisfied. Apollo struck his lyre, and the Muses lifted up their sweet voices, calling and answering one another. When the sun’s glorious light had faded, they went home to bed, each in his own abode, which lame Hephaestus with his consummate skill had fashioned for them. Zeus, the Olympian lord of thunder, went to the bed where he always slept. When he had got into it, he went to sleep, with Hera of the golden throne by his side.

chapters.title: Book 2
paragraphs: A lying dream is sent by Zeus to Agamemnon, who calls the chiefs together and plans to test how his army feels—In the end the army marches out to fight—Catalogue of the Achaean and Trojan forces.

The other gods and the armored warriors on the plain slept soundly, but Zeus lay awake, thinking how he could honor Achilles and destroy great numbers of people at the ships of the Achaeans. In the end he decided that the best plan was to send a lying dream to King Agamemnon. He called one to him and said, “Lying Dream, go to the ships of the Achaeans, into the tent of Agamemnon, and give him my message word for word as I now tell you. Tell him to arm the Achaeans at once, for he is going to take Troy. The gods no longer have divided counsels. Hera has brought them all around to her own view, and disaster awaits the Trojans.”

The dream set off as soon as it had heard its message and quickly reached the ships of the Achaeans. It looked for Agamemnon son of Atreus and found him in his tent, wrapped in deep sleep. It stood over his head in the likeness of Nestor son of Neleus, the councillor whom Agamemnon honored above all the rest, and said:—

“You are sleeping, son of Atreus. A man who carries the welfare of an army and so many other cares on his shoulders should cut short his sleep. Listen to me at once, for I come as a messenger from Zeus. Though he is not near, he thinks of you and pities you. He tells you to arm the Achaeans at once, for you are going to take Troy. The gods no longer have divided counsels; Hera has brought them all around to her own view, and Zeus has doom in store for the Trojans. Remember this, and when you wake do not let it slip away from you.”

Then the dream left him, and Agamemnon thought of things that were surely never to come about. He believed he would take the city of Priam that very day. He had no idea what Zeus intended, who had many more hard-fought battles in store for Danaans and Trojans alike. Soon he woke, the divine message still ringing in his ears. He sat upright and put on his soft shirt, fair and new, and over it his heavy cloak. He bound his sandals onto his comely feet and slung his silver-studded sword over his shoulders. Then he took his father’s imperishable staff and went out to the ships of the Achaeans.

Meanwhile the goddess Dawn made her way up to vast Olympus to announce the day to Zeus and the other immortals. Agamemnon sent the criers around to call the people to assembly, and the people gathered as they were called. But first he summoned the elders to a meeting at the ship of Nestor king of Pylos. When they had come together, he laid a cunning plan before them.

“My friends,” he said, “in the dead of night a dream came to me from heaven. Its face and figure were exactly like Nestor’s. It stood over my head and said, ‘You are sleeping, son of Atreus. A man who carries the welfare of an army and so many other cares on his shoulders should cut short his sleep. Listen to me at once, for I am a messenger from Zeus. Though he is not near, he thinks of you and pities you. He tells you to arm the Achaeans at once, for you are going to take Troy. The gods no longer have divided counsels; Hera has brought them all around to her own view, and Zeus has doom in store for the Trojans. Remember this.’ Then the dream vanished and I woke. Now let us arm the sons of the Achaeans. But it will be well for me to test them first. For that purpose I will tell them to flee with their ships, and you others must go about among the host and stop them from doing so.”

Then he sat down, and Nestor, prince of Pylos, spoke to them with all sincerity and goodwill. “My friends,” he said, “princes and councillors of the Argives, if any other man of the Achaeans had told us of this dream, we would have called it false and paid no attention to it. But the man who saw it is the foremost among us. So we must set about arming the people.”

With this he led the way out of the assembly, and the other scepter-bearing kings rose with him, obeying Agamemnon’s word. The people pressed forward to hear. They swarmed like bees that pour out of a hollow cave and fly in endless crowds among the spring flowers, clustered in knots and clumps. In the same way the great multitude streamed from the ships and tents to the assembly and spread out along the wide-watered shore. Among them ran Wildfire Rumor, the messenger of Zeus, urging them always to the front. So they gathered in wild confusion, and the earth groaned under the tramp of men as they looked for their places. Nine heralds went crying among them to quiet the uproar and make them listen to the kings. At last the people were settled in their places and stopped their noise. Then King Agamemnon rose, holding his scepter. Hephaestus had made it, and he gave it to Zeus the son of Cronus. Zeus gave it to Hermes, slayer of Argus, guide and guardian. King Hermes gave it to Pelops, the mighty charioteer, and Pelops gave it to Atreus, shepherd of his people. When Atreus died he left it to Thyestes, rich in flocks, and Thyestes in turn left it to Agamemnon to carry, so that he might be lord of all Argos and of the isles. Leaning on this scepter, Agamemnon spoke to the Argives.

“My friends,” he said, “heroes, servants of Ares, the hand of heaven has come down heavily on me. Cruel Zeus solemnly promised me that I would sack the city of Priam before I went home. Now he has deceived me, and he orders me to go back to Argos in disgrace, having lost many of my people. This is the will of Zeus, who has laid many a proud city in the dust and will lay others too, for his power is above all. It will be a sorry tale in time to come that an Achaean host so great and valiant fought in vain against men fewer than themselves, and still the end is not in sight. Suppose the Achaeans and Trojans swore a solemn covenant and each side were counted—the Trojans by the roll of their householders, and we by companies of ten. Suppose each of our companies wanted a Trojan householder to pour its wine. We outnumber them so greatly that many a company would have no cup-bearer. But the Trojans have allies from other places in the town, and they are what prevent me from sacking the rich city of Ilium. Nine of Zeus’s years have passed. The timbers of our ships have rotted, and their tackling is no longer sound. Our wives and little ones at home wait anxiously for us, yet the work we came here to do is not done. So now let us all do as I say: let us sail back to our own land, for we shall not take Troy.”

With these words he stirred the hearts of the multitude, all those who did not know Agamemnon’s cunning plan. They surged to and fro like the waves of the Icarian Sea when the east and south winds burst from the clouds of heaven and lash them. Or they swayed like a field of corn when the west wind sweeps over it and the ears bow beneath the blast. In the same way they were tossed about as they ran with loud cries toward the ships, and the dust rose from under their feet to the sky. They cheered one another on to drag the ships into the sea. They cleared the channels in front of them and began pulling away the props from underneath the hulls, and the sky rang with their glad cries, so eager were they to go home.

Then the Argives would surely have gone home in a way that was not fated. But Hera spoke to Athena. “Alas, unwearying daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, are the Argives really going to flee home to their own land over the broad sea? Will they leave Priam and the Trojans the glory of still keeping Helen, for whose sake so many Achaeans have died at Troy, far from their homes? Go among the host at once and speak kindly to them, man by man, so that they do not draw their ships into the sea.”

Athena was quick to obey. She darted down from the topmost summits of Olympus and in a moment was at the ships of the Achaeans. There she found Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in counsel, standing alone. He had not yet laid a hand on his ship, because he was grieved and sorry. She went right up to him and said, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, are you all going to throw yourselves into your ships and run off to your own land like this? Will you leave Priam and the Trojans the glory of still keeping Helen, for whose sake so many Achaeans have died at Troy, far from their homes? Go among the host at once and speak kindly to them, man by man, so that they do not draw their ships into the sea.”

Odysseus knew the voice of the goddess. He threw off his cloak and set off running. His servant Eurybates, a man of Ithaca who waited on him, took charge of the cloak. Odysseus went straight up to Agamemnon and received from him his ancestral, imperishable staff. With it he went about among the ships of the Achaeans.

Whenever he met a king or chieftain, he stood beside him and spoke to him kindly. “Sir,” he said, “this flight is cowardly and unworthy of you. Keep to your post, and tell your people to keep their places too. You do not yet know the full mind of Agamemnon. He was only testing us, and before long he will make the Achaeans feel his displeasure. We were not all at the council to hear what he said. Take care that he does not grow angry and do us harm, for the pride of kings is great, and the hand of Zeus is with them.”

But when he came across a common man who was making noise, he struck him with his staff and scolded him. “You there, be quiet and listen to better men than yourself. You are a coward and no soldier. You count for nothing in fight or council. We cannot all be kings, and it is not good to have many masters. One man must be supreme—one king, to whom the son of scheming Cronus has given the scepter of sovereignty over you all.”

So masterfully did he go among the host, and the people hurried back to the council from their tents and ships. The noise they made was like the thunder of surf crashing down on the shore, when all the sea is in an uproar.

The rest now took their seats and stayed in their own places, but Thersites still went on wagging his unbridled tongue—a man of many words, and unseemly ones, a monger of sedition and a railer against all in authority, who did not care what he said so long as he could set the Achaeans laughing. He was the ugliest man who came to Troy—bandy-legged, lame in one foot, with both shoulders rounded and hunched over his chest. His head ran up to a point, and there was little hair on top of it. Achilles and Odysseus hated him most of all, because he quarreled with them most often. Now, though, in a shrill, squeaky voice, he began heaping abuse on Agamemnon. The Achaeans were angry and disgusted, but he kept on brawling and bawling at the son of Atreus all the same.

“Agamemnon,” he cried, “what is your complaint this time? What else do you want? Your tents are full of bronze and fair women, because we hand you the pick of them whenever we take a town. Is it more gold you want, which some Trojan will bring as a ransom for his son once I or another Achaean has captured him? Or a young girl to hide away and lie with? You are the ruler of the Achaeans, and it is wrong to lead them into such misery. You weak cowards, women rather than men, let us sail home. We will leave this fellow at Troy to stew among his prizes of honor and find out whether we were any use to him or not. Achilles is a far better man than he is, yet look how Agamemnon has treated him—he robbed Achilles of his prize and keeps it for himself. Achilles takes it meekly and shows no fight. If he did, son of Atreus, you would never insult him again.”

So Thersites railed, but Odysseus went straight up to him and rebuked him sternly. “Hold your glib tongue, Thersites,” he said, “and do not babble another word. Do not quarrel with princes when you have no one to back you. No viler creature has come to Troy with the sons of Atreus. Drop this chatter about kings. Do not revile them, and stop harping on going home. We do not yet know how things will turn out, or whether the Achaeans will return with good fortune or bad. How dare you mock Agamemnon because the Danaans have awarded him so many prizes? I tell you this, and it will surely happen: if I catch you talking such nonsense again, I will forfeit my own head and no longer be called father of Telemachus, or else I will take you, strip you stark naked, and whip you out of the assembly until you go blubbering back to the ships.”

Then Odysseus beat him across the back and shoulders with the staff until Thersites sank down in tears. The golden scepter raised a bloody weal on his back. Frightened and in pain, he sat down and wiped the tears from his eyes, looking foolish. The people pitied him, but they laughed heartily all the same, and one man would say to his neighbor, “Odysseus has done many good things before now in fight and council, but he never did the Argives a better service than when he shut this fellow’s mouth. He will not insult the kings any more.”

Such were the people’s words. Then Odysseus rose, scepter in hand, and Athena, in the likeness of a herald, told the people to be still, so that those far off could hear him and weigh his counsel. With all sincerity and goodwill he spoke to them:—

“King Agamemnon, the Achaeans are about to make you a byword among all mankind. They have forgotten the promise they made you when they set out from Argos, that you would not return until you had sacked the town of Troy. Like children or widowed women, they murmur and want to set off for home. It is true that they have had toil enough to lose heart. A man grows restless at being away from his wife even for a single month, when he is on shipboard at the mercy of wind and sea. But we have now been kept here nine long years. So I cannot blame the Achaeans for turning restive. Still, we will be shamed if we go home empty-handed after so long a stay. Therefore, my friends, be patient a little longer, so that we may learn whether the prophecies of Calchas were false or true.

“All of you who have not died since then must remember, as if it were yesterday or the day before, how the ships of the Achaeans were held back at Aulis when we were on our way here to make war on Priam and the Trojans. We were gathered around a fountain, offering great sacrifices to the gods on their holy altars. A fine plane tree stood there, and from beneath it welled a stream of pure water. Then we saw a prodigy. Zeus sent a fearful serpent out of the ground, with blood-red stains on its back, and it darted from under the altar onto the plane tree. On the topmost bough was a brood of young sparrows, quite small, peeping out from under the leaves. There were eight of them, and their mother who had hatched them made nine. The serpent ate the poor cheeping things while the old bird flew about lamenting her little ones. Then the serpent threw his coils around her and caught her by the wing as she screamed. When he had eaten both the sparrow and her young, the god who had sent him made him a sign: the son of scheming Cronus turned him into stone, and we stood there wondering at what had happened. Such a fearful portent had broken in upon our sacrifices, and Calchas at once told us the oracles of heaven. ‘Why are you speechless, Achaeans?’ he said. ‘Zeus has sent us this sign, long in coming and long before it is fulfilled, though its fame will last forever. As the serpent ate the eight fledglings and the sparrow that hatched them, which makes nine, so we shall fight nine years at Troy, but in the tenth we shall take the town.’ This was what he said, and now it is all coming true. So stay here, all of you, until we take the city of Priam.”

At this the Argives raised a shout, and the ships rang with the uproar. Then Nestor, knight of Gerene, spoke to them. “Shame on you,” he cried, “to stand here talking like children when you should be fighting like men. Where are our covenants now, and the oaths we have taken? Will our counsels be thrown into the fire, with our drink-offerings and the right hands of fellowship in which we put our trust? We waste our time in words, and for all our talking here we shall get no further. Son of Atreus, hold to your own steadfast purpose. Lead the Argives on to battle, and leave to rot this handful of men who scheme, and scheme in vain, to get back to Argos before they have learned whether Zeus is true or a liar. For the mighty son of Cronus surely promised that we would succeed, when we Argives set sail to bring death and destruction on the Trojans. He showed us favorable signs by flashing his lightning on our right hands. So let no one hurry to leave until he has lain with the wife of some Trojan and avenged the toil and sorrow he has suffered for the sake of Helen. Nevertheless, if any man is in such haste to be home again, let him lay his hand to his ship, so that he meets his doom in the sight of all. But, O king, consider and listen to my counsel, for what I say should not be lightly neglected. Divide your men, Agamemnon, into their tribes and clans, so that clans and tribes may stand by and help one another. If you do this, and the Achaeans obey you, you will find out who among chiefs and peoples are brave and who are cowards, for they will compete against each other. You will also learn whether it is by the counsel of heaven or by the cowardice of men that you fail to take the town.”

Agamemnon answered, “Nestor, you have once again outdone the sons of the Achaeans in counsel. By Father Zeus, Athena and Apollo, I wish I had ten more such councillors among them! The city of King Priam would soon fall beneath our hands, and we would sack it. But the son of Cronus afflicts me with futile wranglings and strife. Achilles and I are quarreling over this girl, and I was the first to offend. If we can be of one mind again, the Trojans will not hold off destruction for a day. Now go and take your morning meal, so that our hosts may join in fight. Sharpen your spears well, see carefully to the ordering of your shields, give your horses a good feed, and look your chariots over carefully, so that we may do battle the whole day long. We shall have no rest, not for a moment, until night falls to part us. The bands that hold your shields will be wet with sweat on your shoulders, your hands will grow weary on your spears, and your horses will steam in front of your chariots. If I see any man shirking the fight or trying to stay out of it at the ships, there will be no help for him. He will be prey to dogs and vultures.”

So he spoke, and the Achaeans roared their applause. As waves run high before the blast of the south wind and break on some lofty headland, dashing against it and buffeting it without ceasing as storms from every quarter drive them, so the Achaeans rose and hurried in all directions to their ships. There they lit fires at their tents and ate dinner. Every man offered sacrifice to one god or another, praying that he might live to come out of the fight. Agamemnon, king of men, sacrificed a fat five-year-old bull to the mighty son of Cronus, and he invited the princes and elders of his host. He asked Nestor first, and King Idomeneus, then the two Ajaxes and the son of Tydeus, and sixth Odysseus, the equal of the gods in counsel. Menelaus came of his own accord, for he knew how busy his brother was. They stood around the bull with barley meal in their hands, and Agamemnon prayed: “Zeus, most glorious and supreme, you who dwell in heaven and ride upon the storm cloud, grant that the sun may not go down, nor night fall, until the palace of Priam is laid low and its gates are consumed with fire. Grant that my sword may pierce the shirt of Hector about his heart, and that many of his comrades may bite the dust as they fall dying around him.”

So he prayed, but the son of Cronus would not grant his prayer. He accepted the sacrifice, yet he went on adding to their toil. When they had finished praying and had sprinkled barley meal on the victim, they drew back its head, killed it, and flayed it. They cut out the thigh-bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and laid pieces of raw meat on top. They burned these on split logs of firewood. The inward meats they spitted and held in the flames to cook. When the thigh-bones were burned and they had tasted the inward meats, they cut up the rest small, put the pieces on spits, and roasted them until they were done, then drew them off. When the work was finished and the feast was ready, they ate it, and every man had his full share, so that all were satisfied. As soon as they had had enough to eat and drink, Nestor, knight of Gerene, began to speak. “King Agamemnon,” he said, “let us not stay talking here, nor be slow in the work that heaven has put into our hands. Let the heralds summon the people to gather at their ships. Then we will go about among the host, so that we may begin fighting at once.”

So he spoke, and Agamemnon listened to his words. At once he sent the criers around to summon the people to assembly. They called, and the people gathered. The chiefs around the son of Atreus picked out their men and set them in order, while Athena moved among them holding her priceless aegis, which never ages and never dies. A hundred tassels of pure gold hung from it, all finely woven, and each one was worth a hundred oxen. With this she darted furiously everywhere through the armies of the Achaeans, urging them on and putting courage into every man’s heart, so that he would fight and do battle without rest. War became sweeter to them than returning home in their ships. As a great forest fire rages on a mountaintop and its light is seen from far away, so the gleam of their armor, as they marched, flashed up into the sky of heaven.

They were like great flocks of geese, or cranes, or swans on the plain by the waters of Cayster. The birds fly this way and that, proud of their flight, and cry out as they settle, until the marsh is alive with their screaming. In the same way the tribes poured from the ships and tents onto the plain of the Scamander, and the ground rang like brass under the feet of men and horses. They stood on the flower-covered field as thick as the leaves that come out in summer.
As countless swarms of flies buzz around a herdsman’s farmyard in springtime, when the pails are drenched with milk, so the Achaeans swarmed onto the plain to charge the Trojans and destroy them.

The chiefs sorted their men this way and that before the fight began, as easily as goatherds sort their flocks when they have got mixed while feeding. Among them went King Agamemnon. His head and face were like Zeus the lord of thunder, his waist like Ares, and his chest like Poseidon’s. A great bull stands out above the herds on the plain and lords it over them. In the same way Zeus made the son of Atreus stand out beyond all others in the crowd of heroes.

And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell me—for you are goddesses, you are in all places and see all things, while we know nothing except by report—who were the chiefs and princes of the Danaans? As for the common soldiers, I could not name every one of them, even if I had ten tongues, a voice that never failed and a heart of bronze within me, unless you, Olympian Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, were to recount them to me. Still, I will name the captains of the ships and all the ships together.

The Boeotians had five captains: Peneleos, Leitus, Arcesilaus, Prothoenor and Clonius. Their people lived in Hyria and rocky Aulis. They held Schoenus, Scolus and the highlands of Eteonus, along with Thespeia, Graia and the fair city of Mycalessus. Harma, Eilesium and Erythrae were theirs too, as were Eleon, Hyle and Peteon; Ocalea and the strong fortress of Medeon; Copae, Eutresis and Thisbe the haunt of doves; Coronea and the pastures of Haliartus; Plataea and Glisas; the fortress of Thebes the less; holy Onchestus with its famous grove of Poseidon; Arne rich in vineyards; Midea, sacred Nisa, and Anthedon on the sea. Fifty ships sailed from these places, and each carried a hundred and twenty young Boeotian men.

Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares, led the people of Aspledon and Orchomenus, the realm of Minyas. A noble maiden, Astyoche, bore them in the house of Actor son of Azeus. She had gone secretly to an upper room with Ares, and he had lain with her. Thirty ships came with these men.

Schedius and Epistrophus led the Phoceans. They were sons of mighty Iphitus, the son of Naubolus. Their people held Cyparissus, rocky Pytho, holy Crisa, Daulis and Panopeus. Also with them were those who lived in Anemorea and Hyampolis, around the waters of the river Cephissus, and in Lilaea by the springs of the Cephissus. Forty ships came with their chieftains, and the chieftains drew up the forces of the Phoceans, who were stationed next to the Boeotians, on their left.

Ajax, the swift son of Oileus, commanded the Locrians. He was not so great as Ajax the son of Telamon, nor nearly so. He was a little man, and his breastplate was made of linen, but with the spear he surpassed all the Hellenes and the Achaeans. His people lived in Cynus, Opous, Calliarus, Bessa, Scarphe, fair Augeae, Tarphe and Thronium, around the river Boagrius. Forty ships of the Locrians who live beyond Euboea came with him.

The fierce Abantes held Euboea with its cities: Chalcis, Eretria, Histiaea rich in vines, Cerinthus on the sea, and the rock-perched town of Dium. With them were also the men of Carystus and Styra. Elephenor of the race of Ares commanded them. He was the son of Chalcodon and chief over all the Abantes. They followed him, swift-footed and wearing their hair long behind, brave warriors who always fought to tear open their enemies’ corslets with their long ashen spears. Fifty ships came from these.

Then there were those who held the strong city of Athens, the people of great Erechtheus. He was born of the soil itself, but Zeus’s daughter Athena fostered him and set him up at Athens, in her own rich sanctuary. There the Athenian youths worship him year by year with sacrifices of bulls and rams. Menestheus, son of Peteos, commanded them. No man alive could equal him at marshalling chariots and foot soldiers. Only Nestor could rival him, because Nestor was older. Fifty ships came with him.
Ajax brought twelve ships from Salamis and stationed them beside those of the Athenians.

Then came the men of Argos, and those who held the walls of Tiryns, with Hermione and Asine on the gulf; Troezene, Eionae and the vineyard lands of Epidaurus; and the Achaean youths who came from Aegina and Mases. Diomedes of the loud battle cry led them, with Sthenelus son of famed Capaneus. Euryalus also commanded them, son of king Mecisteus, son of Talaus; but Diomedes was chief over them all. Eighty ships came with these.

Those who held the strong city of Mycenae, rich Corinth and Cleonae; Orneae, Araethyrea and Licyon, where Adrastus reigned long ago; Hyperesia, high Gonoessa and Pellene; Aegium and all the coastland around Helice: these sent a hundred ships under King Agamemnon, son of Atreus. His force was by far the finest and the most numerous. In the midst of them was the king himself, glorious in his armor of gleaming bronze. He stood foremost among the heroes, because he was the greatest king and had the most men under him.

And those who lived in Lacedaemon, lying low among the hills: Pharis, Sparta, and Messe the haunt of doves; Bryseae, Augeae, Amyclae and Helos on the sea; also Laas and Oetylus. Menelaus of the loud battle cry, Agamemnon’s brother, led them, and they had sixty ships, drawn up apart from the others. Menelaus himself went among them, strong in zeal, urging his men to fight. He longed to avenge the toil and sorrow he had suffered for Helen’s sake.

The men of Pylos and Arene, and Thryum where the ford of the river Alpheus is; strong Aipy, Cyparisseis and Amphigenea; Pteleum, Helos and Dorium, where the Muses met Thamyris and silenced his minstrelsy forever. He was returning from Oechalia, where Eurytus lived and reigned, and he boasted that he would surpass even the Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, if they should sing against him. The Muses were angry and maimed him. They robbed him of his divine power of song, and from then on he could strike the lyre no more. Nestor, knight of Gerene, commanded these men, and ninety ships came with him.

And those who held Arcadia, under the high mountain of Cyllene, near the tomb of Aepytus, where the people fight hand to hand; the men of Pheneus also, and Orchomenus rich in flocks; of Rhipae, Stratie and bleak Enispe; of Tegea and fair Mantinea; of Stymphelus and Parrhasia. King Agapenor son of Ancaeus commanded these, and they had sixty ships. Many Arcadians, good soldiers, came in each one. But Agamemnon supplied the ships in which they would cross the sea, because they were not a people who busied themselves with the water.

The men of Buprasium and of Elis, as much of it as lies between Hyrmine, Myrsinus on the seashore, the rock Olene and Alesium. They had four leaders, each with ten ships and many Epeans on board. Their captains were Amphimachus and Thalpius—one the son of Cteatus, the other of Eurytus—both of the race of Actor. The other two were Diores, son of Amarynceus, and Polyxenus, son of King Agasthenes, son of Augeas.

And those of Dulichium and the sacred Echinean islands, who lived across the sea from Elis. Meges, peer of Ares, led them. He was the son of valiant Phyleus, who was dear to Zeus. Phyleus had quarreled with his father and gone to settle in Dulichium. Forty ships came with Meges.

Odysseus led the brave Cephallenians, who held Ithaca, Neritum with its forests, Crocylea, rugged Aegilips, Samos and Zacynthus, and the mainland across from the islands. Odysseus, peer of Zeus in counsel, led them, and twelve ships came with him.

Thoas, son of Andraemon, commanded the Aetolians, who lived in Pleuron, Olenus, Pylene, Chalcis by the sea, and rocky Calydon, for the great king Oeneus now had no sons living and was himself dead, as was golden-haired Meleager, who had been set over the Aetolians as their king. Forty ships came with Thoas.

The famous spearsman Idomeneus led the Cretans, who held Cnossus and the well-walled city of Gortys; also Lyctus, Miletus and Lycastus on the chalk; the populous towns of Phaestus and Rhytium, with the other peoples who lived in the hundred cities of Crete. Idomeneus led them all, together with Meriones, peer of murderous Ares. Eighty ships came with these.

Tlepolemus, son of Heracles, a brave man and tall, brought nine ships of lordly warriors from Rhodes. His people lived in Rhodes, which is divided among the three cities of Lindus, Ielysus and Cameirus, which lies on the chalk. Tlepolemus, son of Heracles by Astyochea, commanded them. Heracles had carried her off from Ephyra, on the river Selleis, after sacking many cities of valiant warriors. When Tlepolemus grew up, he killed his father’s uncle Licymnius, who had been a famous warrior in his day but was now old. After this he built himself a fleet, gathered a great following and fled across the sea, because the other sons and grandsons of Heracles threatened him. After a voyage in which he suffered great hardship, he came to Rhodes. There the people divided into three communities, according to their tribes, and Zeus, the lord of gods and men, loved them dearly. So the son of Cronus showered great riches on them.
And Nireus brought three ships from Syme—Nireus, the handsomest man of all the Danaans who came to Ilium, after the son of Peleus. But he was a man of no substance and had only a small following.

Those who held Nisyrus, Crapathus and Casus, with Cos, the city of Eurypylus, and the Calydnian islands, were commanded by Pheidippus and Antiphus, two sons of King Thessalus the son of Heracles. Thirty ships came with them.

Then those who held Pelasgic Argos, Alos, Alope and Trachis, and those of Phthia and Hellas, the land of fair women, who were called Myrmidons, Hellenes and Achaeans: they had fifty ships, and Achilles was in command of them. But they now took no part in the war, because there was no one to marshal them. Achilles stayed by his ships, furious about the loss of the girl Briseis. He had taken her from Lyrnessus at great peril to himself, when he sacked Lyrnessus and Thebe and overthrew Mynes and Epistrophus, sons of king Evenor, son of Selepus. Achilles was still grieving for her sake, but before long he was to join them again.

And those who held Phylace and the flowery meadows of Pyrasus, sanctuary of Demeter; Iton, the mother of sheep; Antrum on the sea, and Pteleum, which lies on the grass lands. Brave Protesilaus had been their captain while he was alive, but now he lay under the earth. He had left a wife behind him in Phylace to tear her cheeks in sorrow, and his house was only half finished. A Dardanian warrior had slain him as he leaped foremost of the Achaeans onto the soil of Troy. Still, though his people mourned their chieftain, they were not without a leader. Podarces, of the race of Ares, marshalled them. He was the son of Iphiclus, rich in sheep, who was the son of Phylacus, and he was own brother to Protesilaus, only younger; Protesilaus was both the elder and the more valiant. So the people were not without a leader, though they mourned the man they had lost. Forty ships came with Podarces.

And those who held Pherae by the Boebean lake, with Boebe, Glaphyrae and the populous city of Iolcus, with their eleven ships, were led by Eumelus, son of Admetus, whom Alcestis bore to him. She was the loveliest of the daughters of Pelias.

And those who held Methone and Thaumacia, with Meliboea and rugged Olizon, were led by the skilled archer Philoctetes. They had seven ships, each with fifty oarsmen, all of them good archers. But Philoctetes was lying in great pain on the island of Lemnos, where the sons of the Achaeans had left him, because a poisonous water snake had bitten him. There he lay sick and sorry, and before long the Argives would come to miss him. But his people, though they felt his loss, were not leaderless. Medon, the bastard son of Oileus by Rhene, set them in array.

Then the men of Tricca and the stony region of Ithome, and those who held Oechalia, the city of Oechalian Eurytus, were commanded by the two sons of Asclepius, Podalirius and Machaon, who were skilled in the art of healing. Thirty ships came with them.
Also the men of Ormenius, and by the fountain of Hypereia, with those who held Asterius and the white crests of Titanus, were led by Eurypylus, the son of Euaemon. Forty ships came with them.

Those who held Argissa and Gyrtone, Orthe, Elone and the white city of Oloosson had brave Polypoetes as their leader. He was the son of Pirithous, who was himself a son of Zeus. Hippodameia bore Polypoetes to Pirithous on the day when Pirithous took his revenge on the shaggy mountain savages and drove them from Mount Pelion to the Aithices. But Polypoetes was not the sole commander. With him was Leonteus, of the race of Ares, son of Coronus, the son of Caeneus. Forty ships came with these.

Guneus brought twenty-two ships from Cyphus. The Enienes and the valiant Peraebi followed him. They lived around wintry Dodona and held the lands around the lovely river Titaresius, which sends its waters into the Peneus. The Titaresius does not mingle with the silver eddies of the Peneus but flows on top of them like oil, because it is a branch of dread Orcus and of the river Styx.
Prothous son of Tenthredon commanded the Magnetes. They lived around the river Peneus and Mount Pelion. Swift-footed Prothous was their leader, and forty ships came with him.
That was the list of the chiefs and princes of the Danaans. Now tell me, O Muse: among the men who followed the sons of Atreus, who was the best, and which was the best horse?

Of the horses, those of the son of Pheres were by far the finest. Eumelus drove them, and they were as swift as birds. They were the same age and color, and perfectly matched in height. Apollo, god of the silver bow, had bred them in Perea. Both were mares, and terrible as Ares in battle. Of the men, Ajax son of Telamon was much the foremost as long as Achilles’s anger lasted, for Achilles excelled him greatly and also had better horses. But Achilles was now holding aloof at his ships because of his quarrel with Agamemnon. His people passed their time on the seashore, throwing discs, aiming spears at a mark, and shooting with the bow. Their horses stood each by his own chariot, champing lotus and wild celery. The chariots were housed under cover, but their owners, for lack of a leader, wandered here and there about the host and did not go out to fight.

So the host marched like a consuming fire, and the earth groaned beneath them, as it does when the lord of thunder is angry and lashes the land around Typhoeus among the Arimi, where they say Typhoeus lies. In the same way the earth groaned beneath them as they sped over the plain.

Meanwhile Zeus sent Iris, swift as the wind, to carry the bad news to the Trojans. Old and young, they were holding an assembly at Priam’s gates. Iris went right up to Priam and spoke in the voice of his son Polites. Polites was swift-footed, and the Trojans had posted him as their watchman on the tomb of old Aesyetes, to look out for any sally by the Achaeans. In his likeness Iris said: “Old man, you talk on and on as if it were peacetime, but war is upon us. I have fought in many battles, yet I have never seen an army like the one now advancing. They are crossing the plain to attack the city, as thick as leaves or as the sands of the sea. Hector, I charge you above all others to do what I say. Allies are scattered all through the city of Priam, men from distant places who speak different tongues. Each chief must give orders to his own people, set them in array separately, and lead them out to battle.”

The goddess had spoken, and Hector knew it. He broke up the assembly at once. The men ran for their arms, every gate was thrown open, and the people poured out, horse and foot, with the tramp of a great multitude.

Before the city, apart from everything else, a high mound rises on the plain. Men call it Batieia, but the gods know it as the tomb of lithe Myrine. The Trojans and their allies divided their forces here.
Great Hector of the gleaming helmet, Priam’s son, commanded the Trojans. By far the greater number, and the most valiant of those who longed for the fray, were drawn up with him.

Brave Aeneas led the Dardanians. Aphrodite bore him to Anchises, when she, goddess though she was, lay with him on the mountain slopes of Ida. He was not alone: with him were the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, both skilled in all the arts of war.

Those who lived in Telea under the lowest spurs of Mount Ida, men of substance who drink the limpid waters of the Aesepus and are of Trojan blood—Pandarus son of Lycaon led them, and Apollo had taught him to use the bow.

Adrestus and Amphius led the men who held Adresteia and the land of Apaesus, with Pityeia and the high mountain of Tereia. Amphius wore a breastplate of linen. The two were sons of Merops of Percote, who excelled in every kind of divination. He told them not to join the war, but they ignored him, because fate was luring them to destruction.

Those who lived around Percote and Practius, with Sestos, Abydos and Arisbe—Asius, son of Hyrtacus, a brave commander, led them. Asius, the son of Hyrtacus, had come from Arisbe, brought by his powerful dark bay horses of the breed from the river Selleis.
The Pelasgian spearsmen of fertile Larissa had two leaders, Hippothous and Pylaeus of the race of Ares. They were the two sons of the Pelasgian Lethus, son of Teutamus.
Acamas and the warrior Peirous commanded the Thracians and those who came from beyond the mighty stream of the Hellespont.
Euphemus, son of Troezenus, the son of Ceos, was captain of the Ciconian spearsmen.
Pyraechmes led the Paeonian archers from distant Amydon, by the broad waters of the river Axius, the fairest that flow on the earth.

Stout-hearted Pylaemanes commanded the Paphlagonians, from Enetae, where the mules run wild in herds. They held Cytorus and the country around Sesamus, with the cities by the river Parthenius, Cromna, Aegialus and lofty Erithini.
Odius and Epistrophus were captains over the Halizoni from distant Alybe, where there are mines of silver.

Chromis and Ennomus the augur led the Mysians. But his skill in augury did not save Ennomus from destruction. He fell by the hand of the swift descendant of Aeacus in the river, who killed other Trojans there as well.
Phorcys and noble Ascanius led the Phrygians from the far country of Ascania, and both were eager for the fray.
Mesthles and Antiphus commanded the Meonians. They were sons of Talaemenes, born to him of the Gygaean lake. They led the Meonians, who lived under Mount Tmolus.

Nastes led the Carians, men of a strange speech. They held Miletus and the wooded mountain of Phthires, the water of the river Maeander and the lofty crests of Mount Mycale. Their commanders were Nastes and Amphimachus, the brave sons of Nomion. Nastes went into the fight wearing gold, like a girl. The fool gained nothing from it. He fell in the river to the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles carried his gold away.
Sarpedon and Glaucus led the Lycians from their distant land, by the eddying waters of the Xanthus.

chapters.title: Book 3
paragraphs: Paris challenges Menelaus—Helen and Priam look out over the Achaeans from the wall—The covenant is made—Paris and Menelaus fight, and Paris gets the worst of it—Aphrodite carries him off to save him—The scene between him and Helen.

Once the companies were arranged, each under its own captain, the Trojans came on like a flight of wild birds, or of cranes. Cranes scream overhead when rain and winter drive them across the flowing waters of Oceanus to bring death and destruction to the Pygmies, and they squabble in the air as they fly. The Achaeans, by contrast, marched in silence, with high courage and the intention of standing by one another.

It was like the south wind spreading a curtain of mist over the mountain tops, bad for shepherds but better than night for thieves, when a man cannot see farther than he can throw a stone. That was how the dust rose from under their feet as they hurried across the plain.

When the armies were close to one another, Paris came forward as the Trojan champion. He carried a panther’s skin on his shoulders, with his bow and his sword, and he brandished two spears tipped with bronze, challenging the bravest of the Achaeans to meet him in single combat. Menelaus saw him stride out in front of the ranks, and he was glad, like a hungry lion that comes upon the carcass of a goat or a horned stag and devours it on the spot, though dogs and young men attack him. In just that way Menelaus was glad when he caught sight of Paris, because he thought he would now have his revenge. He jumped down from his chariot, in his full suit of armor.

Paris lost his nerve when he saw Menelaus coming toward him. Afraid for his life, he shrank back behind his men. A man who suddenly comes upon a snake in a mountain glade jumps back, trembling and pale. In the same way Paris plunged into the crowd of Trojan warriors, terrified at the sight of the son of Atreus.

Then Hector scolded him. “Paris,” he said, “you evil-hearted Paris, so fair to look at, so mad for women, such a liar. I wish you had never been born, or had died unmarried. That would be better than living to be disgraced and looked at sideways. Will the Achaeans not mock us? They will say we sent a champion who is fair to look at but has no brains and no courage. Did you not, being what you are, gather your followers and sail over the seas? Did you not, from a far country, carry off a lovely woman married among a people of warriors—bringing sorrow to your father, your city and your whole country, joy to your enemies, and a hang-dog shame to yourself? And now you do not dare face Menelaus and find out what kind of man he is, whose wife you have stolen? Where would your lyre be then, and your love-tricks, your handsome locks and your fair looks, when you were lying in the dust in front of him? The Trojans are a weak-kneed people. Otherwise you would long ago have been given a shirt of stones for the wrongs you have done them.”

And Paris answered, “Hector, you are right to rebuke me. You are as hard as the axe a shipwright swings at his work, cutting the timber to his liking. The edge of your scorn is as keen as that axe in his hand. Still, do not taunt me with the gifts that golden Aphrodite has given me. They are precious. No man should look down on them, since the gods give them where they choose, and nobody can get them by asking. If you want me to fight Menelaus, tell the Trojans and Achaeans to sit down, while he and I fight in the middle for Helen and all her wealth. Whoever wins and proves the better man will take the woman and everything she has and bring them to his home. The rest of you must swear a solemn covenant of peace, by which you Trojans stay here in Troy and the others go home to Argos and the land of the Achaeans.”

Hector was glad to hear this. He went among the Trojan ranks holding his spear by the middle to keep them back, and at his command they all sat down. But the Achaeans kept aiming stones and arrows at him, until Agamemnon shouted to them, “Hold, Argives, do not shoot, sons of the Achaeans. Hector wants to speak.”

They stopped aiming and were still, and Hector spoke. “Trojans and Achaeans,” he said, “hear from my mouth the proposal of Paris, who caused this quarrel. He asks the Trojans and Achaeans to lay their armor on the ground while he and Menelaus fight in the middle for Helen and all her wealth. Whoever wins and proves the better man is to take the woman and everything she has, and bring them to his own home. The rest of us will swear a solemn covenant of peace.”

So he spoke, and they all fell silent, until Menelaus of the loud battle cry addressed them. “Now hear me too,” he said, “for I am the one most wronged. I think the parting of Achaeans and Trojans is near, as it well may be, since so many have suffered for my quarrel with Paris and the wrong he did me. Let whichever of us is to die, die, and let the others fight no more. Bring two lambs, a white ram and a black ewe, for Earth and Sun, and we will bring a third for Zeus. You must also tell Priam to come and swear to the covenant himself. His sons are arrogant and hard to trust, and the oaths of Zeus must not be broken or taken in vain. Young men’s minds are as light as air, but when an old man comes he looks before and after, and considers what will be fairest for both sides.”

The Trojans and Achaeans were glad to hear this, since they thought they would now get some rest. They backed their chariots toward the ranks, climbed out, and took off their armor, laying it on the ground. The two hosts were close together, with only a small space between them. Hector sent two messengers to the city to fetch the lambs and tell Priam to come. Agamemnon told Talthybius to bring the other lamb from the ships, and he did as Agamemnon said.

Meanwhile Iris went to Helen, taking the form of her sister-in-law, the wife of the son of Antenor. Helicaon, son of Antenor, had married Laodice, the fairest of Priam’s daughters. Iris found Helen in her own room, working at a great web of purple linen. On it she was embroidering the battles between Trojans and Achaeans, which Ares had made them fight for her sake. Iris came up close to her and said, “Come here, child, and see the strange things the Trojans and Achaeans are doing. Until now they have been fighting on the plain, mad with the lust of battle. Now they have stopped fighting. They are leaning on their shields and sitting still, with their spears planted beside them. Paris and Menelaus are going to fight over you, and you are to be the wife of the winner.”

So the goddess spoke, and Helen’s heart longed for her former husband, her city and her parents. She threw a white mantle over her head and hurried from her room, weeping as she went. She was not alone. Two of her handmaids went with her, Aethrae, daughter of Pittheus, and Clymene. Soon they were at the Scaean gates.

The two sages Ucalegon and Antenor, elders of the people, were sitting by the Scaean gates with Priam, Panthous, Thymoetes, Lampus, Clytius, and Hiketaon of the race of Ares. They were too old to fight, but they were fluent speakers. They sat on the tower like cicadas that chirp delicately from the branches of some high tree in a wood. When they saw Helen coming toward the tower, they said softly to one another, “No wonder the Trojans and Achaeans have endured so much for so long for the sake of a woman so marvelously and divinely lovely. Still, fair as she is, let them take her and go. Otherwise she will bring sorrow on us and on our children after us.”

But Priam called her to come near. “My child,” he said, “sit in front of me, so you can see your former husband, your kinsmen and your friends. I do not blame you. The gods are to blame, not you. They brought on this terrible war with the Achaeans. Now tell me, who is that huge hero over there, so great and handsome? I have seen men taller by a head, but none so comely and so royal. He must surely be a king.”

“Sir,” Helen answered, “you are my husband’s father, and I hold you dear and honor you. I wish I had chosen death before following your son here, away from my bridal chamber, my friends, my darling daughter and all the companions of my girlhood. It was not to be, and now my life is tears and sorrow. To answer your question: the hero you ask about is Agamemnon son of Atreus, a good king and a brave soldier. As surely as he lives, he is brother-in-law to my hateful and miserable self.”
