The old man looked at him in wonder. “Happy son of Atreus,” he said, “child of good fortune. I see that great multitudes of Achaeans are subject to you. Once, in Phrygia, I saw a large force of horsemen, the people of Otreus and of Mygdon, camped on the banks of the river Sangarius. I was their ally, and I was with them when the Amazons, the equals of men, attacked them. Even those were not as many as the Achaeans here.”

Next the old man looked at Odysseus. “Tell me,” he said, “who is that other man, a head shorter than Agamemnon but broader across the chest and shoulders? His armor is laid on the ground, and he strides in front of the ranks like some great woolly ram setting his ewes in order.”
Helen replied, “That man is Odysseus, son of Laertes, a man of great craft. He was born in rugged Ithaca, and no one surpasses him in stratagems and subtle cunning.”

Antenor then said, “Madam, you have spoken truly. Odysseus once came here as an envoy about you, and Menelaus came with him. I received them in my own house, so I know both of them by sight and by conversation. When they stood up before the assembled Trojans, Menelaus had the broader shoulders, but when both were seated Odysseus looked the more royal. After a time they delivered their message. The speech of Menelaus ran trippingly off the tongue. He did not say much, being a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point, though he was the younger of the two. Odysseus, on the other hand, when he rose to speak, was at first silent and kept his eyes fixed on the ground. He made no play or graceful movement with his scepter. He held it straight and stiff, like a man unpracticed in oratory, and you might have taken him for a mere churl or simpleton. But when he raised his voice and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, no one could touch him, and nobody thought any more about how he looked.”
Next Priam noticed Ajax. “Who is that huge and handsome warrior?” he asked. “His head and broad shoulders rise above the rest of the Argives.”

“That,” Helen answered, “is huge Ajax, bulwark of the Achaeans. On the other side of him, among the Cretans, stands Idomeneus, looking like a god, with the captains of the Cretans around him. Menelaus often received him as a guest in our house when he came visiting us from Crete. I see many other Achaeans too, whose names I could tell you. But there are two I cannot find anywhere, Castor, breaker of horses, and Pollux the mighty boxer. They are children of my mother, my own brothers. Either they have not left Lacedaemon, or else they have brought their ships but will not show themselves in battle, for the shame and disgrace I have brought on them.”
She did not know that both these heroes were already lying under the earth in their own land of Lacedaemon.

Meanwhile the heralds were carrying the holy oath-offerings through the city: two lambs and a goatskin of wine, the gift of earth. Idaeus carried the mixing-bowl and the golden cups. He came to Priam and said, “Son of Laomedon, the princes of the Trojans and Achaeans call on you to come down to the plain and swear a solemn covenant. Paris and Menelaus are to fight in single combat for Helen, and she and all her wealth will go with whichever of them wins. We are to swear a solemn covenant of peace. Under it the rest of us will live on here in Troy, and the Achaeans will return to Argos and the land of the Achaeans.”

The old man shuddered as he heard this, but he told his followers to yoke the horses, and they did so with all speed. He mounted the chariot and gathered the reins in his hand, and Antenor took his seat beside him. They drove through the Scaean gates onto the plain. When they reached the ranks of the Trojans and Achaeans, they got down from the chariot and walked at a measured pace into the space between the hosts.

Agamemnon and Odysseus both rose to meet them. The attendants brought forward the oath-offerings and mixed the wine in the mixing-bowls. They poured water over the hands of the chieftains. The son of Atreus drew the dagger that hung by his sword and cut wool from the lambs’ heads, and the men-servants handed this around among the Trojan and Achaean princes. Then the son of Atreus lifted up his hands in prayer. “Father Zeus,” he cried, “you who rule from Ida, most glorious in power, and you, Sun, who see and hear all things, Earth and Rivers, and you who in the realms below punish the soul of anyone who has broken his oath, witness these rites and guard them, so that they are not in vain. If Paris kills Menelaus, let him keep Helen and all her wealth, and we will sail home with our ships. But if Menelaus kills Paris, let the Trojans give back Helen and all she has. Let them also pay the Achaeans whatever fine is agreed upon, as a witness among those who will be born hereafter. And if Priam and his sons refuse to pay that fine after Paris has fallen, then I will stay here and go on fighting until I have satisfaction.”

As he spoke he drew his knife across the throats of the victims and laid them on the ground, gasping and dying, for the knife had taken their strength. Then they poured wine from the mixing-bowl into the cups and prayed to the everlasting gods. This was the prayer, Trojans and Achaeans saying it among one another: “Zeus, most great and glorious, and you other everlasting gods, grant that the brains of those who first sin against their oaths—theirs and their children’s—be spilled on the ground just like this wine, and let their wives become the slaves of strangers.”

So they prayed, but Zeus would not yet grant their prayer. Then Priam, descendant of Dardanus, spoke. “Hear me, Trojans and Achaeans,” he said. “I am going back to the wind-beaten city of Ilium. I dare not watch with my own eyes this fight between my son and Menelaus, for only Zeus and the other immortals know which of them will fall.”

With that he laid the two lambs in his chariot and took his seat. He gathered the reins in his hand, Antenor sat beside him, and the two went back to Ilium. Hector and Odysseus measured out the ground. Then they cast lots from a bronze helmet to see which should take aim first. Meanwhile the two hosts lifted their hands and prayed, “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious in power, grant that the man who first brought about this war between us may die and enter the house of Hades, while the rest of us stay at peace and keep our oaths.”

Great Hector turned his head aside as he shook the helmet, and the lot of Paris flew out first. The others took their several stations, each beside his horses and the place where his arms lay. Meanwhile Paris, husband of lovely Helen, put on his fine armor. First he fastened greaves of good make on his legs, fitted with silver ankle-clasps. After that he put on the cuirass of his brother Lycaon and fitted it to his own body. He hung his silver-studded bronze sword about his shoulders, and then his mighty shield. On his handsome head he set a well-made helmet with a horse-hair crest that nodded menacingly above it, and he took up a formidable spear that suited his hands. Menelaus put on his armor in the same way.

When they had armed, each among his own people, they strode into the open space with fierce looks, and Trojans and Achaeans alike were struck with awe at the sight. They stood near each other on the measured ground, brandishing their spears, each furious with the other. Paris aimed first and struck the round shield of the son of Atreus, but the spear did not pierce it, because the shield turned its point. Menelaus took aim next, praying to Father Zeus as he did so. “King Zeus,” he said, “grant me revenge on Paris, who has wronged me. Subdue him under my hand, so that in ages to come men will shrink from doing evil in the house of their host.”

He poised his spear as he spoke and hurled it at the shield of Paris. It went through the shield and the cuirass, and tore the shirt by his flank, but Paris swerved aside and so saved his life. Then the son of Atreus drew his sword and struck at the projecting part of his helmet. The sword shattered into three or four pieces and fell from his hand. Looking up toward Heaven, he cried, “Father Zeus, of all the gods you are the most spiteful. I was sure of my revenge, but now the sword has broken in my hand, my spear was thrown in vain, and I have not killed him.”

With this he flew at Paris, caught him by the horse-hair plume of his helmet, and began dragging him toward the Achaeans. The strap of the helmet under his chin was choking him, and Menelaus would have dragged him off to his own great glory. But Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite was quick to notice and broke the ox-hide strap, so the empty helmet came away in Menelaus’s hand. He flung it to his comrades among the Achaeans and sprang at Paris again to run him through with a spear. But Aphrodite snatched Paris up in a moment (as a god can do), hid him in a cloud of darkness, and carried him to his own bedchamber.

Then she went to fetch Helen, and found her on a high tower, with the Trojan women crowding around her. The goddess took the shape of an old woman who had dressed wool for Helen back in Lacedaemon, and whom Helen loved dearly. Disguised like this, she tugged at Helen’s perfumed robe. “Come with me,” she said. “Paris wants you at the house. He is lying on his bed in his own room, radiant with beauty and dressed in gorgeous clothes. You would never think he had just come from fighting. You would think he was off to a dance, or had just stopped dancing and sat down.”

With these words she stirred Helen’s heart to anger. Helen noticed the goddess’s beautiful neck, her lovely bosom and her sparkling eyes, and she was amazed and said, “Goddess, why do you try to beguile me like this? Are you going to send me still farther afield, to some man you have taken up in Phrygia or fair Meonia? Menelaus has just defeated Paris and is going to take my hateful self back with him. You have come here to betray me. Go and sit with Paris yourself. Give up being a goddess, never let your feet carry you back to Olympus, worry about him and look after him until he makes you his wife—or, for that matter, his slave. But me? I will not go. I can make ready his bed no longer. I would be a by-word among all the women of Troy. Besides, I have trouble on my mind.”

Aphrodite was furious. “Bold hussy,” she said, “do not provoke me. If you do, I will abandon you to your fate and hate you as much as I have loved you. I will stir up fierce hatred between Trojans and Achaeans, and you will come to a bad end.”
Helen was frightened at this. She wrapped her mantle around her and followed the goddess in silence, unnoticed by the Trojan women.

When they reached the house of Paris, the maid-servants went about their work. Helen went into her own room, and the laughter-loving goddess picked up a seat and placed it for her, facing Paris. Helen, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, sat down on it, and with a sidelong look she began to scold her husband.

“So you have come back from the fight,” she said. “I wish you had fallen there instead, by the hand of that brave man who was my husband. You used to brag that you were a better man than Menelaus with hands and spear. Go, then, and challenge him again. But I advise you not to, because if you are foolish enough to meet him in single combat, you will soon fall to his spear.”

And Paris answered, “Wife, do not hurt me with your reproaches. This time Menelaus has beaten me with the help of Athena. Another time I may win, for I too have gods on my side. Come, let us lie down together and make friends. I have never been so passionately in love with you as I am at this moment—not even when I first carried you off from Lacedaemon and sailed away with you, not even when I was with you on the couch of love on the island of Cranae was I so overcome with desire for you as I am now.” With that he led her toward the bed, and his wife went with him.

So they laid themselves down on the bed together. Meanwhile the son of Atreus strode through the crowd, looking everywhere for Paris, and no one, Trojan or ally, could find him. They would not have hidden him if they had seen him, for they all hated him like death itself. Then Agamemnon, king of men, spoke. “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies. The victory has gone to Menelaus. Therefore give back Helen with all her wealth, and pay whatever fine is agreed upon, as a witness among those who will be born hereafter.”
So spoke the son of Atreus, and the Achaeans shouted their approval.

chapters.title: Book 4
paragraphs: Quarrel on Olympus—Athena goes down and persuades Pandarus to break the oaths by wounding Menelaus with an arrow—Agamemnon makes a speech and sends for Machaon—He then goes among his captains and scolds Odysseus and Sthenelus, who both answer him fiercely—Diomedes silences Sthenelus, and the two armies join battle, with great slaughter on both sides.

The gods were sitting in council with Zeus on the golden floor, and Hebe went around pouring them nectar. They raised their golden cups to one another and looked down on the city of Troy. Then the son of Cronus began to tease Hera, speaking at her in order to provoke her. “Menelaus has two good friends among the goddesses,” he said, “Hera of Argos and Athena of Alalcomene. Yet they only sit there and watch. Aphrodite, meanwhile, never leaves Paris’s side, and she keeps him safe from every danger. She has just rescued him when he was sure he was finished, though the victory really belonged to Menelaus. We need to decide what to do about all this. Shall we start the fighting again, or make peace between the two sides? If you agree to the second, Menelaus can take Helen back, and the city of Priam can stay inhabited.”

Athena and Hera sat side by side, plotting trouble for the Trojans, and they muttered their discontent. Athena glared at her father. She was in a furious rage with him, and she said nothing. Hera, however, could not hold herself back. “Dread son of Cronus,” she said, “what do you mean by this? Am I to have all my trouble for nothing? I have sweated and worn out my horses besides, gathering the people against Priam and his children. Do as you like, but the rest of us gods will not all approve of your plan.”

Zeus was angry and answered, “My dear, what harm have Priam and his sons done you, that you are so fiercely set on sacking the city of Ilium? Will nothing satisfy you except walking inside their walls and eating Priam raw, along with his sons and all the other Trojans? Have it your way, then, for I do not want this matter to become a bone of contention between us. But hear this, and take it to heart. If I ever want to sack a city of your friends, you must not stop me. You will have to let me, because I am giving in to you very much against my will. Of all the inhabited cities under the sun and the starry heaven, none was so honored by me as Ilium, with Priam and all his people. My altar never lacked a fair feast, or the savor of burning fat, which is the honor due to us gods.”

“The three cities I love best,” Hera answered, “are Argos, Sparta, and Mycenae. Sack them whenever they displease you. I will not defend them, and I will not care. Even if I did try to hold you back, I would gain nothing, because you are much stronger than I am. But I will not see my own work go to waste. I am a god too, of the same race as you. I am the eldest daughter of Cronus, and I am honored not for that reason alone, but also because I am your wife and you are king over the gods. So let there be give-and-take between us, and the other gods will follow our lead. Tell Athena to go at once and join the fighting, and have her arrange for the Trojans to be the first to break their oaths and attack the Achaeans.”

The father of gods and men listened to her, and he said to Athena, “Go at once to the Trojan and Achaean armies, and arrange for the Trojans to be the first to break their oaths and attack the Achaeans.”

Athena was already eager to do this, so she darted down from the highest peaks of Olympus. She flashed across the sky like a bright meteor, sent by the son of scheming Cronus as a sign to sailors or to some great army, with a fiery trail of light behind it. The Trojans and Achaeans watched in awe. One man turned to his neighbor and said, “Either we are going to have war and the din of battle again, or Zeus, the lord of battle, is about to make peace between us.”

So they talked among themselves. Meanwhile Athena took the form of Laodocus, son of Antenor, and went through the Trojan ranks looking for Pandarus, the redoubtable son of Lycaon. She found him standing among the stalwart fighters who had followed him from the banks of the Aesopus. She went right up to him and said, “Brave son of Lycaon, will you do what I tell you? Dare to shoot an arrow at Menelaus, and you will win honor and thanks from all the Trojans, and most of all from prince Paris. He would be the first to reward you very handsomely if he could see Menelaus laid on his funeral pyre, killed by an arrow from your hand. Take your aim, then, and pray to Lycian Apollo, the famous archer. Vow that when you get home to your strong city of Zelea, you will offer him a great sacrifice of firstling lambs.”

The fool let himself be persuaded and took his bow out of its case. It was made from the horns of a wild ibex that he had once killed. He had stalked the animal as it bounded off a rock, and it fell when his arrow struck it in the heart. The horns were sixteen palms long. A worker in horn had joined them into a bow, smoothed them well, and fitted tips of gold. Pandarus strung the bow and laid it carefully on the ground. His brave followers held their shields in front of him, so that the Achaeans could not attack him before he had shot Menelaus. Then he opened the lid of his quiver and took out a winged arrow that had never been shot, loaded with the pangs of death. He set the arrow on the string and prayed to Lycian Apollo, the famous archer. He vowed that when he got home to his strong city of Zelea, he would offer a great sacrifice of firstling lambs. He fitted the notch of the arrow to the ox-hide string and pulled notch and string back to his chest, until the arrow-head almost touched the bow. When the bow was bent into a half-circle, he let fly. The bow twanged, the string sang, and the arrow sped eagerly over the heads of the crowd.

But the blessed gods did not forget you, Menelaus. Zeus’s daughter, the driver of the spoil, was the first to stand in front of you and fend off the piercing arrow. She turned it away from his skin as a mother brushes a fly off her child when it is sleeping sweetly. She guided it to the place where the golden buckles of his belt were fastened, where the belt overlapped his double cuirass. The arrow struck the belt that fitted tightly around him. It went right through that, and through the cuirass of cunning workmanship, and it also pierced the belt beneath, which he wore next to his skin to keep out darts and arrows. That belt did him the most good, yet the arrow went through it as well and grazed the surface of the skin, and blood began to flow from the wound.

A woman of Meonia or Caria stains a piece of ivory with purple dye, to make a cheek-piece for a horse. It will be laid up in a treasure house. Many a knight longs to wear it, but the king keeps it as an ornament that both horse and driver may be proud of. In the same way, Menelaus, your shapely thighs and your legs down to your fair ankles were stained with blood.

When King Agamemnon saw the blood running from the wound, he was afraid. So was brave Menelaus himself, until he saw that the barbs of the arrow and the thread binding the arrow-head to the shaft were still outside the wound. Then he took heart. Agamemnon, though, heaved a deep sigh as he held Menelaus’s hand in his own, and their comrades groaned together. “Dear brother,” he cried, “I have caused your death by making this covenant and letting you come forward as our champion. The Trojans have trampled on their oaths and wounded you. Even so, the oath, the blood of lambs, the drink-offerings, and the handshakes in which we put our trust will not be in vain. If the ruler of Olympus does not fulfill it here and now, he will fulfill it later. The Trojans will pay dearly with their lives, and with their wives and children. The day will surely come when mighty Ilium is laid low, with Priam and Priam’s people. The son of Cronus will spread his awful aegis over them from his high throne to punish their treachery now. That will surely happen. But how, Menelaus, shall I mourn you if you are fated to die now? I would go back to Argos in disgrace, because the Achaeans will go home at once. We would leave Priam and the Trojans the glory of keeping Helen, and the earth would rot your bones as you lie here at Troy with your task unfinished. Then some boastful Trojan will leap on your tomb and say, ‘May Agamemnon always get his revenge like this! He brought his army here for nothing. He has gone home to his own land with empty ships, and he has left Menelaus behind.’ That is what one of them will say, and on that day may the earth swallow me.”

But Menelaus reassured him. “Take heart,” he said, “and do not alarm the people. The arrow has not hit me in a deadly place. My outer belt of burnished metal stopped it first, and beneath that were my cuirass and the belt of mail that the bronze-smiths made for me.”
Agamemnon answered, “I hope it is as you say, dear Menelaus. But the surgeon must examine your wound and put herbs on it to ease your pain.”

Then he said to Talthybius, “Talthybius, tell Machaon, son of the great physician Asclepius, to come and see Menelaus at once. Some Trojan or Lycian archer has wounded him with an arrow, to our dismay and to his own great glory.”

Talthybius did as he was told and went through the army looking for Machaon. Before long he found him standing among the brave warriors who had followed him from Tricca. He went up to him and said, “Son of Asclepius, King Agamemnon says you are to come and see Menelaus at once. Some Trojan or Lycian archer has wounded him with an arrow, to our dismay and to his own great glory.”

So he spoke, and Machaon was moved to go. They passed through the wide host of the Achaeans until they reached the place where Menelaus had been wounded. He was lying there with the chieftains gathered in a circle around him. Machaon stepped into the middle of the ring and at once pulled the arrow out of the belt. The barbs bent back as he tugged it free. He undid the burnished belt, and beneath it the cuirass and the belt of mail that the bronze-smiths had made. When he had seen the wound, he wiped away the blood and applied soothing drugs, which Chiron had given to Asclepius out of the good will he bore him.
While they were busy with Menelaus, the Trojans advanced on them. They had put on their armor, and now they renewed the fight.

At that moment you would not have found Agamemnon asleep, or cowardly, or unwilling to fight. He was eager for the fray. He left his bronze-decked chariot and his panting horses in the care of Eurymedon, son of Ptolemaeus the son of Peiraeus. He told him to keep them ready for when his limbs grew tired of walking about and giving orders to so many men, for he went among the ranks on foot. When he saw men hurrying to the front, he stood by them and cheered them on. “Argives,” he said, “do not let up in your attack, not for a moment. Father Zeus will not help liars. The Trojans were the first to break their oaths and attack us, so vultures will devour them. We will take their city and carry off their wives and children in our ships.”

But he rebuked those he saw shirking and unwilling to fight, and he was angry. “Argives,” he cried, “you cowardly, miserable creatures, have you no shame? You stand here like frightened fawns that can run no farther across the plain and huddle together without putting up a fight. You are as dazed and spiritless as deer. Will you wait until the Trojans reach the sterns of our ships on the shore, to find out whether the son of Cronus will hold his hand over you to protect you?”

So he went about among the ranks giving his orders. Passing through the crowd, he soon came upon the Cretans, who were arming around Idomeneus. He was at their head, fierce as a wild boar, while Meriones brought up the battalions in the rear. Agamemnon was glad to see him and spoke to him kindly. “Idomeneus,” he said, “I treat you with greater distinction than any other Achaean, in war, in other matters, and at table. When the princes mix my choicest wine in the mixing-bowls, each of them has a fixed allowance. But your cup is always kept full, like my own, so that you may drink whenever you like. Go into battle, then, and show yourself the man you have always been proud to be.”

Idomeneus replied, “You can count on me as a trusty comrade, just as I promised from the first. Go and urge on the other Achaeans, so that we can join battle right away. The Trojans have trampled on their covenants, and since they broke their oaths and attacked us first, death and destruction will be their reward.”

The son of Atreus went on, glad at heart, until he came upon the two Ajaxes arming themselves among a host of foot soldiers. A goat-herd on a high lookout sees a storm come over the sea before the west wind. The offing is black as pitch and a mighty whirlwind rushes toward him, so he is afraid and drives his flock into a cave. In the same way the ranks of stalwart young men moved in a dark mass to battle under the Ajaxes, bristling with shield and spear. King Agamemnon was glad when he saw them. “There is no need,” he cried, “to give orders to leaders of the Argives like you, for you spur your men on to fight with all their might on your own. By father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, I wish everyone were as determined as you are. The city of Priam would soon fall to our hands, and we would sack it.”

Saying this, Agamemnon left them and went on to Nestor, the eloquent speaker of the Pylians. Nestor was drawing up his men and urging them on, together with Pelagon, Alastor, Chromius, Haemon, and Bias shepherd of his people. In the front rank he put the knights with their chariots and horses. Behind them, at the rear, he put the foot soldiers, brave men and many, whom he could trust. The cowards he drove into the middle, so that they would have to fight whether they wanted to or not. His orders went to the knights first. He told them to keep their horses well in hand and so avoid confusion. “No man,” he said, “should trust in his strength or his horsemanship and push out ahead of the others to fight the Trojans alone. Nor should anyone hang back, or you will weaken your attack. When a man meets an enemy chariot, he should throw his spear from his own. That is much the best way. It is how the men of old took towns and strongholds, and that was the thinking behind it.”

So the old man instructed them, for he had been in many a fight, and King Agamemnon was glad. “I wish,” he said to him, “that your limbs were as supple and your strength as sure as your judgment. But age, the common enemy of mankind, has laid its hand on you. I wish it had fallen on some other man, and that you were still young.”

Nestor, knight of Gerene, answered, “Son of Atreus, I would gladly be the man I was when I killed mighty Ereuthalion. But the gods do not give us everything at once. I was young then, and now I am old. Still, I can go with my knights and give them the advice that old men have a right to give. Handling the spear I leave to those who are younger and stronger than I am.”

Agamemnon went on his way glad at heart. Before long he found Menestheus, son of Peteos, standing in his place, with the Athenians, loud of tongue in battle, around him. Cunning Odysseus was standing near him too, with his sturdy Cephallenians about him. They had not yet heard the battle cry, because the Trojan and Achaean ranks had only just begun to move. So they stood still, waiting for some other column of the Achaeans to attack the Trojans and start the fighting. Seeing this, Agamemnon rebuked them. “Son of Peteos,” he said, “and you, steeped in cunning, heart of guile, why do you stand here cowering and waiting on others? You two ought to be foremost of all men when there is hard fighting to be done. You are always the first to accept my invitation when we councillors of the Achaeans hold a feast. Then you are glad enough to eat your fill of roast meat and drink wine as long as you please. Now you would not care even if you saw ten columns of Achaeans go into battle in front of you.”

Odysseus glared at him and answered, “Son of Atreus, what are you saying? How can you call us slack? When the Achaeans are in full fight with the Trojans, you will see, if you care to look, the father of Telemachus joining battle with the foremost of them. You are talking idly.”

Agamemnon saw that Odysseus was angry. He smiled kindly at him and took back his words. “Odysseus,” he said, “noble son of Laertes, excellent in all good counsel, I have no fault to find with you and no orders to give you. I know your heart is right, and that you and I think alike. Enough. I will make up to you for what I have said, and if anything bad has been said just now, may the gods bring it to nothing.”

Then he left them and went on to others. Soon he saw the son of Tydeus, noble Diomedes, standing by his chariot and horses, with Sthenelus the son of Capaneus beside him. At this he began to scold him. “Son of Tydeus,” he said, “why do you stand here cowering at the edge of battle? Tydeus did not shrink like this. He was always ahead of his men when he led them against the enemy. So at least say those who saw him fight, for I never saw him myself. They say no man was like him. He came once to Mycenae, not as an enemy but as a guest, together with Polynices, to gather forces. They were making war on the strong city of Thebes, and they asked our people for a body of picked men to help them. The men of Mycenae were willing to give them one, but Zeus talked them out of it by showing them unfavorable omens. So Tydeus and Polynices went on their way. They came to the deep-meadowed, rush-grown banks of the Aesopus. There the Achaeans sent Tydeus ahead as their envoy, and he found the Cadmeans gathered in great numbers at a banquet in the house of Eteocles. He was a stranger, but he felt no fear at finding himself alone among so many. He challenged them to contests of every kind, and he won every one at once, so mightily did Athena help him. The Cadmeans were furious at his success. They sent fifty youths, with two captains at their head, to lie in wait for him on his way back. The captains were the godlike hero Maeon, son of Haemon, and Polyphontes, son of Autophonus. But Tydeus killed every one of them, except Maeon alone, whom he let go because heaven’s omens told him to. Such was Tydeus of Aetolia. His son can talk more smoothly, but he cannot fight as his father did.”

Diomedes made no answer, for Agamemnon’s rebuke had shamed him. But the son of Capaneus took up the words and said, “Son of Atreus, do not lie, for you can speak the truth if you choose. We claim to be even better men than our fathers. We took seven-gated Thebes, though its wall was stronger and our men were fewer, because we trusted in the omens of the gods and in the help of Zeus. They perished through their own sheer folly. So do not put our fathers on the same level of honor as us.”

Diomedes looked sternly at him and said, “Be quiet, my friend, as I tell you. It is not wrong for Agamemnon to urge the Achaeans on. The glory will be his if we take the city, and the shame will be his if we are beaten. So let us show our courage.”
As he spoke he sprang from his chariot. His armor rang so fiercely around his body that even a brave man might have been frightened to hear it.

As when a mighty wave thunders on the beach after the west wind has whipped it into fury, and has reared its head far out and now comes crashing down on the shore, bowing its arching crest high over the jagged rocks and spewing salt foam in all directions, in just that way the close-packed ranks of the Danaans marched steadily to battle. The chiefs gave orders, each to his own people, but the men said not a word. No one would have thought it possible: huge as the host was, it seemed there was not a tongue among them, so silent were they in their obedience. As they marched, the armor on their bodies glistened in the sun. The noise of the Trojan ranks was different. It was like the sound of many thousand ewes standing in the yards of some rich flock-master, waiting to be milked, and bleating without pause as they answer their lambs. The Trojans had no single speech or language. Their tongues were mixed, and they came from many different places. Ares drove these on, and Athena the others. With them came Panic, Rout, and Strife, whose fury never tires, sister and friend of murderous Ares. She is small at first, but she grows until she lifts her head to heaven while her feet are still on earth. She was the one who went among them and threw down discord, to the increase of sorrow, with an even hand between the two sides.

When they had come together in one place, shield clashed with shield and spear with spear in the rage of battle. The bossed shields beat against one another, and there was a tramp like that of a great multitude. The death cry and the shout of triumph rose together, from the slain and from the slayers, and the earth ran red with blood. Rain-swollen torrents race wildly down their deep channels until the angry floods meet in some gorge, and the shepherd on the hillside hears their roaring from far off. In the same way the hosts toiled and roared as they joined in battle.

Antilochus was the first to kill a man. He killed an armed Trojan warrior fighting in the foremost ranks, Echepolus, son of Thalysius. Antilochus struck at the projecting part of his helmet and drove the spear into his brow. The bronze point went through the bone, and darkness covered his eyes. He fell like a tower in the press of the fight. As he dropped, King Elephenor, son of Chalcodon and captain of the proud Abantes, began dragging him out of reach of the darts that were falling around him. He was in a hurry to strip off the dead man’s armor. But he did not keep at it for long. Agenor saw him hauling the body away and struck him in the side with his bronze-shod spear, because as he stooped his shield left his side unprotected. So Elephenor died. Then the fight between Trojans and Achaeans grew furious over his body, and they leaped at each other like wolves, man crushing against man.

Next Ajax, son of Telamon, killed the fair youth Simoeisius, son of Anthemion. His mother had borne him by the banks of the Simois, when she was coming down from Mount Ida, where she had gone with her parents to see their flocks. That is why he was named Simoeisius. But he did not live to repay his parents for raising him, because mighty Ajax’s spear cut him off too soon. Ajax struck him in the breast by the right nipple as he came on among the foremost fighters. The spear went right through his shoulder, and he fell like a poplar that has grown straight and tall in a meadow by some pond, with its top thick with branches. A wheelwright cuts at its roots with his axe, to shape a rim for the wheel of some fine chariot, and the tree lies seasoning by the waterside. That is how Ajax felled Simoeisius, son of Anthemion. Then Antiphus of the gleaming corslet, son of Priam, threw a spear at Ajax from the crowd. He missed Ajax but hit Leucus, the brave comrade of Odysseus, in the groin, as Leucus was dragging the body of Simoeisius toward the other side. Leucus fell on the body and let go of it. Odysseus was furious when he saw Leucus dead. He strode in full armor through the front ranks until he was very close. Then he glared around and took aim, and the Trojans drew back as he did so. His dart did not fly in vain. It struck Democoon, a bastard son of Priam, who had come from Abydos, where he looked after his father’s mares. Odysseus, enraged at his comrade’s death, hit him with his spear on one temple, and the bronze point came out through the other side of his forehead. Darkness covered his eyes, and he fell heavily to the ground, and his armor clattered around him. Hector and the men in front gave ground, while the Argives raised a shout, dragged away the dead, and pressed still further forward. But Apollo looked down from Pergamus and called aloud to the Trojans, for he was displeased. “Trojans,” he cried, “rush on the enemy, and do not let the Argives beat you like this. Their skins are not stone or iron, so that you do them no harm when you hit them. And Achilles, the son of lovely Thetis, is not fighting. He is nursing his anger at the ships.”

So the mighty god spoke, calling to them from the city. Meanwhile Zeus’s redoubtable daughter, the Trito-born, went among the host of the Achaeans and urged them forward whenever she saw them slacken.

Then fate came upon Diores, son of Amarynceus. A jagged stone hit him near the ankle of his right leg. The man who threw it was Peirous, son of Imbrasus, captain of the Thracians, who had come from Aenus. The pitiless stone crushed the bones and both tendons. Diores fell on his back on the ground and stretched out his hands to his comrades as he died. Peirous, who had wounded him, sprang on him and thrust a spear into his belly, and his bowels came gushing out on the ground, and darkness covered his eyes. As Peirous was leaving the body, Thoas of Aetolia struck him in the chest near the nipple, and the point lodged in his lungs. Thoas came close up to him and pulled the spear out of his chest. Then he drew his sword and struck him in the middle of the belly, and Peirous died. But Thoas did not strip off his armor. Peirous’s Thracian comrades, who wear their hair in a tuft at the top of their heads, stood around the body and held Thoas off with their long spears, for all his great stature and valor. So he was driven back. The two corpses lay stretched on the earth near each other, one the captain of the Thracians and the other of the Epeans. Many others fell around them.

By now no man could have made light of the fighting, if he could have gone about in the middle of it unwounded and untouched, with Athena leading him by the hand and keeping the storm of spears and arrows off him. For on that day many Trojans and Achaeans lay stretched side by side, face down on the earth.

chapters.title: Book 5
paragraphs: The exploits of Diomedes, who keeps fighting even though Pandarus has wounded him—He kills Pandarus and wounds Aeneas—Aphrodite rescues Aeneas, but Diomedes wounds her too, and she hands him over to Apollo’s care and goes to Olympus, where her mother Dione tends her—Ares urges the Trojans on, and Aeneas, cured of his wound, returns to the fight—Athena and Hera help the Achaeans, and on the advice of Athena Diomedes wounds Ares, who goes back to Olympus to be cured.

Then Pallas Athena filled Diomedes, son of Tydeus, with courage, so that he would stand out above all the other Argives and win glory for himself. She made a stream of fire blaze from his shield and helmet, like the star that shines brightest in summer after bathing in the waters of Oceanus. She set that same fire burning on his head and shoulders, and told him to hurry into the thickest of the hurly-burly of the fight.

Among the Trojans there was a rich and honorable man named Dares, a priest of Hephaestus. He had two sons, Phegeus and Idaeus, both skilled in every kind of fighting. These two left the main body of the Trojans and went for Diomedes. They were in their chariot, and he was on foot. When they were close, Phegeus aimed first, but his spear passed over Diomedes’s left shoulder and missed him. Then Diomedes threw, and his spear did not fly in vain: it hit Phegeus on the chest near the nipple, and he fell from the chariot. Idaeus did not dare to stand over his brother’s body. He jumped down from the chariot and ran, and he would have shared his brother’s fate if Hephaestus had not saved him by wrapping him in a cloud of darkness, so that his old father would not be utterly crushed with grief. The son of Tydeus drove off with their horses and told his followers to take them to the ships. The Trojans were frightened when they saw the two sons of Dares, one running in terror and the other lying dead beside his chariot. Then Athena took Ares by the hand and said, “Ares, Ares, bane of men, blood-stained stormer of cities, why do we not leave the Trojans and Achaeans to fight it out, and see to which of them Zeus will grant the victory? Let us go away and so avoid his anger.”

With these words she led Ares out of the battle and sat him down on the steep banks of the Scamander. Then the Danaans pushed the Trojans back, and each of their chieftains killed his man. King Agamemnon was first: he threw mighty Odius, captain of the Halizoni, from his chariot. Odius was turning to run when Agamemnon’s spear caught him in the middle of the back. It struck between his shoulders and went right through his chest, and his armor clattered around him as he fell heavily to the ground.

Next Idomeneus killed Phaesus, son of Borus the Meonian, who had come from Varne. Phaesus was climbing into his chariot when mighty Idomeneus speared him in the right shoulder. He fell heavily from the car, and the darkness of death closed around him.

The squires of Idomeneus stripped Phaesus of his armor. Meanwhile Menelaus, son of Atreus, killed Scamandrius, the son of Strophius, a mighty huntsman and keen lover of the chase. Artemis herself had taught him to kill every kind of wild creature bred in the mountain forests. But neither she nor his famed skill with the bow could save him now. He was running away when the spear of Menelaus struck him in the back, between the shoulders, and went right through his chest. He fell headlong, and his armor clattered around him.

Then Meriones killed Phereclus, son of Tecton and grandson of Hermon, a man whose hands were skilled in every kind of cunning craftsmanship, because Pallas Athena had loved him dearly. He was the one who built the ships for Paris, the beginning of all the trouble, which brought evil on the Trojans and on Paris himself. He had paid no heed to the decrees of heaven. Meriones caught up with him as he ran, and struck him on the right buttock. The point of the spear went through the bone into the bladder. Phereclus cried out, fell forward on his knees, and death came over him.

Meges, too, killed Pedaeus, son of Antenor. Pedaeus was a bastard, but Theano had raised him like one of her own children, out of love for her husband. The son of Phyleus came up close and drove a spear into the back of his neck. It passed under his tongue and in among his teeth, so that he bit the cold bronze and fell dead in the dust.

Eurypylus, son of Euaemon, killed Hypsenor, the son of noble Dolopion. Hypsenor had been made priest of the river Scamander and was honored among the people like a god. Eurypylus chased him as he fled, struck him on the arm with his sword, and cut his strong hand off. The bloody hand fell to the ground, and the shades of death, with a fate no man can withstand, came over Hypsenor’s eyes.

So furiously the battle raged between them. As for the son of Tydeus, you could not tell whether he was fighting among the Achaeans or the Trojans. He swept across the plain like a winter torrent in full flood that has burst its banks. No dikes can hold it back, and no walls of fruitful vineyards can contain it when rain from heaven has swollen it. In a moment it comes tearing on and lays waste many a field that many a strong man’s hand has reclaimed. In the same way the son of Tydeus drove the dense ranks of the Trojans in rout, and many as they were, they dared not stand against his onslaught.

The son of Lycaon saw him sweeping across the plain and driving the Trojans in confusion before him. He aimed an arrow and hit him on the front of his cuirass, near the shoulder. The arrow went right through the metal and into the flesh, and the cuirass was covered with blood. The son of Lycaon shouted in triumph, “Trojan knights, come on! The bravest of the Achaeans is wounded, and he will not last much longer, if King Apollo was truly with me when I set out from Lycia to come here.”

So he boasted, but his arrow had not killed Diomedes. Diomedes pulled back and went to the chariot and horses of Sthenelus, the son of Capaneus. “Dear son of Capaneus,” he said, “come down from your chariot and pull the arrow out of my shoulder.”

Sthenelus jumped down from his chariot and drew the arrow from the wound, and blood came spouting out through the hole it had made in his shirt. Then Diomedes prayed: “Hear me, unwearying daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus. If you ever loved my father and stood by him in the thick of a fight, do the same for me now. Let me come within a spear’s throw of that man and kill him. He was too quick for me and has wounded me, and now he boasts that I will not see the light of the sun much longer.”

So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him. She made his limbs supple and quickened his hands and feet. Then she came close to him and said, “Do not be afraid, Diomedes, to fight the Trojans. I have put into your heart the spirit of your knightly father Tydeus. I have also lifted the veil from your eyes, so that you can tell gods from men. So if any other god comes here and offers you battle, do not fight him. But if Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, comes, strike her with your spear and wound her.”

After saying this Athena went away, and the son of Tydeus took his place again among the foremost fighters. He was three times as fierce as he had been before. He was like a lion that a mountain shepherd has wounded but not killed as it springs over the wall of a sheep-yard to attack the sheep. The shepherd has roused the beast to fury but cannot defend his flock, so he takes shelter in the buildings. The sheep, panic-stricken at being deserted, are smothered in heaps one on top of another, and the angry lion leaps out over the sheep-yard wall. That was how Diomedes went furiously about among the Trojans.

He killed Astynous and Hypeiron, shepherd of his people. He struck Astynous with a spear thrust above the nipple, and Hypeiron with a sword cut on the collarbone that severed his shoulder from his neck and back. He left both of them lying and went after Abas and Polyidus, sons of the old reader of dreams Eurydamas. They never came back for him to read them any more dreams, because mighty Diomedes made an end of them. Next he chased Xanthus and Thoon, the two sons of Phaenops. Both were very dear to their father, who was worn out with age and had no more sons to inherit his possessions. But Diomedes took both their lives and left their father grieving bitterly. He never saw them come home alive from the battle, and his kinsmen divided his wealth among themselves.

Next he met two sons of Priam, Echemmon and Chromius, riding in a single chariot. A lion will leap on the neck of a cow or heifer when the herd is grazing in a coppice, and he leapt on them in the same way. They fought back in vain. He threw both of them out of their chariot and took the armor off their bodies. Then he handed their horses to his comrades, to be led back to the ships.

Aeneas saw him making havoc among the ranks. He went through the fight, through the rain of spears, to look for Pandarus. When he found the brave son of Lycaon, he said, “Pandarus, where are your bow, your winged arrows and your renown as an archer now? No man here can rival you in that, and nobody in Lycia can beat you. Lift your hands to Zeus and send an arrow at this fellow who is going about so masterfully and has done such deadly work among the Trojans. He has killed many a brave man—unless he is some god who is angry with the Trojans about their sacrifices and, in his displeasure, has set his hand against them.”

The son of Lycaon answered, “Aeneas, I take him to be none other than the son of Tydeus. I know him by his shield, by the visor of his helmet and by his horses. He may be a god, but if he is the man I say he is, he is not making all this havoc without heaven’s help. Some god stands by his side, shrouded in a cloud of darkness, and that god turned my arrow aside when it had hit him. I have already shot at him and hit him on the right shoulder. My arrow went through the breast-piece of his cuirass, and I felt sure I had sent him hurrying to the world below. But it seems I have not killed him, so there must be a god who is angry with me. On top of that, I have neither horse nor chariot. In my father’s stables there are eleven excellent chariots, fresh from the builder and quite new, with cloths spread over them, and beside each one stands a pair of horses, champing barley and rye. My old father Lycaon urged me again and again, when I was at home and about to set out, to take chariots and horses with me so that I could lead the Trojans in battle. I would not listen to him. It would have been much better if I had. But I was thinking of the horses, which were used to eating their fill, and I was afraid they would go short of food in such a great gathering of men. So I left them at home and came on foot to Ilium, armed only with my bow and arrows. It seems these are of no use, for I have already hit two chieftains, the sons of Atreus and of Tydeus, and although I certainly drew blood, I have only made them more furious. I did wrong to take my bow down from its peg on the day I led my band of Trojans to Ilium in Hector’s service. If I ever get home again and see my native place, my wife and my great house, may someone cut my head off then and there if I do not break this bow and put it on a hot fire. Those are the tricks it plays on me.”

Aeneas answered, “Say no more. Things will not improve until the two of us go against this man with a chariot and horses and put him to the test of arms. Get into my chariot and see how skillfully the horses of Tros can race this way and that over the plain, in pursuit or in flight. If Zeus grants glory to the son of Tydeus again, they will carry us safely back to the city. So take the whip and reins while I stand on the car to fight. Or else you wait for this man’s attack, and I will look after the horses.”

“Aeneas,” replied the son of Lycaon, “take the reins and drive yourself. If we have to flee from the son of Tydeus, the horses will go better with their own driver. If they miss the sound of your voice when they expect it, they may take fright and refuse to carry us out of the fight. Then the son of Tydeus will kill both of us and take the horses. So drive them yourself, and I will meet him with my spear.”

They climbed into the chariot and drove at full speed toward the son of Tydeus. Sthenelus, son of Capaneus, saw them coming and said to Diomedes, “Diomedes, son of Tydeus, man after my own heart, I see two mighty heroes speeding toward you. One is a skilled archer, Pandarus son of Lycaon. The other is Aeneas, whose father is Anchises and whose mother is Aphrodite. Get into the chariot and let us retreat. I beg you, do not press so furiously forward, or you may get killed.”

Diomedes looked at him angrily and answered, “Do not talk of flight, for I will not listen. I come from a race that knows neither flight nor fear, and my limbs are not yet tired. I have no wish to mount the chariot. I will go against them just as I am. Pallas Athena tells me to be afraid of no man, and even if one of them escapes, their horses will not carry both back. I say more, and take my words to heart. If Athena sees fit to grant me the glory of killing both, stay here with your horses and tie the reins fast to the rim of the chariot. Then be sure to spring on Aeneas’s horses and drive them from the Trojan ranks to the Achaean. They come from the stock that great Zeus gave to Tros in payment for his son Ganymede, and they are the finest that live and move under the sun. King Anchises stole the breed by putting his mares to them without Laomedon’s knowledge, and they bore him six foals. Four are still in his stables, but he gave the other two to Aeneas. We shall win great glory if we can take them.”

So they talked, but the other two had now driven close, and the son of Lycaon spoke first. “Great and mighty son,” he said, “of noble Tydeus, my arrow failed to bring you down, so now I will try my spear.”

As he spoke he poised his spear and hurled it. It struck the shield of the son of Tydeus. The bronze point pierced it and went on until it reached the breastplate. The son of Lycaon shouted out, “You are hit clean through the belly. You will not last long, and the glory of the fight is mine.”
But Diomedes, quite undismayed, answered, “You missed, you did not hit. Before the two of you see the end of this, one or the other of you will glut tough-shielded Ares with his blood.”

With that he hurled his spear, and Athena guided it onto Pandarus’s nose, near the eye. It crashed in among his white teeth. The bronze point cut through the root of his tongue and came out under his chin. His glistening armor clattered around him as he fell heavily to the ground. The horses shied away in fear, and his life and strength were gone.

Aeneas leapt down from his chariot with shield and spear, afraid that the Achaeans would carry off the body. He stood astride it like a lion sure of its strength, holding shield and spear out in front and shouting his battle cry, determined to kill the first man who dared face him. But the son of Tydeus picked up a huge stone. It was so big that, as men are now, it would take two of them to lift it. Even so, he raised it easily by himself, and he hit Aeneas with it on the groin, where the thigh turns in its socket, the joint called the “cup-bone.” The stone crushed the joint and snapped both sinews, and its rough edges ripped away the flesh. The hero dropped to his knees and propped himself up with one hand on the ground, until the darkness of night came over his eyes. Aeneas, king of men, would have died on the spot, but his mother saw it quickly. She was Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, who had conceived him by Anchises while he was herding cattle. She threw her two white arms around her dear son and covered him with a fold of her own fair robe to protect him, so that no Danaan could drive a spear into his chest and kill him.

So Aphrodite carried her dear son out of the fight. But the son of Capaneus had not forgotten the orders Diomedes had given him. He tied his own horses up away from the uproar, fastening the reins to the rim of the chariot. Then he leapt onto Aeneas’s horses and drove them from the Trojan lines over to the Achaean ranks. After that he handed them to his chosen comrade Deipylus, whom he valued above all the others because the two thought alike, and told him to take them to the ships. Then he climbed back into his own chariot, took up the reins, and drove at full speed to look for the son of Tydeus.

Meanwhile the son of Tydeus was chasing the Cyprian goddess with his spear in hand. He knew she was weak, not one of those goddesses who have power over men in battle, like Athena or Enyo, the waster of cities. After a long chase he caught up with her, lunged, and thrust his spear into the flesh of her delicate hand. The point ripped through the ambrosial robe that the Graces had woven for her and pierced the skin between her wrist and the palm of her hand. The immortal blood, or ichor, that runs in the veins of the blessed gods came pouring from the wound. The gods do not eat bread or drink wine, and so they have no blood like ours, and that is why they are immortal. Aphrodite screamed and dropped her son, but Phoebus Apollo caught him in his arms and hid him in a cloud of darkness, so that no Danaan could drive a spear into his chest and kill him. As he left her, Diomedes shouted, “Daughter of Zeus, leave war and battle alone. Is it not enough for you to deceive silly women? If you meddle in fighting, you will get something that makes you shudder at the very name of war.”

The goddess went away dazed and in distress. Iris, swift as the wind, led her out of the throng, in pain, her fair skin all stained. She found fierce Ares waiting on the left of the battle, with his spear and his two swift horses resting on a cloud. Aphrodite fell on her knees before her brother and begged him to let her have his horses. “Dear brother,” she cried, “save me. Give me your horses to carry me to Olympus, where the gods live. A mortal has wounded me badly, the son of Tydeus, who would now fight even with father Zeus.”

At these words Ares gave her his gold-decked horses. She climbed into the chariot, sick at heart and miserable, while Iris sat beside her and took the reins in her hand. Iris whipped the horses on, and they flew ahead willingly. In no time they reached high Olympus, where the gods have their home. There Iris stopped them, unhitched them from the chariot, and fed them ambrosial fodder. Aphrodite threw herself into the lap of her mother Dione, who put her arms around her and stroked her. “Which of the heavenly beings has treated you like this,” she asked, “as if you had been caught doing something wrong in broad daylight?”

Laughter-loving Aphrodite answered, “Proud Diomedes, the son of Tydeus, wounded me because I was carrying my dear son Aeneas, whom I love best of all mankind, out of the fight. This war is no longer just between Trojans and Achaeans. The Danaans are now fighting with the immortals.”

“Bear it, my child,” Dione replied, “and make the best of it. We who live on Olympus put up with a great deal from men, and we also cause one another much suffering. Ares suffered when Otus and Ephialtes, the children of Aloeus, tied him in cruel bonds and kept him locked up for thirteen months in a bronze vessel. Ares would have died there if fair Eeriboea, stepmother to the sons of Aloeus, had not told Hermes. Hermes stole him away when he was already nearly worn out by the harshness of his imprisonment. Hera suffered too, when the mighty son of Amphitryon wounded her in the right breast with a three-barbed arrow, and nothing could ease her pain. So did huge Hades, when this same man, the son of aegis-bearing Zeus, shot him with an arrow at the gates of hell and hurt him badly. Hades went in anger and pain to the house of Zeus on great Olympus. The arrow in his brawny shoulder caused him terrible anguish until Paeeon healed him by spreading soothing herbs on the wound, for Hades was not made of mortal stuff. What a daring, headstrong evildoer, who did not care about his sin in shooting the gods who live on Olympus. And now Athena has urged this son of Tydeus on against you. What a fool he is, not to think that a man who fights with gods will not live long, and will never hear his children prattling about his knees when he comes home from battle. So let the son of Tydeus take care that he does not have to fight someone stronger than you are. Then his brave wife Aegialeia, daughter of Adrestus, will wake her whole household from sleep with her wailing for the loss of her wedded lord, Diomedes, the bravest of the Achaeans.”

With these words she wiped the ichor from her daughter’s wrist with both hands. The pain left her, and her hand was healed. But Athena and Hera had been looking on, and they began to tease Zeus with mocking talk. Athena spoke first. “Father Zeus,” she said, “please do not be angry with me. I think the Cyprian must have been persuading some Achaean woman to go off with the Trojans, of whom she is so very fond. While stroking one or another of those women, she must have cut her delicate hand on the gold pin of the woman’s brooch.”

The father of gods and men smiled and called golden Aphrodite to his side. “My child,” he said, “warfare has not been given to you. From now on, attend to your own delightful duties of marriage, and leave all this fighting to Ares and to Athena.”

So they talked together. Meanwhile Diomedes sprang at Aeneas, though he knew Apollo was holding him in his very arms. He did not fear the mighty god in the least, so set was he on killing Aeneas and stripping off his armor. Three times he leapt forward with all his strength to kill him, and three times Apollo beat his gleaming shield back. When he charged a fourth time, like a god himself, Apollo shouted at him in a terrible voice. “Take care, son of Tydeus, and pull back. Do not think you can match yourself against gods, for men who walk the earth cannot hold their own against the immortals.”

The son of Tydeus gave way a little, to avoid the god’s anger. Apollo carried Aeneas out of the crowd and placed him in sacred Pergamus, where his temple stood. There, inside the mighty sanctuary, Leto and Artemis healed him and made him glorious to look at. Meanwhile Apollo of the silver bow made a phantom in the likeness of Aeneas, armed as Aeneas was. Around this phantom the Trojans and Achaeans hacked at the bucklers on one another’s chests, cutting into round shields and light, hide-covered targets. Then Phoebus Apollo said to Ares, “Ares, Ares, bane of men, blood-stained stormer of cities, can you not go to this man, the son of Tydeus, and draw him out of the battle? He would now fight even with father Zeus. First he went up to the Cyprian and wounded her in the hand near the wrist, and then he sprang at me too, as though he were a god.”

Then Apollo took his seat on the top of Pergamus. Murderous Ares went about among the Trojan ranks to cheer them on, in the likeness of swift Acamas, chief of the Thracians. “Sons of Priam,” he said, “how long will you let the Achaeans slaughter your people like this? Will you wait until they are at the walls of Troy? Aeneas son of Anchises has fallen, and we honored him as highly as Hector himself. Help me, then, to rescue our brave comrade from the thick of the fight.”

These words put heart and spirit into them all. Then Sarpedon rebuked Hector very sharply. “Hector,” he said, “where is your prowess now? You used to say that you could hold the town alone with your brothers and brothers-in-law, even without people or allies. I do not see one of them here. They cower like hounds before a lion, and it is we, your allies, who bear the brunt of the battle. I have come from far away, from Lycia and the banks of the river Xanthus, where I left my wife, my infant son, and great wealth to tempt any needy man. Even so, I lead my Lycian soldiers and stand my ground against anyone who wants to fight me, though I have nothing here for the Achaeans to plunder. You just look on, without even telling your men to stand firm in defense of their wives. Make sure you do not fall into your enemies’ hands like men caught in the mesh of a net, and that they do not sack your fair city at once. Keep this in mind night and day. Beg the captains of your allies to hold on without flinching, and so take their reproaches away from you.”

So Sarpedon spoke, and his words stung Hector. He sprang from his chariot in full armor and went through the army, brandishing his two spears, urging the men to fight and raising the terrible battle cry. They rallied and turned to face the Achaeans again, but the Argives stood close together and firm, and were not driven back. As the breezes play with the chaff on a good threshing floor when men are winnowing—while yellow Demeter blows with the wind to sift the chaff from the grain, and the chaff-heaps grow whiter and whiter—so the Achaeans turned white with the dust that the horses’ hoofs threw up to the sky, as their drivers turned them back into battle and they bore down on the enemy with all their might. Fierce Ares, to help the Trojans, covered them in a veil of darkness and went about everywhere among them. Phoebus Apollo had told him that when he saw Pallas Athena leave the fray, he was to put courage into the hearts of the Trojans, because she was the one helping the Danaans. Then Apollo sent Aeneas out of his rich sanctuary and filled his heart with valor. Aeneas took his place among his comrades, who were overjoyed to see him alive, sound, and in good courage. But they could not ask him how it had all happened, because they were too busy with the turmoil raised by Ares and by Strife, who raged insatiably among them.

The two Ajaxes, Odysseus, and Diomedes cheered the Danaans on, unafraid of the fury and charge of the Trojans. The Danaans stood as still as the clouds that the son of Cronus spreads over the mountain tops when there is no wind and fierce Boreas sleeps, along with the other boisterous winds whose shrill blasts scatter the clouds in every direction—in the same way the Danaans stood firm and unflinching against the Trojans. The son of Atreus went among them urging them on. “My friends,” he said, “be brave men, and avoid disgrace in one another’s eyes in the stress of battle. Men who avoid disgrace live more often than they are killed, but those who run save neither life nor name.”

As he spoke he hurled his spear and hit a man in the front rank, Deicoon son of Pergasus, a comrade of Aeneas. The Trojans honored him as much as the sons of Priam, because he was always quick to put himself among the foremost. King Agamemnon’s spear struck his shield and went right through it, since the shield did not stop it. It drove through his belt into the lower part of his belly, and he fell heavily to the ground, his armor clattering around him.

Then Aeneas killed two champions of the Danaans, Crethon and Orsilochus. Their father was a rich man who lived in the strong city of Phere, and he was descended from the river Alpheus, whose broad stream flows through the land of the Pylians. The river fathered Orsilochus, who ruled over many people and was the father of Diocles. Diocles in his turn fathered twin sons, Crethon and Orsilochus, well skilled in every art of war. When they grew up, they went to Ilium with the Argive fleet, in the cause of Menelaus and Agamemnon, sons of Atreus, and there they both fell. Like two lions that their dam has reared in the depths of a mountain forest to plunder homesteads and carry off sheep and cattle, until men kill them, these two were beaten by Aeneas and fell like tall pine trees to the ground.

Brave Menelaus pitied them as they fell. He made his way to the front, dressed in gleaming bronze and brandishing his spear, because Ares was urging him on, intending that Aeneas should kill him. But Antilochus son of Nestor saw him and sprang forward. He feared that the king might come to harm and so bring all their labor to nothing. Aeneas and Menelaus were setting their hands and spears against each other, eager to fight, when Antilochus placed himself at Menelaus’s side. Bold as Aeneas was, he drew back when he saw the two heroes side by side in front of him. The two men then dragged the bodies of Crethon and Orsilochus to the Achaean ranks and put the two poor fellows into the hands of their comrades. After that they turned back and fought in the front ranks.

They killed Pylaemenes, peer of Ares, leader of the Paphlagonian warriors. Menelaus struck him on the collar-bone as he stood in his chariot. Antilochus hit Mydon son of Atymnius, his charioteer and squire, who was turning his horses to flee. He hit him on the elbow with a stone, and the reins, decorated with white ivory, fell from his hands into the dust. Antilochus rushed at him and struck him on the temples with his sword. Mydon fell head first from the chariot to the ground. There he stood for a while with his head and shoulders buried deep in the dust, for he had fallen on sandy soil, until his horses kicked him and laid him flat on the ground. Antilochus lashed them and drove them off to the host of the Achaeans.

But Hector saw them from across the ranks. He rushed toward them with a loud cry, and the strong battalions of the Trojans followed him. Ares and dread Enyo led them on. She brought the ruthless turmoil of battle with her, while Ares wielded a monstrous spear and went about, now in front of Hector and now behind him.

Diomedes shook with rage when he saw them. A man crossing a wide plain is dismayed to find himself at the edge of a great river rolling swiftly to the sea—he sees its boiling waters and starts back in fear—and in the same way the son of Tydeus gave ground. Then he said to his men, “My friends, why are we surprised that Hector wields the spear so well? Some god is always at his side to protect him, and now Ares is with him in the form of a mortal man. Keep your faces toward the Trojans, but give ground backwards, for we dare not fight with gods.”

As he spoke, the Trojans came close together, and Hector killed two men who were in one chariot, Menesthes and Anchialus, both heroes well versed in war. Ajax son of Telamon pitied them as they fell. He moved in close and hurled his spear at Amphius, the son of Selagus. Amphius was a very wealthy man who lived in Paesus and owned a great deal of land that grew grain, but his fate had led him to come and help Priam and his sons. Ajax struck him in the belt. The spear pierced the lower part of his belly, and he fell heavily to the ground. Ajax ran toward him to strip off his armor, but the Trojans rained spears on Ajax, and many of them landed on his shield. He planted his heel on the body and pulled out his spear. Still, the darts pressed on him so heavily that he could not strip the fine armor from Amphius’s shoulders. Many valiant Trojan chieftains were also crowding around him with their spears, and he did not dare to stay. Great, brave and valiant as he was, they drove him away from them and beat him back.

So the battle raged between them. Then the strong hand of fate drove Tlepolemus, the son of Heracles, a brave man of great height, to fight Sarpedon. The two, son and grandson of great Zeus, came near one another, and Tlepolemus spoke first. “Sarpedon,” he said, “councillor of the Lycians, why are you skulking here, you who are a man of peace? Those who call you a son of aegis-bearing Zeus are liars, for you are very unlike the men who were his children long ago. Heracles was far different, my own brave and lion-hearted father. He came here for the horses of Laomedon. He had only six ships and few men to follow him, yet he sacked the city of Ilium and left her highways a wilderness. You are a coward, and your people are falling away from you. For all your strength, and for all that you have come from Lycia, you will be no help to the Trojans. You will pass the gates of Hades beaten by my hand.”

Sarpedon, captain of the Lycians, answered, “Tlepolemus, your father overthrew Ilium because Laomedon was a fool. Laomedon refused payment to a man who had served him well, and he would not give your father the horses that he had come so far to fetch. As for you, you will meet your death from my spear. You will give me glory, and you will give your soul to Hades of the noble horses.”

So Sarpedon spoke, and Tlepolemus raised his spear. They threw at the same moment. Sarpedon hit his enemy in the middle of the throat; the spear went right through, and the darkness of death fell over his eyes. Tlepolemus’s spear struck Sarpedon in the left thigh with such force that it tore through the flesh and grazed the bone. But his father still kept destruction away from him.

His comrades carried Sarpedon out of the fight. He was in great pain from the weight of the spear dragging in his wound. They were in such haste and distress as they carried him that no one thought to pull the spear out of his thigh so that he could walk upright. Meanwhile the Achaeans carried off the body of Tlepolemus. Odysseus was moved to pity and panted for the fight as he watched them. He could not decide whether to go after the son of Zeus or to slaughter the rank and file of the Lycians. It was not fated that he should kill the son of Zeus, so Athena turned him against the main body of the Lycians. He killed Coeranus, Alastor, Chromius, Alcandrus, Halius, Noemon, and Prytanis, and he would have killed more, but great Hector noticed him. Hector, dressed in his suit of mail, hurried to the front of the fight and filled the Danaans with terror. Sarpedon was glad to see him coming and begged him, “Son of Priam, do not let me lie here and fall into the hands of the Danaans. Help me. And since I am not to return home and gladden the hearts of my wife and my infant son, let me die inside the walls of your city.”

Hector gave him no answer. He rushed on to fall at once on the Achaeans and kill many of them. Sarpedon’s comrades then carried him away and laid him beneath Zeus’s spreading oak tree. Pelagon, his friend and comrade, pulled the spear out of his thigh, but Sarpedon fainted and a mist came over his eyes. Soon he came to himself again. The breath of the north wind, playing on him, gave him new life and brought him out of the deep swoon he had fallen into.

Meanwhile Ares and Hector did not drive the Argives back toward their ships, but the Argives did not attack them either. When they knew that Ares was with the Trojans, they retreated, though they kept their faces turned toward the enemy. Who was the first, and who the last, to be slain by Ares and Hector? They were valiant Teuthras, Orestes the renowned charioteer, Trechus the Aetolian warrior, Oenomaus, Helenus the son of Oenops, and Oresbius of the gleaming girdle. Oresbius had great wealth and lived by the Cephisian lake, with the other Boeotians who lived near him, owners of a fertile country.

When the goddess Hera saw the Argives falling like this, she spoke to Athena. “Alas, unweariable daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, we promised Menelaus that he would not go home until he had sacked the city of Ilium. That promise will come to nothing if we let Ares rage like this. Let us go into the fight at once.”

Athena did not refuse her. Then Hera, the august goddess, daughter of great Cronus, began to harness her horses, which were decked with gold. Hebe quickly fitted the eight-spoked bronze wheels on either side of the iron axle. The rims of the wheels were gold and imperishable, with a tire of bronze over them, wonderful to look at. The hubs of the wheels were silver and turned around the axle on either side. The car itself was made of plaited bands of gold and silver, and it had a double rail running all round it. A silver pole stood out from the body of the car, and on the end of it Hebe bound the golden yoke, with the golden bands that would go under the horses’ necks. Then Hera put her horses under the yoke, horses eager for battle and the war cry.

Meanwhile Athena let her richly embroidered robe, which she had made with her own hands, fall on her father’s threshold, and she put on the tunic of Zeus and armed herself for battle. She threw her tasseled aegis around her shoulders. It was wreathed with Rout like a fringe, and on it were Strife, Strength, and Panic, whose blood runs cold. On it also was the head of the Gorgon, that dread monster, grim and awful to look at, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus. On her head she set her golden helmet, with four plumes, which rose to a peak both in front and behind and was decked with the emblems of a hundred cities. Then she stepped into her flaming chariot and took up her spear, so stout and sturdy and strong, with which she crushes the ranks of heroes who have displeased her. Hera lashed the horses on, and the gates of heaven bellowed as they flew open of their own accord. The Hours guard those gates; Heaven and Olympus are in their hands, to open the dense cloud that hides them or to close it. Through these gates the goddesses drove their obedient horses, and they found the son of Cronus sitting all alone on the topmost ridges of Olympus. There Hera stopped her horses and spoke to Zeus the son of Cronus, lord of all. “Father Zeus,” she said, “are you not angry with Ares for these high doings? What a great and splendid host of the Achaeans he has destroyed, to my great grief, and without either right or reason! Meanwhile the Cyprian and Apollo are enjoying it all at their ease and setting this unrighteous madman on to do more mischief. Father Zeus, I hope you will not be angry if I hit Ares hard and chase him out of the battle.”
Zeus answered, “Set Athena on him, for she punishes him more often than anyone else does.”

Hera did as he said. She lashed her horses, and they flew eagerly forward between earth and sky. As far as a man can see when he looks out over the sea from some high beacon, so far can the loud-neighing horses of the gods leap in a single bound. They reached Troy and the place where its two flowing rivers, Simois and Scamander, meet. There Hera stopped them and took them out of the chariot. She hid them in a thick cloud, and Simois made ambrosia grow for them to eat. The two goddesses went on, flying like turtledoves in their eagerness to help the Argives. They came to the place where the bravest and most numerous men were gathered around mighty Diomedes, fighting like lions or wild boars of great strength and endurance. There Hera stood still and raised a shout like that of brazen-voiced Stentor, whose cry was as loud as the cry of fifty men together. “Argives,” she cried, “shame on you, cowards, brave in appearance only! As long as Achilles was fighting, his spear was so deadly that the Trojans dared not show themselves outside the Dardanian gates. But now they sally far from the city and fight even at your ships.”

With these words she put heart and soul into all of them. Meanwhile Athena sprang to the side of the son of Tydeus. She found him near his chariot and horses, cooling the wound that Pandarus had given him. The hand that carried the weight of his shield made him sweat, and the sweat irritated the hurt. His arm was weary with pain, and he was lifting the strap to wipe away the blood. The goddess laid her hand on the yoke of his horses and said, “The son of Tydeus is not much like his father. Tydeus was a small man, but he could fight. He rushed madly into the fray even when I told him not to. Once he went to the city of Thebes, among the Cadmeans, as an envoy with no one to attend him. I told him to feast in their houses and keep the peace. But with the high spirit that was always in him, he challenged the young Cadmeans and beat them at once in everything he tried, so mightily did I help him. I stand by you too, to protect you, and I tell you to fight the Trojans without delay. But either you are tired out, or you are afraid and have lost heart. In that case I say you are no true son of Tydeus the son of Oeneus.”

Diomedes answered, “I know you, goddess, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, and I will hide nothing from you. I am not afraid or discouraged, and there is no slackness in me. I am only following your own instructions. You told me not to fight any of the blessed gods, except that if Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite came into battle I was to wound her with my spear. That is why I am retreating, and why I am telling the other Argives to gather here. I know that Ares is now lording it over the field.”

“Diomedes, son of Tydeus,” replied Athena, “man after my own heart, fear neither Ares nor any other of the immortals, for I will be your friend. No, drive straight at Ares and strike him in close combat. Do not fear this raging madman, this villain through and through, who is first on one side and then on the other.
