Only now he was talking with Hera and me, saying he would help the Argives and attack the Trojans. Yet he is with the Trojans, and has forgotten the Argives.”

With this she took hold of Sthenelus and lifted him off the chariot onto the ground. He was down in a moment, and the goddess mounted the car and took her place beside Diomedes. The oaken axle groaned aloud under the weight of the awful goddess and the hero. Pallas Athena took the whip and reins and drove straight at Ares. He was stripping huge Periphas, son of Ochesius and bravest of the Aetolians. Bloody Ares was taking his armor, and Athena put on the helmet of Hades so that he would not see her. When Ares saw Diomedes, he made straight for him and left Periphas lying where he had fallen. As soon as they were at close quarters, Ares let fly with his bronze spear over the reins and yoke, thinking to take Diomedes’s life. But Athena caught the spear in her hand and made it fly harmlessly over the chariot. Then Diomedes threw, and Pallas Athena drove the spear into the pit of Ares’s stomach, where his under-girdle went around him. There Diomedes wounded him, tearing his fair flesh, and then drew his spear out again. Ares roared as loudly as nine or ten thousand men in the thick of a fight, and the Achaeans and Trojans were struck with panic, so terrible was the cry he raised.

Diomedes son of Tydeus watched Ares rise into the broad heavens, like a dark cloud in the sky when a wind comes up after heat. Ares quickly reached high Olympus, home of the gods, and sat down in great pain beside Zeus the son of Cronus. He showed Zeus the immortal blood flowing from his wound and spoke piteously. “Father Zeus, are you not angry at such doings? We gods are always suffering the most cruel treatment from one another while we help mortals. And we all hold a grudge against you for having fathered that mad shrew of a daughter, who is always committing some outrage. The rest of us gods must all do as you tell us, but her you neither scold nor punish. You encourage her because the pestilent creature is your daughter. See how she has been inciting proud Diomedes to vent his rage on the immortal gods. First he went up to the Cyprian and wounded her in the hand near her wrist, and then he sprang on me too as though he were a god. If I had not run for it, I would have lain there for a long time in torment among the ghastly corpses, or else been eaten alive by spears until I had no strength left in me.”

Zeus looked at him angrily and said, “Do not come whining to me, Sir Facing-both-ways. Of all the gods in Olympus I hate you most, for you are always fighting and making mischief. You have the intolerable, stubborn spirit of your mother Hera. It is all I can do to manage her, and it is her doing that you are in this plight now. Still, I cannot let you stay in such great pain any longer. You are my own offspring, and it was by me that your mother conceived you. But if you had been the son of any other god, you are so destructive that by now you would have been lying lower than the Titans.”

Then he told Paeeon to heal him, and Paeeon spread pain-killing herbs on his wound and cured him, for Ares was not of mortal make. As the juice of the fig tree curdles milk and thickens it in a moment though it is liquid, so instantly did Paeeon cure fierce Ares. Then Hebe washed him and dressed him in fine clothes, and he took his seat by his father Zeus, glorious to behold.
But Hera of Argos and Athena of Alalcomene had put a stop to the murderous doings of Ares. Now they went back to the house of Zeus.

chapters.title: Book 6
paragraphs: Glaucus and Diomedes—The story of Bellerophon—Hector and Andromache.

Now the battle between the Trojans and the Achaeans raged on unchecked. The tide of war rolled back and forth across the plain, between the streams of Simois and Xanthus, as the two sides aimed their bronze-shod spears at one another.

Ajax son of Telamon, a tower of strength to the Achaeans, was the first to act. He broke a Trojan phalanx and helped his comrades by killing Acamas son of Eussorus, the best man among the Thracians, who was both brave and very tall. Ajax’s spear struck the jutting peak of Acamas’s helmet. The bronze point drove through his forehead into the brain, and darkness covered his eyes.

Next Diomedes killed Axylus son of Teuthranus. Axylus was a rich man from the strong city of Arisbe, and everyone loved him, because his house stood beside the road and he welcomed every passerby. Yet not one of those guests stood in front of him to save his life. Diomedes killed both Axylus and his squire Calesius, who was driving the chariot at the time—and the pair went down beneath the earth.

Euryalus killed Dresus and Opheltius. Then he went after Aesepus and Pedasus, the sons the naiad nymph Abarbarea had borne to noble Bucolion. Bucolion was the eldest son of Laomedon, though he was a bastard. While he was tending his sheep he slept with the nymph, and she conceived twin sons. Now the son of Mecisteus killed them both and stripped the armor from their shoulders. Polypoetes killed Astyalus, Odysseus killed Pidytes of Percote, and Teucer killed Aretaon. Antilochus, Nestor’s son, brought Ablerus down with his spear, and Agamemnon, king of men, killed Elatus, who lived in Pedasus beside the river Satnioeis. Leitus killed Phylacus as he fled, and Eurypylus killed Melanthus.

Then Menelaus of the loud war cry took Adrestus alive. Adrestus’s horses had been running wildly over the plain in flight, and they ran into a tamarisk bush and snapped the pole away from the chariot. They went on toward the city along with the others in full flight, but Adrestus was thrown out and fell flat on his face in the dust beside the wheel of his chariot. Menelaus came up to him with his spear in his hand, and Adrestus clasped him by the knees and begged for his life. “Take me alive, son of Atreus,” he cried, “and you will get a full ransom for me. My father is rich, and he has laid up plenty of treasure in his house: gold, bronze, and wrought iron. From that store he will pay you a large ransom if he hears that I am alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”

So he pleaded, and Menelaus was ready to give in. He meant to hand Adrestus to a squire to take to the ships of the Achaeans. But Agamemnon came running up and scolded him. “My good Menelaus,” he said, “this is no time to show mercy. Has your house been treated so well by the Trojans? We will not spare a single one of them—not even the child still unborn in its mother’s womb. Not one of them may be left alive. Everyone in Ilium must die, ignored and forgotten.”

So he spoke, and his brother was persuaded, because the words were just. Menelaus pushed Adrestus away from him, and King Agamemnon struck him in the flank. Adrestus fell. Then the son of Atreus set his foot on his chest and pulled his spear out of the body.

Meanwhile Nestor called out to the Argives. “My friends, Danaan warriors, servants of Ares, do not let any man hang back to strip the dead so that he can bring a lot of plunder to the ships. Let us kill as many as we can. The bodies will lie on the plain, and you can strip them later, at your leisure.”

His words put heart and soul into every man. The Trojans would now have been routed and driven back into Ilium, if Priam’s son Helenus, the wisest of augurs, had not spoken to Hector and Aeneas. “Hector and Aeneas,” he said, “you two are the mainstays of the Trojans and Lycians, because you always lead the way, in fighting and in counsel alike. Hold your ground here and go among the army, rallying the men in front of the gates. If you do not, they will throw themselves into the arms of their wives, and our enemies will be delighted. Once you have put new heart into all our companies, we will stand firm here and fight the Danaans, however hard they press us, since there is nothing else to be done. Meanwhile, Hector, you go to the city and tell our mother what is happening. Tell her to call the matrons together at the temple of Athena in the acropolis. She should take her key and open the doors of the sacred building. There, on the knees of Athena, she should lay the largest and fairest robe in her house—the one she values most. She should also promise to sacrifice twelve yearling heifers, never yet touched by the goad, in the temple of the goddess, if Athena will pity the town, the wives and the little children of the Trojans, and keep the son of Tydeus from falling on the goodly city of Ilium. He fights in a fury and fills men’s souls with panic. I hold him the mightiest of them all. We did not fear even Achilles, their great champion and the son of a goddess, as we fear this man. His rage knows no bounds, and no one can match him in prowess.”

Hector did what his brother told him. He jumped down from his chariot and went everywhere among the army, brandishing his spears, urging the men to fight, and raising the dreadful battle cry. The Trojans rallied and turned to face the Achaeans again. The Achaeans gave ground and stopped their murderous attack, because they thought one of the immortals must have come down from starry heaven to help the Trojans, so remarkable was their recovery. Then Hector shouted to the Trojans, “Trojans and allies, be men, my friends, and fight with all your might, while I go to Ilium and tell the old men of our council, and our wives, to pray to the gods and vow great sacrifices to them in their honor.”
With that he left, and the black rim of hide around his shield knocked against his neck and his ankles.

Glaucus son of Hippolochus and the son of Tydeus now went out into the open ground between the armies to fight in single combat. When they were near each other, Diomedes of the loud war cry spoke first. “Who are you, my good sir,” he said, “who are you among men? I have never seen you in battle before now. Yet you are bolder than anyone else, if you dare to wait for my attack. Woe to the fathers whose sons face my might. But if you are one of the immortals and have come down from heaven, I will not fight you. Even valiant Lycurgus, son of Dryas, did not live long after he fought with the gods. He is the one who chased the nursing women who looked after frenzied Dionysus through the land of Nysa. They threw their thyrsi on the ground as murderous Lycurgus beat them with his oxgoad. Dionysus himself plunged terrified into the sea, and Thetis took him to her bosom to comfort him, because the fury of the man’s abuse had scared him. The gods who live at ease were angry with Lycurgus for it, and the son of Cronus struck him blind. He did not live much longer, since the immortals had come to hate him. So I will not fight with the blessed gods. But if you are one of those who eat the fruit of the ground, come near and meet your doom.”

The son of Hippolochus answered, “Son of Tydeus, why do you ask about my family line? Men come and go like the leaves on the trees from year to year. The wind scatters the autumn leaves on the ground, but when spring returns the forest bursts into bud with fresh vines. It is the same with the generations of mankind: the new spring up as the old pass away. But if you want to know my descent, many people know it well. There is a city in the heart of Argos, pasture land of horses, called Ephyra. Sisyphus lived there, the craftiest of all mankind. He was the son of Aeolus, and he had a son named Glaucus, who was the father of Bellerophon. Heaven gave Bellerophon the most surpassing good looks and beauty. But Proetus plotted his ruin. Proetus was the stronger, and he drove Bellerophon out of the land of the Argives, over which Zeus had made Proetus ruler. The reason was that Antea, the wife of Proetus, lusted after Bellerophon and wanted him to lie with her in secret. Bellerophon was an honorable man and refused, so she told lies about him to Proetus. ‘Proetus,’ she said, ‘kill Bellerophon or die yourself, for he wanted to lie with me against my will.’ The king was angry, but he shrank from killing Bellerophon. Instead he sent him to Lycia with lying letters of introduction, written on a folded tablet and full of ill against the man who carried it. He told Bellerophon to show these letters to his father-in-law, so that he would die that way. Bellerophon went to Lycia, and the gods escorted him safely.

“He reached the river Xanthus in Lycia, and the king welcomed him with every kindness. He feasted him for nine days and killed nine heifers in his honor. But when rosy-fingered morning appeared on the tenth day, the king questioned him and asked to see the letter from his son-in-law Proetus. Once he had the wicked letter, he first ordered Bellerophon to kill that savage monster, the Chimaera. She was not a human being but a goddess, with the head of a lion and the tail of a serpent, and a body like a goat’s, and she breathed out flames of fire. Bellerophon killed her, for signs from heaven guided him. Next he fought the far-famed Solymi, and that, he said, was the hardest of all his battles. Third, he killed the Amazons, women who were the equals of men. As he was coming back from them, the king devised yet another plan to destroy him. He chose the bravest warriors in all Lycia and set them in ambush, but not one of them ever came home, because Bellerophon killed every one. Then the king knew that Bellerophon must be the valiant offspring of a god. So he kept him in Lycia, gave him his daughter in marriage, and gave him an equal share of honor in the kingdom with himself. The Lycians also gave him a piece of land, the best in the whole country, lovely with vineyards and plowed fields, to have and to hold.

“The king’s daughter bore Bellerophon three children: Isander, Hippolochus, and Laodameia. Zeus, the lord of counsel, lay with Laodameia, and she bore him noble Sarpedon. But Bellerophon came to be hated by all the gods. He wandered in desolation and dismay over the Alean plain, gnawing at his own heart and avoiding the paths of men. Ares, who can never get enough of battle, killed his son Isander while Isander was fighting the Solymi. Artemis of the golden reins killed his daughter, because she was angry with her. Hippolochus was my father. When he sent me to Troy, he urged me again and again to fight always among the foremost and to surpass my peers, so that I would not shame the blood of my fathers, who were the noblest in Ephyra and in all Lycia. This is the descent I claim.”

So he spoke, and Diomedes was glad at heart. He planted his spear in the ground and answered with friendly words. “Then you are an old friend of my father’s house,” he said. “Great Oeneus once entertained Bellerophon for twenty days, and the two exchanged presents. Oeneus gave a belt rich with purple, and Bellerophon gave a double cup, which I left at home when I set out for Troy. I do not remember Tydeus, because he was taken from us while I was still a child, when the army of the Achaeans was cut to pieces before Thebes. From now on, though, I must be your host in middle Argos, and you must be mine in Lycia, if I should ever go there. Let us avoid one another’s spears even in the thick of a general engagement. There are many noble Trojans and allies I can kill, if I overtake them and heaven delivers them into my hand. In the same way, there are many Achaeans whose lives you can take, if you are able. So let the two of us exchange armor, so that everyone here may know of the old ties between us.”

After these words they jumped down from their chariots, clasped each other’s hands, and pledged their friendship. But the son of Cronus made Glaucus lose his wits, for he traded golden armor for bronze, armor worth a hundred head of cattle for armor worth nine.

Hector came to the Scaean gates and the oak tree. The wives and daughters of the Trojans ran up to him, asking about their sons, brothers, kinsmen, and husbands. He told them to start praying to the gods, and many of them were saddened by what they heard.

Soon he came to the splendid palace of King Priam, built with colonnades of hewn stone. Inside were fifty bedchambers—all of hewn stone—built close together, where the sons of Priam slept, each with his wedded wife. Across the courtyard from these were twelve upper rooms, also of hewn stone and built close together, for Priam’s daughters, where his sons-in-law slept with their wives. When Hector arrived, his fond mother came up to him with Laodice, the fairest of her daughters. She took his hand in hers and said, “My son, why have you left the battle and come here? Are the Achaeans, curse them, pressing you hard around the city, so that you have decided to come and lift up your hands to Zeus from the citadel? Wait until I can bring you wine, so that you can make an offering to Zeus and the other immortals, and then drink and be refreshed. Wine gives a man fresh strength when he is weary, as you are now from fighting on behalf of your kinsmen.”

Hector answered, “Do not bring me wine, honored mother. It would unman me, and I would forget my strength. I dare not pour a drink offering to Zeus with unwashed hands, and a man spattered with blood and filth may not pray to the son of Cronus. Gather the matrons and go with offerings to the temple of Athena driver of the spoil. There, on the knees of Athena, lay the largest and finest robe in your house, the one you value most. Promise her also twelve yearling heifers that have never felt the goad, to be sacrificed in her temple, if the goddess will take pity on the town, on the wives and little children of the Trojans, and keep the son of Tydeus away from the good city of Ilium. He fights with fury and fills men’s souls with panic. So go to the temple of Athena, while I look for Paris and urge him on, if he will listen to what I say. I wish the earth would open her jaws and swallow him! Zeus bred him to be a curse on the Trojans, and on Priam and Priam’s sons. If I could only see him go down into the house of Hades, my heart would forget its heaviness.”

His mother went into the house and called her waiting-women, and they gathered the matrons from all over the city. Then she went down to her fragrant storeroom, where her embroidered robes were kept. These were the work of Sidonian women, whom Paris had brought over from Sidon when he sailed the seas on the voyage during which he carried off Helen. Hecuba took out the largest robe, the one most beautifully rich with embroidery, to give to Athena. It glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. She set off with it, and many matrons went with her.

When they reached the temple of Athena, lovely Theano opened the doors. She was the daughter of Cisseus and the wife of Antenor, and the Trojans had made her priestess of Athena. The women raised their hands to the goddess with a loud cry. Theano took the robe and laid it on the knees of Athena, and as she did so she prayed to the daughter of great Zeus. “Holy Athena,” she cried, “protectress of our city, mighty goddess, break the spear of Diomedes and strike him down before the Scaean gates. Do this, and we will sacrifice twelve heifers that have never known the goad in your temple, if you will have pity on the town, on the wives and little children of the Trojans.” So she prayed, but Pallas Athena did not grant her prayer.

While they were praying to the daughter of great Zeus, Hector went to the fine house of Paris. The foremost builders in the land had built it for him: a house, storehouse, and courtyard near those of Priam and Hector on the acropolis. Hector went in, holding a spear eleven cubits long. Its bronze point gleamed ahead of him, fastened to the shaft by a ring of gold. He found Paris inside the house, busy with his armor, his shield and cuirass, and handling his curved bow. Argive Helen sat there too with her women, giving them their various tasks. When Hector saw Paris, he rebuked him with words of scorn. “Sir,” he said, “you do wrong to nurse this bitterness. The people are dying as they fight around this town of ours. You would blame anyone else you saw shirking his part in the fight. Up, then, or before long the city will be in flames.”

Paris answered, “Hector, your rebuke is fair, so listen, and believe me. I am not sitting here so much out of bitterness or ill will toward the Trojans as out of a wish to give way to my grief. My wife was just now gently urging me into battle, and I think it better that I go, for victory is always fickle. Wait while I put on my armor, or go ahead and I will follow. I am sure to catch up with you.”

Hector made no reply, but Helen tried to soothe him. “Brother,” she said, “I am a loathsome, sinful creature. I wish a whirlwind had caught me up on the day my mother gave birth to me and carried me off to some mountain, or into the waves of the roaring sea, to sweep me away before all this mischief came about. But since the gods have planned these evils, I wish at least that I had been wife to a better man, one who could feel the sting of dishonor and of men’s evil talk. This one has never been dependable, and never will be, and he will surely reap what he has sown. Still, brother, come in and rest on this seat. You are the one who bears the brunt of this toil, which was caused by my hateful self and by the sin of Paris. Zeus has doomed us both to be a theme of song among people yet to be born.”

Hector answered, “Do not ask me to sit, Helen, for all the goodwill you show me. I cannot stay. I am in a hurry to help the Trojans, who miss me greatly when I am not among them. But urge your husband on, and let him hurry of his own accord to catch up with me before I am out of the city. I must go home to see my household, my wife and my little son. I do not know whether I will ever return to them, or whether the gods will make me fall at the hands of the Achaeans.”

Hector left Helen and soon reached his own house, but Andromache was not in it. She was out on the wall with her child and one of her maids, weeping bitterly. Finding her gone, he stopped on the threshold of the women’s rooms and called out, “Women, tell me the truth. Where has Andromache gone? Is she with my sisters, or with my brothers’ wives? Or is she at the temple of Athena, where the other women are appeasing the awful goddess?”

His good housekeeper answered, “Hector, since you ask me to tell you the truth: she did not go to your sisters or to your brothers’ wives, and she is not at the temple of Athena, where the other women are appeasing the awful goddess. She is on the high wall of Ilium. She had heard that the Trojans were being hard pressed and that the Achaeans were in great force, so she went to the wall in frenzied haste. The nurse went with her, carrying the child.”

When the housekeeper had finished speaking, Hector hurried from the house and went back down the streets the way he had come. He crossed the city and reached the Scaean gates, by which he would go out onto the plain. There his wife came running toward him. She was Andromache, daughter of great Eetion, who had ruled in Thebe under the wooded slopes of Mt. Placus and was king of the Cilicians. His daughter had married Hector, and now she came to meet him with a nurse who carried his little child in her bosom—a mere babe, Hector’s darling son, lovely as a star. Hector had named him Scamandrius, but the people called him Astyanax, because his father stood alone as chief guardian of Ilium. Hector smiled as he looked at the boy, but he did not speak. Andromache stood beside him weeping and took his hand in hers. “Dear husband,” she said, “your courage will be the death of you. Think of your infant son, and of my unhappy self, who before long will be your widow—for the Achaeans will fall on you all together and kill you. If I lose you, it would be better for me to lie dead and buried, because when you are gone I will have nothing left to comfort me except sorrow. I have neither father nor mother now. Achilles killed my father when he sacked Thebe, the good city of the Cilicians. He killed him, but out of shame he did not strip his body. He burned him in his wondrous armor and raised a barrow over his ashes, and the mountain nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, planted a grove of elms around his tomb. I had seven brothers in my father’s house, and all of them went into the house of Hades on a single day. Achilles killed them as they were with their sheep and cattle. My mother, who had been queen of all the land under Mt. Placus, he brought here with the spoil. He set her free for a great sum, but then the archer-queen Artemis took her in the house of your father. No, Hector—you who are father, mother, brother, and dear husband to me—have mercy on me. Stay here on this wall. Do not make your child fatherless and your wife a widow. As for the army, place them near the fig tree, where the city is easiest to scale and the wall is weakest. Three times their bravest men have come there and attacked it, under the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, the sons of Atreus, and the brave son of Tydeus, either on their own initiative or because some soothsayer had told them to.”

Hector answered, “Wife, I have thought of all this too. But how could I face the Trojans, men or women, if I shirked the fighting like a coward? I cannot. I know nothing except how to fight bravely in the front ranks of the Trojan army and win glory for my father and myself. I know well that the day will surely come when mighty Ilium will be destroyed, with Priam and Priam’s people. Yet I do not grieve for any of them—not for Hecuba, or King Priam, or my many brave brothers who may fall in the dust before their enemies—as I grieve for you, on the day when one of the Achaeans robs you of your freedom forever and takes you away weeping. Perhaps you will have to work the loom in Argos at a mistress’s bidding, or carry water from the springs Messeis or Hypereia, brutally treated by some cruel taskmaster. Then someone who sees you weeping will say, ‘She was the wife of Hector, the bravest warrior among the Trojans in the war before Ilium.’ At that your tears will break out afresh for the man who would have kept that day of captivity from you. May I lie dead under the barrow heaped over my body before I hear your cry as they carry you into bondage.”

He stretched out his arms toward his child, but the boy cried and nestled against his nurse’s bosom. He was scared by the sight of his father’s armor and by the horsehair plume nodding fiercely from the helmet. His father and mother laughed at him. Hector took the helmet off his head and laid it gleaming on the ground. Then he took his darling child, kissed him, and dandled him in his arms, praying over him to Zeus and to all the gods. “Zeus,” he cried, “grant that this child of mine may be like me, chief among the Trojans. Let him be just as excellent in strength, and let him rule Ilium with his might. Then may someone say of him as he comes home from battle, ‘The son is far better than the father.’ May he bring back the blood-stained spoils of the man he has laid low, and let his mother’s heart be glad.”

With this he put the child back in the arms of his wife, who took him to her own soft bosom, smiling through her tears. Her husband watched her, and his heart went out to her. He caressed her fondly and said, “My own wife, do not take these things so bitterly to heart. No one can send me down to Hades before my time. But once a man has been born, whether he is brave or a coward, there is no escape for him when his hour has come. Now go inside the house and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants. War is the business of men, and mine above all others born in Ilium.”

He picked his plumed helmet up from the ground, and his wife went back to her house, weeping bitterly and often looking back at him. When she got home she found her maidens inside and told them all to join in her lament. So they mourned Hector in his own house although he was still alive. They believed they would never see him return safe from the battle and from the furious hands of the Achaeans.

Paris did not stay long in his house. He put on his fine armor overlaid with bronze and hurried through the city as fast as his feet could carry him. As a stabled, well-fed horse breaks loose and gallops proudly over the plain to the place where he is used to bathing in the fair-flowing river—he holds his head high, his mane streams over his shoulders, and he exults in his strength and flies like the wind to the haunts and feeding ground of the mares—in the same way Paris went out from high Pergamus, gleaming like sunlight in his armor, and he laughed aloud as he sped swiftly along. Soon he came upon his brother Hector, who was just turning away from the place where he had talked with his wife. Paris spoke first. “Sir,” he said, “I am afraid I have kept you waiting when you are in a hurry, and I did not come as quickly as you told me to.”

“My good brother,” Hector answered, “you fight bravely, and no one with any fairness can belittle what you do in battle. But you are careless and willfully slack. It grieves me to the heart to hear the bad things the Trojans say about you, for they have suffered much on your account. Let us go. We will put things right later, if Zeus grants that we set the cup of deliverance before the ever-living gods of heaven in our own homes, once we have chased the Achaeans from Troy.”

chapters.title: Book 7
paragraphs: Hector and Ajax fight—Hector is getting the worst of it when night falls and separates them—They exchange gifts—The dead are buried, and the Achaeans build a wall around their ships—The Achaeans buy their wine from Agamemnon and Menelaus.

With these words Hector went out through the gates, and his brother Paris went with him, both eager for the fight. Sailors who have long waited in vain for a breeze, and have worked at their oars until they are faint with exhaustion, are glad when heaven finally sends them one. That was how welcome the sight of these two heroes was to the Trojans.

Then Paris killed Menesthius, the son of Areithous. Menesthius lived in Arne; his father was Areithous the Mace-man, and his mother was Phylomedusa. Hector threw a spear at Eioneus and killed him with a wound in the neck, below the bronze rim of his helmet. Glaucus, son of Hippolochus and captain of the Lycians, fought hand to hand with Iphinous son of Dexius. He struck him on the shoulder as Iphinous was springing onto his chariot behind his swift mares. Iphinous fell from the car to the ground, and there was no life left in him.

Athena saw these men making havoc of the Argives, and she darted down from the summits of Olympus to Ilium. Apollo wanted the Trojans to win. He had been looking on from Pergamus, and he went out to meet her. The two met by the oak tree, and King Apollo son of Zeus spoke first. “What do you want,” he said, “daughter of great Zeus, that your proud spirit has sent you here from Olympus? Do you have no pity on the Trojans? Would you tip the scales of victory toward the Danaans? Let me persuade you—for it will be better this way—stop the fighting for today, and let them take it up again later, until they bring about the doom of Ilium. You goddesses have made up your minds to destroy the city.”

Athena answered, “So be it, Far-Darter. That was my own purpose when I came down from Olympus to the Trojans and Achaeans. Tell me, then, how do you plan to put an end to the fighting that is going on?”
Apollo, son of Zeus, replied, “Let us stir great Hector up to challenge one of the Danaans to single combat. That will shame the Achaeans into finding a man who will fight him.”

Athena agreed. Helenus son of Priam sensed what the gods had in mind, and he went up to Hector. “Hector son of Priam, peer of gods in counsel,” he said, “I am your brother, so let me persuade you. Tell the rest of the Trojans and Achaeans to sit down, all of them. Then challenge the best man among the Achaeans to meet you in single combat. I have heard the voice of the ever-living gods, and the hour of your doom has not yet come.”

Hector was glad to hear this. He went in among the Trojans and held his spear by the middle to push their ranks back, and they all sat down. Agamemnon also told the Achaeans to sit. Athena and Apollo took the shape of vultures and perched in the high oak tree of father Zeus, proud of their men. The ranks sat close together, bristling with shield and helmet and spear. When the rising west wind ruffles the sea, the waters grow dark beneath it. So the companies of Trojans and Achaeans sat on the plain. Then Hector spoke:—

“Hear me, Trojans and Achaeans, so that I may say what is in my mind. Zeus on his high throne has made our oaths and covenants come to nothing. He means harm for both of us, until you either take the towers of Troy or are defeated yourselves at your ships. The princes of the Achaeans are here among you. Let the man who is willing to fight me stand forward as your champion against Hector. This is what I say, and may Zeus be witness between us. If your champion kills me, let him strip off my armor and take it to your ships, but let him send my body home, so that the Trojans and their wives may give me the due of fire when I am dead. In the same way, if Apollo grants me glory and I kill your champion, I will strip off his armor and take it to the city of Ilium, and hang it in the temple of Apollo. But I will give up his body, so that the Achaeans may bury him at their ships and build him a mound by the wide waters of the Hellespont. Then in later days someone sailing his ship over the sea will say, ‘This is the monument of a man who died long ago, a champion who was slain by mighty Hector.’ So someone will say, and my fame will not be lost.”

So he spoke, but they all stayed silent, ashamed to decline the challenge and afraid to accept it. At last Menelaus rose, angry, and rebuked them. “Alas,” he cried, “you empty braggarts, women and not men! The stain on us will be dyed twice over if no man of the Danaans will face Hector now. May every one of you turn into earth and water as you sit there spiritless and without glory in your places. I will go out against this man myself. But how the fight ends is decided on high, in the hands of the immortal gods.”

With these words he put on his armor. And then, Menelaus, your life would have ended at the hands of Hector, who was by far the better man, if the princes of the Achaeans had not sprung up and stopped you. King Agamemnon caught him by the right hand and said, “Menelaus, you are mad. Enough of this folly. Be patient, however angry you are. Do not think of fighting a man so much stronger than yourself as Hector son of Priam, who is feared by many another as well as you. Even Achilles, a far more formidable fighter than you, shrank from meeting him in battle. Go and sit down among your own people, and the Achaeans will send some other champion against Hector. He may be fearless and fond of battle, but I think his knees will gladly bend under him if he comes out alive from the hurly-burly of this fight.”

With these words of sound advice he persuaded his brother, and his squires gladly took the armor off his shoulders. Then Nestor rose and spoke. “Truly,” he said, “the Achaean land has fallen on evil times. The old knight Peleus, counselor and orator among the Myrmidons, loved to question me, when I was in his house, about the race and lineage of all the Argives. How it would grieve him to hear that they are now cowering before Hector! Many times he would lift his hands in prayer that his soul might leave his body and go down to the house of Hades. By father Zeus, Athena and Apollo, I wish I were young and strong again, as I was when the Pylians and Arcadians gathered to fight by the rapid river Celadon, under the walls of Pheia, around the waters of the river Iardanus. The godlike hero Ereuthalion stood forward as their champion, with the armor of King Areithous on his shoulders. Men and women had surnamed Areithous ‘the Mace-man,’ because he fought with neither bow nor spear but broke the battalions of the enemy with his iron mace. Lycurgus killed him, not in fair fight but by trapping him in a narrow way where his mace was of no use to him. Lycurgus was too quick for him and speared him through the middle, and Areithous fell to earth on his back. Then Lycurgus stripped him of the armor that Ares had given him, and wore it in battle from then on. When he grew old and stayed at home, he gave it to his faithful squire Ereuthalion, who wore this same armor when he challenged the foremost men among us. The others quaked and cowered, but my high spirit told me to fight him, though no one else would venture. I was the youngest man of them all. Yet when I fought him, Athena granted me victory. He was the biggest and strongest man I ever killed, and as he lay sprawling on the earth he covered a great deal of ground. I wish I were still as young and strong as I was then, for the son of Priam would soon find someone to face him. But you, the foremost men of the whole host, not one of you has the stomach to fight Hector.”

So the old man rebuked them, and nine men at once started to their feet. First of all rose King Agamemnon, and after him brave Diomedes the son of Tydeus. Next came the two Ajaxes, men clothed in valor as with a garment, and then Idomeneus and Meriones, his brother in arms. After these rose Eurypylus son of Euaemon, Thoas the son of Andraemon, and Odysseus. Then Nestor knight of Gerene spoke again: “Cast lots among you to see who is chosen. If he comes alive out of this fight, he will have done good service to his own soul and to the Achaeans alike.”

So he spoke. Each man marked his lot and threw it into the helmet of Agamemnon son of Atreus. The people lifted their hands in prayer, and one of them would say, looking up into the vault of heaven, “Father Zeus, grant that the lot falls on Ajax, or on the son of Tydeus, or on the king of rich Mycene himself.”

While they were speaking, Nestor knight of Gerene shook the helmet, and out fell the very lot they wanted—the lot of Ajax. The herald carried it around and showed it to all the chieftains of the Achaeans, going from left to right, but none of them claimed it. At last he reached the man who had marked it and put it into the helmet. Brave Ajax held out his hand, and the herald gave him the lot. Ajax saw his mark and knew it, and he was glad. He threw it to the ground and said, “My friends, the lot is mine, and I am delighted, for I shall vanquish Hector. I will put on my armor. Meanwhile, pray to King Zeus in silence among yourselves, so that the Trojans do not hear you—or pray aloud if you like, for we fear no man. No one will overcome me by force or by cunning, for I was born and raised in Salamis, and I can hold my own in all things.”

With this they began praying to King Zeus the son of Cronus, and one of them would say, looking up into the vault of heaven, “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious in power, grant victory to Ajax and let him win great glory. But if you wish Hector well too and would protect him, give each of them equal fame and prowess.”

So they prayed, and Ajax armed himself in his suit of gleaming bronze. When he was fully armed he sprang forward like monstrous Ares going among men whom Zeus has set fighting one another. In the same way huge Ajax, bulwark of the Achaeans, sprang forward with a grim smile on his face, brandishing his long spear and striding on. The Argives were elated when they saw him. The Trojans trembled in every limb, and even Hector’s heart beat fast. But he could not now retreat and withdraw into the ranks behind him, because he had been the challenger. Ajax came up carrying his shield before him like a wall—a shield of bronze with seven folds of ox-hide, the work of Tychius, who lived in Hyle and was by far the best worker in leather. Tychius had made it from the hides of seven full-fed bulls, and over these he had set an eighth layer of bronze. Holding this shield in front of him, Ajax son of Telamon came close up to Hector and threatened him. “Hector,” he said, “you shall now learn, man to man, what kind of champions the Danaans have among them, even besides lion-hearted Achilles, cleaver of the ranks of men. He is staying at the ships now, angry with Agamemnon shepherd of his people. But there are many of us who are well able to face you. So begin the fight.”

Hector answered, “Noble Ajax, son of Telamon, captain of the host, do not treat me as if I were some puny boy or a woman who cannot fight. I have long been used to the blood and butchery of battle. I am quick to turn my leathern shield to the right or the left, and I count that the main thing in battle. I can charge in among chariots and horsemen, and in hand-to-hand fighting I can delight the heart of Ares. Still, I would not take a man like you off his guard—I will strike you openly, if I can.”

With those words Hector lifted his spear and hurled it. It hit the sevenfold shield on its outermost layer, the eighth, which was bronze. The spear tore through six layers of the shield, but it stuck in the seventh hide. Then Ajax threw. He struck the round shield of the son of Priam, and the terrible spear drove through the gleaming shield and on through the finely worked cuirass. It cut the shirt along Hector’s side, but he swerved, and that saved his life. Each man pulled his spear out of the shield, and they crashed together like savage lions, or like wild boars of great strength and endurance. The son of Priam hit the middle of Ajax’s shield, but the bronze did not break, and the point of his spear bent back. Then Ajax sprang forward and drove his spear through Hector’s shield. It went right through and checked Hector as he lunged to attack, and it gashed his neck, so that blood poured from the wound. Even so Hector kept on fighting. He gave ground and grabbed a huge, rugged stone that lay on the plain with his strong hand. With this he hit the boss in the middle of Ajax’s shield, and the bronze rang out. But Ajax snatched up a far larger stone, swung it high, and hurled it with enormous force. That stone, as big as a millstone, smashed Hector’s shield inward and threw him on his back, with the shield crushing him beneath it. Apollo lifted him up at once. They would then have hacked at each other with their swords in close combat, if the heralds, messengers of gods and men, had not come forward, one from the Trojans and one from the Achaeans. These were Talthybius and Idaeus, both honorable men. They parted the two men with their staves, and the good herald Idaeus said, “My sons, stop fighting. You are both brave men, and both are dear to Zeus. We all know that. But night is falling, and it is good to give way when night commands.”
Ajax son of Telamon answered, “Idaeus, tell Hector to say it himself, because he was the one who challenged our princes. Let him speak first, and I will accept what he says.”

Then Hector said, “Ajax, heaven has given you size, strength, and good judgment, and with the spear you are better than all the other Achaeans. Let us stop fighting for today. Later we will fight again until heaven decides between us and gives victory to one or the other. Night is falling, and it is good to give way when night commands. So go and gladden the hearts of the Achaeans at your ships, above all your own followers and clansmen. I will go to the great city of King Priam and bring comfort to the Trojans and their women, who are praying for me and competing with one another in their prayers. And let us also exchange gifts, so that Achaeans and Trojans will say, ‘They fought with all their might, but they made peace and parted as friends.’”

With that Hector gave Ajax a silver-studded sword together with its sheath and its leather baldric. In return Ajax gave him a girdle dyed purple. So they parted. One went to the host of the Achaeans and the other to the host of the Trojans. The Trojans were glad when they saw their hero come back to them safe and unharmed from the strong hands of mighty Ajax. They led him to the city like a man rescued beyond all hope. On the other side, the Achaeans brought Ajax, elated with victory, to Agamemnon.

When they reached the quarters of the son of Atreus, Agamemnon sacrificed a five-year-old bull for them to Zeus, the son of Cronus. They skinned the carcass, prepared it, and cut it into joints. Then they carefully chopped the joints into smaller pieces, put them on spits, roasted them well, and drew them off. When all this was done and the feast was ready, they ate. Every man had a full and equal share, so that all were satisfied. King Agamemnon gave Ajax slices cut lengthwise down the loin, as a mark of special honor. When they had eaten and drunk enough, old Nestor, whose counsel had always proved best, began to speak. He addressed them with complete sincerity and goodwill.

“Son of Atreus and you other chieftains, many of the Achaeans are dead. Ares has shed their blood by the banks of the Scamander, and their souls have gone down to the house of Hades. So when morning comes, it will be well for us to stop fighting. We will then haul our dead together with oxen and mules and burn them not far from the ships, so that when we sail home each man can take the bones of his comrades back to their children. Close by the funeral pyre we will build one barrow, raised from the plain for all the dead in common. Next to it let us build a high wall to shelter ourselves and our ships, and give it well-made gates, so that our chariots can pass through. Just outside it we will dig a deep trench all the way around, to keep off both horses and men on foot, so that the Trojan chieftains cannot press hard on us.”

So Nestor spoke, and the princes shouted their approval. Meanwhile the Trojans held a council on the acropolis, by the gates of King Priam’s palace. They were angry and full of discord, and wise Antenor spoke. “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians, and allies,” he said, “so that I can say what is in my mind. Let us give Argive Helen and her wealth back to the sons of Atreus. We are fighting now in breach of our solemn covenants, and we will not prosper until we do as I say.”

Antenor sat down, and Paris, the husband of lovely Helen, rose to speak. “Antenor,” he said, “I do not like your words. You could find a better thing to say than this, if you tried. But if you really mean it, then heaven has robbed you of your reason. I will speak plainly, and let the Trojans know that I will not give up the woman. The wealth that I brought home with her from Argos I will return, and I will add more of my own.”

When Paris had spoken and taken his seat, Priam of the race of Dardanus, the peer of gods in council, rose and addressed them with complete sincerity and goodwill. “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians, and allies, so that I can say what is in my mind. Eat your suppers now throughout the city as you have been doing, but set your watches and stay awake. At daybreak let Idaeus go to the ships and give Agamemnon and Menelaus, the sons of Atreus, the message from Paris, who caused this quarrel. Let him also press them to stop fighting until we have burned our dead. Later we will fight again, until heaven decides between us and gives victory to one or the other.”

So Priam spoke, and they did as he had said. They ate supper in their companies, and at daybreak Idaeus went to the ships. He found the Danaans, servants of Ares, in council by the stern of Agamemnon’s ship, and he took his place among them. “Son of Atreus,” he said, “and princes of the Achaean host, Priam and the other noble Trojans have sent me to tell you the message of Paris, who caused this quarrel, in case you find it acceptable. Paris will return all the treasure he took to Troy in his ships (I wish he had died before he did it) and will add more of his own. But he will not give up the wedded wife of Menelaus, though the Trojans want him to. Priam also told me to ask whether you will stop fighting until we burn our dead. Later we will fight again, until heaven decides between us and gives victory to one or the other.”
They all kept silent. At last Diomedes of the loud war cry spoke. “Let us accept nothing, neither the treasure nor Helen. Even a child can see that the Trojans’ doom is close.”

The sons of the Achaeans shouted approval of what Diomedes had said, and King Agamemnon then spoke to Idaeus. “Idaeus, you have heard the answer the Achaeans give you, and I give it with them. As for the dead, I allow you to burn them, since no one should begrudge dead men the rites of fire. Let Zeus, the mighty husband of Hera, be witness to this covenant.”

As he spoke, Agamemnon held up his scepter in sight of all the gods. Idaeus went back to the strong city of Ilium. The Trojans and Dardanians were gathered in council, waiting for him. He came and stood among them and gave his message. As soon as they heard it, they set about two tasks, some gathering the corpses and others bringing wood. The Argives likewise hurried from their ships to do the same, some gathering the corpses and others bringing wood.

The sun had just risen into the vault of heaven from the slow, still currents of deep Oceanus, and was beginning to beat on the fields, when the two armies met. They could hardly recognize their dead, but they washed the clotted gore from them, wept over them, and lifted them onto wagons. Priam had forbidden the Trojans to wail aloud. So they piled their dead on the pyre in sorrow and silence, and when the bodies had burned they went back to the city of Ilium. The Achaeans likewise piled their dead on the pyre in sorrow and silence, and when the bodies had burned they went back to their ships.

In the twilight, before it was yet dawn, chosen bands of the Achaeans gathered around the pyre. They built one barrow, raised for all the dead in common, and close to it they built a high wall to shelter themselves and their ships. They gave the wall strong gates so that their chariots could pass through, and just outside it they dug a deep, wide trench, and they planted stakes along the inside of it.

So the Achaeans toiled, and the gods sat beside Zeus, lord of lightning, and marveled at their great work. Then Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, spoke. “Father Zeus, what mortal anywhere in the world will ever again take the gods into his counsel? Do you not see that the Achaeans have built a wall around their ships and dug a trench all along it, and have not offered the gods great sacrifices? The fame of this wall will reach as far as the dawn, and men will think nothing of the wall that Phoebus Apollo and I built for Laomedon with so much labor.”

Zeus was displeased and answered, “What are you talking about, O shaker of the earth? A god less powerful than you might be alarmed at what they are doing, but your fame reaches as far as the dawn. Surely when the Achaeans have gone home with their ships, you can shatter their wall and fling it into the sea. You can cover the beach with sand again, and the great wall of the Achaeans will be wiped out completely.”

So they talked, and by sunset the Achaeans’ work was done. They slaughtered oxen at their tents and ate supper. Many ships had come with wine from Lemnos, sent by Eueneus, the son of Jason, whom Hypsipyle bore to him. The son of Jason had loaded them with ten thousand measures of wine, which he sent especially for the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus. The Achaeans bought their wine from this supply, some paying with bronze, some with iron, some with hides, some with whole heifers, and some with captives. They spread a fine banquet and feasted all night long, and so did the Trojans and their allies in the city. But all the while Zeus was planning evil for them, and he roared with fearful thunder. Pale fear seized them, and they spilled the wine from their cups onto the ground. No one dared drink until he had made an offering to the most mighty son of Cronus. Then they lay down and enjoyed the gift of sleep.

chapters.title: Book 8
paragraphs: Zeus forbids the gods to interfere any further—The fight is even until midday, but then Zeus tips the scales of victory toward the Trojans, who finally chase the Achaeans back inside their wall—Hera and Athena set out to help the Trojans, but Zeus sends Iris to turn them back, though later he promises Hera that she will have her way in the end—Nightfall stops Hector’s triumph—The Trojans camp out on the plain.

At dawn, when Morning in her robe of saffron began to spread light over the earth, Zeus called the gods to a council on the highest crest of many-ridged Olympus. He spoke, and all the other gods listened. “Hear me, gods and goddesses,” he said, “so that I can tell you what I have in mind. Not one of you, goddess or god, is to try to cross me. Every one of you must obey, so that I can finish this business quickly. If I catch any of you slipping away to help either the Trojans or the Danaans, he will be beaten savagely before he gets back to Olympus. Or I will pick him up and throw him down into dark Tartarus, far off in the deepest pit under the earth, where the gates are iron and the floor is bronze, as far below Hades as heaven is high above the earth. Then you will learn how much stronger I am than all of you. Test me and find out for yourselves. Let a golden chain down from heaven, and all of you, gods and goddesses together, take hold of it. Pull as hard as you like. You will never drag Zeus, the supreme counselor, down from heaven to earth. But if I chose to pull on it myself, I would haul you up along with the earth and the sea. Then I would tie the chain around some peak of Olympus and leave all of you hanging in midair. That is how far I stand above all others, gods and men alike.”

They were frightened, and all of them kept silent, because he had spoken with such command. At last Athena answered him. “Father, son of Cronus, king of kings, we all know that no one can resist your strength. But we are still sorry for the Danaan warriors, who are dying and meeting a miserable end. Since you order it, we will keep out of the fighting itself. We will, though, offer the Argives some useful advice, so that they do not all die because of your anger.”
Zeus smiled at her. “Courage, my child, Trito-born,” he said. “I am not truly in earnest, and I want to be kind to you.”

With that he harnessed his swift horses, which had bronze hoofs and manes of shining gold. He put on gold around his body, took up his golden whip, and climbed into his chariot. He lashed the horses, and they flew off willingly, halfway between the earth and the starry heaven. After a while he came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and to Gargarus, where he has his grove and his fragrant altar. There the father of gods and men halted his horses, unhooked them from the chariot, and hid them in a thick cloud. Then, in all his glory, he sat down on the highest crests and looked out over the city of Troy and the ships of the Achaeans.

At the ships the Achaeans hurried through their morning meal, and then put on their armor. The Trojans, for their part, armed themselves throughout the city. They were fewer in number, but they were eager and had no choice but to fight for their wives and children. Every gate was thrown wide open, and horse and foot poured out with the tramp of a vast multitude.

When the two armies met in one place, shield crashed against shield and spear against spear, as mail-clad men fought. The bossed shields pressed hard together, and the noise was enormous—the groans of the dying and the shouts of the killers mingled, and the earth ran red with blood.

All morning, while the day grew brighter, their weapons struck one another and men kept falling. But when the sun stood at the middle of the sky, the father of all raised his golden scales. In them he placed two fates of death, one for the Trojans and one for the Achaeans. He took the balance by its middle and lifted it. The day of the Achaeans sank. Their scale, heavy with death, settled on the ground, while the Trojans’ scale rose toward heaven. Then he thundered loudly from Ida and sent a blaze of lightning at the Achaeans. When they saw it, pale fear fell on them, and they were terrified.

Idomeneus did not dare to stay, nor did Agamemnon, and the two Ajaxes, servants of Ares, would not hold their ground either. Only Nestor, knight of Gerene and bulwark of the Achaeans, remained, and not by his own choice: one of his horses was crippled. Paris, the husband of lovely Helen, had shot it with an arrow on the very top of its head, where the mane starts to grow from the skull, a deadly spot. The horse leaped in agony as the arrow went into its brain, and its thrashing threw the other horses into confusion. The old man at once began cutting the traces with his sword. But Hector’s swift horses were bearing down on him through the rout, with their bold driver, Hector himself, behind them. The old man would have died right there if Diomedes had not seen it quickly. He shouted aloud and called Odysseus to help.

“Odysseus,” he cried, “noble son of Laertes, where are you running to, with your back turned like a coward? Take care that no spear strikes you between the shoulders. Stay here and help me keep this man’s furious charge away from Nestor.”

Odysseus did not listen. He ran on toward the ships of the Achaeans. The son of Tydeus threw himself alone into the thick of the fight and took his stand in front of the horses of the son of Neleus. “Sir,” he said, “these young warriors are pressing you hard. Your strength is gone, old age weighs on you, your squire is useless, and your horses are slow. Get into my chariot and see what the horses of Tros can do. See how skillfully they dart this way and that over the plain, whether fleeing or chasing. I took them from the hero Aeneas. Let our squires look after your horses, and let us drive mine straight at the Trojans, so that Hector learns how furiously I too can use my spear.”

Nestor, knight of Gerene, took his advice. The sturdy squires Sthenelus and kind-hearted Eurymedon looked after Nestor’s horses, while the two men climbed into Diomedes’ chariot. Nestor took the reins and lashed the horses on. Soon they were close to Hector, who was charging at them at full speed, and the son of Tydeus threw a spear at him. He missed Hector but hit his charioteer and squire, Eniopeus, son of noble Thebaeus, in the chest beside the nipple, while the reins were in his hands. Eniopeus fell headlong from the chariot and died on the spot, and the horses swerved. Hector was deeply grieved at the loss of his charioteer, yet for all his sorrow he left him lying there and went to look for another driver. His horses were not without one for long. He soon found brave Archeptolemus, son of Iphitus, and put him up behind the horses, handing the reins to him.

Then all would have been lost beyond help, and the Achaeans would have been penned up in Ilium like sheep, if the father of gods and men had not noticed in time. He hurled a blazing thunderbolt, which landed just in front of Diomedes’ horses with a flash of burning brimstone. The horses were terrified and tried to back under the chariot, and the reins fell from Nestor’s hands. Nestor was afraid, and he said to Diomedes, “Son of Tydeus, turn your horses and flee. Do you not see that the hand of Zeus is against you? Today he grants victory to Hector. Tomorrow, if he wishes, he will grant it to us. No man, however brave, can block the purpose of Zeus, because he is far stronger than anyone.”

Diomedes answered, “Everything you say is true. But one grief pierces me to the heart. Hector will talk among the Trojans and say, ‘The son of Tydeus fled from me to the ships.’ That is the boast he will make, and may the earth swallow me before then.”

“Son of Tydeus,” said Nestor, “what are you saying? Even if Hector calls you a coward, the Trojans and Dardanians will not believe him. Neither will the wives of the mighty warriors you have laid low.”

With these words he turned the horses back through the thick of the battle. With a cry that tore the air, the Trojans and Hector showered their missiles after them. Hector shouted to Diomedes, “Son of Tydeus, until now the Danaans have honored you with a place at table, with meals, and with cups filled with wine. From now on they will despise you, because you have become no better than a woman. Get out, you girl and coward! You will never climb our walls through any flinching on my part, and you will never carry off our wives in your ships. I will kill you with my own hand.”

The son of Tydeus could not decide whether to turn his horses around and fight Hector. Three times he wavered, and three times Zeus thundered from the heights of Ida, a sign to the Trojans that he would turn the battle in their favor. Then Hector shouted to his men, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians, you who love close fighting, be men, my friends, and fight with all your strength. I can see that Zeus intends to give victory and great glory to me, and destruction to the Danaans. What fools they are to have built this weak, worthless wall! It will not hold back my fury. My horses will leap easily over their trench. When I reach their ships, do not forget to bring me fire so that I can burn them, while I slaughter the Argives, who will be dazed and bewildered by the smoke.”

Then he called to his horses: “Xanthus and Podargus, and you, Aethon and goodly Lampus, repay me now for your keep. Andromache, daughter of great Eetion, has fed you honey-sweet grain, and she has mixed wine with water for you to drink whenever you wanted, even before she did so for me, her own husband. Hurry after them, so that we can take the shield of Nestor, whose fame reaches heaven because it is solid gold, arm-rods and all. And let us strip from the shoulders of Diomedes the cuirass that Hephaestus made for him. If we could take these two things, the Achaeans would sail away in their ships this very night.”

So he boasted. But Queen Hera shook with rage on her throne, and high Olympus trembled. She said to the mighty god Poseidon, “What is this, wide-ruling lord of the earthquake? Can you feel no pity in your heart for the dying Danaans? They bring you many welcome offerings at Helice and at Aegae. Wish them well, then. If all of us who side with the Danaans drove the Trojans back and kept Zeus from helping them, he would have to sit there sulking alone on Ida.”
King Poseidon was greatly troubled. “Hera, you reckless talker,” he answered, “what are you saying? The rest of us gods must not set ourselves against Zeus, because he is far stronger than we are.”

So they talked. Meanwhile the whole space enclosed by the ditch, from the ships to the wall, was packed with horses and warriors, penned in there by Hector son of Priam, now that the hand of Zeus was with him. He would even have set the ships on fire and burned them, if Queen Hera had not put it into Agamemnon’s mind to rouse himself and encourage the Achaeans. He went along the ships and tents with a great purple cloak in his hands and took his stand beside the huge black hull of Odysseus’s ship, which lay in the middle of the line. From that spot his voice would carry farthest, both toward the tents of Ajax son of Telamon on one side and those of Achilles on the other. Those two heroes, sure of their own strength, had boldly drawn up their ships at the two ends of the line. From this spot, then, in a voice that could be heard far off, he shouted to the Danaans. “Argives, shame on you, you cowards, brave in appearance only! Where have our boasts gone, that we would win? We made those boasts so proudly in Lemnos, when we ate the flesh of horned cattle and filled our mixing bowls to the brim. You swore that each of you would stand against a hundred or two hundred men. Now you prove no match even for one—for Hector, who will soon be setting our ships ablaze. Father Zeus, did you ever ruin a great king like this and rob him so completely of his greatness? Yet on my way here, to my sorrow, I never let my ship pass one of your altars without burning the fat and thigh-bones of heifers on it, so eager was I to sack the city of Troy. Grant me this prayer, then. Let us at least escape with our lives, and do not let the Trojans crush the Achaeans so utterly.”

So he prayed, and father Zeus pitied his tears and granted that his people should live and not die. At once he sent an eagle, the most reliable omen of all birds, with a young fawn in its talons. The eagle dropped the fawn beside the altar where the Achaeans sacrificed to Zeus, lord of omens. When the people saw that the bird had come from Zeus, they sprang at the Trojans more fiercely and fought more boldly.

Of all the many Danaans, no man could claim that he drove his horses over the trench and went out to fight before the son of Tydeus. He killed an armed Trojan warrior, Agelaus son of Phradmon, long before anyone else could. Agelaus had turned his horses to flee, but the spear struck him in the back between the shoulders and went right through his chest. He fell forward out of his chariot, and his armor clattered around him.

After Diomedes came Agamemnon and Menelaus, sons of Atreus, then the two Ajaxes, clothed in valor as in a garment. Then came Idomeneus and his companion in arms Meriones, a match for murderous Ares, and Eurypylus, the brave son of Euaemon. Ninth came Teucer with his bow, who took his place under the cover of the shield of Ajax son of Telamon. When Ajax raised his shield, Teucer would look out around it. Whenever he hit someone in the crowd, the man fell dead. Then Teucer would dart back to Ajax like a child to its mother, and duck down again under his shield.

Which of the Trojans did brave Teucer kill first? Orsilochus, and then Ormenus, Ophelestes, Daetor, Chromius, godlike Lycophontes, Amopaon son of Polyaemon, and Melanippus. One after another he laid them all low on the earth. King Agamemnon was glad to see him wreaking havoc among the Trojans with his mighty bow. He went up to him and said, “Teucer, man after my own heart, son of Telamon, captain among the host, keep shooting. Be the saving of the Danaans and the glory of your father Telamon, who raised you and cared for you in his own house when you were a child, though you were a bastard. Win him glory even though he is far away. I make you a promise, and I will keep it. If aegis-bearing Zeus and Athena let me sack the city of Ilium, you will have the next best prize of honor after my own—a tripod, or two horses with their chariot, or a woman who will go up into your bed.”

Teucer answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, you do not need to urge me on. Ever since we began to drive them back toward Ilium, I have kept watch, as well as I can, for men I might shoot and kill. I have loosed eight barbed arrows, and every one of them is buried in the flesh of a warlike young man. But this mad dog I cannot hit.”

He spoke, and aimed another arrow straight at Hector, determined to hit him. Again he missed his man. The arrow struck Priam’s brave son Gorgythion in the breast instead. Gorgythion’s mother was fair Castianeira, lovely as a goddess, who had been brought in marriage from Aesyme. Now he bowed his head, as a garden poppy in full bloom bows when spring showers weigh it down. In just that way his head sank under the weight of his helmet.

Teucer aimed at Hector once more, longing to hit him, and once more the arrow missed, because Apollo turned it aside. It struck Hector’s brave charioteer Archeptolemus in the breast, beside the nipple, as he was driving furiously into the fight. He fell headlong from the chariot, the horses swerved away, and no life was left in him. Hector was deeply grieved to lose his charioteer. Even so, he left him lying where he fell, and told his brother Cebriones, who was close by, to take the reins. Cebriones did as he was told. Then Hector sprang from his chariot to the ground with a loud cry. He seized a great stone and went straight for Teucer, meaning to kill him. Teucer had just taken an arrow from his quiver and laid it on the bowstring. But as he took aim and drew the string back to his shoulder, Hector hit him with the jagged stone. It struck him right where the collar-bone divides the neck from the chest, a very deadly spot. It broke the sinew of his arm, so that his wrist went weak, and the bow dropped from his hand as he fell forward on his knees. Ajax saw that his brother had fallen. He ran to him, stood over him, and covered him with his shield. Meanwhile his two trusty squires, Mecisteus son of Echius and Alastor, came up and carried him groaning in great pain to the ships.

Zeus now put fresh courage into the Trojans, and they drove the Achaeans back to their deep trench, with Hector at their head in all his glory. A hound chases a wild boar or a lion, grips it by the flank or buttock, and watches warily for it to wheel around. In the same way Hector stayed close behind the Achaeans, always killing the hindmost as they rushed on in panic. They fled through the set stakes and the trench, and many Achaeans were laid low by the Trojans. At last they halted at their ships. They called to one another, and every man lifted his hands to the gods and prayed hard. Hector, meanwhile, wheeled his horses this way and that, his eyes glaring like those of Gorgo or murderous Ares.

When Hera saw the Achaeans, she pitied them, and she said at once to Athena, “Alas, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, are you and I to give no more thought to the dying Danaans, even if it is the last time we ever do? Look how they are perishing and meeting a bad end before the attack of one single man. Hector the son of Priam is raging with unbearable fury, and he has already done great harm.”

Athena answered, “I wish this fellow would die in his own land, killed by the Achaeans. But my father Zeus is mad with spite. He is always thwarting me, always headstrong and unjust. He forgets how often I saved his son when the labors Eurystheus set him had worn him out. That son would weep until his cry came up to heaven, and then Zeus would send me down to help him. If I had had the sense to see all this coming, he would never have come back alive from the deep waters of the river Styx, when Eurystheus sent him to the house of Hades to fetch the hell-hound from Erebus. And now Zeus hates me, while he lets Thetis have her way, because she kissed his knees and took hold of his beard when she begged him to do honor to Achilles. Next time he starts calling me his gray-eyed darling, I shall know what to do. Get our horses ready, while I go into the house of aegis-bearing Zeus and put on my armor. Then we shall find out whether Priam’s son Hector will be glad to meet us on the highways of battle. Or perhaps the Trojans will glut the hounds and vultures with the fat of their flesh, when they lie dead by the ships of the Achaeans.”

So she spoke, and white-armed Hera, daughter of great Cronus, obeyed her. She set about harnessing her horses with their gold trappings. Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, let her richly woven robe, which she had made with her own hands, fall to the threshold of her father’s house. She put on the shirt of Zeus and armed herself for battle. Then she stepped into her flaming chariot and took up her spear, so stout and sturdy and strong, which she uses to quell the ranks of heroes who have displeased her. Hera lashed the horses. The gates of heaven bellowed and flew open of their own accord. The Hours guard these gates, and heaven and Olympus are in their hands, to open the dense cloud that hides them or to close it. Through these gates the goddesses drove their obedient horses.

But father Zeus saw them from Ida and was very angry. He sent winged Iris to them with a message. “Go, swift Iris,” he said. “Turn them back, and see that they do not come near me, for if we come to fighting there will be trouble. This is what I say, and this is what I mean to do. I will lame their horses. I will hurl them from their chariot and break it in pieces. It will take them ten whole years to heal the wounds my lightning will give them. Then my gray-eyed daughter will learn what it means to quarrel with her father. I am less surprised and angry with Hera, since she always contradicts whatever I say.”

At this Iris set off, swift as the wind, from the heights of Ida to the lofty summits of Olympus. She met the goddesses at the outer gates of its many valleys and gave them her message. “What are you doing?” she said. “Are you mad? The son of Cronus forbids you to go. This is what he says, and this is what he means to do. He will lame your horses. He will hurl you from your chariot and break it in pieces. It will take you ten whole years to heal the wounds his lightning will give you, so that you may learn, gray-eyed goddess, what it means to quarrel with your father. He is less hurt and angry with Hera, because she always contradicts whatever he says. But you, bold hussy, will you really dare to raise your huge spear against Zeus?”

With this Iris left them, and Hera said to Athena, “Truly, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, I am not willing to fight men’s battles any longer against the will of Zeus. Let them live or die as luck decides, and let Zeus pass his judgments on the Trojans and Danaans as he pleases.”

She turned her horses around. The Hours unyoked them, tied them to their ambrosial mangers, and leaned the chariot against the end wall of the courtyard. The two goddesses sat down on their golden thrones among the other gods, but they were very angry.

Before long father Zeus drove his chariot to Olympus and entered the assembly of the gods. The mighty lord of the earthquake unyoked his horses for him, set the car on its stand, and threw a cloth over it. Zeus sat down on his golden throne, and Olympus shook beneath him. Athena and Hera sat apart from Zeus. They did not speak, and they asked him no questions. Zeus knew what they meant, though, and said, “Athena and Hera, why are you so angry? Are you tired from killing so many of your dear friends the Trojans? However that may be, my hands are so mighty that all the gods on Olympus together cannot turn me. You were both trembling all over before you ever saw the fight and its terrible doings. I tell you therefore—and it would surely have happened—I would have struck you with lightning, and your chariots would never have brought you back to Olympus.”

Athena and Hera sat side by side, groaning in spirit and brooding over trouble for the Trojans. Athena sat silent and said not a word, for she was in a furious passion and bitterly angry with her father. Hera could not hold herself in, and she said, “Dread son of Cronus, what are you talking about? We know how great your power is. Even so, we pity the Danaan warriors, who are perishing and meeting a bad end. Since you tell us to, we will keep out of the actual fighting. But we will give the Argives some useful advice, so that they do not all perish under your displeasure.”

Zeus answered, “Tomorrow morning, Hera, if you wish, you will see the son of Cronus destroying great numbers of the Argives. Fierce Hector will not stop fighting until he has roused the son of Peleus, on the day they fight in dire straits at the sterns of the ships, over the body of Patroclus. Whether you like it or not, this is how it is decreed. As for you, I do not care if you go to the lowest depths beneath earth and sea, where Iapetus and Cronus live in lonely Tartarus, with no ray of light and no breath of wind to cheer them. You may go on and on until you get there, and I will not care one bit about your displeasure. You are the greatest vixen alive.”

Hera made him no answer. The sun’s glorious orb sank into Oceanus and drew night down over the land. The Trojans were sorry when the light failed them. The Achaeans, though, welcomed the darkness when it fell, and had prayed for it three times over.

Then Hector led the Trojans back from the ships and held a council in the open space by the river, at a spot clear of corpses. They left their chariots and sat down on the ground to hear what he had to say. In his hand he held a spear eleven cubits long. Its bronze point gleamed at the front, and the ring around the spear-head was gold. Spear in hand, he spoke. “Hear me,” he said, “Trojans, Dardanians, and allies. A moment ago I thought I would destroy the ships and all the Achaeans with them before I went back to Ilium. But darkness came on too soon. That alone saved them and their ships on the sea-shore. So now let us obey the orders of night and prepare our suppers. Take your horses out of their chariots and give them their feed of corn. Then hurry to bring sheep and cattle from the city. Bring wine as well, and corn for your horses, and gather plenty of wood. From dark until dawn we shall burn watchfires, with flames that reach to heaven. The Achaeans may try to flee across the sea by night, and they must not get on board unharmed and unhindered. Many a man among them must take a wound home with him to nurse, hit by spear or arrow as he leaps onto his ship. Then others will be afraid to bring war and weeping on the Trojans. Also, let the heralds tell it around the city that the growing boys and the gray-bearded men are to camp on its heaven-built walls. Let each of the women light a great fire in her house. Let a safe watch be kept, so that the town is not entered by surprise while the army is outside. See to it, brave Trojans, as I have said. Let that be enough for now. At daybreak I will give you further instructions. I pray in hope to Zeus and the other gods that we may then drive these fate-driven hounds out of our land, for it is the fates that have carried them and their ships here. So tonight let us keep watch. With early morning, though, let us put on our armor and rouse fierce war at the ships of the Achaeans. Then I shall know whether brave Diomedes the son of Tydeus will drive me back from the ships to the wall, or whether I shall kill him myself and carry off his blood-stained spoils. Tomorrow let him show his mettle, and let him stand against my spear if he dares. I think that at break of day he will be among the first to fall, and many of his comrades around him. I wish I were as sure of being immortal and never growing old, and of being worshipped like Athena and Apollo, as I am sure that this day will bring evil to the Argives.”

So Hector spoke, and the Trojans shouted their approval. They took their sweating horses out from under the yoke and tied each one beside his own chariot. They hurried to bring sheep and cattle from the city. They brought wine and corn from their houses as well, and gathered plenty of wood. Then they made a great sacrifice of unblemished victims to the immortals, and the wind carried the sweet smell of the sacrifice up to heaven. But the blessed gods took no part in it, for they bitterly hated Ilium, with Priam and Priam’s people. So the Trojans sat all through the night by the highways of war, high in hope, and they kindled many a watchfire. Think of a night when the stars shine clear and the moon is bright. There is not a breath of air. Every peak and glade and jutting headland stands out in the matchless radiance that breaks from the calm of heaven. All the stars can be counted, and the shepherd’s heart is glad. Just so shone the watchfires of the Trojans before Ilium, midway between the ships and the river Xanthus.
