A thousand camp-fires gleamed on the plain, and in the glow of each sat fifty men. The horses stood beside their chariots, champing oats and corn, and waited for dawn to come.

chapters.title: Book 9
paragraphs: The Embassy to Achilles.

The Trojans kept watch. But Panic, the comrade of blood-stained Rout, had taken a firm hold on the Achaeans, and all their princes were in despair. As when the two winds that blow from Thrace, the north wind and the northwest wind, spring up suddenly and stir the sea to fury, and at once the dark waves lift their heads and scatter seaweed in every direction, so were the hearts of the Achaeans troubled.

In dismay, the son of Atreus told the heralds to call the people to a council one by one, but not to shout the news aloud. He hurried to call them himself as well, and they sat in the assembly, sick at heart. Agamemnon wept like a running stream or a waterfall down the side of a sheer cliff. With many heavy sighs he spoke to the Achaeans. “My friends,” he said, “princes and councilors of the Argives, heaven has laid a heavy hand on me. Cruel Zeus solemnly promised me that I would sack the city of Troy before I went home. He has cheated me. Now he orders me to go back to Argos with no glory, after losing so many of my people. This is the will of Zeus, who has brought down many proud cities and will bring down others, for his power is above all. So now let us all do as I say. Let us sail back to our own country, for we will not take Troy.”

So he spoke, and the sons of the Achaeans sat sorrowful for a long while, and all of them kept silent. At last Diomedes of the loud battle cry answered. “Son of Atreus, I will rebuke your folly, as is my right in council. Do not be angry that I do. First, you attacked me in front of all the Danaans and called me a coward and no soldier. The Argives, young and old, know that you did. But the son of scheming Cronus gave you only half his gifts. He gave you honor as our chief ruler, but he did not give you valor, which is the highest of both right and might. Sir, do you really think the sons of the Achaeans are as unwarlike and cowardly as you say they are? If your own mind is set on going home, then go. The way is open to you. The many ships that followed you from Mycene stand lined up on the seashore. But the rest of us will stay here until we have sacked Troy. And even if these men too turn homeward with their ships, Sthenelus and I will go on fighting until we reach the goal of Ilium, for heaven was with us when we came.”

The sons of the Achaeans shouted their approval of what Diomedes had said, and soon Nestor rose to speak. “Son of Tydeus,” he said, “your prowess in war is beyond question, and in council you excel all men of your own age. None of the Achaeans can brush aside what you say or argue against it. But you have not yet reached the end of the matter. You are young. You could be the youngest of my own children. Still, you have spoken wisely, and you have advised the chief of the Achaeans with good judgment. Even so, I am older than you, and I will tell you everything. So let no man, not even King Agamemnon, ignore what I say, for whoever stirs up civil strife is a clanless, hearthless outlaw.

“Now, though, let us obey the commands of night and get our suppers. Let the sentinels, every one of them, camp by the trench outside the wall. These are my instructions to the young men. When they have been seen to, son of Atreus, you give your orders, for you are the most royal of us all. Prepare a feast for your councilors. It is right and reasonable that you should. There is plenty of wine in your tents, which the ships of the Achaeans bring from Thrace every day. You have everything you need to entertain guests, and you have many subjects. When many are gathered, you can follow the man whose counsel is wisest. And we badly need shrewd and prudent counsel, for the enemy has lit his watchfires close to our ships. Who can help being dismayed? This night will either ruin our army or save it.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said. The sentinels went out in their armor under Nestor’s son Thrasymedes, a captain of the host, and the bold warriors Ascalaphus and Ialmenus. With them were Meriones, Aphareus and Deipyrus, and the son of Creion, noble Lycomedes. There were seven captains of the sentinels, and a hundred youths armed with long spears went with each of them. They took their places midway between the trench and the wall. Then they lit their fires, and every man got his supper.

The son of Atreus then invited many councilors of the Achaeans to his quarters and prepared a great feast in their honor. They helped themselves to the good things set before them. When they had had enough to eat and drink, old Nestor, whose counsel was always truest, was the first to lay his thoughts before them. He addressed them sincerely and with goodwill, in these words.

“Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, with you I will both begin my speech and end it, for you are king over many people. Zeus has also granted you the scepter and the duty to uphold justice, so that you may look after the people under you. That is why you, above all others, must both speak and listen, and act on the advice of anyone else who chooses to speak wisely. Everything depends on you and your commands, so I will say what I think is best. No man will have a truer mind than mine has been since the hour when you, sir, angered Achilles by taking the girl Briseis from his tent, against my judgment. I urged you not to do it. But you gave in to your own pride and dishonored a hero whom heaven itself had honored, for you still hold the prize that was awarded to him. Now let us think how we can appease him, with presents and with fair words that will win him over.”

And King Agamemnon answered, “Sir, you have rightly rebuked my folly. I was wrong. I admit it. A man whom heaven befriends is an army in himself, and Zeus has shown that he befriends this man by destroying so many of the Achaeans. I was blinded by passion and gave in to my worse mind. So I will make amends and give him great gifts as atonement. I will name them in front of you all. I will give him seven tripods that have never yet been on the fire, and ten talents of gold. I will give him twenty iron cauldrons and twelve strong horses that have won races and carried off prizes. A man is rich indeed in land and gold if he has as many prizes as my horses have won me. I will give him seven excellent workwomen, Lesbians, whom I chose for myself when he took Lesbos, all of surpassing beauty. I will give him these, and with them the one I took from him earlier, the daughter of Briseus. And I swear a great oath that I never went up into her bed, and never lay with her as men and women do.

“All this I will give him now. And if later the gods grant that I sack the city of Priam, let him come when we Achaeans are dividing the spoil and load his ship with as much gold and bronze as he likes. Let him also take twenty Trojan women, the loveliest after Helen herself. Then, when we reach Achaean Argos, wealthiest of all lands, he will be my son-in-law. I will show him the same honor as my own dear son Orestes, who is being raised in all abundance. I have three daughters, Chrysothemis, Laodice, and Iphianassa. Let him take whichever he chooses to the house of Peleus, freely and without wedding gifts. I will add a dowry besides, such as no man ever gave his daughter. I will give him seven well-established cities: Cardamyle, Enope, and Hire, where there is grass; holy Pherae and the rich meadows of Anthea; Aepea too, and the vine-clad slopes of Pedasus. All of them are near the sea, on the borders of sandy Pylos. The men who live there are rich in cattle and sheep. They will honor him with gifts as though he were a god, and obey his mild decrees. All this I will do if he gives up his anger now. Let him yield. Only Hades is utterly ruthless and unyielding, and that is why he is the god most hated by mankind. Besides, I am older and more royal than he is. So let him obey me now.”

Then Nestor answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men: the gifts you offer are not small ones. Let us send chosen messengers to the tent of Achilles son of Peleus without delay. Let those go whom I name. Let Phoenix, dear to Zeus, lead the way. Let Ajax and Odysseus follow, and let the heralds Odius and Eurybates go with them. Now bring water for our hands, and tell everyone to keep silent while we pray to Zeus the son of Cronus, in case he will have mercy on us.”

So he spoke, and his words pleased them well. Servants poured water over the guests’ hands, and pages filled the mixing bowls with wine and water and handed it around, giving every man his drink offering. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as each wanted, the envoys set out from the tent of Agamemnon son of Atreus. Nestor looked first at one and then at another, but most especially at Odysseus, and urged them hard to win over the noble son of Peleus.

They went along the shore of the sounding sea and prayed earnestly to earth-encircling Poseidon that the proud spirit of the son of Aeacus would be favorable to them. They reached the ships and tents of the Myrmidons and found Achilles playing a lyre, a beautiful one of skilled workmanship, with a silver cross-bar. It was part of the spoils he had taken when he sacked the city of Eetion. He was entertaining himself with it and singing the deeds of heroes. He was alone with Patroclus, who sat opposite him in silence, waiting for him to stop singing. Odysseus and Ajax now came in, with Odysseus leading the way, and stood before him. Achilles sprang from his seat with the lyre still in his hand, and Patroclus rose too when he saw the strangers. Achilles greeted them. “Welcome, all hail. You must have come on some great matter, you who are still dearest to me of the Achaeans, for all my anger.”

With this he led them forward and had them sit on seats covered with purple rugs. Then he spoke to Patroclus, who was close by him. “Son of Menoetius, set a larger bowl on the table, mix less water with the wine, and give every man his cup. These are very dear friends, and they are under my roof now.”

Patroclus did as his comrade told him. He set the chopping block in front of the fire and laid on it the loin of a sheep, the loin of a goat, and the chine of a fat hog. Automedon held the meat while Achilles chopped it. Then Achilles sliced the pieces and put them on spits, while the son of Menoetius made the fire burn high. When the flame had died down, Patroclus spread out the embers, laid the spits over them, lifted them and set them on the spit racks, and sprinkled them with salt. When the meat was roasted, he put it on platters and passed bread around the table in fair baskets, while Achilles dealt out the portions. Then Achilles took his seat facing Odysseus, against the opposite wall, and told his comrade Patroclus to offer sacrifice to the gods. Patroclus cast the offerings into the fire, and they helped themselves to the good things set before them. When they had had enough to eat and drink, Ajax made a sign to Phoenix. Odysseus saw it, filled his cup with wine, and drank to Achilles.

“Hail, Achilles,” he said. “We have had no lack of good cheer, either in the tent of Agamemnon or here. There has been plenty to eat and drink, but our thoughts are not on such things. Sir, we face great disaster, and without your help we do not know whether we will save our fleet or lose it. The Trojans and their allies have camped close to our ships and the wall. They have lit watchfires throughout their host and think nothing can now stop them from falling on our fleet. Zeus has also sent lightning on their right. Hector, in all his glory, rages like a maniac. Confident that Zeus is with him, he fears neither god nor man. He has gone raving mad and prays for the day to come. He vows to hew the high sterns of our ships to pieces, set fire to their hulls, and slaughter the Achaeans while they are dazed and choked with smoke. I fear greatly that heaven will make his boasting good, and that it will be our lot to die at Troy, far from our home in Argos. Up, then, and late though it is, save the sons of the Achaeans, who are failing before the fury of the Trojans. You will bitterly regret it later if you do not, for once the harm is done there will be no curing it. Think before it is too late, and save the Danaans from destruction.

“My good friend, when your father Peleus sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, did he not give you this charge? ‘My son, Athena and Hera will make you strong if they choose, but keep your high temper in check, for goodwill is the better course. Avoid pointless quarrels, and the Achaeans, old and young, will respect you more for it.’ Those were his words, but you have forgotten them. Even now, though, calm down and put your anger aside. Agamemnon will make you great amends if you forgive him. Listen, and I will tell you what he said in his tent that he will give you. He will give you seven tripods that have never yet been on the fire, and ten talents of gold; twenty iron cauldrons, and twelve strong horses that have won races and carried off prizes. A man is rich indeed in land and gold if he has as many prizes as these horses have won for Agamemnon. He will also give you seven excellent workwomen, Lesbians, whom he chose for himself when you took Lesbos, all of surpassing beauty. He will give you these, and with them the one he took from you earlier, the daughter of Briseus, and he will swear a great oath that he never went up into her bed and never lay with her as men and women do. He will give you all this right now. And if later the gods grant that he sack the city of Priam, you can come when we Achaeans are dividing the spoil and load your ship with as much gold and bronze as you like. You can take twenty Trojan women, the loveliest after Helen herself. Then, when we reach Achaean Argos, wealthiest of all lands, you will be his son-in-law, and he will show you the same honor as his own dear son Orestes, who is being raised in all abundance. Agamemnon has three daughters, Chrysothemis, Laodice, and Iphianassa. You may take whichever you choose to the house of Peleus, freely and without wedding gifts. He will add a dowry besides, such as no man ever gave his daughter, and will give you seven well-established cities: Cardamyle, Enope, and Hire, where there is grass; holy Pherae and the rich meadows of Anthea; Aepea too, and the vine-clad slopes of Pedasus. All of them are near the sea, on the borders of sandy Pylos. The men who live there are rich in cattle and sheep. They will honor you with gifts as though you were a god, and obey your mild decrees. All this he will do if you give up your anger now. And even if you hate both him and his gifts with all your heart, still pity the rest of the Achaeans, who are being worn down throughout their host. They will honor you as a god, and you will win great glory from them. You might even kill Hector. He will come within your reach, for he is infatuated, and he declares that not one Danaan the ships have brought can stand against him.”

Achilles answered, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, I must tell you plainly, and with a fixed purpose, that I want no more of this cajoling, from whatever quarter it comes. I hate like the gates of hell the man who says one thing while hiding another in his heart. So I will say what I mean. Neither Agamemnon son of Atreus nor any other of the Danaans will appease me, for I see that I get no thanks for all my fighting. The man who fights fares no better than the man who does not. Coward and hero are held in equal honor, and death deals the same measure to the man who works and the man who is idle. I have gained nothing from all my hardships, with my life always in my hand. A bird, when she has found a morsel, takes it to her nestlings and goes hungry herself. In the same way I have lain awake many a long night, and fought many a bloody battle by day against men who were fighting for their women. With my ships I have taken twelve cities, and eleven more around Troy I have stormed with my men by land. From every one of them I took great store of wealth, and I gave all of it up to Agamemnon son of Atreus. He stayed where he was by his ships, and of what came to him he gave out little and kept much himself.

“Still, he did hand out some prizes of honor among the chieftains and kings, and they have them yet. From me alone of the Achaeans he took the woman I delighted in. Let him keep her and sleep with her. Why, tell me, must the Argives fight the Trojans? What made the son of Atreus gather the host and bring them? Was it not for the sake of Helen? Are the sons of Atreus the only men in the world who love their wives? Any man of common decent feeling loves and cherishes his own woman, as I loved this one with my whole heart, though she was only the fruit of my spear. Agamemnon has taken her from me. He has cheated me. I know him. Let him tempt me no further, for he will not move me. Let him look to you, Odysseus, and the other princes, to save his ships from burning. He has done much without me already. He has built a wall. He has dug a trench, deep and wide, all around it, and planted stakes inside it. But even so he cannot stop the murderous might of Hector. As long as I fought among the Achaeans, Hector did not let the battle range far from the city walls. He would come as far as the Scaean gates and the oak tree, and no further. Once he stood to meet me, and he barely escaped my onslaught. Now, since I am in no mood to fight him, I will offer sacrifice to Zeus and all the gods tomorrow. I will draw my ships into the water and stock them properly. Tomorrow morning, if you care to look, you will see my ships on the Hellespont and my men rowing out to sea with all their might. If great Poseidon grants me a fair passage, in three days I will be in Phthia. I have much there that I left behind when I came here to my sorrow. I will bring back still more gold, red copper, fair women, and iron, my share of the spoils we have taken. But one prize, the man who gave it has insolently taken away. Tell him all this as I now tell you, and tell him in public, so that the Achaeans may hate him and beware of him, in case he thinks he can still dupe others, for his effrontery never fails him.

“As for him, the hound does not even dare to look me in the face. I will not sit in council with him, and I will have no share in any plan of his. He has wronged and deceived me enough. He will not cheat me a second time. Let him go his own way, since Zeus has taken away his reason. I hate his presents, and I do not care a straw for the man himself. Let him offer ten times what he has offered now, or twenty—no, not even if he gave me everything he owns in the world, now or ever. Let him promise me the wealth of Orchomenus or of Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the whole world, which has a hundred gates, and through each gate two hundred men can drive out at once with their chariots and horses. Let him offer gifts as many as the sands of the sea or the dust of the plain. Even so he will not move me until I have paid him back in full for the bitter wrong he did me. I will not marry his daughter. She could be as beautiful as Aphrodite and as skilled as Athena, and I would still have none of her. Let some other man take her, one who suits her better and rules a larger kingdom. If the gods bring me safely home, Peleus himself will find me a wife. There are Achaean women in Hellas and Phthia, daughters of kings who rule cities, and I can take whichever of them I like and marry her. Many times, back home in Phthia, I longed to court a wife who would suit me and to enjoy the riches of my old father Peleus. My life is worth more to me than all the wealth of Ilium in the days when it was at peace, before the Achaeans came, or than all the treasure that lies on the stone floor of Apollo’s temple under the cliffs of Pytho. Cattle and sheep can be won by raiding, and a man can buy tripods and horses if he wants them. But once a man’s life has left him, it can be neither bought nor raided back.

“My mother Thetis tells me that death can come to me in one of two ways. If I stay here and fight, I will not get home alive, but my name will live forever. If I go home, my name will die, but I will live a long time before death takes me. To the rest of you I say, ‘Go home. You will never take Ilium.’ Zeus has held his hand over the city to protect it, and its people have taken heart. So go, as is your duty, and give the princes of the Achaeans the message I am sending. Tell them to find some other plan to save their ships and their people, because the one they have settled on now will not work while my anger lasts. As for Phoenix, let him sleep here, so that he can sail home with me in the morning if he wishes. But I will not take him by force.”

They all stayed silent, shaken by how harshly he had refused them. At last the old knight Phoenix, in his great fear for the ships of the Achaeans, burst into tears and spoke. “Noble Achilles, if you are really set on going home, and your fierce anger will not let you do anything to save the ships from burning, then how can I stay here without you, my son? Your father Peleus sent me with you on the day he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, when you were only a boy. You knew nothing yet of war, or of the skills that make men known in council. He sent me to train you in every excellence of speech and action. So, my son, I will not stay here without you—no, not even if heaven itself were to strip the years from me and make me as young as I was when I first left Hellas, the land of fair women. I was running from the anger of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus. He was furious with me over his concubine, whom he loved, to the wrong of his wife, my mother. My mother begged me without stopping to sleep with the woman myself, so that she would come to hate my father, and in time I gave in. But my father soon found out, and cursed me bitterly, calling the dreadful Erinyes to witness. He prayed that no son of mine would ever sit on his knees—and the gods, Zeus of the world below and awful Persephone, fulfilled his curse. I made up my mind to kill him, but some god held back my rashness. He made me think of what men’s evil tongues would say, and how I would be branded the murderer of my father. Even so, I could not bear to stay in my father’s house with him so bitter against me. My cousins and kinsmen gathered around me and pressed me hard to stay. They slaughtered many sheep and many oxen, set many fat hogs to roast before the fire, and broached many jars of my father’s wine. For nine whole nights they set a guard over me, taking turns to watch, and they kept a fire burning always, both in the cloister of the outer court and in the inner court at the doors of the room where I lay. But when the darkness of the tenth night came, I broke through the closed doors of my room and climbed the wall of the outer court, after slipping quickly and unseen through the guards and the women servants. Then I fled through Hellas until I came to fertile Phthia, mother of sheep, and to King Peleus. He welcomed me and treated me as a father treats an only son who will inherit all his wealth. He made me rich and put me over many people, setting me on the borders of Phthia, where I ruled as chief over the Dolopians.

“It was I, Achilles, who made you what you are. I loved you with all my heart. You would not eat at home, or anywhere else you went, until I had set you on my knees, cut up the tasty morsel for you, and held the wine cup to your lips. Many times you dribbled your wine over my shirt in a baby’s helplessness. I had endless trouble with you. But I knew that heaven had given me no child of my own, so I made a son of you, Achilles, so that in my hour of need you would protect me. Now I tell you: fight your pride and beat it. Do not nurse your anger forever. The might and majesty of heaven are greater than ours, and even heaven can be appeased. When a man has sinned, he prays to the gods and wins them back with his pitiful cries, with frankincense, with drink offerings and the smell of burnt sacrifice. For prayers are like daughters of great Zeus. They are lame and wrinkled, and they squint, and they follow in the footsteps of sin. Sin is fierce and swift-footed, so it leaves them far behind, and, a curse to mankind always, it outruns them to the ends of the world. Still, the prayers come limping after, and heal what sin has done. If a man respects these daughters of Zeus when they come near him, they bless him and listen to his prayers as well. But if he refuses them and will not listen, they go to Zeus the son of Cronus and pray that sin will overtake him, so that he comes to regret it bitterly. So, Achilles, give these daughters of Zeus the reverence they are due, and bow before them as all good men bow. If the son of Atreus were not offering you gifts and promising more later—if he were still furious and unyielding—I would not be the one to tell you to throw off your anger and help the Achaeans, however great their need. But he is giving much now, and will give more later. He has sent his captains to plead for him, and chosen the men who are dearest to you of all the Argives. Do not make their words and their coming useless. Until now your anger was justified. We have heard in song how heroes of old quarreled when fury seized them, yet gifts could still win them over, and fair words could soothe them.

“I have an old story in my mind—a very old one—but you are all friends, so I will tell it. The Curetes and the Aetolians were fighting and killing one another around Calydon, the Aetolians defending the city and the Curetes trying to destroy it. Artemis of the golden throne was angry and did them harm, because Oeneus had not offered her the first fruits of his harvest. The other gods had all been feasted with great sacrifices, but to the daughter of great Zeus alone he had made no sacrifice. He had forgotten her, or somehow it had slipped his mind, and this was a grievous sin. In her anger the archer goddess sent a monstrous creature against him, a savage wild boar with great white tusks. It did great harm to his orchard lands, uprooting apple trees in full bloom and flinging them to the ground. But Meleager son of Oeneus gathered huntsmen and hounds from many cities and killed it. The boar was so huge that not a few men were needed, and it laid many a man on his funeral pyre. Then the goddess set the Curetes and the Aetolians fighting furiously over the boar’s head and skin.

“As long as Meleager was in the field, things went badly for the Curetes, and for all their numbers they could not hold their ground under the city walls. But in time Meleager grew angry, as even a wise man sometimes will. He was enraged at his mother Althaea, and so he stayed at home with his wedded wife, fair Cleopatra. She was the daughter of Marpessa daughter of Euenus, and of Ides, the man who was then alive. This Ides took up his bow and faced King Apollo himself for the sake of fair Marpessa. After that, her father and mother named her Alcyone, because her mother had cried out in grief like the halcyon bird when Phoebus Apollo carried her off. So Meleager stayed at home with Cleopatra, feeding the anger he felt over his mother’s curses. His mother was grieving for her brother’s death. She prayed to the gods and beat the earth with her hands, calling on Hades and on awful Persephone. She was on her knees, and her bosom was wet with tears, as she prayed that they would kill her son. And Erinys, who walks in darkness and knows no pity, heard her from Erebus.

“Soon the din of battle was heard around the gates of Calydon, and the dull thud of battering against the walls. The elders of the Aetolians begged Meleager. They sent the most important of their priests to ask him to come out and help them, and promised him a great reward. They told him to choose fifty plow-gates in the most fertile part of the plain of Calydon, half of it vineyard and half open plowland. The old warrior Oeneus pleaded with him, standing at the threshold of his room and beating on the doors in supplication. His sisters and his mother herself begged him hard, but he refused them all the more. Those of his comrades who were nearest and dearest to him prayed to him too, but they could not move him. That went on until the foe was battering at the very doors of his chamber, and the Curetes had scaled the walls and were setting fire to the city. Then at last his sorrowing wife described to him the horrors that fall on people whose city is taken. She reminded him how the men are slain, and the city is given over to the flames, while the women and children are carried off into captivity. When he heard all this, his heart was touched, and he put on his armor and went out. So he saved the city of the Aetolians of his own free will. But they no longer gave him any of the rich rewards they had offered before, and though he saved the city he gained nothing by it. Do not let yourself think this way, my son. Do not let heaven lure you into any such course. When the ships are burning, it will be harder to save them. Take the gifts and go, for then the Achaeans will honor you like a god. But if you fight without taking them, you may beat the battle back, but you will not be held in the same honor.”

And Achilles answered, “Phoenix, old friend and father, I have no need of that kind of honor. I have honor from Zeus himself, and it will stay with me at my ships as long as I have breath in my body and strength in my limbs. And I tell you this—take it to heart—stop upsetting me with this weeping and lamenting for the sake of the son of Atreus. If you love him so well, you may lose the love I bear you. You should rather help me trouble those who trouble me. Be king as much as I am, and share equal honor with me. The others will carry back my answer. You stay here yourself and sleep comfortably in your bed, and at daybreak we will decide whether to stay or go.”

Then he nodded quietly to Patroclus, as a sign that he should prepare a bed for Phoenix and that the others should leave. Ajax son of Telamon spoke next. “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, let us go. I can see that our journey is useless. We must take our answer, unwelcome as it is, to the Danaans, who are waiting for it. Achilles is savage and without mercy. He is cruel, and cares nothing for the love his comrades gave him more than all the others. He is unforgiving. Yet when a man’s brother or son has been killed, he will accept a payment as compensation from the killer, and the wrongdoer, having paid in full, stays in peace among his own people. But you, Achilles—the gods have put a wicked, unforgiving spirit in your heart, and all this over one single girl, when we are now offering you the seven best we have, and much else besides. Be more gracious, and respect the hospitality of your own roof. We are here with you as messengers from the host of the Danaans, and we would gladly be held nearest and dearest to you of all the Achaeans.”

“Ajax,” replied Achilles, “noble son of Telamon, what you have said pleases me well. But my blood boils when I think it over and remember how the son of Atreus treated me with contempt, as if I were some vile tramp, and in front of the Argives too. So go and deliver your message. Say that I will have nothing to do with fighting until Hector, son of noble Priam, reaches the tents of the Myrmidons in his murderous course and throws fire on their ships. For all his lust for battle, I think he will be held back once he is at my own tent and ship.”

After that, each man took his double cup, made his drink offering, and went back to the ships, with Odysseus leading the way. Patroclus told his men and the maidservants to make a comfortable bed for Phoenix, and they did, with sheepskins, a rug, and a sheet of fine linen. The old man lay down and waited for morning. Achilles slept in an inner room, and beside him lay the daughter of Phorbas, lovely Diomede, whom he had carried off from Lesbos. Patroclus lay on the other side of the room, and with him fair Iphis, whom Achilles had given him when he took Scyros, the city of Enyeus.

When the envoys reached the tents of the son of Atreus, the Achaeans rose, raised cups of gold to them, and began to question them. King Agamemnon was the first. “Tell me, Odysseus,” he said, “will he save the ships from burning, or did he refuse, and is he still furious?”

Odysseus answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, Achilles will not be calmed. He is angrier than ever, and he rejects both you and your gifts. He tells you to take counsel with the Achaeans and save the ships and the host as best you can. As for himself, he said that at daybreak he would drag his ships down into the water. He also said he would advise everyone to sail home too, because you will never reach your goal of Ilium. ‘Zeus,’ he said, ‘has laid his hand over the city to protect it, and its people have taken heart.’ That is what he said, and the others who were with me can tell you the same story: Ajax and the two heralds, both men who can be trusted. The old man Phoenix stayed where he was to sleep, because Achilles wanted it so, to let him go home with him in the morning if he wished. But Achilles will not take him by force.”

They all stayed silent, sitting for a long time quiet and downcast at how harshly Achilles had refused them. At last Diomedes spoke. “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, you should not have pleaded with the son of Peleus or offered him gifts. He is proud enough already, and you have pushed him further into his pride. Let him stay or go as he wishes. He will fight later, when he is in the mood and heaven puts it in his mind. Now let us all do as I say. We have eaten and drunk our fill, so let us rest, for in rest there is both strength and support. But when fair rosy-fingered Dawn appears, bring your host and your horsemen out in front of the ships at once, urging them on, and fight yourself among the foremost.”
So he spoke, and the other chieftains approved his words. They made their drink offerings, and each man went to his own tent, where they lay down and enjoyed the gift of sleep.

chapters.title: Book 10
paragraphs: Odysseus and Diomedes go out as spies and meet Dolon, who gives them information. They then kill him, and using what he told them, they kill Rhesus king of the Thracians and take his horses.

All the other princes of the Achaeans slept soundly through the night, but Agamemnon son of Atreus was troubled and could find no rest. As when the husband of fair Hera flashes his lightning as a sign of heavy rain, or hail, or a snowfall that turns the ground white, or else as a sign that he will open the wide jaws of hungry war, so Agamemnon heaved many a heavy sigh, for his soul trembled within him. When he looked out over the plain of Troy, he marveled at the many watchfires burning in front of Ilium, and at the sound of pipes and flutes and the hum of men. But when he turned toward the ships and the armies of the Achaeans, he tore his hair out by handfuls before Zeus on high, and groaned aloud, so uneasy was his soul. In the end he decided it was best to go at once to Nestor son of Neleus, and see whether the two of them could find some way to save the Achaeans from destruction. So he got up, put on his shirt, tied his sandals on his comely feet, threw over his shoulders the skin of a huge tawny lion—a skin that reached his feet—and took his spear in his hand.

Menelaus could not sleep either. He too feared disaster for the Argives, who had sailed far over the seas for his sake to fight the Trojans. He draped the skin of a spotted panther over his broad back, set a bronze helmet on his head, and took his spear in his strong hand. Then he went to wake his brother, who was by far the most powerful of the Achaeans and was honored by the people as if he were a god. He found Agamemnon by the stern of his ship, already putting his fine armor on his shoulders, and Agamemnon was very glad that his brother had come.

Menelaus spoke first. “My dear brother,” he said, “why are you arming? Are you going to send one of our comrades to scout the Trojans? I am afraid no one will do you this service, to spy on the enemy alone in the dead of night. It would take great daring.”

King Agamemnon answered, “Menelaus, both of us need shrewd advice to save the Argives and our ships. Zeus has changed his mind, and favors Hector’s sacrifices over ours. I never saw or heard of any one man doing so much damage in a single day as Hector has now done to the sons of the Achaeans—and he did it all by himself, though he is the son of neither god nor goddess. The Argives will regret it long and bitterly. Now run quickly along the line of the ships and call Ajax and Idomeneus. Meanwhile I will go to Nestor and tell him to get up and go among our companies of sentinels to give them their instructions. They will listen to him sooner than to anyone, since his own son and Meriones, the brother in arms of Idomeneus, are the captains over them. It was to those two especially that we gave this charge.”

Menelaus replied, “What exactly do you mean? Should I stay with them and wait for you to come, or come back here once I have delivered your orders?” “Wait there,” King Agamemnon answered, “because there are so many paths through the camp that we might miss each other. Call every man you pass, and tell him to get up. Address him by his family and his father’s name, and give each the full respect due to him. Do not stand on your own dignity. We must take our full share of the work, since Zeus laid this heavy burden on us at our birth.”

With these instructions he sent his brother off, and went on to Nestor, shepherd of his people. He found him asleep in his tent near his own ship. His fine armor lay beside him—his shield, his two spears and his helmet. Beside him also lay the gleaming belt that the old man put on when he armed to lead his people into battle, for age did not hold him back. Nestor raised himself on his elbow and looked up at Agamemnon. “Who is this,” he said, “walking alone through the army and along the ships in the dead of night, while other men are sleeping? Are you looking for one of your mules, or for a comrade? Do not just stand there silent. Speak. What is your business?”

Agamemnon answered, “Nestor, son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, it is I, Agamemnon son of Atreus. Zeus has laid labor and sorrow on me for as long as I have breath in my body and my limbs carry me. I am out like this because sleep will not settle on my eyelids. My heart is heavy with the war and with the danger the Achaeans are in. I fear greatly for the Danaans. I am adrift at sea, with no sure counsel; my heart pounds as though it would leap out of my body, and my limbs fail me. So if you can do anything—for you cannot sleep either—let us make the round of the watch and see whether the sentinels are drowsy with toil and sleeping instead of doing their duty. The enemy is camped close by, and for all we know he may attack us by night.”

Nestor replied, “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, Zeus will not give Hector everything Hector expects. He will have plenty of troubles yet, if Achilles will put aside his anger. I will go with you, and we will wake others: the son of Tydeus, or Odysseus, or swift Ajax and the valiant son of Phyleus. Someone should also go and call Ajax and King Idomeneus, since their ships are not close at hand but the farthest of all. But I cannot help blaming Menelaus, much as I love and respect him—and I will say so plainly, even at the risk of offending you—for sleeping and leaving all this trouble to you alone. He ought to be going around begging for help from all the princes of the Achaeans, for we are in extreme danger.”

Agamemnon answered, “Sir, you may sometimes blame him justly, for he is often slow and unwilling to exert himself. It is not from laziness or carelessness, but because he looks to me and expects me to take the lead. This time, though, he was awake before I was and came to me of his own accord. I have already sent him to call the very men you named. Now let us go. We will find them with the watch outside the gates, since that is where I said we would meet them.”
“Then,” said Nestor, “no Argive will find fault with him, or ignore his orders, when he calls on them to fight or tells them what to do.”

With this Nestor put on his shirt and tied his sandals on his comely feet. He fastened on his purple coat, which was double-thick, large, and rough and shaggy, took up his formidable bronze-shod spear, and made his way along the line of the Achaean ships. First he called loudly to Odysseus, peer of gods in counsel, and woke him; Odysseus was roused at once by the sound of the battle cry. He came outside his tent and said, “Why are you going alone through the army and along the ships in the stillness of the night? What is so urgent?” Nestor, knight of Gerene, answered, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, do not take it badly, for the Achaeans are in great trouble. Come with me and let us wake someone else, who can help us decide whether we should fight or flee.”

At this Odysseus went straight into his tent, slung his shield over his shoulders and came out with them. They went first to Diomedes son of Tydeus. They found him outside his tent in full armor, with his comrades sleeping around him and using their shields as pillows. Their spears stood upright on the spikes at their butt ends, driven into the ground, and the burnished bronze flashed far off like the lightning of father Zeus. The hero was sleeping on the skin of an ox, with a piece of fine carpet under his head. Nestor went up to him and nudged him with his heel to wake him, scolding him and urging him to get moving. “Wake up,” he cried, “son of Tydeus. How can you sleep on like this? Do you not see that the Trojans are camped on the brow of the plain close to our ships, with only a little space between us and them?”

At these words Diomedes leaped up and said, “Old man, your heart is iron. You do not rest from your labors for a single moment. Are there no younger men among the Achaeans who could go around and wake the princes? Nothing wears you out.”

Nestor, knight of Gerene, replied, “My son, everything you say is true. I have good sons, and plenty of other men who could call the chieftains. But the Achaeans are in the gravest danger. Life and death hang, as it were, on the edge of a razor. So go, since you are younger than I am, and out of courtesy wake Ajax and the swift son of Phyleus.”

Diomedes threw the skin of a great tawny lion over his shoulders—a skin that reached his feet—and took up his spear. He woke the heroes and brought them back with him. Then they made the round of the men on guard, and found the captains not sleeping at their posts but awake and sitting with their arms about them. As sheep dogs guard their penned flocks and hear a wild beast coming toward them through the mountain forest, and at once dogs and men raise a cry and sleep is broken, so sleep was driven from the eyes of the Achaeans as they kept the watches of that wicked night, for they kept turning toward the plain whenever they heard any stir among the Trojans. The old man was glad and told them to take heart. “Keep watching, my children,” he said, “and do not let sleep take hold of you, or our enemies will triumph over us.”

With this Nestor crossed the trench, and the other chiefs of the Achaeans who had been called to the council went with him. Meriones and the brave son of Nestor went too, because the princes told them to. Beyond the trench that was dug around the wall, they held their meeting on open ground, where there was a clear space free of corpses. It was here that Hector had turned back from his attack on the Argives when night fell. They sat down and talked it over together.

Nestor spoke first. “My friends,” he said, “is any man bold enough to venture among the Trojans, and cut off some straggler, or bring us news of what the enemy mean to do? Will they stay here by the ships, away from the city, or now that they have beaten the Achaeans, will they retire inside their walls? If he could learn all this and come back here safely, his fame would reach as high as heaven in the mouths of all men, and he would be richly rewarded. The chiefs from all our ships would each give him a black ewe with her lamb—a gift of surpassing value—and he would be invited as a guest to all feasts and clan gatherings.”

They all kept silent, but Diomedes of the loud war cry spoke. “Nestor,” he said, “I will gladly go to the army of the Trojans opposite us. But if another man will go with me, I will do it with more confidence and comfort. When two men are together, one of them may notice some opportunity that the other has missed. A man alone is less resourceful, and his wit is weaker.”

At this several men offered to go with Diomedes. The two Ajaxes, servants of Ares, Meriones, and the son of Nestor all wanted to go, and so did Menelaus son of Atreus. Odysseus also wished to go among the army of the Trojans, for he was always full of daring. Then Agamemnon, king of men, spoke. “Diomedes,” he said, “son of Tydeus, man after my own heart, choose your comrade yourself. Take the best man of those who have offered, for many would go with you now. Do not out of delicacy turn down the better man and take the worse out of respect for his birth, because he is of more royal blood.”

Agamemnon said this because he feared for Menelaus. Diomedes answered, “If you tell me to take the man of my own choice, how can I fail to think of Odysseus? No man is more eager to face every kind of danger, and Pallas Athena loves him well. If he went with me, we could pass safely through fire itself, for he is quick to see and understand.”

“Son of Tydeus,” Odysseus replied, “say neither good nor bad about me, for you are among Argives who know me well. Let us go, for the night is waning and dawn is near. The stars have moved on, two-thirds of the night is already gone, and only the third part is left to us.”

Then they put on their armor. Brave Thrasymedes gave the son of Tydeus a sword and a shield (for Diomedes had left his own at his ship), and set a helmet of bull’s hide on his head, without peak or crest. It is called a skull-cap and is a common headgear. Meriones found a bow and quiver for Odysseus, and set on his head a leather helmet. It was lined inside with a strong weaving of leather thongs, and on the outside it was thickly studded with boar’s teeth, skillfully and well set into it; next to the head was an inner lining of felt. Autolycus had stolen this helmet out of Eleon, when he broke into the house of Amyntor son of Ormenus. He gave it to Amphidamas of Cythera to take to Scandea, and Amphidamas gave it as a guest-gift to Molus, who gave it to his son Meriones. Now it was set on the head of Odysseus.

When the pair had armed, they set out and left the other chieftains behind. Pallas Athena sent them a heron by the wayside on their right. They could not see it in the dark, but they heard its cry. Odysseus was glad to hear it and prayed to Athena. “Hear me,” he cried, “daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus. You watch over all my ways and are with me in all my hardships. Be my friend now, in this hour, and grant that we may return to the ships covered with glory, after achieving some mighty exploit that will bring sorrow to the Trojans.”

Then Diomedes of the loud war cry prayed as well. “Hear me too,” he said, “unwearying daughter of Zeus. Be with me as you were with my noble father Tydeus, when he went to Thebes as an envoy sent by the Achaeans. He left the Achaeans by the banks of the river Aesopus and went to the city carrying a message of peace to the Cadmeians. On his way back, with your help, goddess, he did great deeds of daring, for you were his ready helper. In the same way guide me and guard me now, and in return I will sacrifice to you a broad-browed heifer a year old, unbroken, never yet brought under the yoke by any man. I will gild her horns and offer her up to you in sacrifice.”

So they prayed, and Pallas Athena heard them. When they had finished their prayer to the daughter of great Zeus, they set off, like two lions prowling in the night through the armor and the blood-stained bodies of the fallen.

Hector did not let the Trojans sleep either. He too called together the princes and councillors of Troy, so that he could lay his plan before them. “Is there anyone,” he said, “who will do me a service for a great reward? I will tell you what it is. He will be well paid if he does it. I will give him a chariot and a pair of horses, the swiftest to be found at the ships of the Achaeans, if he has the courage for this task. He will also win endless honor. He must go to the ships and find out whether they are still guarded as before, or whether the Achaeans, now that we have beaten them, plan to flee and are neglecting their watches out of sheer exhaustion.”

They all kept silent. But among the Trojans there was a man named Dolon, son of Eumedes the famous herald, and rich in gold and bronze. He was ugly but a good runner, and he was the only son among five sisters. He now spoke up to the Trojans. “Hector,” he said, “I will go to the ships and spy them out. But first raise your scepter and swear to me that you will give me the chariot decked with bronze, and the horses that carry the noble son of Peleus. I will be a good scout for you and will not fail you. I will cross the whole host from one end to the other until I reach the ship of Agamemnon, where I expect the princes of the Achaeans are meeting to decide whether they will fight or flee.”

When he had finished, Hector raised his scepter and swore the oath. “May Zeus, the thundering husband of Hera, be my witness,” he said, “that no Trojan but you will ride behind those horses, and that they will be yours to do with as you like forever.”

The oath was empty, but it made Dolon all the keener to go. He slung his bow over his shoulder and put on the skin of a gray wolf as a cloak, with a cap of ferret skin on his head. Then he took a pointed javelin and left the camp for the ships. He would never come back with news for Hector. He left the horses and the troops behind and hurried on his way, but Odysseus saw him coming and said to Diomedes, “Diomedes, someone is coming from the camp. I cannot tell whether he is a spy or a thief out to strip the bodies of the dead. Let him pass us by a little, and then we can leap on him and catch him. If he outruns us, go after him with your spear and drive him toward the ships, away from the Trojan camp, so that he cannot get back to the town.”

With that they left the path and lay down among the corpses. Dolon suspected nothing and soon went past them. When he had gone about as far as a furrow plowed by mules is longer than one plowed by oxen (for mules work fallow land faster than oxen), they ran after him. He heard their footsteps and stopped, sure that they were friends from the Trojan camp, sent by Hector to call him back. But when they were only a spear’s cast away, or less, he saw they were enemies and ran as fast as his legs would carry him. The two gave chase at once. As two well-trained hounds press hard after a doe or a hare that runs screaming ahead of them, so the son of Tydeus and Odysseus hunted Dolon and cut him off from his own people. He had almost reached the ships and would soon have run into the outposts, when Athena gave fresh strength to the son of Tydeus. She did it so that no other Achaean could win the glory of hitting Dolon first and leave Diomedes only second. He sprang forward with his spear and called out, “Stop, or I will throw my spear, and then I will soon finish you.”

As he spoke he threw, but he missed on purpose. The spear flew over the man’s right shoulder and stuck in the ground. Dolon stood stock still, trembling and terrified. His teeth chattered and his face went pale. The two came up to him out of breath and seized his hands, and he began to weep. “Take me alive,” he said. “I will pay my own ransom. We have plenty of gold, bronze and wrought iron, and my father will give you a very large ransom out of it if he hears that I am alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”

“Do not be afraid,” answered Odysseus. “Put all thought of death out of your mind. But tell me, and tell me the truth. Why are you going about alone like this in the dead of night, away from your camp and toward the ships, while other men sleep? Do you mean to strip the bodies of the slain? Or did Hector send you to spy out what is going on at the ships? Or did you come here on your own whim?”

Dolon answered, his legs shaking under him. “Hector lured me away from my better judgment with his empty, flattering promises. He said he would give me the horses of the noble son of Peleus and his chariot decked with bronze. He told me to go through the darkness of the fleeting night, get close to the enemy, and find out whether the ships are still guarded as before, or whether the Achaeans, now that we have beaten them, plan to flee and are neglecting their watches out of sheer exhaustion.”

Odysseus smiled at him and answered, “You certainly set your heart on a great reward. But the horses of the descendant of Aeacus are hard for any mortal man to control or drive, except Achilles himself, whose mother was an immortal. Now tell me, and tell me the truth. Where did you leave Hector when you set out? Where are his armor and his horses? How are the watches and the sleeping places of the Trojans arranged? What are their plans? Will they stay here by the ships, away from the city? Or now that they have beaten the Achaeans, will they go back inside their walls?”

Dolon answered, “I will tell you everything truthfully. Hector and the other councillors are holding a conference at the monument of great Ilus, away from the general noise. As for the guards you ask about, no watch has been chosen to protect the host. The Trojans have their watchfires, because they must, so they are awake and urge one another to do their duty as sentinels. But the allies who have come from other lands are asleep. They leave the guarding to the Trojans, since their own wives and children are not here.”
Odysseus then said, “Now tell me this. Are they sleeping mixed in with the Trojan troops, or do they lie apart? Explain it so that I understand.”

“I will tell you everything truthfully,” replied Dolon. “Toward the sea lie the Carians, the Paeonian bowmen, the Leleges, the Cauconians and the noble Pelasgi. The Lycians, the proud Mysians, the Phrygians and the Meonians have their place on the side toward Thymbra. But why ask about all this? If you want to find a way into the Trojan host, there are the Thracians, who have only just arrived. They lie apart from the others at the far end of the camp, and their king is Rhesus son of Eioneus. His horses are the finest and strongest I have ever seen. They are whiter than snow and swifter than any wind. His chariot is decked with silver and gold, and he has brought his marvelous golden armor, of the rarest workmanship. It is too splendid for any mortal man to wear and fit only for the gods. Now take me to the ships, or tie me up securely here until you come back and have tested my words to see whether they are false or true.”

Diomedes looked at him sternly and answered, “Dolon, do not think that you will escape now that you are in our hands, however useful your information has been. If we ransom you or let you go, you will come back to the ships of the Achaeans some other time, as a spy or as an open enemy. But if I kill you and put an end to you, you will give no more trouble.”

Dolon was reaching for his beard to plead with him further, but Diomedes struck him with his sword in the middle of the neck and cut through both sinews, so that his head fell rolling in the dust while he was still speaking. They took the ferret-skin cap from his head, and the wolf skin, the bow and the long spear. Odysseus hung them up aloft in honor of Athena, goddess of plunder, and prayed, “Accept these, goddess. We give them to you before all the gods on Olympus. Now guide us further, to the horses and the sleeping place of the Thracians.”

With these words he took the spoils and set them on a tamarisk tree. They marked the place by pulling up reeds and gathering tamarisk boughs, so that they would not miss it when they came back through the fleeting hours of darkness. The two then went on through the fallen armor and the blood, and soon came to the company of Thracian soldiers. They were sleeping, worn out by the day’s labor. Their fine armor lay on the ground beside them in three neat rows, and each man had his pair of horses next to him. Rhesus slept in the middle, and close by him his horses were tied to the top rim of his chariot. Odysseus saw him from a little way off and said, “Diomedes, this is the man, and these are the horses Dolon told us about, the one we killed. Do your utmost. Do not waste time on your armor. Loose the horses at once, or else kill the men yourself while I see to the horses.”

Then Athena put courage into the heart of Diomedes, and he struck the Thracians right and left. They groaned horribly as they were hacked down, and the earth was red with their blood. As a lion falls furiously on a flock of sheep or goats when it finds them without their shepherd, so the son of Tydeus fell on the Thracian soldiers until he had killed twelve. As he killed them, Odysseus came and dragged them aside by the feet, one by one, so that the horses could go forward freely and not be frightened as they passed over the dead bodies, since they were not yet used to them. When the son of Tydeus reached the king, he killed him too, which made thirteen. The king was breathing hard, for by the counsel of Athena an evil dream, the offspring of Oeneus, hovered over his head that night. Meanwhile Odysseus untied the horses, fastened them to one another and drove them off, striking them with his bow, because he had forgotten to take the whip from the chariot. Then he whistled as a signal to Diomedes.

But Diomedes stayed where he was, thinking what other bold deed he could do. He wondered whether to take the chariot where the king’s armor lay and pull it out by the pole, or to lift the armor out and carry it off, or whether he should kill still more Thracians. While he was hesitating, Athena came up to him and said, “Get back to the ships, Diomedes, or you may be driven there, if some other god rouses the Trojans.”
Diomedes knew it was the goddess and sprang at once onto the horses. Odysseus beat them with his bow, and they flew on toward the ships of the Achaeans.

But Apollo was not keeping a careless watch when he saw Athena with the son of Tydeus. He was angry with her. He went to the Trojan host and woke Hippocoon, a counsellor of the Thracians and a noble kinsman of Rhesus. Hippocoon started up from his sleep and saw that the horses were no longer in their place and that the men were gasping in their death agony. He groaned aloud and called his friend by name. Then the whole Trojan camp was in uproar, as the people kept rushing together, and they marveled at what the heroes had done before getting away toward the ships.

When they reached the place where they had killed Hector’s scout, Odysseus stopped his horses. The son of Tydeus leapt to the ground, put the blood-stained spoils in the hands of Odysseus, and remounted. Then he lashed the horses on, and they flew toward the ships, willingly, as if by their own choice. Nestor was the first to hear the beat of their hooves. “My friends,” he said, “princes and counsellors of the Argives, will I guess right or wrong? Still, I must say what I think. There is a sound in my ears like the beat of horses’ hooves. I hope it is Diomedes and Odysseus driving horses in from the Trojans, but I greatly fear that the bravest of the Argives may have come to some harm at their hands.”

He had hardly finished speaking when the two men came in and dismounted. The others shook their hands warmly and congratulated them. Nestor, knight of Gerene, was the first to question them. “Tell me, renowned Odysseus,” he said, “how did you two get these horses? Did you slip in among the Trojan forces, or did a god meet you and give them to you? They are like sunbeams. I know the Trojans well, for old warrior though I am, I never hold back by the ships. But I have never seen or heard of horses like these. A god must surely have met you and given them to you, for you are both dear to Zeus, and to Zeus’s daughter Athena.”

Odysseus answered, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, heaven, if it so wills, can give us even better horses than these, for the gods are far mightier than we are. But the horses you ask about have just come from Thrace. Diomedes killed their king along with the twelve bravest of his companions. Close by the ships we took a thirteenth man, a scout whom Hector and the other Trojans had sent to spy on our ships.”

He laughed as he spoke and drove the horses over the ditch, and the other Achaeans followed him gladly. When they reached the strongly built quarters of the son of Tydeus, they tied the horses with leather thongs to the manger, where the horses of Diomedes stood eating their sweet corn. Odysseus hung the blood-stained spoils of Dolon at the stern of his ship, so that they could prepare a sacred offering to Athena. They themselves went into the sea and washed the sweat from their bodies, their necks and their thighs. When the sea water had washed all the sweat off them and refreshed them, they went into the baths and washed again. After that they anointed themselves with oil and sat down to the meal. They drew wine from a full mixing bowl and poured a drink offering to Athena.

chapters.title: Book 11
paragraphs: In the forenoon the fight is even, but Agamemnon swings the day toward the Achaeans until he is wounded and leaves the field—Hector then drives all before him until Diomedes wounds him—Paris wounds Diomedes—Odysseus, Nestor, and Idomeneus do astonishing feats of valor—Machaon is wounded—Nestor takes him off in his chariot—Achilles sees the two driving toward the camp and sends Patroclus to ask who the wounded man is—This is the beginning of evil for Patroclus—Nestor makes a long speech.

Dawn was rising from her couch beside Tithonus, bringing light to mortals and immortals alike, when Zeus sent fierce Discord to the ships of the Achaeans, with the ensign of war in her hands. She stopped beside the huge black hull of Odysseus’s ship, which lay in the middle of the line, so that her voice would carry farthest in both directions: toward the tents of Ajax son of Telamon on one side, and toward those of Achilles on the other. These two heroes, sure of their own strength, had bravely drawn up their ships at the two ends of the line. There she stood and gave a cry, loud and shrill, that filled the Achaeans with courage. It gave them heart to fight steadily and with all their might, and they would sooner stay and do battle than sail home in their ships.

The son of Atreus shouted aloud and told the Argives to gird themselves for battle, while he put on his own armor. First he fastened his fine greaves around his legs, with ankle-clasps of silver. Then he put on the breastplate that Cinyras had once given him as a guest-gift. News had spread as far as Cyprus that the Achaeans were about to sail for Troy, and that was why Cinyras gave it to the king. It had ten courses of dark cyanus, twelve of gold, and ten of tin. Serpents of cyanus reared up toward the neck, three on each side, like the rainbows that the son of Cronus has set in heaven as a sign to mortal men. Over his shoulders he slung his sword, studded with bosses of gold; its scabbard was silver, with a chain of gold to hang it by. He also took up his richly decorated shield, which covered his body in battle. It was fair to see, with ten circles of bronze running all round it. On the body of the shield were twenty bosses of white tin, with one of dark cyanus in the middle. This center boss was made to show a Gorgon’s head, fierce and grim, with Rout and Panic on either side. The band for the arm to go through was silver, and on it was a writhing snake of cyanus with three heads that sprang from a single neck and wound in and out among one another. On his head Agamemnon set a helmet with a peak in front and behind, and four plumes of horsehair nodded menacingly above it. Then he took two formidable bronze-shod spears. The gleam of his armor shot up from him like a flame into the sky, while Hera and Athena thundered in honor of the king of rich Mycene.

Each man now left his horses with his charioteer, to hold them ready by the trench, and went into battle on foot in full armor. A mighty uproar rose into the dawn. The chiefs were armed and at the trench before the horses got there; the horses came up soon after. The son of Cronus sent an evil portent through their host: the dew fell red with blood, for he was about to send many a brave man hurrying down to Hades.

On the other side, on the rising slope of the plain, the Trojans gathered around great Hector, noble Polydamas, and Aeneas, whom the Trojans honored like an immortal. With them were the three sons of Antenor, Polybus, Agenor, and young Acamas, beautiful as a god. Hector’s round shield showed in the front rank. As a baneful star shines for a moment through a rent in the clouds and is hidden again beneath them, so Hector was seen now in the front ranks and now in the rearmost, and his bronze armor gleamed like the lightning of aegis-bearing Zeus.

As a band of reapers mow swathes of wheat or barley on a rich man’s land, and the sheaves fall thick before them, so the Trojans and Achaeans attacked one another. Neither side would yield; they fought like wolves, and neither got the better of the other. Discord was glad as she watched them, for she was the only god among them. The others were not there; they sat quietly, each in his own home, among the dells and valleys of Olympus. All of them blamed the son of Cronus for wanting to give victory to the Trojans, but father Zeus paid them no heed. He held aloof from them all and sat apart in his all-glorious majesty, looking down on the city of the Trojans, the ships of the Achaeans, the gleam of bronze, and the slayers and the slain alike.

So long as the day was growing and it was still morning, their darts rained thick on both sides and men died. But when the hour came near at which a woodman working in some mountain forest gets his midday meal—for he has felled trees until his hands are weary, he is tired out, and must now have food—then the Danaans, with a cry that rang through all their ranks, broke the enemy battalions. Agamemnon led them on. He killed Bienor first, a leader of his people, and then Bienor’s comrade and charioteer Oileus, who sprang down from his chariot and came straight at him. Agamemnon struck him on the forehead with his spear. His bronze visor was no use against the weapon, which pierced bronze and bone together, so that his brains were battered in and he died in the thick of the fight.

Agamemnon stripped the shirts from their bodies and left them lying where they had fallen, their breasts bare. Then he went on to kill Isus and Antiphus, two sons of Priam, one a bastard and the other born in wedlock. They rode in the same chariot, the bastard driving while noble Antiphus fought beside him. Achilles had once taken both of them prisoner in the glades of Ida, as they were shepherding, and had bound them with fresh withes, but he had accepted a ransom for them. Now Agamemnon son of Atreus struck Isus in the chest, above the nipple, with his spear, and hit Antiphus hard by the ear and threw him from his chariot. At once he stripped off their fine armor, and he recognized them, for he had seen them at the ships when Achilles brought them in from Ida. Just as a lion fastens on the fawns of a hind and crushes them in his great jaws, robbing them of their tender life as he goes back to his lair—and the hind can do nothing for them even if she is close by, for she is in an agony of fear and flees through the thick forest, sweating, at her utmost speed before the mighty beast—so no man of the Trojans could help Isus and Antiphus, for they were themselves fleeing in panic before the Argives.

Then King Agamemnon took the two sons of Antimachus, Pisander and brave Hippolochus. Antimachus had been the foremost in preventing Helen from being given back to Menelaus, since Paris had bribed him heavily. Now Agamemnon caught his two sons in the same chariot, trying to bring their horses to a stand. They had lost hold of the reins, and the horses were mad with fear. The son of Atreus sprang at them like a lion, and the pair begged him from their chariot. “Take us alive, son of Atreus,” they cried, “and you will receive a great ransom for us. Our father Antimachus has a great store of gold, bronze, and wrought iron, and from it he will pay you a very large ransom if he hears that we are alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”

They begged the king with such piteous words and tears, but the answer they heard was not pitying. “If you are sons of Antimachus,” said Agamemnon, “who once proposed at a council of the Trojans that Menelaus and Odysseus, who had come to you as envoys, should be killed and not allowed to return, then you will now pay for your father’s foul wickedness.”

As he spoke he struck Pisander in the chest with his spear and felled him from his chariot to the earth, so that he lay face upward on the ground. Hippolochus fled, but Agamemnon struck him down too. He cut off his hands and his head, and sent the head rolling in among the crowd like a ball. He left them both lying there and flew to wherever the ranks were thickest, while the other Achaeans followed. Foot soldiers drove the enemy foot soldiers in rout before them and killed them, and horsemen did the same to horsemen, while the thundering tramp of the horses raised a cloud of dust from the plain. King Agamemnon came after them, always slaying and cheering on the Achaeans. As when some mighty forest is all ablaze, and the eddying gusts whirl the fire in all directions until the thickets shrivel and are consumed before the blast of the flame, so the heads of the fleeing Trojans fell before Agamemnon son of Atreus. Many a noble pair of horses drew an empty chariot along the highways of war, for want of drivers who lay on the plain, more use now to vultures than to their wives.

Zeus drew Hector away from the darts and dust, the carnage and the din of battle, but the son of Atreus rushed on, calling out loudly to the Danaans. They sped past the tomb of old Ilus, son of Dardanus, in the middle of the plain, and past the wild fig tree, always making for the city, with the son of Atreus still shouting and his hands all smeared with gore. When they reached the Scaean gates and the oak tree, they halted and waited for the others to come up. Meanwhile the Trojans kept fleeing over the middle of the plain like a herd of cows maddened with fright when a lion attacks them in the dead of night. He springs on one of them, seizes her neck in the grip of his strong teeth, laps up her blood, and gorges himself on her entrails. In the same way King Agamemnon son of Atreus pursued the enemy, always slaughtering the hindmost as they fled pell-mell before him. Many a man was flung headlong from his chariot by the hand of the son of Atreus, for he wielded his spear with fury.

But when Agamemnon was just about to reach the high wall and the city, the father of gods and men came down from heaven and sat on the crest of many-fountained Ida, with a thunderbolt in his hand. He told Iris of the golden wings to carry a message for him. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “and tell Hector this. As long as he sees Agamemnon at the head of his men, making havoc of the Trojan ranks, he is to keep aloof and tell the others to bear the brunt of the battle. But when Agamemnon is wounded by spear or arrow and takes to his chariot, then I will grant Hector strength to slay until he reaches the ships and night falls at the going down of the sun.”

Iris listened and obeyed. She went down from the crests of Ida to strong Ilium, where she found Hector son of Priam standing by his chariot and horses. “Hector son of Priam,” she said, “peer of gods in counsel, father Zeus has sent me with this message for you. While you see Agamemnon leading his men and making havoc of the Trojan ranks, keep aloof and tell the others to bear the brunt of the battle. But once Agamemnon is wounded by spear or arrow and takes to his chariot, Zeus will grant you strength to slay, until you reach the ships and night falls at the going down of the sun.”

Having said this, Iris left him. Hector leaped fully armed from his chariot to the ground. He went all through the host, brandishing his spear, urging his men to fight and stirring up the dread strife of battle. The Trojans wheeled round to face the Achaeans again, and the Argives on their side strengthened their battalions. Now the battle lines were drawn and the two sides stood face to face, with Agamemnon pressing ahead of everyone in his eagerness to be first.

Tell me now, you Muses who dwell in the mansions of Olympus: who, of the Trojans or their allies, was first to face Agamemnon? It was Iphidamas son of Antenor, a man both brave and of great stature, who was brought up in fertile Thrace, the mother of sheep. Cisses, his mother’s father, raised him in his own house when he was a child—Cisses, father of fair Theano. When Iphidamas reached manhood, Cisses wanted to keep him there and was ready to give him his daughter in marriage. But as soon as he was married, he set out to fight the Achaeans with the twelve ships that followed him. He had left these at Percote and come on by land to Ilium. This was the man who now met Agamemnon son of Atreus. When they were close to each other, the son of Atreus missed his aim, and Iphidamas hit him on the girdle below the cuirass, then threw himself on him, trusting in the strength of his arm. But the girdle was not pierced, not nearly, for the point of the spear struck against the silver and was turned aside as though it were lead. King Agamemnon caught the spear and, with the fury of a lion, pulled it toward him out of Iphidamas’s hand. Then he drew his sword and killed Iphidamas by striking him on the neck. So the poor fellow lay there, sleeping a sleep as it were of bronze, killed in defense of his fellow citizens, far from his wedded wife, of whom he had had no joy though he had given much for her. He had paid a hundred head of cattle down and had promised later to give a thousand sheep and goats mixed, from the countless flocks he owned. Agamemnon son of Atreus then despoiled him and carried his armor off into the host of the Achaeans.

When noble Coon, Antenor’s eldest son, saw this, his eyes were sore at the sight of his fallen brother. Unseen by Agamemnon, he got beside him, spear in hand, and wounded him in the middle of the arm below the elbow, so that the point of the spear went right through the arm. Agamemnon was convulsed with pain, but even so he did not leave off struggling and fighting. He grasped his spear, which flew swift as the wind, and sprang upon Coon. Coon was trying to drag off the body of his brother, his father’s son, by the foot, and was crying for help to all the bravest of his comrades. Agamemnon struck him with a bronze-shod spear and killed him as he dragged the dead body through the press of men under cover of his shield. Then, standing over the body of Iphidamas, he cut off Coon’s head. So the sons of Antenor met their fate at the hands of the son of Atreus and went down into the house of Hades.

While the blood still ran warm from his wound, Agamemnon kept charging the enemy ranks with spear and sword and great handfuls of stone. Then the bleeding stopped and the wound dried, and the pain grew terrible. A woman in labor is sent sharp pangs by the Eilithuiae, the goddesses of childbirth, who are daughters of Hera and dispense cruel pain. The pangs that struck the son of Atreus were as sharp as those. He leaped onto his chariot and ordered his charioteer to drive to the ships, because he was in great agony. In a loud clear voice he called out to the Danaans, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, you must defend the ships yourselves. Zeus has not allowed me to fight the whole day through against the Trojans.”

The charioteer then swung his horses around toward the ships, and they raced ahead willingly. Foam whitened their chests and dust whitened their bellies as they carried the wounded king out of the battle.

Hector saw Agamemnon leave the field, and he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians. “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanian warriors, be men, my friends, and fight bravely. Their best man has left them, and Zeus has granted me a great triumph. Drive your chariots at the enemy, and win still greater glory.”

Those words put heart and soul into every one of them. A huntsman sets his dogs on a lion or a wild boar, and in the same way Hector, the equal of Ares, set the proud Trojans on the Achaeans. Full of hope, he plunged in among the foremost fighters. He fell on the battle like a fierce storm that swoops down on the sea and whips its deep blue waters into a fury.

Who, then, were all those that Hector son of Priam killed in the hour of triumph that Zeus gave him? First Asaeus, Autonous, and Opites; Dolops son of Clytius, Opheltius and Agelaus; Aesymnus, Orus and Hipponous, steadfast in battle. These were the Achaean chieftains Hector killed, and then he fell on the rank and file. It was like the west wind shoving the clouds of the white south and beating them down in its fury: the waves of the sea roll high, and the spray is flung up in the rage of the wandering wind. In just that way the heads of the men who fell by Hector’s hand lay thick.

Everything would have been lost then, with no remedy, and the Achaeans would have fled in a jumble to their ships, if Odysseus had not called out to Diomedes. “Son of Tydeus, what has come over us, that we forget our fighting strength? Come, my good fellow, stand beside me and help me. We will be shamed forever if Hector takes the ships.”
Diomedes answered, “I will hold my ground, whatever comes. But we will get little joy from it, because Zeus wants to give victory to the Trojans rather than to us.”

With these words Diomedes knocked Thymbraeus from his chariot to the ground, driving his spear into his left breast. Odysseus killed Molion, who was his squire. They left these two lying there, since the pair had ended their fighting. The two heroes then went on wreaking havoc on the enemy, like two wild boars that wheel around in fury and tear the hounds hunting them. So they turned on the Trojans and killed them, and the Achaeans were grateful for a breathing space in their flight from Hector.

Next they took two princes along with their chariot: the two sons of Merops of Percote, who surpassed all other men in the art of divination. He had forbidden his sons to go to the war, but they did not obey him, because fate was luring them to their deaths.
