Diomedes son of Tydeus killed them both and stripped them of their armor, while Odysseus killed Hippodamus and Hypeirochus.

Now the son of Cronus, looking down from Ida, ordained that neither side should gain the advantage, and they kept on killing one another. The son of Tydeus speared Agastrophus son of Paeon in the hip joint. Agastrophus had no chariot at hand to escape in, so blindly confident had he been. His squire was holding it some distance away, while he fought on foot among the foremost until he lost his life. Hector soon noticed the havoc Diomedes and Odysseus were causing. He bore down on them with a loud cry, and the Trojan ranks followed him. Brave Diomedes was dismayed at the sight and said to Odysseus beside him, “Great Hector is bearing down on us, and we will be undone. Let us stand firm and wait for his attack.”

He poised his spear as he spoke and hurled it, and he did not miss his mark. He had aimed at Hector’s head near the top of the helmet, but bronze was turned by bronze. The spear was stopped by the visored helmet of three metal plates that Phoebus Apollo had given Hector, and Hector was untouched. He sprang back with a great bound under cover of the ranks. He fell on his knees and propped himself up with his brawny hand on the ground, because darkness had fallen over his eyes. The son of Tydeus, having thrown his spear, dashed in among the foremost fighters to where he had seen it strike the ground. Meanwhile Hector recovered, sprang back into his chariot, and mingled with the crowd, and so he saved his life. But Diomedes came at him with his spear and said, “Dog, you have got away again, though death was close on your heels. Phoebus Apollo, to whom I think you pray before you go into battle, has saved you again. Still, I will meet you and make an end of you later, if any god will stand by me too and help me. For now I must go after the ones I can lay hands on.”

While he spoke, Diomedes began stripping the spoils from the son of Paeon. But Paris, husband of lovely Helen, was leaning against a pillar of the monument that men had raised long ago to Ilus son of Dardanus, a ruler in days of old, and from there he aimed an arrow at him. Diomedes had taken the cuirass from Agastrophus’s breast, along with his heavy helmet and the shield from his shoulders, when Paris drew his bow and let fly an arrow. It did not leave his hand in vain. It pierced the flat of Diomedes’s right foot, went right through it, and fixed itself in the ground. Paris sprang out from his hiding place with a hearty laugh and taunted him. “You are wounded—my arrow was not shot in vain. I wish it had hit you in the belly and killed you. Then the Trojans, who fear you as goats fear a lion, would have had a break from their misery.”

Diomedes answered, quite undaunted, “Archer, you are nothing without your bow. Slanderer, seducer! If you were tried in single combat, fighting in full armor, your bow and arrows would do you little good. Your boast is empty, just because you have scratched the sole of my foot. I care no more than if a girl or some silly boy had hit me. A worthless coward can inflict only a light wound. When I wound a man, even if I only graze his skin, it is another matter, because my weapon lays him low. His wife will tear her cheeks in grief and his children will be fatherless. He will rot there, reddening the earth with his blood, and vultures, not women, will gather around him.”

So he spoke, and Odysseus came up and stood over him. Under this cover Diomedes sat down and drew the arrow from his foot, and the pain was sharp as he did it. Then he sprang onto his chariot and told the charioteer to drive him to the ships, for he was sick at heart.

Odysseus was now alone. Not one of the Argives stood by him, because panic had seized them all. “Alas,” he said to himself in dismay, “what will become of me? It is bad if I turn and run from these odds, but worse if I am left alone and taken prisoner, since the son of Cronus has struck the rest of the Danaans with panic. But why do I talk to myself like this? I know well that cowards quit the field, while a hero, whether he wounds or is wounded, must stand firm and hold his own.”

While he was torn between two choices, the Trojan ranks advanced and closed around him, and they would bitterly regret it. It was as when hounds and strong young men set upon a wild boar that charges out of his lair, whetting his white tusks. They attack him from every side and hear his jaws gnashing, yet for all his fierceness they hold their ground. In the same way the Trojans furiously attacked Odysseus. First he sprang at Deiopites, spear in hand, and wounded him on the shoulder with a downward blow. Then he killed Thoon and Ennomus. After these he struck Chersidamas in the loins, under his shield, as the man had just leapt down from his chariot. Chersidamas fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the hollow of his hand. Odysseus left these men lying and went on to wound Charops son of Hippasus, own brother to noble Socus. Socus, hero that he was, hurried to help his brother. When he was close to Odysseus he said, “Far-famed Odysseus, insatiable for craft and toil, today you will either boast of killing both sons of Hippasus and stripping them of their armor, or you will fall to my spear.”

With these words Socus struck the shield of Odysseus. The spear went through the shield and on through his richly wrought cuirass, tearing the flesh from his side, but Pallas Athena did not let it pierce the hero’s entrails. Odysseus knew that his hour had not yet come. He gave ground and said to Socus, “Wretch, now you will surely die. You have kept me from fighting further against the Trojans, but you will fall to my spear, giving glory to me and your soul to Hades of the noble horses.”

Socus had turned to run, but as he did, the spear struck him in the back midway between the shoulders and went right through his chest. He fell heavily to the ground, and Odysseus boasted over him. “Socus, son of Hippasus, tamer of horses, death has been too quick for you, and you have not escaped it. Poor wretch, not even in death will your father and mother close your eyes. The ravening vultures will cover you with the flapping of their dark wings and devour you. But if I fall, the Achaeans will give me the proper rites of burial.”

With that, Odysseus drew Socus’s heavy spear out of his flesh and out of his shield. The blood welled out when the spear was pulled free, and that dismayed him badly. When the Trojans saw that Odysseus was bleeding, they raised a great shout and came at him in a body. He gave ground and called to his comrades to come help him. Three times he cried as loudly as a man can, and three times brave Menelaus heard him. Menelaus turned to Ajax, who was close beside him, and said, “Ajax, noble son of Telamon, captain of your people, the cry of Odysseus rings in my ears, as though the Trojans had cut him off and were getting the better of him, alone as he is. Let us make our way through the throng and defend him. I fear he may come to harm, for all his valor, if he is left without support, and the Danaans would miss him badly.”

Menelaus led the way, and mighty Ajax went with him. The Trojans had gathered around Odysseus like ravenous mountain jackals around the carcass of a horned stag that has been hit with an arrow. The stag runs at full speed as long as his blood is warm and his strength lasts; when the arrow overcomes him, the savage jackals devour him in the shady glades of the forest. Then heaven sends a fierce lion their way, the jackals run in terror, and the lion robs them of their prey. In the same way many brave Trojans gathered around crafty Odysseus, but the hero stood at bay and kept them off with his spear. Then Ajax came up with his shield before him like a wall and stood close by, and the Trojans fled in all directions. Menelaus took Odysseus by the hand and led him out of the press while his squire brought up his chariot. Ajax rushed furiously at the Trojans and killed Doryclus, a bastard son of Priam. Then he wounded Pandocus, Lysandrus, Pyrasus, and Pylartes. Ajax was like a swollen torrent that rushes in full flood from the mountains onto the plain, big with the rain of heaven. It engulfs many a dry oak and many a pine, and it brings down much mud and casts it into the sea. So brave Ajax chased the enemy furiously over the plain, slaying men and horses alike.

Hector did not yet know what Ajax was doing. He was fighting on the far left of the battle by the banks of the river Scamander, where the slaughter was thickest and the war cry loudest around Nestor and brave Idomeneus. Hector was making great slaughter among them with his spear and furious driving, destroying the ranks that stood against him. Even so, the Achaeans would not have given ground if Paris, husband of lovely Helen, had not stopped the prowess of Machaon, shepherd of his people, by wounding him in the right shoulder with a triple-barbed arrow. The Achaeans were in great fear that, with the fight turned against them, the Trojans might take Machaon prisoner. Idomeneus said to Nestor, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, get into your chariot at once. Take Machaon with you and drive your horses to the ships as fast as you can. A physician is worth more than several other men put together, because he can cut out arrows and spread healing herbs.”

Nestor, knight of Gerene, did as Idomeneus had advised. He got into his chariot at once, and Machaon, son of the famed physician Asclepius, went with him. Nestor lashed the horses, and they flew toward the ships without hesitation, as if of their own free will.

Then Cebriones saw the Trojans in confusion and spoke to Hector from his place beside him. “Hector, the two of us are fighting out here on the far wing of the battle, while the other Trojans are in a jumbled rout, themselves and their horses. Ajax son of Telamon is driving them before him. I know him by the breadth of his shield. Let us turn our chariot and horses to where horse and foot are fighting hardest and the battle cry is loudest.”

Cebriones lashed his fine horses. They felt the whip and pulled the chariot at full speed into the Achaeans and Trojans, over the bodies and shields of the fallen. Blood spattered the axle, and the rail around the car was covered with splashes thrown up by the horses’ hoofs and the tires of the wheels. Hector tore his way through and flung himself into the thick of the fight. The Danaans fell into confusion when he appeared, since his spear was never idle for long. He went among the ranks with sword and spear and threw great stones, yet he kept clear of Ajax son of Telamon, because Zeus would have been angry if Hector had fought a better man than himself.

Then father Zeus on his high throne struck fear into the heart of Ajax. Ajax stood there dazed and threw his shield behind him. He looked fearfully at the throng of his enemies like some wild beast, turning this way and that but backing away slowly, crouching. It was like peasants and their hounds driving a lion from their stockyard and keeping watch by night to stop him carrying off the pick of their herd. He makes his greedy spring, but in vain, for darts from many a strong hand fall thick around him, and burning brands scare him for all his fury, and when morning comes he slinks away, foiled and angry. In the same way Ajax, sorely against his will, retreated angrily before the Trojans, fearing for the ships of the Achaeans. Or he was like a lazy ass that has had many a cudgel broken on his back. He goes into a field and starts eating the corn. Boys beat him, but he is too much for them, and though they lay about with their sticks they cannot hurt him. Still, when he has had his fill, they finally drive him from the field. In the same way the Trojans and their allies pursued great Ajax, ever striking the middle of his shield with their darts. Now and again he would turn and show fight, holding back the Trojan battalions, and then he would retreat again. But he kept any of them from making his way to the ships. He stood alone midway between the Trojans and Achaeans. Of the spears that sped from their hands, some stuck in his mighty shield, while many fell to the ground, though thirsting for his blood, before they could reach him and wound his fair flesh.

Eurypylus, the brave son of Euaemon, saw that the rain of arrows was overpowering Ajax. He went up to him and hurled his spear, and it struck Apisaon son of Phausius in the liver, below the midriff, and laid him low. Eurypylus sprang on him and stripped the armor from his shoulders. But Paris saw him at it and aimed an arrow at him. It hit him in the right thigh and broke off, and the point left in the wound dragged at the thigh. So Eurypylus drew back among his comrades to save his life. As he went, he shouted to the Danaans, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, rally to the defense of Ajax, who is being overpowered. I doubt he will come out of this fight alive. Come here, then, and rescue great Ajax son of Telamon.”

He cried out like this when he was wounded, and the others came near and gathered around him, holding their shields up from their shoulders to cover him. Ajax then moved toward them, and as soon as he reached his men he turned around to stand at bay.

So they fought, like a flaming fire. Meanwhile the mares of Neleus, all in a lather of sweat, were carrying Nestor out of the fight, and Machaon, shepherd of his people, with him. Achilles saw them and took note. He was standing on the stern of his ship, watching the hard stress and struggle of the battle. He called out from the ship to his comrade Patroclus. Patroclus heard him in the tent and came out looking like Ares himself—this was the beginning of the evil that soon befell him. “Achilles,” he said, “why do you call me? What do you want with me?” Achilles answered, “Noble son of Menoetius, man after my own heart, I think the Achaeans will soon be praying at my knees, for they are in great straits. Go, Patroclus, and ask Nestor who it is that he is carrying away wounded from the field. From behind I would say it was Machaon son of Asclepius, but I could not see his face, because the horses went past me at full speed.”
Patroclus did what his dear comrade had told him and ran off past the ships and tents of the Achaeans.

Nestor and Machaon reached the tents of the son of Neleus and dismounted, and an esquire, Eurymedon, took the horses from the chariot. The two men stood in the breeze by the seaside to dry the sweat from their shirts. Then they went inside and took their seats. Fair Hecamede mixed them a mess. Nestor had been awarded her from Tenedos when Achilles took it; she was the daughter of wise Arsinous, and the Achaeans had given her to Nestor because he excelled all of them in counsel. First she set before them a fair, well-made table with feet of cyanus. On it were a bronze vessel, an onion to give relish to the drink, and honey and cakes of barley meal. There was also a cup of rare workmanship that the old man had brought from home, studded with bosses of gold. It had four handles, and on each handle two golden doves were feeding; it stood on two feet. Anyone else would hardly have been able to lift it from the table when it was full, but Nestor lifted it quite easily. In this cup the woman, as fair as a goddess, mixed them a mess with Pramnian wine. She grated goat’s milk cheese into it with a bronze grater and threw in a handful of white barley meal. When the mess was ready she told them to drink it. They drank and quenched their thirst, and then they fell to talking with one another. At this moment Patroclus appeared at the door.

The old man saw him, sprang from his seat, seized his hand and led him into the tent, and told him to take a place among them. But Patroclus stayed where he was. “Noble sir,” he said, “I may not stay. You cannot persuade me to come in. The man who sent me is not one to be trifled with, and he told me to ask who the wounded man was that you were carrying away from the field. I can see for myself now that it is Machaon, shepherd of his people. I must go back and tell Achilles. You, sir, know what a terrible man he is, and how ready to blame even where no blame is due.”

Nestor answered, “Why should Achilles care to know how many of the Achaeans are wounded? He pays no heed to the dismay that reigns in our host. Our most valiant chieftains lie disabled. Brave Diomedes, son of Tydeus, is wounded, and so are Odysseus and Agamemnon. Eurypylus has been hit in the thigh with an arrow, and I have just brought this man from the field, also wounded with an arrow. Yet Achilles, valiant as he is, does not care and knows no pity. Will he wait until the ships are in a blaze, do what we may, and we perish one on top of another? As for me, I have no strength or staying power left. I wish I were still young and strong, as in the days when a fight broke out between us and the men of Elis over some cattle raiding. I killed Itymoneus then, the valiant son of Hypeirochus, who lived in Elis. I was driving off the spoil, and he was hit by a dart thrown from my hand as he fought in the front rank to defend his cows. He fell, and the country people around him were in great fear. We drove off a vast quantity of booty from the plain: fifty herds of cattle and as many flocks of sheep, fifty droves of pigs, and as many wide-spreading flocks of goats. We also seized a hundred and fifty horses, all of them mares, and many had foals running with them. We drove all these by night to Pylus, the city of Neleus, and took them inside the city. Neleus was glad that I had taken so much, though it was the first time I had ever been in the field. At daybreak the heralds went around crying that all in Elis who were owed a debt should come, and the leading Pylians assembled to divide the spoils. The Epeans owed chattels to many people, for we men of Pylus were few and had been oppressed with wrong. In former years Heracles had come and laid his hand heavy on us, and all our best men had perished. Neleus had had twelve sons, but I alone was left; the others had all been killed. The Epeans presumed on all this, looked down on us and did us much evil. My father chose a herd of cattle and a great flock of sheep, three hundred in all, and took their shepherds with him. A great debt was due to him in Elis, namely four prize-winning horses. They and their chariots had gone to the games to run for a tripod, but King Augeas took them and sent back their driver, grieving for the loss of his horses. Neleus was angered by what Augeas had said and done, and took great value in return. The rest he divided, so that no man would have less than his full share.

“So we arranged everything and offered sacrifices to the gods throughout the city. Three days later the Epeans came in a body, many in number, with their chariots, in full array. The two Moliones came with them in their armor, though they were still lads and unused to fighting. Now there is a certain town, Thryoessa, perched on a rock by the river Alpheus, the border city of Pylus. The Epeans wanted to destroy it, and they pitched their camp around it. But when they had crossed their whole plain, Athena darted down by night from Olympus and told us to set ourselves in array. She found willing soldiers in Pylos, for the men meant to fight. Neleus would not let me arm. He hid my horses, for he said I could not yet know anything about war. Nevertheless Athena so ordered the fight that I, all on foot as I was, fought among our mounted forces and vied with the foremost of them. There is a river Minyeius that falls into the sea near Arene. There those of us who were mounted (and I with them) waited until morning, when the companies of foot soldiers came up with us in force. From there, in full panoply and equipment, we came toward noon to the sacred waters of the Alpheus. There we offered victims to almighty Zeus, with a bull to Alpheus, another to Poseidon, and a herd heifer to Athena. After this we took supper in our companies and lay down to rest, each in his armor, by the river.

“The Epeans were besieging the city and were determined to take it, but before that could happen a desperate fight was in store for them. When the sun’s rays began to fall on the earth we joined battle, praying to Zeus and Athena. Once the fight had begun, I was the first to kill my man and take his horses, the warrior Mulius. He was son-in-law to Augeas, married to his eldest daughter, golden-haired Agamede, who knew the virtues of every herb that grows on the face of the earth. I speared him as he came toward me. When he fell headlong in the dust I sprang onto his chariot and took my place in the front ranks. The Epeans fled in all directions when they saw the captain of their horsemen, the best man they had, laid low. I swept down on them like a whirlwind and took fifty chariots, and in each of them two men bit the dust, slain by my spear. I would even have killed the two Moliones, sons of Actor, if their real father, Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, had not hidden them in a thick mist and carried them out of the fight. Then Zeus granted the Pylians a great victory. We chased the Epeans far over the plain, killing the men and gathering their armor, until we brought our horses to Buprasium, rich in wheat, and to the Olenian rock, and the hill called Alision, where Athena turned the people back. There I killed the last man and left him. Then the Achaeans drove their horses back from Buprasium to Pylos, and gave thanks to Zeus among the gods, and among mortal men to Nestor.

“That is what I was among my peers, as surely as ever any man was, but Achilles means to keep all his valor for himself. He will bitterly regret it later, when the host is being cut to pieces. My good friend, did Menoetius not give you this charge on the day he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon? Odysseus and I were inside the house and heard everything he said to you. We had come to the fair house of Peleus while recruiting throughout all Achaea, and when we arrived we found Menoetius and yourself there, and Achilles with you. The old knight Peleus was in the outer court, roasting the fat thigh-bones of a heifer for Zeus, lord of thunder. He held a gold chalice in his hand and poured drink offerings of wine over the burning sacrifice. You two were busy cutting up the heifer, and just then we stood at the gates. Achilles sprang to his feet, led us by the hand into the house, seated us at table, and set before us the hospitality that guests expect. When we had had enough meat and drink, I said my say and urged both of you to join us. You were ready enough, and the two old men gave you many strict charges. Old Peleus told his son Achilles to fight always among the foremost and to outdo his peers. Menoetius the son of Actor spoke to you like this: ‘My son, Achilles is of nobler birth than you, but you are older than he, though he is far the better man of the two. Counsel him wisely, guide him the right way, and he will follow you to his own profit.’ That was your father’s charge to you, but you have forgotten it. Even now, though, say all this to Achilles, if he will listen to you. Who knows whether, with heaven’s help, you may talk him over? It is good to take a friend’s advice. But if he is fearful about some oracle, or if his mother has told him something from Zeus, then let him send you, and let the rest of the Myrmidons follow with you, in case you may bring light and rescue to the Danaans. And let him send you into battle dressed in his own armor, so that the Trojans may mistake you for him and stop fighting. The sons of the Achaeans may then have time to get their breath, for they are hard pressed and there is little breathing time in battle. You are fresh, and might easily drive a tired enemy back to his walls, away from the tents and ships.”

Nestor’s words moved the heart of Patroclus, and he ran off along the line of the ships toward Achilles, descendant of Aeacus. Near the ships of Odysseus, where the Achaeans held their assemblies and their court of justice, and where their altars to the gods stood, he met Eurypylus son of Euaemon. Eurypylus was limping out of the fight with an arrow in his thigh. Sweat rained from his head and shoulders, and black blood welled from his cruel wound, yet his mind did not wander. The son of Menoetius felt compassion at the sight and spoke to him piteously. “Unhappy princes and counselors of the Danaans! Are you doomed, then, to feed the hounds of Troy with your fat, far from your friends and your native land? Tell me, noble Eurypylus, can the Achaeans hold great Hector in check, or will they fall now before his spear?”

Wounded Eurypylus answered, “Noble Patroclus, the Achaeans have no hope left. They will perish at their ships. Every man who was a prince among us lies struck down and wounded by the Trojans, and the Trojans are growing stronger and stronger. But save me. Take me to your ship, cut the arrow out of my thigh, and wash the black blood from it with warm water. Then lay on it those gracious herbs that Achilles showed you, so they say, and that Chiron, most righteous of all the centaurs, showed to him. As for the physicians Podalirius and Machaon, I hear that one is lying wounded in his tent and needs healing himself, while the other is fighting the Trojans on the plain.”

“Hero Eurypylus,” the brave son of Menoetius replied, “what can be done? How can this be? I am on my way to noble Achilles with a message from Nestor of Gerene, bulwark of the Achaeans. Even so, I will not forget your distress.”

With this he put his arm around Eurypylus’s middle and led him into the tent. A servant saw him and spread bullock-skins on the ground for him to lie on. Patroclus laid him at full length and cut the sharp arrow out of his thigh. He washed the black blood from the wound with warm water. Then he crushed a bitter herb between his hands and spread it on the wound. This was a virtuous herb that killed all pain, and the wound soon dried and the blood stopped flowing.

chapters.title: Book 12
paragraphs: Led by Hector, the Trojans and their allies break through the wall.

While the son of Menoetius tended Eurypylus’s wound inside the tent, the Argives and Trojans went on fighting desperately. But the trench and the high wall above it were not going to hold the Trojans back much longer. The Achaeans had built the wall to protect their ships, and had dug the trench all around it to keep both the ships and the rich spoils they had taken safe. But they had never offered a great sacrifice to the gods. Because it was built without the immortals’ consent, it did not last. As long as Hector lived, Achilles kept up his anger, and Priam’s city stayed unsacked, the great wall of the Achaeans stood firm. Then the bravest of the Trojans died, and many of the Argives too, though some were still alive. In the tenth year the city was sacked, and the Argives sailed home to their own country. After that Poseidon and Apollo made a plan to destroy the wall. They turned the streams of all the rivers that run from Mount Ida to the sea onto it: the Rhesus, the Heptaporus, the Caresus, the Rhodius, the Grenicus, the Aesopus, and goodly Scamander, and the Simois, where many a shield and helmet had fallen and many a hero of the race of demigods had bitten the dust. Phoebus Apollo brought the mouths of all these rivers together and sent them flowing against the wall for nine days. Zeus rained the whole time, so that the wall would be washed into the sea sooner. Poseidon himself, trident in hand, looked over the work. He threw into the sea all the foundations of beams and stones that the Achaeans had laid with so much toil. He leveled everything along the mighty stream of the Hellespont, and when the wall was swept away he spread a great beach of sand over the place where it had stood. Then he turned the rivers back into their old channels.

That was what Poseidon and Apollo would do in later times. For now, battle and turmoil still raged around the wall, and its timbers rang under the blows that rained on them. Cowed by the scourge of Zeus, the Argives were penned in at their ships, afraid of Hector, the mighty minister of Rout, who fought as before with the force and fury of a whirlwind. A lion or wild boar turns fiercely on the dogs and men who attack him. They stand together in a solid wall and shower javelins at him as they face him. His courage is not shaken at all, but his high spirit will be the death of him. Many times he charges at his pursuers to scatter them, and each time they give way. In the same way Hector went about among the host, urging his men on and calling them to cross the trench.

But the horses did not dare. They stood neighing at the edge, because the width of it frightened them. They could neither jump it nor cross it. It had overhanging banks all the way around on both sides, and above these were the sharp stakes that the sons of the Achaeans had planted close and strong to guard against anyone who attacked. A horse could not get down into it and pull his chariot after him. The men on foot, though, kept trying with all their strength. Then Polydamas went up to Hector and said, “Hector, and you other captains of the Trojans and allies, it is madness to try to drive our horses across the trench. It will be very hard to cross, because it is full of sharp stakes, and beyond them is the wall. The horses cannot get down into it, and they would be no use if they did. It is also a narrow place, and we would come to harm. If great Zeus really means to help the Trojans, and in his anger will utterly destroy the Achaeans, I would gladly see them perish here and now, far from Argos. But suppose they rally, and we are driven back from the ships in a jumble into the trench. Then not one man will get back to the city to tell the tale. So let us all do as I say. Let our squires hold our horses by the trench, and let us follow Hector in a body on foot, in full armor. If the day of their doom is near, the Achaeans will not be able to stand against us.”

So Polydamas spoke, and Hector liked what he said. He sprang to the ground in full armor, and when the other Trojans saw him do it, they all left their chariots too. Each man handed his horses to his charioteer, to hold them ready for him at the trench. Then they formed into companies, got themselves ready, and followed their leaders in five bodies. The ones who went with Hector and Polydamas were the bravest and the most numerous, and the most determined to break through the wall and fight at the ships. Cebriones joined them as third in command, since Hector had left his chariot in the care of a less valiant soldier. Paris, Alcathous and Agenor led the next company. Helenus and Deiphobus, two sons of Priam, led the third, and with them was the hero Asius, son of Hyrtacus, whose great black horses of the breed from the river Selleis had carried him from Arisbe. Aeneas, the valiant son of Anchises, led the fourth, together with the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, men well versed in every art of war. Sarpedon was captain of the allies. He took with him Glaucus and Asteropaeus, whom he considered the most valiant after himself, for he was far the best of them all. They helped one another put on their ox-hide shields, and then charged straight at the Danaans. They were sure the Danaans could not hold out any longer, and that they themselves would now fall on the ships.

The rest of the Trojans and their allies now followed the advice of Polydamas. But Asius, son of Hyrtacus, would not leave his horses and his squire behind. In his foolhardiness he took them on toward the ships, and it brought him to his end. He was never to return to wind-beaten Ilium, boasting in his chariot and his horses. Before that, death with its ill-omened name overshadowed him, and he fell by the spear of Idomeneus, the noble son of Deucalion. He had driven toward the left wing of the ships, the way the Achaeans used to come back from the plain with their chariots and horses. He drove there and found the gates standing wide open, with the great bar down, because the gatemen kept them open to let in any comrades who might be fleeing toward the ships. Asius steered his horses there on purpose, and his men followed with a loud cry. They were sure the Achaeans could not hold out any longer and that they would now fall on the ships. They little knew that at the gates they would find two of the bravest chieftains, proud sons of the fighting Lapithae. One was Polypoetes, the mighty son of Pirithous, and the other was Leonteus, peer of murderous Ares. These two stood before the gates like two high oak trees on the mountains, which tower up from their wide-spreading roots and battle the wind and rain year after year. In the same way these two men awaited the onset of great Asius with confidence, without flinching. The Trojans raised a loud battle cry and made straight for the wall, holding their shields of dry ox-hide above their heads. They were led by Asius and by Iamenus, Orestes, Adamas the son of Asius, Thoon and Oenomaus. For a while the two defenders stayed inside and called on the Achaeans to stand firm in defense of their ships. But then they saw the Trojans attacking the wall, while the Danaans cried out for help and were routed. They rushed outside and fought in front of the gates like two wild boars on the mountains. The boars wait for the attack of men and dogs, and charging at them from either side they break down the wood all around, tearing it up by the roots, and one can hear the clattering of their tusks until someone hits them and ends them. So the gleaming bronze rattled about the breasts of the two men as the weapons fell on them. They fought with great fury, trusting in their own prowess and in the men on the wall above them. These threw great stones at the attackers to defend themselves, their tents and their ships. The stones fell as thick as flakes of snow, when a fierce blast drives them from the dark clouds and showers them down in sheets upon the earth. So the weapons fell from the hands of Trojans and Achaeans alike. Helmet and shield rang out as the great stones rained on them. Asius, son of Hyrtacus, cried out in dismay and struck his two thighs. “Father Zeus,” he cried, “truly you too are altogether given to lying. I was sure the Argive heroes could not withstand us. But they are like slim-waisted wasps, or bees that have their nests in the rocks by the wayside. These do not leave the holes they have built undefended, but fight for their little ones against anyone who would take them. In the same way these men, though they are only two, will not be driven from the gates. They stand firm to kill or be killed.”

He spoke, but he did not change the mind of Zeus, whose plan at that time was to give glory to Hector. Meanwhile the rest of the Trojans were fighting at the other gates. I, however, am no god, and cannot tell about all these things, for the battle raged everywhere around the stone wall like a fiery furnace. The Argives, beaten though they were, were forced to defend their ships, and all the gods who were defending the Achaeans were vexed in spirit. But the Lapithae kept on fighting with all their might.

Then Polypoetes, mighty son of Pirithous, hit Damasus on his cheek-pierced helmet with a spear. The helmet did not protect him. The point of the spear went through it and broke the bone, so that the brain inside was scattered about, and he died fighting. Polypoetes then killed Pylon and Ormenus. Leonteus, of the race of Ares, killed Hippomachus the son of Antimachus, by striking him on the girdle with his spear. Then he drew his sword and sprang first on Antiphates, whom he killed in close combat, and who fell face upward on the ground. After him he killed Menon, Iamenus and Orestes, and laid them low one after another.

While the two Lapiths were busy stripping the armor from these heroes, the young men led by Polydamas and Hector were still standing by the trench, unsure what to do. These were the greater part and the most valiant of those trying to break through the wall and set fire to the ships. They had seen a sign from heaven when they tried to cross. An eagle soared along the left wing of their host, carrying a monstrous blood-red snake in its talons, still alive and struggling to escape. The snake had not given up its revenge. It twisted and wriggled backward until it struck the bird that held it, on the neck and breast. In pain, the bird let it fall into the middle of the host, and then flew off down the wind with a sharp cry. The Trojans were struck with terror when they saw the snake, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus, writhing in the midst of them. Polydamas went up to Hector and said, “Hector, at our councils of war you are always rebuking me, even when I speak wisely. It seems it is not right, you say, for one of the people to cross your will, either in the field or at the council board. You want them to support you always. Still, I will say what I think is best. Let us not go on now to fight the Danaans at their ships. I know what will happen, if this soaring eagle that skirted the left wing of our host with a monstrous blood-red snake in its talons (the snake still alive) was really sent as an omen to the Trojans as they tried to cross the trench. The eagle let go her hold. She did not manage to take the snake home to her little ones, and so it will be with us. Even if by a mighty effort we break through the gates and wall of the Achaeans, and they give way before us, we shall still not return in good order the way we came. We shall leave many a man behind, whom the Achaeans will put to death in defense of their ships. This is how any seer who was expert in these matters, and trusted by the people, would read the portent.”

Hector looked fiercely at him and said, “Polydamas, I do not like your reading. You can find a better thing to say than this, if you try. But if you have spoken in good earnest, then heaven has robbed you of your reason. You would have me pay no heed to the counsels of Zeus, or to the promises he made me, when he bowed his head in confirmation. You tell me to be ruled instead by the flight of wild birds. What do I care whether they fly toward dawn or dark, or whether they are on my right hand or my left? Let us put our trust rather in the counsel of great Zeus, king of mortals and immortals. There is one omen, and one only: that a man should fight for his country. Why are you so afraid? Even if all the rest of us are killed at the ships of the Argives, you are not likely to be killed yourself, because you are neither steadfast nor courageous. If you will not fight, or if you talk others out of fighting, you shall fall at once before my spear.”

He led the way with these words, and the others followed with a shout that tore the air. Then Zeus, lord of thunder, sent a blast of mighty wind down from the mountains of Ida, and it carried the dust toward the ships. In this way he lulled the Achaeans into feeling secure, and he gave victory to Hector and the Trojans. They trusted in their own strength and in the signs he had shown them, and they tried to break through the great wall of the Achaeans. They tore the breastworks off the walls and threw down the battlements. They heaved up the buttresses, which the Achaeans had planted in front of the wall to hold it up. Once these were pulled down, the Trojans felt sure they would break through the wall. But the Danaans showed no sign of giving ground. They kept the battlements fenced with their shields of ox-hide, and hurled missiles down on any enemy who came below the wall.

The two Ajaxes went all along the walls, cheering on the Achaeans. They spoke kindly to some, and sharply to anyone they saw holding back. “My friends,” they cried, “Argives one and all—good, bad and indifferent, for there was never yet a fight in which all were equal in prowess—there is work enough now for all of you, as you very well know. Make sure that none of you turns in flight toward the ships, daunted by the shouting of the enemy. Press forward and keep one another’s courage up. Perhaps Olympian Zeus, lord of lightning, will grant that we repel our foes and drive them back toward the city.”

So the two went about shouting and urging the Achaeans on. The stones fell as thickly as the flakes of snow on a winter’s day, when Zeus is minded to snow and show mankind these arrows of his. He lulls the wind to rest and snows hour after hour, until he has buried the tops of the high mountains, the headlands that jut into the sea, the grassy plains and the tilled fields of men. The snow lies deep on the forelands and the harbors of the gray sea, but the waves rolling in hold it back so that it can come no further, though everything else is wrapped as in a mantle, so heavy are the heavens with snow. Just so thickly did the stones fall on both sides, some thrown at the Trojans, and some by the Trojans at the Achaeans, and the whole wall was in an uproar.

The Trojans and brave Hector would still not have broken down the gates and the great bar, if Zeus had not turned his son Sarpedon against the Argives, like a lion against a herd of horned cattle. Sarpedon held before him his shield of hammered bronze, which the smith had beaten so fair and round and lined with ox-hides, fastening them with rivets of gold all around the shield. He held this in front of him and brandished two spears, and he came on like a lion of the wilderness that has long been famished for want of meat and will dare to break even into a well-fenced homestead to get at the sheep. The lion may find shepherds keeping watch over their flocks with dogs and spears, but he has no mind to be driven from the fold before he has made his try. Either he will spring on a sheep and carry it off, or a strong hand will hit him with a spear. In just that way Sarpedon was eager to attack the wall and break down its battlements. Then he said to Glaucus son of Hippolochus, “Glaucus, why do we in Lycia receive special honor in our place at table? Why are the choicest portions served to us and our cups kept brimming, and why do men look up to us as though we were gods? Besides, we hold a large estate by the banks of the river Xanthus, fair with orchard lawns and wheat-growing land. So it is right for us to take our stand at the head of all the Lycians and bear the brunt of the fight. Then one man can say to another, ‘Our princes in Lycia eat the fat of the land and drink the best wine, but they are fine fellows. They fight well and are always at the front in battle.’ My good friend, if we could get out of this fight and then escape old age and death forever after, I would neither press forward myself nor tell you to. But death in ten thousand shapes hangs always over our heads, and no man can elude him. So let us go forward and either win glory for ourselves or yield it to another.”

Glaucus listened to what he said, and the pair at once led on the host of Lycians. Menestheus son of Peteos was dismayed when he saw them, for they were coming against his part of the wall, bringing destruction with them. He looked along the wall for some chieftain to support his comrades, and he saw the two Ajaxes, men always eager for the fray, with Teucer, who had just come from his tent, standing near them. But he could not make his voice heard by shouting to them, so great was the uproar of crashing shields and helmets and the battering at the gates, a din that reached the skies. All the gates had been closed, and the Trojans were hammering at them to try to break through. So Menestheus sent Thootes with a message to Ajax. “Run, good Thootes,” he said, “and call Ajax—or better still, tell both to come, for it will soon be all over with us here. The leaders of the Lycians are upon us, men who have always fought desperately before. But if they have too much on their hands to come, then at least let Ajax son of Telamon come, and let Teucer, the famous bowman, come with him.”

The messenger did as he was told. He ran along the wall of the Achaeans until he reached the Ajaxes, and said to them, “Sirs, princes of the Argives, the son of noble Peteos begs you to go to him for a while and help. It would be best if you both came, or it will soon be all over with him. The leaders of the Lycians are upon him, men who have always fought desperately in the past. If you are too busy for both to leave, then Ajax son of Telamon must come at least, and Teucer, the famous bowman, with him.”

Great Ajax son of Telamon heard the message and spoke at once to the son of Oileus. “Ajax,” he said, “you two, yourself and brave Lycomedes, must stay here and keep the Danaans fighting as hard as they can. I am going over there to take my part in the fray. As soon as I have given them the help they need, I will come straight back.”

Ajax son of Telamon set off at once, and Teucer, his brother by the same father, went too, with Pandion carrying Teucer’s bow. They went along inside the wall. They came to the tower where Menestheus was, and found him hard pressed indeed. The brave captains and leaders of the Lycians were storming the battlements like a thick dark cloud, fighting at close quarters and raising the battle cry aloud.

First, Ajax son of Telamon killed brave Epicles, a comrade of Sarpedon. He hit him with a jagged stone that lay by the battlements at the very top of the wall. As men are now, even one in the bloom of youth could hardly lift it with both hands, but Ajax raised it high and flung it down. It smashed Epicles’ four-crested helmet and crushed the bones of his head to pieces, and he fell from the high wall like a diver, with no life left in him. Then Teucer wounded Glaucus, the brave son of Hippolochus, as he was coming on to attack the wall. Teucer saw his shoulder bare and aimed an arrow at it, and this made Glaucus stop fighting. He sprang down out of sight, for fear some of the Achaeans might see that he was wounded and taunt him. Sarpedon was stung with grief when he saw Glaucus leave him, but he did not stop fighting. He aimed his spear at Alcmaon son of Thestor and hit him. He drew the spear back again, and Alcmaon came down headlong after it, his bronzed armor clattering around him. Then Sarpedon seized the battlement in his strong hands and tugged at it until it all gave way together, and a breach was made through which many could pass.

Ajax and Teucer both turned on him. Teucer’s arrow struck the strap that carried the shield over his body, but Zeus saved his son from destruction, for he was not to fall by the ships’ sterns. At the same moment Ajax sprang at him and pierced the shield, though the spear did not go clean through it. It shoved Sarpedon back, so that he could advance no further. He gave up a little space by the battlement, though not all his ground, since he still thought to cover himself with glory. Then he turned and shouted to the brave Lycians, “Lycians, why do you fail me like this? For all my prowess, I cannot break through the wall alone and open a way to the ships. Follow close behind me. The more of us there are, the better.”

The Lycians, shamed by his rebuke, pressed closer around their counselor and king. The Argives, for their part, got their men into fighting order inside the wall, and a deadly struggle began between them. The Lycians could not break through the wall and force their way to the ships, and the Danaans could not drive the Lycians from the wall now that they had reached it. As two men, measuring-rods in hand, quarrel over the boundaries of a field they own in common and argue stubbornly for their rights though it is only a narrow strip, so now the battlements became a bone of contention, and the two sides beat one another’s round shields for possession of them. Many a man’s body was wounded by the pitiless bronze when he turned and bared his back to the foe, and many were struck clean through their shields. The wall and battlements were everywhere drenched with the blood of Trojans and Achaeans alike. Even so, the Trojans could not rout the Achaeans, who held on. As some honest hard-working woman weighs wool in her balance and checks that the scales are true, because she wants to win a pitiful wage for her little ones, so evenly was the fight balanced between them, until the time came when Zeus gave the greater glory to Hector son of Priam, who was first to spring toward the wall of the Achaeans. When he had done so, he cried aloud to the Trojans, “Up, Trojans, break the wall of the Argives and fling fire upon their ships.”

So he drove them on, and they rushed at the wall in one body, as he had ordered, and climbed the battlements with sharp spears in their hands. Just outside the gates lay a stone, thick at one end and pointed at the other, and Hector took hold of it. Two of the best men in a town, as men are now, could hardly have heaved it from the ground onto a wagon, but Hector lifted it easily by himself, since the son of scheming Cronus made it light for him. A shepherd picks up a ram’s fleece in one hand and finds it no burden. That is how easily Hector lifted the great stone and drove it at the doors that closed the gates, so strong and so firmly set. The doors were double and high, held shut by two crossbars that had only one key. He came close, then strode forward so that his blow would gain force, and struck the middle of them, leaning his whole weight against them. Both hinges broke, and the stone dropped inside, so heavy it was. The portals re-echoed with the sound, the bars gave way, and the doors burst open, one flying each way, from the force of the blow. Then brave Hector leaped inside, his face as dark as flying night. The gleaming bronze flashed fiercely about his body, and he had two spears in his hand. No one but a god could have withstood him as he flung himself into the gateway, and his eyes glared like fire. Turning to the Trojans, he called on them to scale the wall, and they obeyed. Some climbed straight over the wall while others came through the gates. The Danaans fled in panic toward their ships, and all was uproar and confusion.

chapters.title: Book 13
paragraphs: Poseidon helps the Achaeans—The feats of Idomeneus—Hector at the ships.

Now that Zeus had brought Hector and the Trojans to the ships, he left them to their endless toil. He turned his keen eyes away and looked elsewhere, toward the horse-breeders of Thrace, the Mysians who fight at close quarters, the noble Hippemolgi who live on milk, and the Abians, the most just of mankind. He no longer cast even a glance toward Troy. He did not think that any of the immortals would go to help either the Trojans or the Danaans.

But King Poseidon had not been keeping a careless watch. He sat on the highest peaks of wooded Samothrace and gazed at the battle in admiration. From there he could see all of Ida, with the city of Priam and the ships of the Achaeans. He had come up from under the sea to take this seat, because he pitied the Achaeans, who were being beaten by the Trojans, and he was furiously angry with Zeus.

Soon he left his post on the mountaintop. He strode swiftly on, and the high hills and the forest shook under his immortal feet. He took three strides, and with the fourth he reached his destination, Aegae, where his glittering golden palace stands in the depths of the sea, never to decay. When he arrived, he harnessed his swift bronze-footed horses, whose golden manes streamed in the wind. He put on clothing of gold, took up his golden whip, and stepped onto his chariot. As he drove out over the waves, the sea monsters left their lairs, for they knew their lord. They came playing around him from every part of the deep, and the sea in her gladness opened a path for his chariot. The horses flew so lightly that the bronze axle of the car stayed dry beneath it. In this way his bounding horses carried him to the ships of the Achaeans.

In the depths of the sea, midway between Tenedos and rocky Imbrus, there is a huge cavern. Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, stopped his horses there, unyoked them, and set ambrosial fodder before them. He tied their feet with golden hobbles that no one could loosen or break, so that they would stay in that place until their lord came back. Then he went on to the army of the Achaeans.

The Trojans were following Hector son of Priam in close formation, like a storm cloud or a blaze of fire. They fought with all their strength and raised the battle cry, for they believed they would take the ships of the Achaeans and kill all their greatest heroes then and there. Meanwhile earth-encircling Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, was encouraging the Argives. He had come up out of the sea and taken the form and voice of Calchas.

He spoke first to the two Ajaxes, who were already doing their best. “Ajaxes,” he said, “you two can save the Achaeans, if you give all your strength and refuse to be frightened. I am not afraid for any other part of the line, though the Trojans have crossed the wall in force. The Achaeans can hold them all back there. But I fear greatly that some evil will fall on us here, where furious Hector is leading them on like a pillar of flame. He boasts that he is the son of great Zeus himself. May some god put it into your hearts to make a firm stand here and to urge others to do the same. Then you will drive him from the ships, even if Zeus himself inspires him.”

As he spoke, the earth-encircling lord of the earthquake struck them both with his scepter and filled their hearts with courage. He made their legs light and quick, and their hands and feet as well. Then, as a soaring falcon hovers on the wing high above a sheer rock and soon swoops down to chase a bird over the plain, so Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, took wing into the air and left them. Swift Ajax son of Oileus was the first of the two to realize who had been speaking with them. He said to Ajax son of Telamon, “Ajax, this is one of the gods who live on Olympus. He has taken the likeness of the prophet to tell us to fight hard by our ships. It was not Calchas, the seer and reader of omens. I knew him at once by his feet and knees as he turned away, for gods are easily recognized. And I feel the lust for battle burning more fiercely inside me, while my hands and feet beneath me are more eager for the fight.”
Ajax son of Telamon answered, “I feel it too. My hands grip my spear more firmly, my strength is greater, and my feet are quicker. I even long to meet furious Hector son of Priam in single combat.”

So they talked, delighting in the hunger for battle that the god had put into them. Meanwhile the earth-encircler stirred up the Achaeans who were resting in the rear by the ships. They were worn out at once by hard fighting and by grief at seeing that the Trojans had crossed the wall in force. Tears fell from their eyes as they watched, for they were sure they would not escape destruction. But the lord of the earthquake moved lightly among them and drove their battalions to the front.

He went first to Teucer and Leitus, the hero Peneleos, Thoas and Deipyrus, and Meriones and Antilochus, valiant warriors. He urged them all on. “Shame on you, young Argives,” he cried. “I relied on your prowess to save our ships. If you do not fight with all your strength, this very day will see us beaten by the Trojans. I truly see with my own eyes a great and terrible portent that I never thought I would see: Trojans at our ships! They used to be like panic-stricken deer in a forest, prey for jackals and wolves, with no strength except in flight, since they cannot defend themselves. Until now the Trojans did not dare face the attack of the Achaeans for a single moment. Now they have come far out from their city and are fighting at our very ships, because of our leader’s cowardice and the disaffection of the people themselves. In their discontent they do not care to fight in defense of the ships, and they are being slaughtered beside them. It is true that King Agamemnon son of Atreus is the cause of our disaster, because he insulted the son of Peleus. Still, that is no reason for us to stop fighting. Let us be quick to heal, for the hearts of the brave heal quickly. You do wrong to be so slack, you who are the finest soldiers in our whole army. I do not blame a man for staying out of battle if he is a weakling, but I am angry with men like you. My good friends, this slackness will soon make matters even worse. Each of you, think of your own honor and reputation, for the danger of the fight is extreme. Great Hector is now fighting at our ships. He has broken through the gates and the strong bolt that held them.”

So the earth-encircler addressed the Achaeans and urged them on. Strong bands of men gathered around the two Ajaxes. Not even Ares, or Athena who marshals the hosts, could have made light of them had they gone among them, for these were the picked men of all who were waiting for the attack of Hector and the Trojans. They made a living fence, spear to spear, shield to shield, buckler to buckler, helmet to helmet, and man to man. The horsehair crests on their gleaming helmets touched as they nodded forward, so close were they packed. The spears in their strong hands were interlaced, and their hearts were set on battle.

The Trojans advanced in a dense body, with Hector at their head pressing straight on, like a rock that comes thundering down a mountainside after winter torrents have torn it from the brow. Floods of rain have loosened the foundations of the dull thing, and as it bounds headlong on its way it sets the whole forest roaring. It swerves neither right nor left until it reaches level ground, but there, for all its fury, it can go no further. In the same way Hector for a while seemed as though he would rampage through the tents and ships of the Achaeans, slaughtering as he went, until he reached the sea. But the closely packed battalions stopped him when he reached them. The sons of the Achaeans thrust at him with swords and with spears pointed at both ends, and drove him back so that he staggered and gave ground. Then he shouted to the Trojans, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians, fighters in close combat, stand firm! The Achaeans have set themselves up as a wall against me, but they will not hold me for long. They will give way before me, if the mightiest of the gods, the thundering husband of Hera, has truly inspired my attack.”

With these words he put heart and soul into them all. Deiphobus son of Priam went among them, intent on deeds of daring. He held his round shield before him and strode quickly forward under its cover. Meriones took aim at him with a spear and did not miss, hitting the broad circle of ox-hide. But he was far from piercing it. The spear broke in two long before it could, and Deiphobus had also seen it coming and held his shield well away from him. Meriones drew back among his comrades, angry both at failing to defeat Deiphobus and at breaking his spear. So he turned toward the ships and tents to fetch a spear he had left behind in his tent.

The others went on fighting, and the cry of battle rose to the heavens. Teucer son of Telamon was the first to kill his man, the warrior Imbrius, son of Mentor, rich in horses. Until the Achaeans came, Imbrius had lived in Pedaeum and had married Medesicaste, a bastard daughter of Priam. When the Danaan fleet arrived, he went back to Ilium. He became a great man among the Trojans and lived near Priam himself, who gave him the same honor as his own sons. Now the son of Telamon struck him with a spear under the ear, then drew it back out. Imbrius fell headlong, like an ash tree felled on the crest of a high mountain beacon, when its delicate green foliage comes toppling to the ground. So he fell, with his bronze-wrought armor ringing harshly around him. Teucer sprang forward, meaning to strip off his armor, but as he did, Hector took aim at him with a spear. Teucer saw it coming and swerved aside. The spear hit Amphimachus, son of Cteatus son of Actor, in the chest as he was coming into the battle, and his armor clattered around him as he fell heavily to the ground. Hector sprang forward to pull the helmet from Amphimachus’s temples. At once Ajax threw a spear at him but did not wound him, because he was covered all over in his terrible armor. Still, the spear struck the boss of his shield with such force that it drove him back from the two corpses, and the Achaeans pulled them away. Stichius and Menestheus, captains of the Athenians, carried Amphimachus to the host of the Achaeans, while the two brave and impetuous Ajaxes did the same for Imbrius. As when two lions snatch a goat from hounds that have it in their fangs and carry it in their jaws, high off the ground, through thick brushwood, so the Ajaxes carried Imbrius’s body aloft and stripped off its armor. Then the son of Oileus, in revenge for the death of Amphimachus, cut the head from the neck and sent it whirling through the crowd like a ball, until it fell in the dust at Hector’s feet.

Poseidon was exceedingly angry that his grandson Amphimachus had fallen. He went to the tents and ships of the Achaeans to urge the Danaans on still further and to devise evil for the Trojans. Idomeneus met him as he was leaving a comrade who had just come from the fight, wounded in the knee. His fellow soldiers had carried the man off the field. Idomeneus gave orders to the physicians and went on to his tent, for he was still thirsting for battle. Poseidon spoke in the likeness and with the voice of Thoas son of Andraemon, who ruled the Aetolians of all Pleuron and high Calydon and was honored among his people as if he were a god. “Idomeneus,” he said, “lawgiver to the Cretans, what has become of the threats the sons of the Achaeans used to make against the Trojans?”

Idomeneus, chief among the Cretans, answered, “Thoas, as far as I know, no one is at fault, for we can all fight. Neither fear nor slackness holds anyone back. It seems to be the will of almighty Zeus that the Achaeans should perish without glory here, far from Argos. You, Thoas, have always been staunch, and you keep others in heart when you see anyone fail in duty. So do not be slack now, but urge everyone to do his utmost.”

Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, answered him, “Idomeneus, may the man who is slack in fighting this day by his own choice never return from Troy, but stay here for the dogs to feast on. Get your armor and come. We must hurry together, if we can be of any use, though we are only two. Even cowards gain courage from company, and we two can hold our own against the bravest.”

With that the god went back into the thick of the fight. Idomeneus reached his tent, put on his armor, took up his two spears, and rushed out. His armor gleamed about him as he ran, like the lightning that the son of Cronus brandishes from bright Olympus when he wants to show a sign to mortals, and its flash shines far and wide. His sturdy squire Meriones met him while he was still near his tent (Meriones was going to fetch his spear), and Idomeneus said:

“Meriones, swift son of Molus, best of comrades, why did you leave the fight? Has a weapon’s point wounded you and left you in pain? Or did someone send you to bring me back? I need no one to bring me. I would much prefer to fight than stay in my tent.”
“Idomeneus,” Meriones answered, “I have come for a spear, if I can find one in my tent. I broke the one I had when I threw it at the shield of Deiphobus.”

Idomeneus, captain of the Cretans, answered, “If you want one spear, or twenty, you will find them standing against the end wall of my tent. I took them from Trojans I have killed, for I do not keep my enemy at arm’s length. That is why I have spears, bossed shields, helmets, and burnished corslets.”

Then Meriones said, “I also have spoils taken from the Trojans, in my tent and at my ship, but they are not at hand. I have always been brave, and wherever the fighting was hard I have held my own among the foremost. There may be Achaeans who do not know how I fight, but you know it well enough yourself.”

Idomeneus answered, “I know you are a brave man, and you need not tell me. Suppose the best men at the ships were being chosen for an ambush—nothing shows what a man is made of like that, for it comes out then who is a coward and who is brave. The coward changes color at every turn. He is full of fear and keeps shifting his weight, first on one knee and then on the other. His heart beats fast as he thinks of death, and you can hear his teeth chattering. The brave man does not change color or take fright on finding himself in ambush, but longs the whole time to go into action. If the best men were being chosen for such a service, no one could make light of your courage or your feats of arms. If you were hit by a dart or struck in close combat, it would not be from behind, in your neck or back. The weapon would hit you in the chest or belly as you pressed forward to a place in the front ranks. But let us stop standing here talking like children, or we will be spoken ill of. Go and fetch your spear from the tent at once.”

At this, Meriones, peer of Ares, went to the tent and got himself a bronze spear. He followed after Idomeneus, set on great deeds of valor. As when baneful Ares goes out to battle, and his son Panic, strong and dauntless, goes with him to strike terror even into the heart of a hero—the pair have left Thrace to arm themselves among the Ephyri or the brave Phlegyans, but they will not listen to both of the contending armies, and will give victory to one side or the other—so Meriones and Idomeneus, captains of men, went out to battle in their bronze armor. Meriones spoke first. “Son of Deucalion,” he said, “where would you have us begin fighting? On the right wing of the army, in the center, or on the left wing, where I think the Achaeans will be weakest?”

Idomeneus answered, “There are others to defend the center: the two Ajaxes and Teucer, the finest archer of all the Achaeans and good in a hand-to-hand fight too. They will give Hector son of Priam all he can handle. Fight as he may, he will find it hard to overcome their indomitable fury and set fire to the ships, unless the son of Cronus hurls a firebrand on them with his own hand. Great Ajax son of Telamon will yield to no man who is of mortal mold and eats the grain of Demeter, so long as bronze and great stones can bring him down. He would not give way even to Achilles in hand-to-hand fighting, and in speed of foot no one can beat him. So let us turn toward the left wing, and find out at once whether we will give glory to someone else, or he to us.”
Meriones, peer of swift Ares, then led the way until they came to the part of the army that Idomeneus had named.

When the Trojans saw Idomeneus coming at them like a flame of fire, he and his squire in their richly wrought armor, they shouted and moved against him all together. A furious hand-to-hand fight raged beside the ships’ sterns. The fury of the combat was like the shrill winds that whistle on a day when dust lies deep on the roads and the gusts raise it in a thick cloud. With all their might they hacked at each other with spear and sword throughout the army. The field bristled with the long, deadly spears they carried. The sheen of their gleaming helmets, their freshly burnished breastplates, and their glittering shields was dazzling as they joined battle. His courage must be iron indeed who could take pleasure in the sight of such turmoil and look on it without dismay.

So the two mighty sons of Cronus plotted evil for mortal heroes. Zeus meant to give victory to the Trojans and to Hector, to honor swift-footed Achilles. Yet he did not mean to destroy the Achaean army utterly before Ilium. He only wanted to glorify Thetis and her valiant son. Poseidon, on the other hand, went among the Argives to urge them on. He had come up from the gray sea in secret, because he was grieved to see them beaten by the Trojans and was furiously angry with Zeus. The two gods shared the same race and country, but Zeus was born first and knew more. So Poseidon was afraid to defend the Argives openly. In the likeness of a man, he kept encouraging them throughout their army. In this way the two gods tied a knot of war and battle that no one could undo or break, and set both sides tugging at it, until the men’s knees failed beneath them.

Now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with gray, called loudly to the Danaans and spread panic among the Trojans as he leaped in among them. He killed Othryoneus of Cabesus, a visitor who had only lately come to join the war. Othryoneus had sought Cassandra, the fairest of Priam’s daughters, in marriage, but offered no gifts of wooing. He promised something great instead: that he would drive the sons of the Achaeans from Troy, whether they liked it or not. Old King Priam had agreed and promised her to him, and Othryoneus fought on the strength of those promises. Idomeneus aimed a spear and hit him as he came striding on. His bronze cuirass did not protect him, and the spear stuck in his belly, so that he fell heavily to the ground. Then Idomeneus boasted over him. “Othryoneus,” he said, “there is no one in the world I will admire more than you, if you really do what you promised Priam son of Dardanus in return for his daughter. We also will make you an offer. We will give you the loveliest daughter of the son of Atreus and bring her from Argos for you to marry, if you will sack the goodly city of Ilium with us. So come along with me, and we will make a covenant about the marriage at the ships. We will not be hard on you about gifts of wooing.”

With this Idomeneus began dragging him by the foot through the thick of the fight. But Asius came up to protect the body, on foot, in front of his horses. His squire drove them so close behind him that he could feel their breath on his shoulder. Asius longed to strike Idomeneus down, but before he could, Idomeneus struck him with his spear in the throat under the chin, and the bronze point went clean through. He fell like an oak, a poplar, or a pine that shipwrights have felled on the mountains with whetted axes for ship’s timber. So he lay at full length in front of his chariot and horses, grinding his teeth and clutching at the blood-stained dust. His charioteer was struck with panic. He did not dare turn his horses around and escape. Then Antilochus hit him in the middle of his body with a spear. His bronze cuirass did not protect him, and the spear stuck in his belly. He fell gasping from his chariot, and Antilochus, great Nestor’s son, drove his horses away from the Trojans to the Achaeans.

Deiphobus then came close to Idomeneus to avenge Asius and aimed a spear at him. But Idomeneus was on the lookout and dodged it, covered by the round shield he always carried—a shield of ox-hide and bronze with two arm-rods on the inside. He crouched under it, and the spear flew over him. The shield rang out as the spear grazed it, yet the weapon did not leave the strong hand of Deiphobus in vain. It struck Hypsenor son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver under the midriff, and his limbs gave way beneath him. Deiphobus boasted over him and cried out in a loud voice, “Truly, Asius has not fallen unavenged. He will be glad even as he passes into the house of Hades, the strong gatekeeper, that I have sent someone to escort him.”

So he boasted, and the Argives were stung by his words. Noble Antilochus was angrier than anyone, but grief did not make him forget his friend and comrade. He ran to him, stood over him, and covered him with his shield. Then two of his staunch comrades, Mecisteus son of Echius and Alastor, stooped down and carried him groaning heavily to the ships. But Idomeneus did not ease his fury. He kept striving, again and again, either to wrap some Trojan in the darkness of death, or to fall himself while warding off the evil day from the Achaeans. Then Alcathous fell, son of noble Aesyetes. He was son-in-law to Anchises, having married his eldest daughter Hippodameia. She was the darling of her father and mother and surpassed all her generation in beauty, accomplishments, and understanding, and so the bravest man in all Troy had taken her as his wife. Poseidon laid this man low by the hand of Idomeneus. He blinded his bright eyes and bound his strong limbs in fetters, so that Alcathous could neither go back nor step aside, but stood stock still like a pillar or a lofty tree when Idomeneus struck him with a spear in the middle of his chest. The coat of mail that had protected his body until then was broken, and it rang harshly as the spear tore through it. He fell heavily to the ground, and the spear stuck in his heart. The heart still beat, and made the butt-end of the spear quiver, until dread Ares put an end to his life. Idomeneus boasted over him and cried out in a loud voice, “Deiphobus, since you are in the mood to boast, shall we call it even now that we have killed three men to your one? No, sir, stand and fight me yourself, so that you learn what kind of man I am, born of Zeus, who have come here. Zeus first fathered Minos, chief ruler in Crete, and Minos in his turn fathered a son, noble Deucalion. Deucalion fathered me to rule over many men in Crete, and now my ships have brought me here to be the bane of you, your father, and the Trojans.”

So he spoke, and Deiphobus could not decide what to do. He wondered whether to go back and bring some other Trojan to help him, or to take up the challenge alone. In the end he thought it best to fetch Aeneas. He found him standing at the rear of the army, still sore at Priam, who gave him no share of honor to match his brave deeds. Deiphobus went up to him and said, “Aeneas, prince among the Trojans, if you feel any tie of kinship, help me now to defend the husband of your sister. Come with me to save Alcathous. He married your sister and raised you in his house when you were a child, and now Idomeneus has killed him.”

With these words he moved the heart of Aeneas, who went after Idomeneus, eager for great deeds of valor. But Idomeneus was not to be frightened like a small child. He stood his ground like a wild boar at bay in the mountains, waiting for a great crowd of men to reach him in some lonely place. The bristles stand up along its back, its eyes flash fire, and it whets its tusks, eager to defend itself against hounds and men. In just that way famed Idomeneus held firm and did not give way as Aeneas came on. He called out to his comrades, looking toward Ascalaphus, Aphareus, Deipyrus, Meriones and Antilochus, all brave soldiers. “Come to me, my friends,” he cried, “and do not leave me alone. I am in great fear of swift Aeneas, who is coming at me and is a fearsome dealer of death in battle. He is also in the flower of youth, when a man’s strength is greatest. If I were his age and had my present spirit, either he or I would soon carry off the prize of victory.”

At this they all gathered around him as one man, with shields on their shoulders. On the other side Aeneas called to his comrades, looking toward Deiphobus, Paris and Agenor, who led the Trojans together with himself. The people followed them as sheep follow the ram when they go down to drink after feeding, and the shepherd’s heart is glad. In the same way the heart of Aeneas was gladdened when he saw his people follow him.

Then they fought furiously hand to hand over the body of Alcathous, swinging their long spears. The bronze armor on their bodies rang fearfully as they aimed at one another in the crush of the fight. The two heroes Aeneas and Idomeneus, peers of Ares, outdid everyone in their longing to hack at each other with sword and spear. Aeneas took the first throw, but Idomeneus was watching and dodged the spear. It left the strong hand of Aeneas in vain and stuck quivering in the ground. Idomeneus in turn struck Oenomaus in the middle of the belly and broke the plate of his corslet. His bowels came gushing out, and he fell sprawling in the dust, clutching the earth in the palms of his hands. Idomeneus pulled his spear out of the body but could not strip off the rest of Oenomaus’s armor, because a rain of darts was showered on him. His strength was also beginning to fail, so that he could no longer charge. He could not spring forward to recover his own weapon, and he could not swerve aside from one aimed at him. So although he still defended himself in hand-to-hand fighting, his heavy feet could not carry him swiftly out of the battle. Deiphobus threw a spear at him as he slowly retreated from the field, for his bitterness against him was as fierce as ever. Again he missed, and he hit Ascalaphus, the son of Ares. The spear went through his shoulder, and he fell sprawling in the dust, clutching the earth in the palms of his hands.

Grim Ares of the awful voice did not yet know that his son had fallen. He was sitting on the summits of Olympus under the golden clouds, by command of Zeus, where the other gods also sat, forbidden to take part in the battle. Meanwhile the men fought furiously over the body. Deiphobus tore the helmet from the head of Ascalaphus, but Meriones leapt at him and struck him on the arm with a spear. The visored helmet fell from Deiphobus’s hand and came ringing down on the ground. Meriones then sprang on him like a vulture, drew the spear out of his shoulder, and fell back under cover of his men. Then Polites, own brother of Deiphobus, put his arms around Deiphobus’s waist and carried him out of the battle, until he reached his horses. They were standing at the rear of the fight with the chariot and their driver. These took him toward the city, groaning in great pain, with blood flowing from his arm.

The others kept on fighting, and the battle cry rose to heaven without ceasing. Aeneas sprang on Aphareus son of Caletor and struck him with a spear in the throat, which was turned toward him. Aphareus’s head fell to one side, his helmet and shield came down with him, and death, the enemy of life, was poured around him. Antilochus saw his chance and flew at Thoon, wounding him as he turned around. He laid open the vein that runs all the way up the back to the neck, cutting it clean away along its whole length. Thoon fell in the dust on his back, stretching out his hands toward his comrades and pleading for help. Antilochus sprang on him and stripped the armor from his shoulders, glaring fearfully around him as he did it. The Trojans closed in on every side and struck his broad, gleaming shield, but they could not wound his body, for Poseidon stood guard over the son of Nestor, though the darts fell thickly around him. He was never clear of the enemy but always in the thick of the fight. His spear was never idle. He poised and aimed it in every direction, so eager was he to hit someone from a distance or to fight him hand to hand.

Adamas, son of Asius, saw him aiming among the crowd. He rushed at him and struck him with a spear in the middle of his shield, but Poseidon made the point useless, for he begrudged Adamas the life of Antilochus. One half of the spear stuck fast in the shield of Antilochus like a charred stake, and the other half lay on the ground. Adamas then drew back under cover of his men, but Meriones went after him and hit him with a spear midway between the private parts and the navel, where a wound is especially painful to wretched mortals.
