There Meriones transfixed him, and Adamas writhed around the spear like a bull that mountain herdsmen have bound with ropes of withes and are dragging away by force. In the same way he writhed for a while, though not for long, until Meriones came up and drew the spear out of his body, and darkness veiled his eyes.

Then Helenus struck Deipyrus with a great Thracian sword. He hit him on the temple in close combat and tore the helmet from his head. The helmet fell to the ground and rolled at the feet of one of the Achaean fighters, who took charge of it. But the eyes of Deipyrus closed in the darkness of death.

Menelaus was grieved at this and went menacingly at Helenus, brandishing his spear. Helenus drew his bow, and the two attacked at the same moment, one with his spear, the other with his bow and arrow. The son of Priam hit the breastplate of Menelaus’s corslet, but the arrow glanced off it. As black beans or peas come pattering onto a threshing floor from the broad winnowing shovel, blown by shrill winds and shaken by the shovel, so the arrow glanced off and bounced away from the shield of Menelaus. He in his turn wounded the hand that Helenus carried his bow with. The spear went right through the hand and stuck in the bow itself. Helenus retreated under cover of his men to save his life, with his hand dragging at his side, for the spear weighed it down until Agenor pulled it out and bound the hand carefully in a woolen sling that his squire had with him.

Pisander then went straight at Menelaus. His evil destiny was luring him on to his doom, for he was to fall in the fight with you, Menelaus. When the two were close together, the spear of the son of Atreus turned aside and missed. Pisander then struck the shield of brave Menelaus but could not pierce it, for the shield stopped the spear and the shaft broke. Even so he was glad and sure of victory. But the son of Atreus drew his sword at once and sprang at him. Pisander took the bronze battle-axe that hung at his side under his shield, with its long, polished handle of olive wood, and the two went at each other. Pisander struck the peak of Menelaus’s crested helmet just under the crest itself. Menelaus hit Pisander as he came on, on the forehead, just where the nose begins. The bones cracked, and Pisander’s two eyes, drabbled in gore, fell at his feet in the dust. He fell backward to the ground. Menelaus set his heel on him, stripped him of his armor, and boasted over him. “This is how you Trojans will leave the ships of the Achaeans, proud and insatiable for battle as you are. You will not be spared any of the disgrace and shame that you have heaped on me. You cowardly she-wolves, you did not fear the anger of dread Zeus, avenger of violated hospitality, who will one day destroy your city. You stole my wedded wife and wickedly carried off much treasure when you were her guest. Now you want to fling fire on our ships and kill our heroes. A day will come when, rage as you may, you will be stopped. Father Zeus, they say you are above all, both gods and men, in wisdom, and that everything that befalls us comes from you. How can you favor the Trojans like this, men so proud and overbearing that they never tire of fighting? Everything palls after a while: sleep, love, sweet song, stately dance. Still, these are things a man would surely rather have his fill of than of battle, yet it is of battle that the Trojans cannot get enough.”
With that, Menelaus stripped the blood-stained armor from the body of Pisander and handed it to his men. Then he took his place again among those at the front of the fight.

Harpalion, son of King Pylaemenes, then sprang at him. He had come to fight at Troy with his father, and he never went home again. He struck the middle of Menelaus’s shield with his spear but could not pierce it. To save his life he drew back under cover of his men, looking around on every side in case he should be wounded. But Meriones aimed a bronze-tipped arrow at him as he left the field and hit him on the right buttock. The arrow went through the bone and into the bladder. He sat down where he was and breathed his last in the arms of his comrades, stretched like a worm on the ground, watering the earth with the blood that flowed from his wound. The brave Paphlagonians tended him with all due care. They lifted him into his chariot and carried him sadly to the city of Troy. His father went with him, weeping bitterly, but no ransom could bring his dead son back to life.

Paris was deeply grieved by the death of Harpalion, who had been his host when he went among the Paphlagonians, and he aimed an arrow to avenge him. There was a man named Euchenor, son of Polyidus the prophet, brave and wealthy, whose home was in Corinth. Euchenor had sailed for Troy knowing well that it would be his death. His good old father Polyidus had often told him that he must either stay at home and die of a terrible disease, or go with the Achaeans and perish at the hands of the Trojans. So he chose to avoid the heavy fine the Achaeans would have laid on him and, at the same time, to escape the pain and suffering of disease. Now Paris struck him on the jaw under the ear. The life went out of him, and the darkness of death enshrouded him.

So they fought, like a flaming fire. But Hector had not yet heard, and did not know, that the Argives were making havoc of his men on the left wing of the battle. There the Achaeans would soon have triumphed over them, so vigorously did Poseidon cheer them on and help them. Hector held on instead at the point where he had first forced his way through the gates and the wall, breaking through the serried ranks of Danaan warriors. Here the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus were drawn up by the seashore. Here the wall was lowest, and the fighting of men and horses raged most fiercely. The Boeotians, the Ionians with their long tunics, the Locrians, the men of Phthia, and the famous force of the Epeans could hardly hold Hector back as he rushed on toward the ships. They could not drive him away from them, for he was like a wall of fire. The chosen men of the Athenians were in the front, led by Menestheus son of Peteos. With him were Pheidas, Stichius and stalwart Bias. Meges son of Phyleus, Amphion and Dracius commanded the Epeans, and Medon and staunch Podarces led the men of Phthia. Of these, Medon was a bastard son of Oileus and brother of Ajax, but he lived in Phylace, away from his own country, because he had killed the brother of his stepmother Eriopis, the wife of Oileus. The other, Podarces, was the son of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus. These two stood in front of the Phthians and defended the ships along with the Boeotians.

Ajax son of Oileus never left the side of Ajax son of Telamon for a moment. Two dark oxen strain with all their might at the plow they are drawing in a fallow field, and sweat steams up from the roots of their horns, with nothing but the yoke between them as they break up the ground to the end of the field. In just that way the two Ajaxes stood shoulder to shoulder. Many brave comrades followed the son of Telamon, to take his shield from him when he was overcome with sweat and toil. The Locrians did not follow so close behind the son of Oileus, for they could not hold their own in hand-to-hand fighting. They had no bronze helmets with plumes of horse-hair, no shields and no ashen spears. They had come to Troy armed with bows and with slings of twisted wool, from which they showered missiles to break the ranks of the Trojans. So the others, in their heavy armor, bore the brunt of the fight against the Trojans and Hector, while the Locrians shot from behind them, under their cover. And so the Trojans began to lose heart, for the arrows threw them into confusion.

The Trojans would now have been driven in sorry plight from the ships and tents back to windy Ilium, if Polydamas had not spoken to Hector. “Hector, there is no persuading you to take advice. Because heaven has so richly endowed you with the arts of war, you think you must also excel others in counsel. But you cannot claim preeminence in everything. Heaven has made one man an excellent soldier. Another it has made a dancer, or a singer and player on the lyre. In yet another Zeus has planted a wise understanding, from which many men reap benefit and are saved, and he himself knows more about it than anyone. So I will say what I think is best. The fight has hemmed you in like a circle of fire. Even now that the Trojans are inside the wall, some of them stand aloof in full armor, while others fight scattered and outnumbered near the ships. Draw back, therefore, and call your chieftains around you, so that we can consider together whether to fall on the ships now, in the hope that heaven may grant us victory, or to retreat while we can still do so safely. I greatly fear that the Achaeans will pay us their debt of yesterday in full, for there is one at their ships who never tires of battle, and he will not hold aloof much longer.”

So spoke Polydamas, and his words pleased Hector well. He sprang from his chariot in full armor and said, “Polydamas, gather the chieftains here. I will go over there into the fight, and I will return at once when I have given them their orders.”

He then rushed onward, towering like a snowy mountain, and flew through the ranks of the Trojans and their allies with a loud cry. When they heard his voice, they all hurried to gather around Polydamas, the excellent son of Panthous. Hector kept going among the foremost, looking everywhere for Deiphobus, prince Helenus, Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus. He could no longer find them alive and unharmed. The last two were lying by the sterns of the Achaean ships, killed by the Argives, and the others had also been stricken and wounded by them. But on the left wing of the dread battle he found Paris, husband of lovely Helen, cheering his men and urging them on to fight. He went up to him and reproached him. “Paris,” he said, “evil-hearted Paris, fair to see but woman-mad and false of tongue, where are Deiphobus and King Helenus? Where are Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus? Where is Othryoneus too? Ilium is undone and will surely fall now!”

Paris answered, “Hector, why find fault when there is no one to blame? Of all days, this is the one on which I would least hold back from battle, for my mother bore me with nothing of the coward in me. From the moment you set our men fighting about the ships, we have been here, doing battle with the Danaans. The comrades you ask about are dead. Only Deiphobus and King Helenus have left the field, both of them wounded in the hand, but the son of Cronus kept them alive. Now lead on wherever you want us to go, and we will follow with right goodwill. You will not find us failing you, as far as our strength holds out. But no man can do more than is in him, however willing he may be.”

With these words he satisfied his brother, and the two went to the part of the battle where the fight was thickest, around Cebriones, brave Polydamas, Phalces, Orthaeus, godlike Polyphetes, Palmys, Ascanius, and Morys son of Hippotion. These had come from fertile Ascania the day before to relieve other troops. Then Zeus urged them on to fight. They surged forward like the blasts of a fierce wind that strikes the earth ahead of a thunderstorm. Such winds buffet the salt sea into an uproar, and many mighty waves come crashing in one after another on the shore, their arching heads crested with foam. In the same way rank behind rank of Trojans in gleaming armor followed their leaders. Hector son of Priam, peer of murderous Ares, led the way, with his round shield before him, a shield of ox-hides covered with plates of bronze, and his gleaming helmet on his temples. He kept stepping forward in every direction under cover of his shield, testing the ranks to see if they would give way before him, but he could not daunt the courage of the Achaeans. Ajax was the first to stride out and challenge him. “Sir,” he cried, “come near. Why do you think you can dismay the Argives to no purpose? We Achaeans are excellent soldiers, but the scourge of Zeus has fallen heavily on us. Your heart, of course, is set on destroying our ships, but we too have hands that can keep you at bay, and your own fair town will be taken and sacked by us sooner than that. The time is near when you will pray to Zeus and all the gods, as you flee, that your horses may be swifter than hawks as they raise the dust on the plain and carry you back to your city.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right hand, and the host of the Achaeans shouted, for they took heart at the omen. But Hector answered, “Ajax, braggart and false of tongue, I wish I were as sure of being son for evermore to aegis-bearing Zeus, with Queen Hera for my mother, and of being honored as Athena and Apollo are, as I am sure that this day brings destruction to the Achaeans. You will fall among them if you dare to face my spear. It will rend your fair body and make you glut our hounds and birds of prey with your fat and your flesh, as you fall by the ships of the Achaeans.”

Having said this, he went ahead, and the rest came after him with a cry that split the air, the whole host shouting at their backs. The Argives shouted back. They remembered their prowess and held firm against the charge of the Trojan chieftains. The noise from both armies rose up to heaven, to the brightness where Zeus is present.

chapters.title: Book 14
paragraphs: Agamemnon proposes that the Achaeans should sail home, and Odysseus rebukes him—Hera deceives Zeus—Hector is wounded.

Nestor sat drinking his wine, but the noise of battle did not escape him. He said to the son of Asclepius, “Noble Machaon, what does all this mean? The shouts of men fighting by our ships keep growing louder. Stay here and go on with your wine, while fair Hecamede heats a bath for you and washes the clotted blood off your body. I will go straight to the lookout post and find out what is happening.”

He took the shield of his son Thrasymedes from the tent, where it lay gleaming with bronze, since Thrasymedes had taken his father’s shield. He also picked up his redoubtable bronze-shod spear. As soon as he was outside he saw the disastrous rout of the Achaeans. Their wall was overthrown, and they were fleeing in confusion before the Trojans. As when there is a heavy swell on the sea and the waves are dumb, they watch for the quarter from which the fierce winds may spring on them, but they stay where they are and roll neither this way nor that, until some particular wind sweeps down from heaven to decide for them. In the same way the old man was torn over whether to make for the crowd of Danaans or go in search of Agamemnon. In the end he thought it best to go to the son of Atreus. Meanwhile the armies kept fighting and killing one another, and the hard bronze rattled on their bodies as they thrust at each other with swords and spears.

The wounded kings met Nestor as they came up from their ships: the son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon son of Atreus. Their ships were drawn up some way from the fighting, on the shore itself, because they had been beached first, and the wall had been built behind the hindmost. The shore, wide as it was, had no room for all the ships, and the army was cramped for space. So the ships had been placed in rows, one behind another, and they filled the whole opening of the bay between the two points that formed it. The kings were leaning on their spears and coming out to look at the fight. They were very anxious, and when old Nestor met them they were filled with dismay. King Agamemnon said to him, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor to the Achaean name, why have you left the battle and come here? I fear that dread Hector’s words will come true. He boasted among the Trojans that he would not go back to Ilium until he had set our ships on fire and killed us. That is what he said, and now it is all coming true. Alas! Other Achaeans, like Achilles, are so angry with me that they refuse to fight at the sterns of our ships.”

Then Nestor, knight of Gerene, answered, “It is just as you say. It is all coming true at this moment, and even Zeus who thunders from on high cannot stop it. The wall has fallen, the wall we trusted as an impregnable bulwark for ourselves and our fleet. The Trojans are fighting stubbornly at the ships and never let up. Look where you may, you cannot tell from what quarter the rout of the Achaeans is coming. They are being killed in a confused mass, and the battle cry rises to heaven. Let us think, if thinking can help, what we had better do. But I do not advise going into battle ourselves, for a man cannot fight when he is wounded.”

And King Agamemnon answered, “Nestor, the Trojans are indeed fighting at the rear of our ships, and neither the wall nor the trench has done us any good. The Danaans toiled so hard over them, and thought they would be an impregnable bulwark for ourselves and our fleet. So I see it must be the will of Zeus that the Achaeans should perish here without glory, far from Argos. I knew when Zeus was willing to defend us, and I know now that he is raising the Trojans to equal honor with the gods, while he has bound us hand and foot. Now let us all do as I say. Let us bring down the ships that are on the beach and draw them into the water. We will make them fast to their mooring stones a little way out, against the fall of night, in case the Trojans will stop fighting even by night. Then we may draw down the rest of the fleet. There is nothing wrong with fleeing from ruin, even by night. It is better for a man to flee and be saved than to be caught and killed.”

Odysseus looked fiercely at him and said, “Son of Atreus, what are you talking about? Wretch, you should have commanded some other, baser army, and not be ruler over us. Zeus has given us a life of hard fighting from youth to old age, until every one of us perishes. Is this how you would leave the city of Troy, which we have suffered so much hardship to win? Be quiet, or some other Achaean may hear you say what no man who knows how to give good counsel should ever have let fall from his lips, and no king over so great a host as the Argives. I utterly despise your judgment for what you have been saying. Would you have us draw our ships down into the water while the battle is raging, and so play further into the hands of the conquering Trojans? It would be ruin. The Achaeans will not go on fighting when they see the ships being drawn into the water. They will stop attacking and keep turning their eyes toward the ships. So your counsel, sir captain, would be our destruction.”

Agamemnon answered, “Odysseus, your rebuke has stung me to the heart. But I am not ordering the Achaeans to draw their ships into the sea against their will. Someone, old or young, may be able to offer us better advice, and I will be glad to hear it.”

Then Diomedes said, “That man is close by. You need not look far, if you will listen to me and not resent my speaking, though I am younger than any of you. By lineage I am the son of a noble father, Tydeus, who lies buried at Thebes. Portheus had three noble sons. Two of them, Agrius and Melas, lived in Pleuron and rocky Calydon. The third was the knight Oeneus, my father’s father, and he was the most valiant of them all. Oeneus stayed in his own country, but my father, as Zeus and the other gods ordained, moved to Argos. He married into the family of Adrastus. His house had great abundance: he had large estates of rich grain-growing land, with much orchard ground as well, and he had many sheep. He also excelled all the Argives in the use of the spear. You must have heard for yourselves whether these things are true. So when I speak well, do not despise my words as though I were a coward or of ignoble birth. I say, then, that we must go to the fight, wounded though we are. When we get there, we can stay out of the battle and beyond the range of spears, so that we get no fresh wounds on top of the ones we already have. But we can spur on the others, who have been indulging their ill temper and holding back from the battle until now.”
So he spoke. They did as he said and set out, with King Agamemnon in the lead.

Meanwhile Poseidon had been keeping a sharp lookout. He came up to them looking like an old man, took Agamemnon’s right hand in his own, and said, “Son of Atreus, I think Achilles is glad now, seeing the Achaeans routed and slain, for he has no remorse at all. May he come to a bad end, and may heaven confound him. As for you, the blessed gods are not yet so bitterly angry with you. The princes and counselors of the Trojans will again raise the dust on the plain, and you will see them fleeing from the ships and tents toward their city.”

With this he gave a mighty battle cry and rushed out to the plain. His voice came from a deep chest, and it was like the voice of nine or ten thousand men shouting in the thick of a fight. It gave the Achaeans fresh courage to wage war and fight without ceasing.

Hera of the golden throne stood on a peak of Olympus and looked down. Her heart was gladdened to see him who was both her brother and her brother-in-law hurrying back and forth amid the fighting. Then she turned her eyes to Zeus, sitting on the topmost crests of many-fountained Ida, and she loathed him. She set herself to think how she could hoodwink him. In the end she decided it was best to go to Ida dressed in rich attire, in the hope that Zeus would become enamored of her and want to embrace her. While he was occupied with that, a sweet and careless sleep might be made to steal over his eyes and senses.

She went, then, to the room her son Hephaestus had made for her. He had cunningly fastened its doors with a secret key, so that no other god could open them. She went in and shut the doors behind her. With ambrosia she cleaned all the dirt from her fair body, and then she anointed herself with olive oil, ambrosial, very soft, and scented specially for her. If it was so much as shaken in the bronze-floored house of Zeus, its scent filled the universe of heaven and earth. With this she anointed her delicate skin. Then she braided the fair ambrosial locks that flowed in a stream of golden tresses from her immortal head. She put on the wondrous robe that Athena had made for her with supreme skill and embroidered with many designs. She fastened it over her bosom with golden clasps, and belted herself with a girdle that had a hundred tassels. Then she put her earrings, three brilliant pendants that glistened most beautifully, through the pierced lobes of her ears, and threw a lovely new veil over her head. She bound her sandals on her feet. When she had dressed herself perfectly to her satisfaction, she left her room and called Aphrodite aside to speak to her. “My dear child,” she said, “will you do what I am going to ask of you, or will you refuse me because you are angry that I am on the Danaan side while you are on the Trojan?”

Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, answered, “Hera, august queen of goddesses and daughter of mighty Cronus, tell me what you want. I will do it for you right away, if I am able and if it can be done at all.”

Then Hera told her a lying tale. “I want you to give me some of those fascinating charms, whose spells bring all things, mortal and immortal, to your feet. I am going to the world’s end to visit Oceanus (from whom all we gods are descended) and mother Tethys. They received me in their house, took care of me, and brought me up, after taking me over from Rhaea when Zeus imprisoned great Cronus in the depths under earth and sea. I must go and see them to make peace between them. They have been quarreling, and are so angry that they have not slept with one another for a long while. If I can bring them around and restore them to one another’s embraces, they will be grateful to me and love me forever afterward.”
Laughter-loving Aphrodite replied, “I cannot and must not refuse you, since you sleep in the arms of Zeus, who is our king.”

As she spoke she unfastened from her bosom the curiously embroidered girdle in which all her charms had been wrought: love, desire, and that sweet flattery which steals the judgment even of the most prudent. She gave the girdle to Hera and said, “Take this girdle, which holds all my charms, and lay it in your bosom. If you wear it, I promise you that your errand, whatever it may be, will not fail.”
Hera smiled at these words, and still smiling she tucked the girdle into her bosom.

Aphrodite went back into the house of Zeus, and Hera darted down from the summits of Olympus. She crossed Pieria and fair Emathia and kept going until she reached the snowy mountains of the Thracian horsemen. She sped over their highest peaks without once touching the ground. At Athos she left the land and went on over the waves of the sea to Lemnos, the city of noble Thoas. There she met Sleep, own brother to Death. She caught his hand and said, “Sleep, you who rule over mortals and immortals alike, if you ever did me a service in the past, do one for me now, and I will be grateful to you ever after. Close the keen eyes of Zeus in slumber for me while I hold him clasped in my embrace. In return I will give you a beautiful golden seat that can never fall to pieces. My clubfooted son Hephaestus shall make it, with a footstool for you to rest your fair feet on when you are at table.”

Then Sleep answered, “Hera, great queen of goddesses, daughter of mighty Cronus, I would lull any other god to sleep without hesitation, even the waters of Oceanus, from whom all of them are descended. But I dare not go near Zeus, or send him to sleep unless he tells me to. I have already had one lesson from doing what you asked. It was the day when the mighty son of Zeus, Heracles, set sail from Ilium after sacking the city of the Trojans. At your bidding I poured my sweet self over the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus and laid him to rest. Meanwhile you hatched a plot against Heracles and set the blasts of the angry winds beating on the sea, until you carried him to the goodly city of Cos, away from all his friends. When Zeus woke he was furious, and began hurling the gods about all over the house. He was looking for me most of all, and would have flung me down through space into the sea, where I should never have been heard of again, if Night, who cows both men and gods, had not protected me. I fled to her, and Zeus left off looking for me, angry as he was, for he did not dare do anything to displease Night. And now you are asking me again to do something I cannot venture.”

Hera said, “Sleep, why do you get such notions into your head? Do you think Zeus will be as eager to help the Trojans as he was for his own son? Come, I will give you one of the youngest of the Graces in marriage, and she will be yours—Pasithea, the one you have always wanted to marry.”

Sleep was glad to hear it. “Then swear it to me,” he answered, “by the dread waters of the river Styx. Put one hand on the bounteous earth and the other on the sheen of the sea, so that all the gods who live below with Cronus will be our witnesses, and will see that you truly give me one of the youngest of the Graces—Pasithea, whom I have always wanted to marry.”

Hera did as he asked. She swore the oath and called on all the gods of the nether world, the ones called Titans, as witnesses. When the oath was complete, the two wrapped themselves in a thick mist and hurried on, leaving Lemnos and Imbrus behind them. Soon they came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and to Lectum, where they left the sea and went on over land. The tops of the forest trees rustled beneath their feet. Sleep stopped here. Before Zeus could catch sight of him, he climbed a lofty pine—the tallest that lifted its head toward heaven on all Ida. He hid among the branches and sat there looking like the sweet-singing bird of the mountains, which the gods call Chalcis and men call Cymindis. Hera then went on to Gargarus, the topmost peak of Ida, and Zeus, driver of the clouds, saw her. The moment he did, he was filled with the same passionate desire for her that he had felt when they first enjoyed each other’s embraces and slept together without their dear parents knowing anything about it. He went up to her and said, “What do you want, that you have come here from Olympus, and with no chariot or horses to carry you?”

Then Hera told him a lie. “I am on my way to the end of the world,” she said, “to visit Oceanus, from whom all we gods come, and mother Tethys. They took me into their house, looked after me and raised me. I must go and see them to make peace between them. They have been quarreling, and are so angry that they have not slept together for a long time. The horses that will carry me over land and sea are waiting on the lowest slopes of many-fountained Ida, and I came here from Olympus specially to consult you. I was afraid you might be angry with me later if I went to the house of Oceanus without telling you.”

And Zeus said, “Hera, you can visit Oceanus some other time. For now let us give ourselves to love and to enjoying each other. Never has passion overpowered me like this, for goddess or mortal woman, as it does at this moment for you—not even when I loved the wife of Ixion, who bore me Pirithous, the peer of gods in counsel, nor Danae, the daintily-ankled daughter of Acrisius, who bore me the famed hero Perseus. Then there was the daughter of Phoenix, who bore me Minos and Rhadamanthus. There was Semele, and Alcmena in Thebes, by whom I fathered my lion-hearted son Heracles, while Semele became the mother of Dionysus, comforter of mankind. There was queen Demeter too, and lovely Leto, and yourself. But with none of these was I ever so much in love as I am now with you.”

Hera again answered him with a lie. “Most dread son of Cronus,” she exclaimed, “what are you saying? Would you have us make love here on the top of Mount Ida, where everything can be seen? What if one of the ever-living gods saw us sleeping together and told the others? It would be such a scandal that after I rose from your embrace I could never show myself in your house again. But if you are willing, there is a room your son Hephaestus made for me, and he gave it good strong doors. If that is what you want, let us go there and lie down.”

And Zeus answered, “Hera, you need not fear that god or man will see you. I will wrap both of us in a golden cloud so dense that not even the sun, for all his bright piercing beams, can see through it.”

With this the son of Cronus took his wife in his arms. At once the earth sprouted a cushion of fresh grass for them, with dew-bespangled lotus, crocus and hyacinth, so soft and thick that it lifted them well above the ground. They lay down there, and a fair cloud of gold covered them overhead, from which glittering dewdrops fell.

So the father of all things lay peacefully on the crest of Ida, overcome by sleep and love, with his wife in his arms. Meanwhile Sleep ran off to the ships of the Achaeans to tell earth-encircling Poseidon, lord of the earthquake. Having found him, he said, “Now, Poseidon, you can help the Danaans wholeheartedly and give them victory, though only for a short while, since Zeus is still sleeping. I have sent him into a sweet slumber, and Hera has beguiled him into going to bed with her.”

Sleep then left and went on his way among mankind, leaving Poseidon more eager than ever to help the Danaans. He darted out among the foremost ranks and shouted, “Argives, are we going to let Hector son of Priam take our ships and cover himself in glory? That is what he says he will do, because Achilles is still sulking at his ship. We will manage very well without him if we keep each other’s spirits up and stand by one another. So now, all of you, do as I say. Each of us should take the best and largest shield he can lay hands on, put on his helmet, and march out with his longest spear in his hand. I will lead you, and Hector son of Priam, rage as he may, will not dare to hold out against us. If any good, steady soldier has only a small shield, let him hand it to a worse man and take a larger one for himself.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said. The son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, wounded though they were, put the others in order and went everywhere arranging the exchanges of armor. The most valiant took the best armor and gave the worse to the worse man. When they had put on their bronze armor, they marched on with Poseidon at their head. In his strong hand he gripped his terrible sword, sharp of edge and flashing like lightning. Woe to anyone who meets it in the day of battle; all men shake with fear and keep away from it.

On the other side Hector put the Trojans in array. Then Poseidon and Hector waged fierce war against each other—Hector on the Trojan side and Poseidon on the Argive. The uproar was mighty as the two forces met. The sea came rolling in toward the ships and tents of the Achaeans. But waves do not thunder on the shore more loudly when Boreas drives them with his blast, nor do the flames of a forest fire roar more fiercely when it is well alight on the mountains, nor does the wind bellow with ruder music as it tears through the treetops when it is blowing its hardest, than the terrible shout the Trojans and Achaeans raised as they sprang at one another.

Hector threw his spear first, aiming at Ajax, who was turned full toward him, and he did not miss. The spear struck where two bands crossed Ajax’s chest—the band of his shield and that of his silver-studded sword—and these protected his body. Hector was angry that his spear had been thrown in vain, and he drew back under cover of his men. As he retreated, Ajax son of Telamon struck him with a stone. Many lay about under the men’s feet as they fought, brought there to prop up the sides of the ships as they lay on the shore. Ajax caught up one of them and hit Hector above the rim of his shield, close to the neck. The blow made him spin like a top and reel in every direction. As an oak falls headlong when the lightning flash of father Zeus uproots it, and there is a terrible smell of brimstone—no man standing near can help being dismayed, for a thunderbolt is a very awful thing—so Hector fell to the earth and bit the dust. His spear dropped from his hand, but his shield and helmet stayed fast about his body, and his bronze armor rang around him.

The sons of the Achaeans ran toward him with a loud cry, hoping to drag him away, and they showered darts on the Trojans. But none of them could wound him before he was surrounded and covered by the princes Polydamas, Aeneas, Agenor, Sarpedon captain of the Lycians, and noble Glaucus. None of the others forgot him either, and they held their round shields over him. His comrades lifted him off the ground and carried him from the battle to the place where his horses stood waiting at the rear of the fight with their driver and the chariot. These took him toward the city, groaning in great pain. When they reached the ford of the fair stream of Xanthus, begotten of immortal Zeus, they lifted him from the chariot and laid him on the ground. They poured water over him, and as they did he breathed again and opened his eyes. Then he got up on his knees and vomited blood, but soon fell back on the ground, and his eyes closed again in darkness, for the blow still held him stunned.

When the Argives saw Hector leaving the field, they took heart and attacked the Trojans even more furiously. Swift Ajax son of Oileus led off by springing on Satnius son of Enops and wounding him with his spear. A fair naiad nymph had borne him to Enops while Enops was herding cattle by the banks of the river Satnioeis. The son of Oileus came up and struck him in the flank, so that he fell, and a fierce fight between Trojans and Danaans raged round his body. Polydamas son of Panthous came near to avenge him and wounded Prothoenor son of Areilycus in the right shoulder. The terrible spear went right through the shoulder, and he clutched the earth as he fell in the dust. Polydamas boasted loudly over him: “Once again I think the spear has not flown in vain from the strong hand of the son of Panthous. An Argive has caught it in his body, and it will serve him as a staff on his way down to the house of Hades.”

The Argives were maddened by this boasting. Ajax son of Telamon was angrier than any, because the man had fallen right beside him. He aimed at Polydamas as he retreated, but Polydamas saved himself by swerving aside, and the spear struck Archelochus son of Antenor, for heaven had decided on his destruction. It hit him where the head joins the neck, at the top joint of the spine, and cut through both tendons at the back of the head. His head, mouth and nostrils reached the ground long before his legs and knees could, and Ajax shouted to Polydamas, “Think, Polydamas, and tell me truly: is this man not as well worth killing as Prothoenor was? He seems rich, and of a rich family—a brother, it may be, or a son of the knight Antenor, for he is very like him.”

But he knew well who it was, and the Trojans were greatly angered. Acamas then stood astride his brother’s body and wounded Promachus the Boeotian with his spear, because Promachus was trying to drag the body away. Acamas boasted loudly over him: “Argive archers, braggarts that you are, toil and suffering will not be for us alone. Some of you will fall here as well as we. See how Promachus now sleeps, vanquished by my spear. Payment for my brother’s blood was not long delayed. A man may well be thankful, therefore, if he leaves a kinsman in his house to avenge his fall.”

The Argives were infuriated by his taunts, and Peneleos was more enraged than any of them. He sprang at Acamas, but Acamas did not stand his ground, and Peneleos killed Ilioneus son of the rich flock-master Phorbas, whom Hermes had favored and given more wealth than any other Trojan. Ilioneus was Phorbas’s only son. Peneleos wounded him in the eye under the eyebrows, tearing the eyeball from its socket. The spear went right through the eye into the nape of the neck, and he fell, stretching out both hands in front of him. Peneleos then drew his sword and struck him on the neck, so that head and helmet both tumbled to the ground with the spear still sticking in the eye. He held up the head as though it were a poppy head and showed it to the Trojans, boasting over them as he did. “Trojans,” he cried, “tell the father and mother of noble Ilioneus to mourn for him in their house. The wife of Promachus son of Alegenor will not be gladdened either by her dear husband’s coming, when we Argives sail home from Troy with our ships.”
As he spoke, fear took hold of them all, and each man looked about for a way to escape.

Tell me now, Muses who live on Olympus, who was the first of the Argives to carry off blood-stained spoils after Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, had turned the fortune of war. Ajax son of Telamon was first: he wounded Hyrtius son of Gyrtius, captain of the staunch Mysians. Antilochus killed Phalces and Mermerus, Meriones slew Morys and Hippotion, and Teucer killed Prothoon and Periphetes. The son of Atreus then wounded Hyperenor, shepherd of his people, in the flank. The bronze point tore in among his entrails and made them gush out, and his life came hurrying out of him at the place where he was wounded, and his eyes closed in darkness. Ajax son of Oileus killed more than any other, for no man was so swift as he in chasing down fleeing enemies when Zeus had spread panic among them.

chapters.title: Book 15
paragraphs: Zeus wakes up and orders Apollo to heal Hector, and the Trojans become victorious once more.

The Trojans fled past the trench and the set stakes, and many fell to the Danaans along the way. When they reached their chariots they halted, routed and pale with fear. Then Zeus woke on the crests of Ida, where he had been lying beside golden-throned Hera. He sprang to his feet and saw the Trojans and Achaeans. The Trojans were in confusion, and the Achaeans were driving them headlong before them, with King Poseidon among them. He saw Hector lying on the ground with his comrades gathered around him. Hector was gasping for breath, his mind wandering, and vomiting blood, for the man who had struck him was not the feeblest of the Achaeans.

The father of gods and men pitied Hector and glared at Hera. “I see it, Hera, you mischief-making trickster,” he said. “Your cunning has kept Hector from fighting and has routed his army. I am half inclined to thrash you, and you would be the first to reap the fruits of your scurvy knavery. Do you not remember the time I hung you up? I fastened two anvils to your feet and bound your hands in a golden chain that no one could break, and you dangled in mid-air among the clouds. All the gods of Olympus raged, but they could not get near enough to set you free. Any of them I caught, I seized and hurled from the heavenly threshold until he came fainting down to earth. Even that did not ease my mind of its constant anxiety about noble Heracles. You and Boreas had spitefully carried him off across the seas to Cos, after you had won the tempests over to your scheme. But I rescued him, and in spite of all his mighty labors I brought him back to Argos. I remind you of this so that you will learn to stop your deceit, and see how much you are likely to gain from the embraces you left to come here and trick me.”

Hera trembled at his words. “Let heaven above and earth below be my witnesses,” she said, “and the waters of the river Styx—the most solemn oath a blessed god can take—and I swear also by your own almighty head and by our marriage bed, things I could never swear falsely by: Poseidon is not punishing Hector and the Trojans and helping the Achaeans because of anything I did. He acts entirely of his own accord, because he was sorry to see the Achaeans hard pressed at their ships. If I were advising him, I would tell him to do as you command.”

The father of gods and men smiled and answered, “Hera, if you always backed me when we sit in council of the gods, Poseidon, whether he liked it or not, would soon come round to your way of thinking and mine. So if you are telling the truth and mean what you say, go among the throng of the gods and tell Iris and Apollo, lord of the bow, that I want them. Iris is to go to the Achaean army and tell Poseidon to stop fighting and go home. Apollo is to send Hector back into battle and give him fresh strength. Hector will then forget his present sufferings and drive the Achaeans back in confusion, until they fall among the ships of Achilles son of Peleus. Achilles will then send his comrade Patroclus into battle. Hector will kill him in front of Ilium, after Patroclus has slain many warriors, among them my own noble son Sarpedon. To avenge Patroclus, Achilles will kill Hector. From that time on I will see to it that the Achaeans keep driving the Trojans back until Athena’s counsels are fulfilled and they take Ilium. But I will not give up my anger, and I will not let any god help the Danaans, until I have granted the wish of the son of Peleus. That is the promise I made, bowing my head, on the day Thetis touched my knees and begged me to give him honor.”

Hera heeded his words and went down from the heights of Ida to great Olympus. Her flight was as swift as a thought. A man’s fancy carries him over vast lands, and he says to himself, “Now I will be here, or there,” and wishes for all manner of things. That swiftly Hera flew until she reached high Olympus and entered the house of Zeus, where the gods were gathered. When they saw her, they all hurried to her and held out their cups in greeting. She ignored the others but took the cup from lovely Themis, who had been first to run up to her. “Hera,” Themis said, “why have you come? You seem troubled. Has your husband, the son of Cronus, been frightening you?”

Hera answered, “Themis, do not ask me about it. You know how proud and cruel my husband is. Take the gods to the feast, and there you and all the immortals will hear the wicked plans he has declared. Many, mortal and immortal, will be angered by them, however peacefully any of them may be feasting now.”

Hera sat down, and the gods throughout the house of Zeus were troubled. Laughter sat on her lips, but her brow was furrowed with care, and she spoke out in a rage. “What fools we are,” she cried, “to be so madly angry with Zeus! We keep wanting to go to him and stop him, by force or by persuasion, but he sits apart and cares for nobody, because he knows he is much stronger than any other immortal. So make the best of whatever evils he chooses to send each of you. Ares, I think, has already had a taste of them, for his son Ascalaphus has fallen in battle—the man he loved more dearly than any other, and whose father he admits himself to be.”

When Ares heard this, he struck his two sturdy thighs with the flat of his hands and said in anger, “Do not blame me, you gods who live in heaven, if I go to the ships of the Achaeans to avenge my son’s death, even if it ends with Zeus’s lightning striking me and I lie in blood and dust among the corpses.”

As he spoke he ordered his horses Panic and Rout to be yoked, and he put on his armor. Then Zeus would have been roused to fiercer and more implacable enmity against the other immortals, if Athena, alarmed for the safety of the gods, had not sprung from her seat and hurried outside. She tore the helmet from his head and the shield from his shoulders, took the bronze spear from his strong hand, and set it to one side. Then she said to Ares, “Madman, you are undone! Either you have ears that do not hear, or you have lost all judgment and understanding. Have you not heard what Hera said when she came straight from the presence of Olympian Zeus? Do you want to go through every kind of suffering before you are brought back to Olympus sick and sorry, after causing infinite mischief to the rest of us? Zeus would leave the Trojans and Achaeans to themselves at once. He would come to Olympus to punish us, and would grab us one after another, guilty or not. So give up your anger over your son’s death. Better men than he have been killed already or will fall hereafter, and one cannot protect everyone’s whole family.”

With these words she took Ares back to his seat. Meanwhile Hera called Apollo outside, together with Iris, the messenger of the gods. “Zeus,” she told them, “wants you to go to him on Mt. Ida at once. When you have seen him, you are to do whatever he then commands.”

Hera then left them and went back to her seat inside, while Iris and Apollo hurried on their way. They came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and found Zeus sitting on topmost Gargarus, a fragrant cloud wreathed around his head like a diadem. They stood before him. He was pleased that they had obeyed his wife’s orders so quickly.

He spoke to Iris first. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “and give King Poseidon this message of mine—and tell him truly. He is to stop fighting and either join the company of the gods or go down into the sea. If he pays no attention and disobeys me, let him consider carefully whether he is strong enough to stand against me if I attack him. I am older and much stronger than he is. Yet he is not afraid to set himself up as my equal, though all the other gods stand in awe of me.”

Iris, swift as the wind, obeyed him. She sped down as swiftly as cold hail or snowflakes flying out of the clouds before the blast of Boreas, until she came close to the great shaker of the earth. Then she said, “O dark-haired king who holds the world in his embrace, I have come with a message from Zeus. He orders you to stop fighting and either join the company of the gods or go down into the sea. But if you pay no attention and disobey, he says he will come down here and fight you. He wants you to keep out of his reach, because he is older and much stronger than you are. Yet you are not afraid to set yourself up as his equal, though all the other gods stand in awe of him.”

Poseidon was very angry. “Great heavens!” he said. “Strong as Zeus may be, he has said more than he can do if he threatens violence against me, who am his equal in honor. We were three brothers whom Rhea bore to Cronus: Zeus, myself, and Hades, who rules the world below. Heaven and earth were divided three ways, and each of us was to have an equal share. When we cast lots, the sea fell to me as my dwelling forever. Hades took the darkness of the realms under the earth, while air and sky and clouds were the portion that fell to Zeus. But earth and great Olympus belong to all of us in common. So I will not walk as Zeus would have me. For all his strength, let him stay in his own third share and be content, without threatening to lay hands on me as though I were nobody. Let him save his bragging talk for his own sons and daughters, who have no choice but to obey him.”

Iris, swift as the wind, answered, “Poseidon, am I really to carry this bold and unyielding message to Zeus, or will you think again about your answer? Sensible people can be argued with, and you know that the Erinyes always take the side of the older person.”

Poseidon answered, “Goddess Iris, what you say is well timed. It is good when a messenger shows such discretion. Even so, it cuts me to the heart when anyone rebukes so angrily one who is his own peer and has equal power. Now, though, I will give way, in spite of my displeasure. And let me tell you something more, and I mean it: if Zeus spares steep Ilium and will not let the Achaeans have the great triumph of sacking it, against the wishes of myself, of Athena, driver of the spoil, of Hera, of Hermes, and of King Hephaestus, then let him understand that he will bring on himself our implacable resentment.”

Poseidon then left the field and went down under the sea, and the Achaeans sorely missed him. Zeus then said to Apollo, “Dear Phoebus, go to Hector. Poseidon, who holds the earth in his embrace, has gone down under the sea to escape the severity of my anger. If he had not, the gods below with Cronus would have heard of the fight between us. It is better for both of us that he curbed his anger and kept out of my reach, for I would have had much trouble with him. Now take your tasseled aegis and shake it furiously to throw the Achaean heroes into a panic. And take brave Hector into your own care, O Far-Darter, and rouse him to daring deeds until the Achaeans are sent flying back to their ships and the Hellespont. From there I will think the matter over, and decide how the Achaeans may get a respite from their troubles.”

Apollo did as his father said. He left the crests of Ida and flew down like a falcon, the swiftest of all birds and the bane of doves. Hector was no longer lying on the ground. He was sitting up, having just come to himself, and he recognized the men around him. The sweat and the hard breathing had left him the moment the will of aegis-bearing Zeus revived him. Apollo stood beside him and asked, “Hector son of Priam, why are you so faint, and why are you sitting here apart from the others? Has some mishap befallen you?”

Hector answered in a weak voice, “Which of the gods are you, kind sir, to ask me this? Do you not know that Ajax struck me on the chest with a stone while I was killing his comrades at the ships of the Achaeans, and made me stop fighting? I was sure that this very day I would breathe my last and go down into the house of Hades.”

Then King Apollo said to him, “Take heart. The son of Cronus has sent you a mighty helper from Ida to stand by you and defend you: I, Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword, who have guarded not only you but your city until now. So order your horsemen to drive their chariots to the ships in great numbers. I will go ahead of your horses and smooth the way for them, and I will turn the Achaeans in flight.”

As he spoke he filled the shepherd of his people with great strength. A horse that has been stabled and well fed breaks loose and gallops gloriously across the plain to the place where he is used to bathing in the river. He tosses his head, his mane streams over his shoulders, and in all the pride of his strength he flies at full speed to the pastures where the mares are feeding. So Hector, when he heard the god’s words, urged his horsemen on and rushed forward as fast as his limbs could carry him. Or think of country peasants who set their hounds on a horned stag or wild goat. It has taken shelter under a rock or thicket, and they cannot find it, but then a bearded lion, roused by their shouts, stands in their path, and they have no more heart for the chase. So the Achaeans had been charging on in a body, using their swords and spears pointed at both ends, but when they saw Hector going about among his men they were afraid, and their hearts fell down into their feet.

Then Thoas son of Andraemon, leader of the Aetolians, spoke. He was a man who could make a good throw, staunch in close fight, and few could surpass him in debate when opinions were divided. With complete sincerity and goodwill he addressed them: “In heaven’s name, what do I see? Is that not Hector, come to life again? Everyone was sure he had been killed by Ajax son of Telamon, but it seems one of the gods has rescued him again. He has already killed many of us Danaans, and I think he will go on doing so, for the hand of Zeus must be with him, or he would never dare show himself so masterful in the forefront of the battle. So let us all do as I say. Let us order the main body of our forces to fall back on the ships. But those of us who claim to be the flower of the army should stand firm and see whether we can hold Hector back with the points of our spears as soon as he comes near us. I expect that he will then think better of it before he tries to charge into the press of the Danaans.”

So he spoke, and they did exactly as he had said. Those around Ajax and King Idomeneus, along with the followers of Teucer, Meriones, and Meges, peer of Ares, called all their best men about them and held the fight against Hector and the Trojans. The main body fell back on the ships of the Achaeans.

The Trojans came on in a dense body, and Hector strode at their head. Phoebus Apollo walked in front of him, with cloud wrapped around his shoulders. In his hands he carried the terrible aegis, shaggy with fringe, that Hephaestus the smith had given to Zeus to strike terror into men’s hearts. Holding it, Apollo led the Trojans on.

The Argives held together and stood their ground. The battle cry rose high from both sides, and arrows flew from the bowstrings. Many a spear sped from strong hands and fastened in the bodies of valiant warriors, while others dropped to earth midway, before they could taste man’s fair flesh and glut themselves with blood. As long as Phoebus Apollo held his aegis quietly, without shaking it, the weapons on both sides struck home and men fell. But when he shook it straight in the Danaans’ faces and raised his mighty battle cry, their hearts fainted within them and they forgot their former prowess. Two wild beasts spring in the dead of night on a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep when the herdsman is not there. In the same way the Danaans were struck helpless, for Apollo filled them with panic and gave victory to Hector and the Trojans.

The fighting grew more scattered after that, and each man killed whomever he could. Hector killed Stichius and Arcesilaus, one a leader of the Boeotians and the other a friend and comrade of Menestheus. Aeneas killed Medon and Iasus. Medon was a bastard son of Oileus and a brother of Ajax. He lived in Phylace, away from his own country, because he had killed a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, whom Oileus had married. Iasus had become a leader of the Athenians and was the son of Sphelus, the son of Boucolos. Polydamas killed Mecisteus, and Polites killed Echius, both in the front of the battle, while Agenor slew Clonius. Paris struck Deiochus from behind, low on the shoulder, as he fled among the foremost fighters, and the spear point went clean through him.

While they were stripping these heroes of their armor, the Achaeans fled headlong to the trench and the set stakes and were forced back inside their wall. Hector then shouted to the Trojans, “Forward to the ships, and leave the spoils! If I see any man hanging back on the far side of the wall, away from the ships, I will have him killed. His kinsmen and kinswomen will not give him his due of fire; dogs will tear him to pieces in front of our city.”

As he spoke he laid his whip across his horses’ shoulders and called to the Trojans all along their ranks. The Trojans shouted with a cry that rent the air and kept their horses neck and neck with his. Phoebus Apollo went ahead and kicked the banks of the deep trench down into its middle, making a great broad bridge, as wide as a spear’s throw when a man is testing his strength. The Trojan battalions poured over the bridge, with Apollo and his formidable aegis leading the way. He kicked down the wall of the Achaeans as easily as a child kicks down a house of sand that he has built, playing on the sea shore, and so destroys it. In the same way, O Apollo, you poured toil and trouble on the Argives, filling them with panic and confusion.

So the Achaeans were hemmed in at their ships, calling out to one another and raising their hands to heaven with loud cries, every man of them. Nestor of Gerene, tower of strength to the Achaeans, lifted his hands to the starry firmament of heaven and prayed more fervently than any. “Father Zeus,” he said, “if anyone in wheat-growing Argos ever burned you the fat thigh-bones of a sheep or heifer and prayed to return safely home, and you bowed your head to him in assent, remember it now. Do not let the Trojans triumph over the Achaeans like this.”

All-counseling Zeus thundered loudly in answer to the prayer of the aged son of Neleus. When the Trojans heard Zeus thunder, they flung themselves still more fiercely on the Achaeans. A wave breaks over the bulwarks of a ship when the sea runs high before a gale—the force of the wind is what makes the waves so great. In the same way the Trojans sprang over the wall with a shout and drove their chariots onward. The two sides fought hand to hand with their double-pointed spears, the Trojans from their chariots, and the Achaeans from up in their ships, wielding the long pikes that lay on the decks ready for a sea fight, jointed and shod with bronze.

For as long as the Achaeans and Trojans were fighting around the wall and had not yet got inside it or reached the ships, Patroclus stayed sitting in the tent of good Eurypylus. He kept him company with his talk and spread herbs over his wound to ease the pain. But then he saw the Trojans swarming through the breach in the wall while the Achaeans screamed in panic. He cried out and struck both his thighs with the flat of his hands. “Eurypylus,” he said in dismay, “I know you need me badly, but I cannot stay with you any longer, because the fighting has turned hard. A servant will look after you now. I must hurry to Achilles and try to get him to fight. Who knows, with the help of heaven I may persuade him. A man does well to listen to a friend’s advice.”

With that he went on his way. The Achaeans held firm against the Trojan attack. The Trojans were fewer in number, yet the Achaeans could not push them back from the ships, and the Trojans could not break the Achaean ranks and force their way in among the tents and ships. A carpenter’s line gives a true edge to a piece of ship’s timber in the hand of a skilled workman, whom Athena has taught all kinds of useful arts. In the same way the fight between the two sides stayed level, as they fought, some around one ship and some around another.

Hector went straight for Ajax, and the two of them fought fiercely around the same ship. Hector could not push Ajax back and set the ship on fire, and Ajax could not drive Hector away from the spot where heaven had brought him.

Then Ajax struck Caletor son of Clytius in the chest with his spear as Caletor was carrying fire toward the ship. Caletor fell heavily to the ground, and the torch dropped from his hand. Hector saw his cousin lying in front of the ship and shouted to the Trojans and Lycians. “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians good in close fight, do not give up an inch of ground. Rescue the son of Clytius, or the Achaeans will strip him of his armor now that he has fallen.”

Then he threw a spear at Ajax and missed him. But he hit Lycophron, a follower of Ajax. Lycophron came from Cythera, and he lived with Ajax because he had killed a man among the Cythereans. Hector’s spear struck him on the head below the ear, and he fell headlong from the ship’s prow to the ground, with no life left in him. Ajax shook with rage and spoke to his brother. “Teucer, my good fellow, our trusted comrade the son of Mastor has fallen. He came from Cythera to live with us, and we honored him as much as our own parents. Hector has just killed him. Quickly, fetch your deadly arrows and the bow that Phoebus Apollo gave you.”

Teucer heard him and hurried to his side with his bow and quiver in his hands. At once he sent a shower of arrows at the Trojans. He hit Cleitus son of Pisenor, a comrade of Polydamas, the noble son of Panthous. Cleitus had the reins in his hands and was tending his horses. He was in the very thickest part of the fight, doing good service to Hector and the Trojans, but now evil had come upon him, and none of those who wanted to could keep it off him, because the arrow struck him on the back of the neck. He fell from his chariot, and his horses swerved aside and shook the empty car. King Polydamas saw what had happened and was the first to reach the horses. He put them in the charge of Astynous son of Protiaon and ordered him to watch and keep the horses close at hand. Then he went back and took his place in the front ranks.

Teucer then aimed another arrow at Hector. If he had hit and killed him there and then, there would have been no more fighting at the ships. But Zeus, who watched over Hector, kept his eyes on Teucer and robbed him of his triumph. Just as Teucer was drawing the bow and about to take aim, Zeus broke the bowstring. The arrow went astray and the bow dropped from his hands. Teucer shook with anger and spoke to his brother. “Alas, see how heaven thwarts us in everything we do. It has broken my bowstring and snatched the bow from my hand, though I strung it this very morning so that it would serve me for many arrows.”

Ajax son of Telamon answered, “My good fellow, leave your bow and your arrows alone, because Zeus has made them useless to spite the Danaans. Take your spear, put your shield on your shoulder, and fight the Trojans yourself and urge the others to fight too. They may be winning for the moment, but if we fight as we ought, they will find the ships hard to take.”

Teucer then took his bow and put it away in his tent. He hung a shield four hides thick from his shoulders, and on his fine head he set a well-made helmet with a crest of horse-hair that nodded menacingly above it. He took up his formidable bronze-tipped spear, and at once he was at Ajax’s side.

Hector saw that Teucer’s bow was no use to him any more, and he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians. “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians good in close fight, be men, my friends, and show your courage here at the ships. I have seen the weapon of one of their chieftains made useless by the hand of Zeus. It is easy to tell when Zeus is helping people and means to help them still more, and again when he is bringing them down and will do nothing for them. Now he is on our side and is turning against the Argives. So swarm around the ships and fight. If any of you is struck by spear or sword and loses his life, let him die. A man who dies fighting for his country dies with honor. He leaves his wife and children safe behind him, and his house and allotment unplundered, if only the Achaeans can be driven back to their own land, they and their ships.”

With these words he put heart and soul into all of them. On the other side Ajax urged on his comrades. “Shame on you, Argives! Now we are utterly lost unless we can save ourselves by driving the enemy from our ships. If Hector takes them, do you think you will get home by land? Can you not hear him cheering on his whole army to set our fleet on fire? He tells them to remember that they are in a battle, not at a dance. Our only course is to fight them with all our strength. We had better take our chance, life or death, once and for all, than be hemmed in at our ships by worse men than ourselves and fight a long time with no result.”

With these words he put life and soul into all of them. Then Hector killed Schedius son of Perimedes, leader of the Phoceans, and Ajax killed Laodamas, a captain of foot soldiers and son of Antenor. Polydamas killed Otus of Cyllene, a comrade of the son of Phyleus and chief of the proud Epeans. Meges saw this and sprang at Polydamas, but Polydamas crouched down and Meges missed him, because Apollo would not allow the son of Panthous to fall in battle. The spear hit Croesmus in the middle of the chest instead, and he fell heavily to the ground, and Meges stripped him of his armor. At that moment the valiant soldier Dolops son of Lampus charged in. Lampus was a son of Laomedon and famous for his valor, and his son Dolops knew every way of war. Dolops attacked at close quarters and struck the middle of the shield of the son of Phyleus with his spear, but his good corslet, made with plates of metal, saved him. Phyleus had brought it from Ephyra and the river Selleis, where his host, King Euphetes, had given it to him to wear in battle for protection. Now it saved the life of his son. Then Meges struck the topmost crest of Dolops’s bronze helmet with his spear and tore off its plume of horse-hair. It had just been dyed scarlet, and it tumbled into the dust. Dolops was still fighting, confident of victory, when Menelaus came up to help Meges and got to Dolops’s side without being noticed. He speared him in the shoulder from behind, and the point, driven with great force, went through into his chest, and Dolops fell headlong. The two of them then went toward him to strip off his armor. But Hector called on all his brothers for help, and he especially reproached brave Melanippus son of Hiketaon. Before the war broke out, Melanippus used to pasture his herds of cattle in Percote. When the ships of the Danaans came, he went back to Ilium, where he was eminent among the Trojans and lived near Priam, who treated him like one of his own sons. Hector now rebuked him. “Why, Melanippus, are we so slack? Do you take no notice of the death of your kinsman? Do you not see how they are trying to take Dolops’s armor? Follow me. We must not fight the Argives from a distance now, but in close combat, until either we kill them or they take the high wall of Ilium and slay her people.”

He led the way as he spoke, and the hero Melanippus went after him. Meanwhile Ajax son of Telamon kept cheering on the Argives. “Be men, my friends,” he cried, “and dread disgrace. Behave in battle so that each of you earns the respect of the others. Men who care what their fellows think are less likely to be killed than men who do not. In flight there is neither gain nor glory.”

So he urged on men who were already set on driving back the Trojans. They took his words to heart and fenced the ships in as with a wall of bronze, while Zeus urged on the Trojans. Menelaus of the loud battle cry urged on Antilochus. “Antilochus,” he said, “you are young, and none of the Achaeans is more swift-footed or more valiant than you. See if you cannot spring upon some Trojan and kill him.”

Having spurred on Antilochus, Menelaus hurried away. Antilochus darted out at once from the front ranks, looked carefully around him, and threw a spear. The Trojans fell back as he threw, and the dart did not leave his hand in vain. It struck Melanippus, the proud son of Hiketaon, in the breast by the nipple as he was coming forward, and Melanippus fell heavily to the ground with his armor ringing and rattling around him. Antilochus sprang on him as a dog springs on a fawn that a hunter has hit as it broke from its hiding place, and killed it. In the same way, O Melanippus, stalwart Antilochus sprang on you to strip you of your armor. But noble Hector saw him and came running at him through the thick of the battle. Brave soldier though he was, Antilochus would not wait to face him. He fled like a savage creature that knows it has done wrong, and runs, after killing a dog or a man herding his cattle, before a crowd of men can gather to attack it. So the son of Nestor fled, and Hector and the Trojans showered their weapons after him with a cry that tore the air. He did not turn around and stop his flight until he had reached his comrades.

The Trojans, fierce as lions, kept rushing toward the ships to carry out the commands of Zeus. He kept spurring them on to new feats of daring, while he deadened the courage of the Argives and defeated them by encouraging the Trojans. For he meant to give glory to Hector son of Priam and let him throw fire upon the ships, until he had granted the unrighteous prayer that Thetis had made to him. So Zeus bided his time until he should see the glare of a blazing ship. From that hour he meant to arrange that the Trojans would be driven back from the ships and that the Achaeans would be given glory. With this purpose he inspired Hector son of Priam, who was eager enough already, to attack the ships. His fury was like that of Ares, or like a fire raging in the glades of a dense forest upon the mountains. He foamed at the mouth, his eyes glared under his terrible eyebrows, and his helmet quivered on his temples with the fury of his fighting. Zeus from heaven was with him, and though Hector was one man against many, Zeus granted him victory and glory. For he was doomed to an early death, and already Pallas Athena was hurrying on the hour of his destruction at the hands of the son of Peleus. For now, however, he kept trying to break the enemy ranks wherever he saw them thickest and in the finest armor. Whatever he did, he could not break through them, for they stood like a four-sided tower, or like a high cliff rising from the gray sea that stands against the anger of the gale and of the waves thundering up against it. He fell upon them like flames of fire from every side. A wave raised mountain high by wind and storm breaks over a ship and buries it deep in foam. The fierce winds roar against the mast, the sailors’ hearts fail them for fear, and they are saved from destruction by only a very little. In the same way the hearts of the Achaeans were fainting within them. Or think of a savage lion attacking a herd of cows feeding by the thousands in the low-lying meadows by some wide-watered shore. The herdsman is at his wit’s end how to protect his herd, and keeps going about, now in front of his cattle and now behind them, while the lion springs into the thick of them and fastens on a cow, so that they all tremble with fear. In the same way the Achaeans were utterly panic-stricken by Hector and father Zeus. Even so, Hector killed only Periphetes of Mycenae. He was the son of Copreus, who used to carry the orders of King Eurystheus to mighty Heracles, but the son was a far better man than his father in every way. He was swift-footed and a valiant warrior, and in understanding he ranked among the foremost men of Mycenae. It was he who gave Hector his triumph. As he turned back, he stumbled against the rim of his shield, which reached his feet and kept the javelins off him. He tripped on it and fell on his back, and his helmet rang loudly about his head as he fell. Hector saw him fall and ran up to him. He thrust a spear into his chest and killed him close to his own comrades. For all their sorrow, they could not help him, because they were themselves terribly afraid of Hector.

By now the Argives had reached the ships, and the prows of the ships drawn up first were on every side of them, but the Trojans came pouring after them. The Argives were driven back from the first row of ships, but they made a stand by their tents and did not break up and scatter. Shame and fear held them. They kept shouting to one another without stopping. Nestor of Gerene, tower of strength to the Achaeans, was loudest of all, begging every man by his parents to stand firm.

“Be men, my friends,” he cried, “and respect one another’s good opinion. Every one of you, think of your children, your wives, your property, and your parents, whether they are alive or dead. For their sake, though they are not here, I beg you to stand firm and not to turn in flight.”

With these words he put heart and soul into all of them. Athena took the thick veil of darkness away from their eyes, and a great light fell on them, on the side of the ships and on the side where the fight was raging alike. They could see Hector and all his men: those in the rear, who were taking no part in the battle, and those fighting by the ships.

Ajax could not bring himself to retreat with the rest. He strode from deck to deck with a great sea-pike in his hands, twelve cubits long and jointed with rings. A man skilled in feats of horsemanship couples four horses together and comes tearing at full speed along the public road from the country into some large town. Many men and women marvel as they watch him, because he keeps changing his horse, springing from one to another without ever missing his footing while the horses gallop. In the same way Ajax went striding from one ship’s deck to another, and his voice went up into the heavens. He kept shouting orders to the Danaans, urging them to defend their ships and tents. Hector, for his part, did not stay inside the main body of the Trojan warriors. A dun eagle swoops down on a flock of wild birds feeding near a river, geese, it may be, or cranes, or long-necked swans. In the same way Hector made straight for a dark-prowed ship and rushed right at it, for Zeus with his mighty hand drove him forward and roused his people to follow him.

Now the battle raged furiously at the ships again. You would have thought the men were coming on fresh and unwearied, so fiercely did they fight. This was the state of mind they were in. The Achaeans did not believe they would escape destruction but thought themselves doomed, while there was not a Trojan whose heart did not beat high with the hope of setting the ships on fire and putting the Achaean heroes to the sword.

That was how the two sides felt. Then Hector seized the stern of the good ship that had brought Protesilaus to Troy but never carried him back to his native land. Around this ship a close hand-to-hand fight raged between Danaans and Trojans. They did not fight at a distance with bows and javelins. With one mind they hacked at each other in close combat with their mighty swords and spears pointed at both ends. They also fought with keen battle-axes and with hatchets. Many a good stout blade, hilted and scabbarded with iron, fell from hand or shoulder as they fought, and the earth ran red with blood. Hector had seized the ship and would not let go. He held on to its curved stern and shouted to the Trojans, “Bring fire, and all of you raise the battle cry together. Zeus has granted us a day that will pay us back for all the rest. Today we shall take the ships that came here against the will of heaven, and that have caused us such endless suffering through the cowardice of our councillors. When I wanted to do battle at the ships, they held me back and forbade the army to follow me. If Zeus did then indeed warp our judgment, he himself now commands me and cheers me on.”

As he spoke, the Trojans sprang still more fiercely on the Achaeans. Ajax no longer held his ground. The darts flung at him overcame him, and he was sure he was doomed. So he left the raised deck at the stern and stepped back onto the seven-foot bench of the oarsmen. There he stood on the lookout, and with his spear he held back any Trojan he saw bringing fire to the ships. All the while he kept shouting at the top of his voice and urging on the Danaans. “My friends,” he cried, “Danaan heroes, servants of Ares, be men, my friends, and fight with all your might. Can we hope to find helpers later, or a wall to shield us more surely than the one we have? There is no strong city within reach from which we could draw fresh forces to turn the scales in our favor. We are on the plain of the armed Trojans with the sea behind us, far from our own country. Our salvation, therefore, is in the strength of our hands and in hard fighting.”

As he spoke, he wielded his spear with still greater fury. Whenever any Trojan made for the ships with fire at Hector’s bidding, Ajax was watching for him and drove at him with his long spear. In this way he killed twelve men in hand-to-hand fight before the ships.

chapters.title: Book 16
paragraphs: Fire is now set to the ship of Protesilaus, and Patroclus goes into battle in the armor of Achilles—He pushes the Trojans back, but in the end Euphorbus and Hector kill him.

So the fight went on around the ship of Protesilaus. Meanwhile Patroclus came up to Achilles with tears welling in his eyes, like a spring whose clear water spills down the ledges of a high cliff. Achilles saw him crying and felt sorry for him. He said, “Patroclus, why are you standing there in tears like a silly little girl who runs to her mother and begs to be picked up and carried? She clings to her mother’s dress and holds her back though her mother is in a hurry, and she keeps looking up at her with wet eyes until her mother lifts her. You are shedding tears just like that, Patroclus. Do you have something to tell the Myrmidons, or me? Or have you had news from Phthia that only you know? They tell me that Menoetius son of Actor is still alive, and that Peleus son of Aeacus is still alive among the Myrmidons. We two would grieve bitterly to lose either of them. Or are you mourning for the Argives, and for the way they are being killed at the ships because of their own arrogance? Do not hide anything from me. Say it, so that both of us know.”

Then, knight Patroclus, you answered with a deep sigh, “Achilles, son of Peleus, greatest champion of the Achaeans, do not be angry. I weep because of the disaster that has fallen on the Argives. Every man who has been their champion until now is lying at the ships, wounded by sword or spear. Brave Diomedes son of Tydeus has been hit by a spear. Famed Odysseus and Agamemnon have both taken sword wounds. Eurypylus has been struck in the thigh by an arrow. Skilled healers are tending these heroes and curing their wounds. And you, Achilles, are you still so unyielding? May I never carry the kind of rage you carry, to the ruin of your own good name. Who in later stories will speak well of you if you do not save the Argives from destruction now? You have no pity. The knight Peleus was not your father, and Thetis was not your mother. The gray sea bore you and the sheer cliffs gave you life, so cruel and hard are you. But perhaps you are holding back because you know of some oracle, or because your mother Thetis has told you something from the mouth of Zeus. If so, at least send me out, and the Myrmidons with me, in case I can bring the Danaans some relief. And let me wear your armor.
