The Trojans may take me for you and leave the field, and the hard-pressed sons of the Achaeans can get a chance to breathe. They have hardly had one while fighting. We are fresh, and we could easily drive these tired men back from our ships and tents to their own city.”

He did not know what he was asking, or that he was begging for his own death. Achilles was deeply moved, and he answered, “Noble Patroclus, what are you saying? I am not heeding any prophecy that I know of, and my mother has told me nothing from the mouth of Zeus. What cuts me to the heart is that a man of my own rank should dare to rob me, only because he has more power than I do. After everything I have been through, it is more than I can bear. The girl the sons of the Achaeans picked out for me, whom I won with my spear when I sacked a city—King Agamemnon took her from me as if I were some common vagrant. Still, let bygones be bygones. No man can keep his anger forever. I said I would not give way until the battle and the war cry reached my own ships. But now, strap my armor around your shoulders and lead the Myrmidons into the fight. The dark cloud of Trojans has burst furiously over our fleet. The Argives are pushed back onto the beach and penned into a narrow space, and the whole people of Troy has grown bold enough to come out against them, because they do not see the visor of my helmet gleaming close by. If they had seen it, they would have fled, and there would not be a creek or gully that was not filled with their dead. That is how it would have gone, if only King Agamemnon had treated me fairly. As things are, the Trojans have surrounded our army. Diomedes son of Tydeus no longer wields his spear to defend the Danaans, and I have not heard the voice of the son of Atreus coming from his hated head. What rings in my ears is the voice of murderous Hector giving orders to the Trojans, who triumph over the Achaeans and fill the whole plain with their battle cry. But even so, Patroclus, fall on them and save the fleet, or the Trojans will burn it and cut off our way home. Do exactly as I now tell you, so that you win me great honor from all the Danaans, and they give the girl back to me with splendid gifts besides. When you have driven the Trojans from the ships, come back. Even if Hera’s thundering husband puts victory within your reach, do not fight the Trojans further without me, or you will rob me of glory that should be mine. And do not let your lust for battle carry you into killing more Trojans, or leading the Achaeans on toward Ilium. One of the ever-living gods may come down from Olympus and attack you, for Phoebus Apollo loves the Trojans well. Return once you have freed the ships from danger, and let others fight on the plain. By father Zeus, Athena and Apollo, I wish that not one Trojan were left alive, and not one Argive either, and that only we two were left to tear off the veil that covers the brow of Troy.”

So they spoke together. Meanwhile Ajax could no longer hold his ground under the shower of darts that rained on him. The will of Zeus and the Trojan javelins were too much for him. The helmet gleaming at his temples rang without pause as the missiles kept pouring onto it and onto the cheek-pieces that guarded his face. His left shoulder was also worn out from holding his shield so long. Still, however hard they threw at him, they could not make him give way. He could hardly breathe. Sweat ran from every pore of his body. He had not a moment’s rest, and danger upon danger pressed on him from every side.

And now, Muses who have your homes on Olympus, tell me how fire was thrown on the ships of the Achaeans. Hector came up close and swung his great sword at the ashen spear of Ajax. He cut it clean in two, just behind the place where the point was fixed to the shaft. So Ajax was left holding a headless spear, while the bronze point flew off some distance and landed ringing on the ground. Ajax saw the hand of heaven in this. He was dismayed to see that Zeus had left him completely defenseless and wanted the Trojans to win. So he drew back, and the Trojans hurled fire at the ship, which at once was wrapped in flames.

The fire was now blazing around the ship’s stern. Achilles slapped his two thighs and said to Patroclus, “Up, noble knight! I can see the glare of enemy fire at our fleet. Up, before they destroy our ships and leave us no way to retreat. Put on your armor at once while I call our people together.”

As he spoke, Patroclus began to arm. First he strapped greaves of good make on his legs, fitted with silver ankle-clasps. After that he put on the cuirass of the son of Aeacus, richly inlaid and studded. He hung his silver-studded sword of bronze from his shoulders, and then took up his mighty shield. On his handsome head he set the well-made helmet, with its crest of horse-hair nodding threateningly above. He took two sturdy spears that fitted his hands. But he did not take the spear of noble Achilles, so stout and strong, because no other Achaean could wield it, though Achilles handled it easily. It was an ashen spear from Mount Pelion. Chiron had cut it on a mountain top and given it to Peleus, to deal out death among heroes. Patroclus told Automedon to yoke the horses quickly. Next to Achilles, Automedon was the man he honored most, and the one he could most firmly rely on in battle. So Automedon yoked the swift horses Xanthus and Balius, who could fly like the wind. The harpy Podarge had borne them to the west wind as she grazed in a meadow by the waters of the river Oceanus. In the side traces he set the noble horse Pedasus. Achilles had taken him away when he sacked the city of Eetion, and though Pedasus was a mortal horse, he could keep pace with the immortal ones.

Meanwhile Achilles went everywhere among the tents and told his Myrmidons to put on their armor. As fierce, ravening wolves feast on a horned stag they have killed in the mountains, their jaws red with blood, and then go in a pack to lap water from a clear spring with their long thin tongues, reeking of blood and slaughter and knowing no fear because hunger drives them, so the leaders and counselors of the Myrmidons gathered around the good squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles himself stood among them, urging on both men and horses.

Noble Achilles had brought fifty ships to Troy, and each had a crew of fifty oarsmen. Over them he set five captains he could trust, and he himself commanded them all. Menesthius of the gleaming corslet led the first company. He was the son of the river Spercheius, which streams down from heaven. Fair Polydora, daughter of Peleus, had borne him to ever-flowing Spercheius—a woman joined to a god. But he was called the son of Borus son of Perieres, who lived with his mother as her husband, and who had given great wealth to win her. Noble Eudorus, the son of an unmarried woman, led the second company. Polymele, daughter of Phylas the graceful dancer, bore him. The mighty slayer of Argus had fallen in love with her when he saw her among the singing women at a dance in honor of Artemis, the rushing huntress of the golden arrows. So Hermes, giver of all good, went up with her to an upper chamber and lay with her in secret. She bore him a noble son, Eudorus, who was singularly swift-footed and valiant in a fight. Ilithuia, goddess of the pains of childbirth, brought him into the light, and he saw the face of the sun. Then mighty Echecles son of Actor took the mother as his wife, giving great wealth to win her. Her father Phylas brought the child up and cared for him, doting on him as fondly as if he were his own son. Pisander son of Maemalus led the third company. Among all the Myrmidons he was the finest spearman, after Achilles’s own comrade Patroclus. The old knight Phoenix was captain of the fourth company, and Alcimedon, noble son of Laerceus, of the fifth.

When Achilles had chosen his men and stationed them all with their captains, he gave them a stern charge. “Myrmidons,” he said, “remember the threats you made against the Trojans at the ships, in the time of my anger, when you were all complaining of me. ‘Cruel son of Peleus,’ you would say, ‘your mother must have fed you on gall, you are so ruthless. You keep us here at the ships against our will. If you are going to be this relentless, we had better go home over the sea.’ Often you have gathered and scolded me like that. Now the hour has come for the great feats of arms you have so long been longing for. So let every one of you keep a high heart to do battle with the Trojans.”

With these words he put heart and soul into every man, and when they heard their king’s words they closed their companies up even tighter. As a builder fits stones tightly into the wall of a high house that must give shelter from the winds, so closely were the helmets and bossed shields set against one another. Shield pressed on shield, helm on helm, and man on man. They stood so close that the horse-hair plumes on the gleaming ridges of their helmets touched as they bent their heads.

In front of them all, two men armed themselves—Patroclus and Automedon—two men with one mind, to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went into his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest that silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and had filled with shirts, cloaks against the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he kept a cup of rare workmanship. No man but himself might drink from it, and he made offerings from it to no god except father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulphur. Then he rinsed it in clean water, washed his hands, and drew wine. He stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven and pouring out the wine as a drink offering. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, you who live far away and rule wintry Dodona, where your prophets the Selli live around you with unwashed feet and beds made on the ground—if you heard me when I prayed to you before, and honored me by sending disaster on the Achaeans, grant me now the fulfillment of one more prayer. I will stay here where my ships are lying, but I am sending my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory goes with him. Put your courage into his heart, so that Hector learns whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is unbeatable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fighting and the battle cry away from the ships, grant that he returns unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”

So he prayed, and all-counselling Zeus heard his prayer. He granted part of it, but not all. He agreed that Patroclus would thrust war and battle back from the ships, but he refused to let him come out of the fight safely.
When Achilles had poured his drink offering and prayed, he went back into his tent and put the cup away in his chest.
Then he came out again, because he still loved to watch the fierce fight raging between the Trojans and Achaeans.

Meanwhile the armed band around Patroclus marched on until they sprang at the Trojans, high in hope. They swarmed out like wasps whose nests are by the roadside, and which silly children love to tease, so that anyone passing by may get stung. Or again, if a traveler on the road annoys them by accident, every wasp comes flying out in a fury to defend its young. With that same rage and courage the Myrmidons swarmed from their ships, and their battle cry rose to the heavens. Patroclus called to his men at the top of his voice, “Myrmidons, followers of Achilles son of Peleus, be men, my friends! Fight with all your might and main, so that we win glory for the son of Peleus, who is by far the foremost man at the ships of the Argives—he and his close-fighting followers. Then King Agamemnon, son of Atreus, will learn his folly in showing no respect to the bravest of the Achaeans.”

With these words he put heart and soul into every man, and they fell on the Trojans in a body. The ships rang again with the cry the Achaeans raised. When the Trojans saw the brave son of Menoetius and his squire, both gleaming in their armor, they lost heart and their battalions fell into confusion. They thought the swift son of Peleus must have put aside his anger and made peace with Agamemnon. Every man looked around to see where he could flee to safety.

Patroclus was the first to aim a spear. He threw it into the middle of the crowd, where men were packed most thickly, by the stern of the ship of Protesilaus. He hit Pyraechmes, who had led his Paeonian horsemen from Amydon and the broad waters of the river Axius. The spear struck him in the right shoulder and he fell backward in the dust with a groan. His men fell into confusion, because by killing their leader, the finest soldier among them, Patroclus had struck panic into them all. So he drove them away from the ship and put out the fire that was blazing there, leaving the half-burnt ship where it lay. The Trojans were driven back with a shout that split the skies, and the Danaans poured after them from their ships, shouting just as ceaselessly. As when Zeus, gatherer of the thunder cloud, spreads a dense canopy over the top of a lofty mountain, and all the peaks, the jutting headlands and the forest glades show out in the great light flashing from the bursting heavens, so the Danaans, having driven the fire back from their ships, took a short breath. But the fury of the fight was not over. The Trojans had not been driven back in utter rout. They still gave battle, and were forced from their ground only by sheer fighting.

The fighting now broke up into scattered clashes, and the chieftains killed one another whenever and however they could. The valiant son of Menoetius was first. As Areilycus was turning around, he drove a spear into his thigh. The point went straight through and broke the bone, and Areilycus fell forward. Menelaus struck Thoas in the chest, at the place near the rim of his shield where it was left exposed, and Thoas fell dead. The son of Phyleus saw Amphiclus about to attack him. Before Amphiclus could, he aimed at the top of his thigh, where the muscle is thicker than anywhere else. The spear tore through all the sinews of the leg, and darkness closed Amphiclus’s eyes. Of Nestor’s sons, Antilochus speared Atymnius. He drove the point of the spear through his throat, and Atymnius went down. Then Maris sprang at Antilochus in hand-to-hand fight, to avenge his brother. He stood over the body with his spear in hand. But valiant Thrasymedes was too quick for him. Before Maris could land a blow, Thrasymedes struck him in the shoulder. His aim was true. The spear severed all the muscles at the root of the arm and tore them right down to the bone, so Maris fell heavily to the ground, and darkness closed his eyes. In this way two noble comrades of Sarpedon went down to Erebus, killed by the two sons of Nestor. They were the warrior sons of Amisodorus, who had raised the invincible Chimaera, to the harm of many. Ajax son of Oileus sprang on Cleobulus, who was caught in the crush, and took him alive. But he killed him then and there with a sword blow on the neck. The sword was drenched in his blood, while dark death and the strong hand of fate seized him and closed his eyes.

Peneleos and Lycon now met in close combat, because their spears had missed. Both had thrown without effect, so now they drew their swords. Lycon struck the plumed crest of Peneleos’s helmet, but his sword broke off at the hilt. Peneleos struck Lycon on the neck under the ear. The blade went in so deep that the head hung by nothing but the skin, and no life was left in him. Meriones chased Acamas on foot and caught him just as he was about to mount his chariot. He drove a spear through his right shoulder, and Acamas fell headlong from the car, and darkness closed his eyes. Idomeneus speared Erymas in the mouth. The bronze point of the spear went straight through, beneath the brain, crashing in among the white bones and smashing them. All his teeth were knocked out, and blood gushed in a stream from both his eyes. It also came gurgling up from his mouth and nostrils, and the darkness of death wrapped around him.

So each of these Danaan chieftains killed his man. Ravening wolves seize kids or lambs that have strayed from the main flock through the shepherd’s carelessness and are alone on the hillsides. When the wolves see them, they pounce at once, because the young animals cannot defend themselves. In the same way the Danaans now fell on the Trojans, who fled with ill-omened cries in their panic and had no fight left in them.

Meanwhile great Ajax kept trying to drive his spear into Hector. But Hector was skilled enough to keep his broad shoulders well covered by his ox-hide shield, always listening for the whizzing of arrows and the heavy thud of spears. He knew well that the fortunes of the day had turned, yet he stood his ground and tried to protect his comrades.

As a cloud rises into heaven from Olympus out of a clear sky when Zeus is brewing a gale, so the Trojans now fled in panic-stricken rout, with no order in their going. Hector’s swift horses carried him and his armor out of the fight, and he left the Trojan host penned in against their will by the deep trench. Many a team of horses snapped the pole of their chariot in the trench and left their master’s car behind. Patroclus chased them, calling fiercely on the Danaans and full of fury against the Trojans. They were no longer in a body, and they filled every road with their cries of panic and rout. The air was dark with the clouds of dust they raised, and the horses strained every nerve in their flight from the tents and ships toward the city.

Patroclus kept steering his horses toward wherever he saw the most men fleeing in confusion, cheering on his men as he went. Chariots were being smashed in all directions, and many a man tumbled from his own car and fell beneath the wheels of Patroclus’s chariot. Its immortal horses, which the gods had given to Peleus, sprang over the trench in a single bound as they raced on. Patroclus was set on getting near Hector, for he had his heart fixed on spearing him, but Hector’s horses were now hurrying him away. As the whole dark earth bows before a tempest on an autumn day, when Zeus rains his hardest to punish men who give crooked judgments in their courts, drive justice out of them and ignore the decrees of heaven, and all the rivers run full, and the torrents tear many a new channel as they roar headlong from the mountains to the dark sea, and it goes badly for the works of men, so great was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight.

Patroclus now cut off the battalions nearest to him and drove them back toward the ships. They were doing their best to reach the city, but he would not let them. He bore down on them in the space between the river, the ships and the wall, and he avenged many a fallen comrade there. First he hit Pronous with a spear in the chest, where it was exposed near the rim of his shield, and Pronous fell heavily to the ground. Next he sprang at Thestor son of Enops. Thestor sat huddled in his chariot, because he had lost his head and the reins had been torn from his hands. Patroclus went up to him and drove a spear into his right jaw. The spear hooked him by the teeth and pulled him over the rim of his car. It was like a man sitting on the end of a jutting rock who draws a strong fish out of the sea with a line and hook. In the same way Patroclus pulled Thestor, gaping, from his chariot with the spear. He threw him down on his face, and Thestor died as he fell. Then Erylaus came on to attack him, and Patroclus struck him full on the head with a stone. His brains were all battered inside his helmet, and he fell headlong to the ground, and the pangs of death took hold of him. After that Patroclus laid low, one after another, Erymas, Amphoterus, Epaltes, Tlepolemus, Echius son of Damastor, Pyris, Ipheus, Euippus and Polymelus son of Argeas.

Sarpedon saw his comrades, the men who wore ungirdled tunics, being beaten down by Patroclus son of Menoetius. He rebuked the Lycians, saying, “Shame on you! Where are you running to? Show your mettle. I will meet this man in fight myself and find out who it is that is so masterful. He has done us great harm and has stretched many a brave man on the ground.”

As he spoke he sprang from his chariot, and Patroclus, seeing this, leaped to the ground as well. The two rushed at each other with loud cries, like eagle-beaked crook-taloned vultures that scream and tear at one another on some high mountain crag.

The son of scheming Cronus looked down on them with pity and spoke to Hera, who was his wife and sister. “Alas, it is the fate of Sarpedon, whom I love so dearly, to die by the hand of Patroclus. I am in two minds. Shall I catch him up out of the fight and set him down safe and sound in the fertile land of Lycia, or let him fall now by the hand of the son of Menoetius?”

Hera answered, “Most dread son of Cronus, what are you saying? Would you snatch a mortal man out of the jaws of death, when his doom was fated long ago? Do as you wish, but the rest of us will not all agree with you. And I tell you this, so take it to heart. If you send Sarpedon safely home, some other god will want to carry his own son out of the battle too. Many sons of gods are fighting around the city of Troy, and you will make every one of them jealous. But if you are fond of him and pity him, let him fall by the hand of Patroclus. Then, as soon as the life has gone out of him, send Death and sweet Sleep to carry him off the field and take him to the broad lands of Lycia. There his brothers and kinsmen will bury him with mound and pillar, as the dead are rightly honored.”
The father of gods and men gave his consent. Yet for the sake of his son, whom Patroclus was about to kill far from home on the rich plain of Troy, he let a rain of blood fall on the earth.

When they had come close to one another, Patroclus struck Thrasydemus, the brave squire of Sarpedon, in the lower belly and killed him. Then Sarpedon aimed a spear at Patroclus and missed him, but he hit the horse Pedasus in the right shoulder. It screamed aloud and lay groaning in the dust until the life went out of it. The other two horses began to plunge. The chariot pole cracked, and they tangled in the reins because the horse yoked with them had fallen. But Automedon knew what to do. Without losing a moment he drew the keen blade that hung by his sturdy thigh and cut the third horse loose. Then the other two straightened themselves, pulled hard at the reins and went together into battle again.

Sarpedon took a second aim at Patroclus and again missed him. The point of the spear flew over his left shoulder and did not touch him. Then Patroclus took aim in his turn, and his spear did not leave his hand in vain. It struck Sarpedon exactly where the midriff encloses the ever-beating heart. He fell as an oak or silver poplar or tall pine falls when woodmen on the mountains have laid their axes to it, to make timber for ship-building. So he lay stretched at full length in front of his chariot and horses, moaning and clutching at the blood-stained dust. A lion springs with a bound on a herd of cattle and fastens on a great black bull, which dies bellowing in its clutches. In just that way the leader of the Lycian warriors struggled in death, brought down by the hand of Patroclus. He called to his trusty comrade and said, “Glaucus, my brother, hero among heroes, put forth all your strength. Fight with might and main, and now, if ever, behave like a valiant soldier. First go among the Lycian captains and tell them to fight for Sarpedon. Then do battle yourself to save my armor from being taken. My name will haunt you from now on and forever if the Achaeans rob me of my armor now that I have fallen at their ships. Do your very utmost and call all my people together.”

Death closed his eyes as he spoke. Patroclus planted his heel on his breast and pulled the spear from his body. His senses came out with it, so that he drew out spear-point and Sarpedon’s soul together. Close by, the Myrmidons held his snorting horses, who were wild with panic at finding themselves deserted by their lords.

Glaucus was overcome with grief when he heard what Sarpedon said, because he could not help him. He had to hold up one arm with his other hand, for he was in great pain from the wound that Teucer’s arrow had given him when Teucer was defending the wall and he, Glaucus, was attacking it. So he prayed to far-darting Apollo, saying, “Hear me, O king. You may be in the rich land of Lycia or in Troy, but in all places you can hear the prayer of someone in distress, as I am now. I have a grievous wound. My hand aches with pain, there is no staunching the blood, and my whole arm drags because of my hurt, so I cannot grasp my sword or go among my foes and fight them, though our prince, Sarpedon, the son of Zeus, is slain. Zeus did not defend his son. So you, O king, heal my wound, ease my pain and give me strength both to cheer on the Lycians and to fight alongside them around the body of him who has fallen.”

So he prayed, and Apollo heard him. The god eased his pain, stopped the flow of black blood from the wound and gave him new strength. Glaucus felt it, and he was glad that the mighty god had answered his prayer. At once he went among the Lycian captains and told them to come fight about the body of Sarpedon. From them he strode on among the Trojans, to Polydamas son of Panthous and to Agenor. Then he went looking for Aeneas and Hector, and when he found them he said, “Hector, you have utterly forgotten your allies. They are wearing themselves out here for your sake, far from friends and home, and you do nothing to support them. Sarpedon, leader of the Lycian warriors, has fallen—he who was at once the right and might of Lycia. Ares has struck him down by the spear of Patroclus. Stand by him, my friends. Do not let the Myrmidons strip him of his armor or abuse his body, in revenge for all the Danaans we have speared at the ships.”

At his words the Trojans were plunged into extreme and ungovernable grief. Sarpedon, foreigner though he was, had been one of the main supports of their city, both because he had many people with him and because he was himself the foremost of them all. Led by Hector, who was infuriated by Sarpedon’s fall, they made straight for the Danaans with all their might. Meanwhile the undaunted spirit of Patroclus son of Menoetius cheered on the Achaeans. First he spoke to the two Ajaxes, men who needed no urging. “Ajaxes,” he said, “may it please you now to show yourselves the men you have always been, or even better. Sarpedon is fallen—he who was first to leap over the wall of the Achaeans. Let us take his body and outrage it. Let us strip the armor from his shoulders and kill his comrades if they try to rescue his body.”

The men he spoke to were already eager. Both sides, the Trojans and Lycians on one hand and the Myrmidons and Achaeans on the other, closed up their battalions and fought desperately over the body of Sarpedon, with fierce shouting all the while. The din of their armor was mighty as they met. Zeus spread a thick darkness over the fight, to make the toil of the battle over his son’s body harder.

At first the Trojans made some headway against the Achaeans, because one of the best men among the Myrmidons was killed: Epeigeus, son of noble Agacles, who had once been king in the good city of Budeum. Having killed a valiant kinsman of his own, he had taken refuge with Peleus and Thetis, who sent him to Ilium, the land of noble horses, to fight the Trojans under Achilles. Now Hector struck him on the head with a stone just as he had caught hold of the body. His brains were all battered in inside his helmet, and he fell face foremost on the body of Sarpedon and died there. Patroclus was enraged by his comrade’s death. He sped through the front ranks as swiftly as a hawk that swoops on a flock of daws or starlings. So swiftly, O noble knight Patroclus, did you make straight for the Lycians and Trojans to avenge your comrade. At once he struck Sthenelaus the son of Ithaemenes on the neck with a stone and broke the tendons that join it to the head and spine. Hector and the front rank of his men gave ground. The Trojans retreated before the Achaeans as far as a man can throw a javelin when he competes for some prize, or even in battle. Glaucus, captain of the Lycians, was the first to rally them, by killing Bathycles son of Chalcon, who lived in Hellas and was the richest man among the Myrmidons. Bathycles was pursuing Glaucus and about to lay hold of him when Glaucus turned round suddenly and drove his spear right into the middle of his chest. Bathycles fell heavily to the ground. The fall of so good a man filled the Achaeans with dismay, while the Trojans were exultant and came up in a body round the corpse. Even so, the Achaeans, mindful of their prowess, bore straight down on them.

Next Meriones killed a helmeted Trojan, Laogonus son of Onetor. Laogonus was priest of Zeus on Mt. Ida, and the people honored him like a god. Meriones struck him beneath the jaw and ear, and the life went out of him as the darkness of death seized him. Then Aeneas threw a spear at Meriones, hoping to hit him under the shield while he was advancing. Meriones saw it coming and stooped low to dodge it. The spear flew past him and its point stuck in the ground, and the butt-end went on quivering until Ares drained its force away. So the spear left Aeneas’s hand for nothing and fell quivering to the ground. Aeneas was angry and said, “Meriones, you are a fine dancer, but if I had hit you, my spear would have put an end to you soon enough.”

Meriones answered, “Aeneas, brave as you are, you cannot finish off every man who comes against you. You are only a mortal, like me. If I hit you square in the middle of your shield with my spear, however strong and sure of yourself you are, I would quickly beat you, and you would give up your life to Hades of the noble horses.”

At this the son of Menoetius scolded him. “Meriones, you are a hero, but you should not talk this way,” he said. “Taunting, my good friend, will not make the Trojans pull away from the dead body. Some of them must go under the ground first. Blows are for battle, and words are for council. So fight, and say nothing.”

Patroclus led the way as he spoke, and the hero went forward with him. Woodcutters work in some forest glade on the mountains, and the thud of their axes is heard from far away. A din just like that now rose from the earth, the clash of bronze armor and good ox-hide shields, as men struck at each other with swords and with spears pointed at both ends. A man would have needed sharp eyes to recognize Sarpedon, so covered was he from head to foot with spears, blood and dust. Men swarmed around the body like flies that buzz around the full milk-pails in spring, when the pails are brimming with milk. In the same way they crowded around Sarpedon. Zeus did not turn his keen eyes from the fight for a single moment. He kept watching it all the time, while he worked out how best to kill Patroclus. He was weighing whether Hector should be allowed to finish Patroclus now, in the fight over the body of Sarpedon, and strip off his armor, or whether Patroclus should give the Trojans still more trouble. In the end Zeus decided that the brave squire of Achilles son of Peleus should first drive Hector and the Trojans back toward the city and take many lives. So he began by making Hector lose heart. Hector got into his chariot and fled, telling the other Trojans to flee as well, because he saw that the scales of Zeus had tipped against him. The brave Lycians did not stand firm either. They were dismayed to see their king lying struck to the heart in a heap of corpses, for when the son of Cronus made the fight grow hot, many had fallen on top of him. The Achaeans stripped the gleaming armor from Sarpedon’s shoulders, and the brave son of Menoetius gave it to his men to carry to the ships. Then Zeus, lord of the storm cloud, said to Apollo, “Dear Phoebus, go now, I ask you, and take Sarpedon out of range of the weapons. Wipe the black blood from him, carry him a long way off, and wash him in the river. Anoint him with ambrosia and dress him in immortal clothing. When that is done, give him into the arms of the two swift messengers, Death and Sleep. They will carry him straight to the rich land of Lycia. There his brothers and kinsmen will bury him and raise a mound and a pillar to his memory, as is the due honor of the dead.”

So he spoke. Apollo obeyed his father’s word and came down from the heights of Ida into the thick of the fight. At once he lifted Sarpedon out of range of the weapons and carried him a long way off. There he washed him in the river, anointed him with ambrosia and dressed him in immortal clothing. Then he gave him into the arms of the two swift messengers, Death and Sleep, who soon set him down in the rich land of Lycia.

Meanwhile Patroclus, shouting again and again to his horses and to Automedon, chased the Trojans and Lycians, proud and foolish in his heart. If only he had obeyed the command of the son of Peleus, he would have escaped death and come to no harm. But the plans of Zeus are beyond human understanding. Zeus will put even a brave man to flight and snatch victory out of his hands, and at another time he will push him on to fight, as he did now when he put a high spirit into the heart of Patroclus.

Who was the first, and who the last, that you killed, O Patroclus, when the gods had called you to meet your doom? First came Adrestus, Autonous, Echeclus, Perimus son of Megas, Epistor and Melanippus. After these you killed Elasus, Mulius and Pylartes. These you slew, and the rest saved themselves by running away.

The sons of the Achaeans would have taken Troy then, by the hands of Patroclus, whose spear flew in every direction. But Phoebus Apollo took his stand on the wall to ruin his plan and help the Trojans. Three times Patroclus charged at a corner of the high wall, and three times Apollo drove him back, striking his shield with his own immortal hands. When Patroclus came on like a god for a fourth time, Apollo shouted at him in a terrible voice. “Draw back, noble Patroclus,” he said. “It is not your fate to sack the city of the Trojan chieftains. It will not be the fate of Achilles either, and he is a far better man than you.” At these words Patroclus pulled back some distance, to avoid the anger of Apollo.

Meanwhile Hector was waiting with his horses inside the Scaean gates. He could not decide whether to drive out and fight again, or to call the army back inside the gates. While he hesitated, Phoebus Apollo came up to him looking like Asius, a young and lusty warrior. Asius was Hector’s uncle, a brother of Hecuba and a son of Dymas, who lived in Phrygia by the waters of the river Sangarius. In this likeness Apollo, son of Zeus, spoke to Hector. “Hector, why have you stopped fighting? It is badly done. If I were as much better a man than you as I am worse, you would soon regret your slackness. Drive straight at Patroclus, and perhaps Apollo will grant you a triumph over him, and you will overpower him.”

With that the god went back into the uproar, and Hector told Cebriones to drive into the fight again. Apollo passed in among the ranks and struck panic into the Argives, while he gave triumph to Hector and the Trojans. Hector left the other Danaans alone and killed no one, but drove straight at Patroclus. Patroclus jumped down from his chariot to the ground, holding a spear in his left hand and in his right a jagged stone as big as his hand could hold. He stood still and threw it. It did not go far before it hit someone, and the cast was not wasted. The stone struck Cebriones, Hector’s charioteer and a bastard son of Priam, as he held the reins in his hands. It hit him on the forehead and drove his brows into his head, because the bone was smashed, and his eyes fell to the ground at his feet. He dropped dead from the chariot like a diver, and no life was left in him. Over him you then boasted, O knight Patroclus: “Bless my heart, how nimble he is, and how well he dives! If we were at sea, this fellow would dive from the ship’s side and bring up as many oysters as the whole crew could eat, even in rough water, since he has dived so beautifully off his chariot onto the ground. So it seems the Trojans have divers too.”

As he spoke he threw himself on Cebriones, leaping like a lion that attacks a stockyard and is struck in the chest, so that his own courage is the death of him. With the same fury, O Patroclus, you then leapt on Cebriones. Hector sprang down from his chariot to the ground as well. The two of them fought over the body of Cebriones. Two lions fight fiercely on some high mountain over the body of a stag they have killed. In the same way these two mighty warriors, Patroclus son of Menoetius and brave Hector, hacked and hewed at each other over the corpse of Cebriones. Once Hector had caught Cebriones by the head, he would not let go, while Patroclus kept a firm hold on his feet. A fierce fight raged between the other Danaans and Trojans. The east wind and the south wind buffet each other when they beat on a dense forest in the mountains, where there are beech and ash and spreading cornel. The tops of the trees roar as they crash together, and you can hear the boughs cracking and breaking. In the same way the Trojans and Achaeans leapt at one another and cut each other down, and neither side would give way. Many a pointed spear fell to the ground, and many a winged arrow flew from its bowstring around the body of Cebriones. Many a great stone also beat on many a shield as they fought around him. But there he lay in the whirling clouds of dust, huge in his hugeness, heedless now of his driving.

As long as the sun stood high in mid-heaven, the weapons of both sides were equally deadly, and men fell. But when the sun sank toward the time when men unyoke their oxen, the Achaeans proved, beyond all expectation, to be the stronger. They dragged Cebriones out of range of the darts and the tumult of the Trojans and stripped the armor from his shoulders. Then Patroclus rushed on the Trojans like Ares, with fierce purpose and a terrible shout, and three times he killed nine men. But while he kept coming on like a god, O Patroclus, the hour of your end was drawing near, for Phoebus met you in deadly earnest. Patroclus did not see him moving about in the crush, because the god was wrapped in thick darkness. Apollo struck him from behind, on his back and broad shoulders, with the flat of his hand, and his eyes spun. Phoebus Apollo knocked the helmet from his head, and it rolled rattling under the horses’ feet, where its horse-hair plumes were smeared with dust and blood. That helmet had never fared this way before, for it had protected the head and comely forehead of the godlike hero Achilles. Now, however, Zeus handed it over to be worn by Hector. Even so, the end of Hector was near too. The bronze-shod spear, so great and so strong, broke in the hand of Patroclus. His shield, which covered him from head to foot, fell to the ground together with the band that held it, and Apollo undid the fastenings of his corslet.

At this his mind clouded over. His limbs failed him, and he stood dazed. Then Euphorbus son of Panthous, a Dardanian, came up behind him and struck him in the back with a spear, between the shoulders. Euphorbus was the best spearman of his time, and also the finest horseman and the swiftest runner. As soon as he had first come up with his chariot, he had unseated twenty men, so skilled was he in all the arts of war. He it was, O knight Patroclus, who first drove a weapon into you, but he did not quite overpower you. Euphorbus pulled his ashen spear out of the wound and ran back into the crowd. He would not stand and wait for Patroclus to attack him, unarmed though Patroclus now was. But Patroclus, unnerved by the blow from the god and by the spear wound, drew back among his men, afraid for his life. Hector saw that he was wounded and giving ground. He forced his way through the ranks, and when he was close he struck Patroclus in the lower belly with a spear, driving the bronze point right through. Patroclus fell heavily to the ground, to the great grief of the Achaeans. As when a lion has fought a fierce wild boar and beaten him—the two fight furiously on the mountains over some little spring where both want to drink, and the lion has beaten the boar until he can hardly breathe—in the same way Hector son of Priam took the life of the brave son of Menoetius, who had killed so many. He struck him from close at hand and boasted over him as he did it. “Patroclus,” he said, “you thought you would sack our city, rob our Trojan women of their freedom and carry them off in your ships to your own country. Fool! Hector and his swift horses were always straining their utmost to defend them. I am the foremost of all the Trojan warriors in keeping the day of slavery away from them. As for you, vultures will devour you here. Poor wretch, Achilles with all his bravery was no help to you. And yet I think that when you left him he gave you strict orders. He said, ‘Do not come back to the ships, knight Patroclus, until you have torn the blood-stained shirt of murderous Hector on his body.’ That, I think, is how he charged you, and your foolish heart answered him ‘yes’ within you.”

Then, as the life ebbed out of you, you answered, O knight Patroclus: “Hector, boast as you like, for Zeus the son of Cronus and Apollo have granted you victory. They have beaten me so easily, and they have stripped the armor from my shoulders. If twenty men like you had attacked me, every one of them would have fallen to my spear. Fate and the son of Leto have overpowered me, and among mortal men, Euphorbus. You are only third in my killing. I say one thing more, so take it to heart. You too will live only a little while. Death and the day of your doom are close on you, and they will lay you low at the hands of Achilles son of Aeacus.”

With those words death closed his eyes. His soul slipped out of his body and flitted down to the house of Hades, grieving over its sad fate and leaving behind the youth and vigor of its manhood. Patroclus was dead, but Hector spoke to him anyway. “Patroclus, why prophesy my doom? Who knows whether Achilles, son of lovely Thetis, may be struck down by my spear and die before me?”

As he spoke, Hector drew the bronze spear out of the wound. He planted his foot on the body, shoved it off and let it lie on its back. Then, spear in hand, he went after Automedon, squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, longing to lay him low. But the immortal horses, which the gods had given to Peleus as a rich gift, carried Automedon swiftly from the field.

chapters.title: Book 17
paragraphs: The battle over the body of Patroclus.

Brave Menelaus son of Atreus now learned that Patroclus had fallen. He pushed through the front ranks in full armor and stood astride the body. A cow stands lowing over her first calf, and yellow-haired Menelaus stood over Patroclus in the same way. He held his round shield and his spear out in front of him, ready to kill anyone who dared to face him. But the son of Panthous had also seen the body. He came up to Menelaus and said, “Menelaus, son of Atreus, step back. Leave the body and let the bloody spoils alone. I was the first of the Trojans and their brave allies to drive a spear into Patroclus. So let me have my full glory among the Trojans, or I will aim at you and kill you.”

Menelaus answered this in great anger. “By father Zeus, boasting is an ugly thing. The leopard is not bolder, nor the lion, nor the savage wild boar, which is the fiercest and most fearless of all creatures, than the proud sons of Panthous are. Yet Hyperenor did not live out his youth after he made light of me and stood against me, thinking me the weakest soldier among the Danaans. His own feet never carried him home to gladden his wife and parents. In the same way I will finish you too if you stand against me. Get back into the crowd and do not face me, or it will go worse for you. Even a fool can be wise after the event.”

Euphorbus would not listen. “Now, Menelaus, you will pay for the death of my brother,” he said. “You boasted over him. You made his wife a widow in her bridal chamber, and you brought unspeakable grief on his parents. I will comfort those poor people if I bring your head and armor and put them in the hands of Panthous and noble Phrontis. The time has come to fight this matter out and settle it, for me or against me.”

As he spoke he struck Menelaus squarely on the shield, but the spear did not go through, because the shield bent its point back. Then Menelaus took aim and prayed to father Zeus. Euphorbus was drawing back, and Menelaus struck him at the base of the throat, leaning his whole weight on the spear to drive it home. The point went straight through his neck. He fell heavily to the ground, and his armor clattered around him. His hair, which was like the hair of the Graces, and his locks so neatly bound in bands of silver and gold, were all soaked with blood. Think of a man who has grown a fine young olive tree in a clear place with plenty of water. The plant is full of promise, and though the winds beat on it from every direction, it keeps putting out its white blossoms, until the blasts of some fierce hurricane sweep down and level it with the ground. In the same way Menelaus stripped the fair youth Euphorbus of his armor after he had killed him. Or think of a fierce lion on the mountains, proud of his strength, who fastens on the finest heifer in a herd as it feeds. First he breaks her neck with his strong jaws, and then he gorges on her blood and entrails. Dogs and shepherds raise a hue and cry against him, but they keep their distance and will not come close, for they are pale with fear. In the same way no one had the courage to face valiant Menelaus. The son of Atreus would then have carried off the armor of the son of Panthous with ease, if Phoebus Apollo had not been angry. In the form of Mentes, chief of the Cicons, Apollo urged Hector to attack him. “Hector,” he said, “you are chasing after the horses of the noble son of Aeacus, but you will not take them. A mortal man cannot hold them in hand and drive them, except Achilles, whose mother is immortal. Meanwhile Menelaus son of Atreus has stood over the body of Patroclus and killed the noblest of the Trojans, Euphorbus son of Panthous, so that he can fight no more.”

Then the god went back into the toil and turmoil. Hector’s soul was darkened by a cloud of grief. He looked along the ranks and saw Euphorbus lying on the ground, the blood still flowing from his wound, and Menelaus stripping off his armor. At that he made his way to the front like a flame of fire, in his gleaming armor, crying out in a loud voice. When the son of Atreus heard him, he was dismayed and said to himself, “Alas, what shall I do? I cannot let the Trojans take the armor of Patroclus, who fell fighting on my behalf, in case some Danaan who sees me cries shame on me. Yet if I fight Hector and the Trojans alone for the sake of my honor, there will be too many for me, because Hector is bringing them up in force. But why should I hesitate like this? When a man fights against heaven, against an opponent whom a god befriends, he will soon regret it. Let no Danaan think badly of me if I give way to Hector, for the hand of heaven is with him. Still, if I could find Ajax, the two of us would fight Hector and heaven too, if only we might save the body of Patroclus for Achilles son of Peleus. Of many evils, that would be the least.”

While he was torn between two courses, the Trojans came up with Hector at their head. So he drew back and left the body. He turned away like a bearded lion that dogs and men are chasing from a stockyard with spears and shouting, so that he loses heart and slinks sulkily off. In the same way Menelaus son of Atreus turned and left the body of Patroclus. When he was back among his own men, he looked around for mighty Ajax son of Telamon. Soon he saw him on the far left of the fight, cheering on his men and urging them to keep fighting, for Phoebus Apollo had spread a great panic among them. Menelaus ran up to him and said, “Ajax, my good friend, come with me at once to dead Patroclus, in case we can bring the body to Achilles. Hector already has his armor.”

These words stirred the heart of Ajax, and he made his way among the front ranks with Menelaus beside him. Hector had stripped the armor from Patroclus and was dragging him away, meaning to cut off his head and fling the body to the dogs of Troy. But Ajax came up with his shield like a wall in front of him. Hector withdrew under cover of his men and sprang onto his chariot. He gave the armor to the Trojans to take to the city as a great trophy for himself. Ajax covered the body of Patroclus with his broad shield and stood over it. A lion stands over his cubs when hunters come upon him in a forest with his little ones, and in the pride and fierceness of his strength he pulls his knit brows down until they cover his eyes. In the same way Ajax stood over the body of Patroclus, and beside him stood Menelaus son of Atreus, with great sorrow in his heart.

Then Glaucus son of Hippolochus glared at Hector and rebuked him harshly. “Hector,” he said, “you make a fine show, but in fighting you are sadly lacking. A runaway like you has no claim to such a great reputation. Think how you can save your town and citadel now, with the help of your own people born in Ilium. You will get no Lycians to fight for you, seeing what thanks they have had for their endless hardships. Are you likely, sir, to do anything to help a man of lesser note, when you left Sarpedon, your guest and comrade in arms, to be the spoil and prey of the Danaans? As long as he lived he served both your city and you well, yet you had no stomach to save his body from the dogs. If the Lycians listen to me, they will go home and leave Troy to its fate. If the Trojans had any of that daring, fearless spirit that seizes men who fight for their country and harass those who would attack it, we would soon carry Patroclus off into Ilium. If we could get this dead man away and bring him into the city of Priam, the Argives would readily give up the armor of Sarpedon, and we would get his body as well. For the man whose squire has just been killed is the foremost man at the ships of the Achaeans, he and his close-fighting followers. Even so, you did not dare to stand against Ajax or face him eye to eye with the battle all around you, because he is a braver man than you are.”

Hector scowled at him and answered, “Glaucus, you should know better. Until now I considered you wiser than anyone in all Lycia, but now I despise you for saying I am afraid of Ajax. I fear neither battle nor the din of chariots. But the will of Zeus is stronger than ours. Zeus at one time makes even a strong man draw back and snatches victory from his grasp, and at another time he sets him on to fight. Come here, my friend, stand by me, and see for yourself whether I will play the coward the whole day through, as you say, or whether I will stop even some of the boldest Danaans from fighting around the body of Patroclus.”

As he spoke he called loudly to the Trojans, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians, you who fight in close combat, be men, my friends, and fight with all your might, while I put on the fine armor of Achilles, which I took when I killed Patroclus.”

With this Hector left the fight and ran at full speed after his men, who were carrying the armor of Achilles to Troy but had not gone far. He stood for a while apart from the woeful fight and changed his armor. He sent his own to the strong city of Ilium and to the Trojans, and put on the immortal armor of the son of Peleus. The gods had given it to Peleus, and in his old age Peleus gave it to his son. But the son did not grow old in his father’s armor.

Zeus, lord of the storm cloud, saw Hector standing aloof and arming himself in the armor of the son of Peleus. He shook his head and muttered to himself, “Ah, poor wretch! You arm yourself in the armor of a hero before whom many a man trembles, and you pay no heed to the doom already close upon you. You have killed his comrade, so brave and strong, but it was not right to strip the armor from his head and shoulders. I do give you great might now, but in exchange you will not come back from battle to lay the armor of the son of Peleus before Andromache.”

The son of Cronus bowed his ominous brows, and Hector fitted the armor to his body. Terrible Ares entered into him and filled his whole body with might and valor. With a shout he strode in among the allies, and his armor flashed around him, so that to all of them he looked like the great son of Peleus himself. He went among them and cheered them on: Mesthles, Glaucus, Medon, Thersilochus, Asteropaeus, Deisenor and Hippothous, Phorcys, Chromius, and Ennomus the augur. He urged all of these, saying, “Hear me, allies from other cities, here in your thousands. I did not call you here, each from his own city, to have a crowd around me. I called you so that with heart and soul you would defend the wives and little children of the Trojans from the fierce Achaeans. For this I wear down my people with food for you and with the gifts that make you rich. So turn and charge the enemy, to stand or fall as the game of war decides. Whoever brings Patroclus, dead though he is, into the hands of the Trojans and makes Ajax give way before him, I will give him half the spoils and keep the other half myself. He will share the same honor as I do.”

When he had spoken, they charged with full weight at the Danaans, spears held out in front of them. Each man’s hopes ran high that he would force Ajax son of Telamon to give up the body. Fools they were, for Ajax was about to take the lives of many. Then Ajax said to Menelaus, “My good friend Menelaus, you and I will hardly come out of this fight alive. I am less worried about the body of Patroclus, who will soon be meat for the dogs and vultures of Troy, than about the safety of my own head and yours. Hector has wrapped us in a storm of battle from every side, and our destruction now looks certain. Call on the princes of the Danaans, in case any can hear us.”

Menelaus did as he said and shouted for help to the Danaans at the top of his voice. “My friends,” he cried, “princes and counselors of the Argives, all you who drink at the public cost with Agamemnon and Menelaus and who give orders, each to his own people, as Zeus grants you power and glory: the fight is so thick around me that I cannot make out each of you. Come on, every man of you unbidden, and be ashamed that Patroclus should become meat and morsel for Trojan hounds.”

Swift Ajax son of Oileus heard him. He was the first to force his way through the fight and run to help. Next came Idomeneus and Meriones his esquire, the peer of murderous Ares. As for the others who came into the fight after these, who could name them by himself?

The Trojans charged in a body with Hector at their head. They came on with a roar like a great wave thundering in at the mouth of some heaven-born river, while the rocks that jut into the sea ring with the roar of the breakers that beat and buffet them. But the Achaeans stood firm in singleness of heart around the son of Menoetius and fenced him in with their bronze shields. Zeus also hid the brightness of their helmets in a thick cloud. He had borne no grudge against the son of Menoetius while he was alive and squire to the descendant of Aeacus. So he was unwilling to let him fall prey to the dogs of his foes the Trojans, and he urged his comrades on to defend him.

At first the Trojans drove the Achaeans back, and the Achaeans withdrew from the dead man, daunted. The Trojans did not manage to kill anyone, but they did drag the body away. The Achaeans did not lose it for long, though. Ajax, foremost of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus in both stature and prowess, quickly rallied them and made for the front. He was like a wild boar on the mountains that stands at bay in the forest glades and routs the hounds and lusty youths who have attacked him. In the same way Ajax son of Telamon passed easily in among the phalanxes of the Trojans and scattered those who stood over Patroclus and were most set on winning glory by dragging him off to their city. At this moment Hippothous, brave son of the Pelasgian Lethus, in his zeal for Hector and the Trojans, was dragging the body off by the foot through the press of the fight. He had bound a strap around the sinews near the ankle. But disaster soon befell him, and none of those who would gladly have done so could save him from it. The son of Telamon sprang forward and struck him on his bronze-cheeked helmet. The plumed headpiece broke around the point of the weapon, hit at once by the spear and by the strong hand of Ajax, and the bloody brain came oozing out through the crest-socket. His strength failed him, and he let Patroclus’s foot drop from his hand as he fell full length, dead, on the body. So he died far from the fertile land of Larissa and never repaid his parents for raising him, because the spear of mighty Ajax cut his life short. Then Hector aimed a spear at Ajax, but Ajax saw it coming and only just avoided it. The spear passed on and struck Schedius son of noble Iphitus, captain of the Phoceans, who lived in famed Panopeus and ruled over many people. It struck him under the middle of the collar-bone, and the bronze point went right through him and came out at the bottom of his shoulder-blade. He fell heavily to the ground, and his armor clattered around him. In his turn Ajax struck noble Phorcys son of Phaenops in the middle of the belly as he stood over Hippothous. The spear broke the plate of his cuirass and tore out his entrails, and he clutched the ground in his palm as he fell to earth. Hector and those in the front rank then gave ground, while the Argives raised a loud cry of triumph. They dragged away the bodies of Phorcys and Hippothous and soon stripped them of their armor.

The Trojans would now have been beaten by the brave Achaeans and driven back to Ilium through their own cowardice. And the Argives, so great were their courage and endurance, would have won a triumph even against the will of Zeus, if Apollo had not roused Aeneas. He came in the likeness of Periphas son of Epytus, an attendant who had grown old in the service of Aeneas’s aged father and was devoted to him at all times. In that likeness Apollo said, “Aeneas, can you not manage to save high Ilium, even though heaven is against us? I have known men whose numbers, courage, and self-reliance saved their people in spite of Zeus. In this case he would much rather give the victory to us than to the Danaans, if you would only fight instead of being so terribly afraid.”

Aeneas knew Apollo when he looked straight at him, and he shouted to Hector, “Hector and all you other Trojans and allies, shame on us if the Achaeans beat us and drive us back to Ilium through our own cowardice. A god has just come up to me and told me that Zeus, the supreme disposer, will be with us. So let us go at the Danaans, and let it go hard with them before they carry dead Patroclus off to the ships.”

As he spoke he sprang far out in front of the others, who then rallied and faced the Achaeans again. Aeneas speared Leiocritus son of Arisbas, a valiant follower of Lycomedes. Lycomedes felt pity as he saw him fall. He went close up and speared Apisaon son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver under the midriff, and Apisaon died. He had come from fertile Paeonia and was the best man of them all after Asteropaeus. Asteropaeus flew forward to avenge him and attack the Danaans, but this could no longer be. Those around Patroclus were well covered by their shields and held their spears in front of them, for Ajax had given them strict orders. No man was to give ground, and none was to stand out before the others. All were to hold close together around the body and fight hand to hand. So huge Ajax ordered them, and the earth ran red with blood as the corpses fell thick on one another, on the side of the Trojans and allies and on that of the Danaans alike. The Danaans too fought no bloodless fight, though far fewer of them perished, because of the care they took to defend and stand by one another.

So they fought, like a flaming fire. It seemed as though it had gone hard even with the sun and moon, for they were hidden over all that part where the bravest heroes were fighting about the dead son of Menoetius. The other Danaans and Achaeans fought at their ease in full daylight, with brilliant sunshine all around them and not a cloud to be seen on plain or mountain. These others would also rest for a while and stop fighting, since they were some distance apart, beyond range of one another’s weapons. But those in the thick of the fray suffered from both battle and darkness. The best of them were being worn out by the great weight of their armor. The two valiant heroes Thrasymedes and Antilochus had not yet heard of the death of Patroclus. They believed he was still alive and leading the van against the Trojans, and they were keeping themselves in reserve against the death or rout of their own comrades, as Nestor had ordered when he sent them from the ships into battle.

All through the long day they waged fierce war, and the sweat of their labor ran constantly down their legs, their hands and their eyes as they fought over the squire of the swift son of Peleus. It was like a man handing a great ox-hide, soaked through with fat, to his workers and telling them to stretch it. They stand around it in a ring and pull until the moisture leaves it, and the fat sinks in under the tugging of so many hands, and the hide is stretched well. In just that way the two sides tugged the dead body back and forth within a very small space. The Trojans were set on dragging it into Ilium, and the Achaeans were just as set on taking it to their ships, and the fight between them was fierce. Not even Ares, the lord of hosts, nor Athena, at the height of their fury, could have made light of such a battle.

That was the terrible turmoil of men and horses that Zeus ordained that day around the body of Patroclus. Meanwhile Achilles did not know that Patroclus had fallen, because the fight was under the wall of Troy, a long way from the ships. He had no idea that Patroclus was dead. He thought his friend would come back alive once he had gone close to the gates. He also knew that Patroclus was not going to sack the city, with him or without him, because his mother had often told him so when he sat alone with her, and she had passed on to him the plans of great Zeus. This time, though, she had not told him what a great disaster had struck him in the death of the one who was dearest to him of all his comrades.

The others kept charging at one another around the body with their pointed spears, killing each other. Then one of them would say, “My friends, we can never again show our faces at the ships. It would be better, far better, for the earth to open and swallow us right here than to let the Trojans have the triumph of carrying Patroclus off to their city.”

The Trojans, for their part, spoke to one another too. “Friends,” they said, “even if we all fall beside this body, let none of us hold back from fighting.” With such words they urged each other on. They fought and fought, and an iron clang rose through the empty air to the bronze vault of heaven. The horses of the descendant of Aeacus stood apart from the fight and wept when they heard that their driver had been laid low by the hand of murderous Hector. Automedon, the valiant son of Diores, lashed them again and again. Many times he spoke kindly to them, and many times he scolded them, but they would not go back to the ships by the waters of the broad Hellespont, and they would not go into battle among the Achaeans either. They stood stock still with their chariot, like a pillar set over the tomb of some dead man or woman, and bowed their heads to the ground. Hot tears fell from their eyes as they mourned the loss of their charioteer, and their noble manes hung wet and drooping from under the yoke-straps on either side of the yoke.

The son of Cronus saw them and pitied them in their sorrow. He shook his head and muttered to himself, “Poor things, why did we give you to King Peleus, a mortal, when you are ageless and immortal yourselves? Was it so that you could share the sorrows of mankind? Of all the creatures that live and move on the earth, none is so pitiable as man. Still, Hector son of Priam shall not drive you or your chariot. I will not have it. It is enough that he has the armor he boasts of so vainly. And I will give you strength of heart and limb to carry Automedon safely from the battle to the ships. I mean to let the Trojans triumph further still, and keep killing until they reach the ships. Then night will fall and darkness will cover the land.”

As he spoke he breathed spirit and strength into the horses. They shook the dust from their manes and carried their chariot swiftly into the fight raging between Trojans and Achaeans. Behind them fought Automedon, full of sorrow for his comrade, like a vulture among a flock of geese. In and out, here and there, at full speed he dashed through the crowd of the Trojans. But for all the fury of his pursuit he killed no man, because he could not wield his spear and also keep his horses under control while alone in the chariot. At last a comrade, Alcimedon, son of Laerces son of Haemon, caught sight of him and came up behind his chariot. “Automedon,” he said, “what god has put this folly into your heart and robbed you of your right mind, that you fight the Trojans in the front rank all alone? The man who was your comrade is dead, and Hector struts about, proud to be armed in the armor of the descendant of Aeacus.”

Automedon son of Diores answered, “Alcimedon, no one else can control and guide the immortal horses as well as you can, except Patroclus, peer of gods in counsel, while he was alive. Take the whip and reins, then, while I get down from the car and fight.”

Alcimedon sprang onto the chariot and took up the whip and reins, while Automedon leaped down from the car. Hector saw this and said to Aeneas, who was near him, “Aeneas, counselor of the mail-clad Trojans, I can see the horses of the swift son of Aeacus coming into battle with weak hands to drive them. I am sure we could take them, if you agree. They will not dare to face us if we both attack.”

The valiant son of Anchises agreed, and the pair went straight ahead, their shoulders covered by shields of tough, dry ox-hide overlaid with much bronze. Chromius and Aretus went with them, and their hearts beat high with hope of killing the men and capturing the horses. Fools that they were, they were not to return unharmed from their meeting with Automedon, who prayed to father Zeus and was at once filled with courage and abounding strength. He turned to his trusty comrade Alcimedon and said, “Alcimedon, keep your horses so close that I can feel their breath on my back. I doubt that we can hold back Hector son of Priam until he has killed us and mounted behind the horses. Then he will either spread panic through the ranks of the Achaeans or be killed himself among the foremost.”

With that he called out to the two Ajaxes and Menelaus, “Ajaxes, captains of the Argives, and Menelaus, hand the dead body over to those best able to defend it, and come to the rescue of us who are living. Hector and Aeneas, the two best men among the Trojans, are pressing us hard in the full tide of war. Still, the outcome lies in the lap of heaven. So I will hurl my spear and leave the rest to Zeus.”

As he spoke he took aim and hurled. The spear struck the round shield of Aretus and went right through it, because the shield did not stop it, and it was driven through his belt into the lower part of his belly. Think of a sturdy youth with an axe in his hand who deals a blow behind the horns of an ox and cuts the tendons at the back of its neck, so that it springs forward and then drops. In the same way Aretus gave one bound and then fell on his back, the spear quivering in his body until it finished him. Then Hector aimed a spear at Automedon, but Automedon saw it coming and stooped forward to avoid it. It flew past him, and its point stuck in the ground, while the butt-end went on quivering until Ares took its force away. They would then have fought hand to hand with swords, if the two Ajaxes had not forced their way through the crowd when they heard their comrade calling, and parted them in spite of their fury. Hector, Aeneas and Chromius were afraid and drew back, leaving Aretus lying there, struck to the heart. Automedon, peer of swift Ares, stripped him of his armor and boasted over him, “I have done little to ease my sorrow for the son of Menoetius, because the man I have killed is not as good as he was.”
As he spoke he took the blood-stained spoils and laid them in his chariot. Then he mounted the car, his hands and feet steeped in gore, like a lion that has been gorging on a bull.

Now the fierce, groaning fight raged again around Patroclus, because Athena had come down from heaven and stirred up its fury. Far-seeing Zeus, who had changed his mind, had commanded her and sent her to encourage the Danaans. Just as Zeus bends his bright bow in heaven as a sign to mankind of either war or the chill storms that keep men from their work and plague their flocks, in the same way, wrapped in such radiant raiment, Athena went into the host and spoke to each man in turn. First she took the form and voice of Phoenix and spoke to Menelaus son of Atreus, who was standing near her. “Menelaus,” she said, “it will be a shame and a dishonor to you if dogs tear apart the noble comrade of Achilles under the walls of Troy. So stand firm, and urge your men to do the same.”

Menelaus answered, “Phoenix, my good old friend, may Athena grant me strength and keep the darts off me. Then I will stand by Patroclus and defend him. His death has gone to my heart. But Hector is like a raging fire and strikes blow after blow without stopping, because Zeus is now granting him a time of triumph.”

Athena was pleased that he had named her before any of the other gods. So she put strength into his knees and shoulders, and made him as bold as a fly. Drive a fly off, and it will come back and bite if it can, so dearly does it love human blood. She made Menelaus as bold as that as he stood over Patroclus and threw his spear. Now there was among the Trojans a man named Podes, son of Eetion, who was both rich and valiant. Hector held him in the highest honor, because he was his comrade and boon companion. The spear of Menelaus struck this man in the girdle just as he turned to flee, and went right through him. He fell heavily forward, and Menelaus son of Atreus dragged his body away from the Trojans and into the ranks of his own people.

Then Apollo went up to Hector and spurred him on to fight. He took the likeness of Phaenops son of Asius, who lived in Abydos and was the most favored of all Hector’s guests. In that likeness Apollo said, “Hector, which of the Achaeans will fear you from now on, when you have shrunk back from Menelaus, who has always been rated poorly as a soldier? Yet now he has carried a corpse away from the Trojans all by himself, and has killed your own true comrade, a man brave among the foremost, Podes son of Eetion.”

A dark cloud of grief fell on Hector as he heard this, and he made his way to the front, clad in full armor. Then the son of Cronus seized his bright tasselled aegis and veiled Ida in cloud. He sent out lightnings and thunders, and as he shook his aegis he gave victory to the Trojans and routed the Achaeans.

The panic began with Peneleos the Boeotian. He kept his face turned toward the enemy, and a spear hit him on the upper part of the shoulder. It was thrown by Polydamas, who had come up close to strike him, and it grazed the top of the bone. Then Hector, in close combat, struck Leitus son of noble Alectryon in the hand by the wrist and disabled him from fighting any further. Leitus looked about him in dismay, knowing that he would never again wield a spear in battle against the Trojans. While Hector was in pursuit of Leitus, Idomeneus struck Hector on the breastplate over his chest, near the nipple. But the spear broke in the shaft, and the Trojans cheered aloud. Then Hector aimed at Idomeneus son of Deucalion as he stood on his chariot, and missed him by a very narrow margin. The spear hit Coiranus instead, a follower and charioteer of Meriones, who had come with him from Lyctus. Idomeneus had left the ships on foot, and he would have given the Trojans a great triumph if Coiranus had not driven quickly up to him. Coiranus thus brought life and rescue to Idomeneus, but he himself fell by the hand of murderous Hector. Hector hit him on the jaw under the ear. The end of the spear drove out his teeth and cut his tongue in two pieces, so that he fell from his chariot and let the reins drop to the ground. Meriones gathered them up from the ground and took them into his own hands. Then he said to Idomeneus, “Keep lashing until you get back to the ships. You can see for yourself that the day is no longer ours.”
At this Idomeneus lashed the horses toward the ships, because fear had taken hold of him.

Ajax and Menelaus saw how Zeus had tipped the scale in favor of the Trojans, and Ajax was the first to speak. “Alas,” he said, “even a fool can see that father Zeus is helping the Trojans. All their weapons strike home. It makes no difference whether a brave man or a coward throws them, since Zeus speeds them all alike, while ours fall to the ground without effect. What, then, is our best course, both for rescuing the body and for returning to the joy of our friends? They will be grieving as they look this way, and they will be sure that nothing can now check the terrible hands of Hector, and that he will fling himself on our ships. I wish someone would go and tell the son of Peleus at once. I do not think he can have heard yet the sad news that the dearest of his friends has fallen. But I cannot see a single man among the Achaeans to send, because they and their chariots are all hidden in darkness. O father Zeus, lift this cloud from over the sons of the Achaeans. Make the sky clear, and let us see. If you want us to perish, let us at least fall by daylight.”

Father Zeus heard him and pitied his tears. He drove the cloud of darkness away immediately, the sun shone out, and the whole fight lay in view. Ajax then spoke to Menelaus. “Look around, Menelaus. If Antilochus son of Nestor is still living, send him right away to tell Achilles that the comrade far dearest to him of them all has fallen.”

Menelaus took his words to heart and went on his way, like a lion leaving a stockyard. The lion is tired of attacking the men and hounds, who keep watch all night long and will not let him feast on the fat of their herd. In his lust for meat he rushes straight at them, but in vain, because darts from strong hands hit him, along with burning brands that daunt him for all his hunger. So in the morning he slinks sulkily away. In just that way Menelaus left Patroclus, very much against his will and in great fear that the Achaeans would be driven back in rout and let the body fall into the hands of the enemy. He gave strict orders to Meriones and the two Ajaxes, “Ajaxes and Meriones, leaders of the Argives, remember now how good Patroclus was. He was always courteous while he lived. Bear it in mind now that he is dead.”

With this Menelaus left them, looking around him as keenly as an eagle, whose sight, they say, is keener than that of any other bird. However high he is in the heavens, not a hare that runs can escape him by crouching under a bush or thicket, because he swoops down on it and makes an end of it. In the same way, O Menelaus, your keen eyes ranged around the mighty host of your followers to see if you could find the son of Nestor still alive. Soon Menelaus spotted him at the far left of the battle, encouraging his men and urging them to fight boldly. Menelaus went to him and said, “Antilochus, come here and hear sad news. I wish it were not true. You can see for yourself that heaven is piling disaster on the Danaans and giving victory to the Trojans. Patroclus, the bravest of the Achaeans, has fallen, and the Danaans will badly miss him. Run to the ships now and tell Achilles. Let him come to rescue the body and carry it back to the ships. As for the armor, Hector already has it.”

Horror struck Antilochus. He stood speechless for a long time, his eyes filling with tears, unable to find his voice. Then he did what Menelaus had told him. He handed his armor to a comrade, Laodocus, who was turning his horses around close beside him, and ran off.

So he ran weeping from the field to carry the bad news to Achilles son of Peleus. And you, O Menelaus, were not minded to help his harassed comrades after Antilochus had left the Pylians, who missed him greatly. Instead you sent them noble Thrasymedes, and went back to Patroclus yourself. You came running up to the two Ajaxes and said, “I have sent Antilochus to the ships to tell Achilles. But however much he rages against Hector, he cannot come, since he cannot fight without armor. What will be our best plan, then, both for rescuing the dead and for escaping death ourselves amid the battle cries of the Trojans?”

Ajax answered, “Menelaus, you have spoken well. You and Meriones should stoop down, lift the body and carry it out of the fray. We two will stay behind you and keep off Hector and the Trojans. We are one in heart as in name, and we have long been used to fighting side by side.”

Menelaus and Meriones then took the dead man in their arms and, with a great effort, heaved him high. Behind them the Trojan host raised a hue and cry as they watched the Achaeans carry the body off. They flew after them like hounds attacking a wounded boar, running at the head of a band of young huntsmen. For a while the hounds fly at him as though they would tear him to pieces, but now and again he turns on them in a fury, scaring them and scattering them in every direction. In the same way the Trojans charged for a while in a body, striking with swords and with spears pointed at both ends. But when the two Ajaxes faced them and stood at bay, they turned pale, and no man dared press on to fight any further about the dead.

In this way the two heroes strained every nerve to carry the body to the ships out of the fight. The battle raged around them like fierce flames that, once kindled, spread like wildfire over a city, until the houses fall in the glare of the burning. Such was the roar and tramp of men and horses pursuing them as they carried Patroclus from the field. Or think of mules putting forth all their strength to haul some beam or great piece of ship’s timber down a rough mountain track, panting and sweating as they go.
