In the same way Menelaus and Meriones panted and sweated as they carried the body of Patroclus. Behind them the two Ajaxes held out stoutly. Some wooded mountain-spur stretches across a plain and turns water aside, checking the flow even of a great river, and no stream is strong enough to break through it. In the same way the two Ajaxes faced the Trojans and stemmed the tide of their fighting, though the Trojans kept pouring toward them, and foremost among them all were Aeneas son of Anchises and valiant Hector. A flock of daws or starlings falls to screaming and chattering when it sees a falcon, foe to all small birds, come soaring near. In the same way the Achaean youth raised a babel of cries as they fled before Aeneas and Hector, forgetting their former prowess. In the rout of the Danaans much goodly armor fell around the trench, and of fighting there was no end.

chapters.title: Book 18
paragraphs: Achilles grieves for Patroclus—Thetis visits Hephaestus, and Hephaestus makes armor for Achilles.

So the fighting went on, blazing like a fire. Meanwhile Antilochus, the swift runner who had been sent as messenger, reached Achilles. He found him sitting by his tall ships, with a foreboding of what was in fact only too true. “Alas,” he said to himself in the heaviness of his heart, “why are the Achaeans scouring the plain again and crowding toward the ships? I pray the gods are not now bringing on me the sorrow my mother Thetis spoke of. She said that while I was still alive, the bravest of the Myrmidons would fall before the Trojans and no longer see the light of the sun. I fear the brave son of Menoetius has fallen through his own daring. Yet I told him to come back to the ships as soon as he had driven off the men who were bringing fire against them, and not to join battle with Hector.”

While he was turning this over in his mind, the son of Nestor came up and told him the sad news, weeping bitterly all the while. “Alas,” he cried, “son of noble Peleus, I bring you bad tidings. I wish they were untrue. Patroclus has fallen, and men are fighting around his naked body—for Hector holds his armor.”

A dark cloud of grief came over Achilles as he listened. He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his head. It spoiled his handsome face, and the grime settled on his fine new shirt. He threw himself down at full length, a huge man hugely stretched out, and tore his hair with his hands. The bondswomen whom Achilles and Patroclus had taken captive screamed aloud in grief. They beat their breasts, and their limbs gave way under them for sorrow. Antilochus bent over him, weeping and holding both his hands as he lay groaning, for he feared Achilles might cut his own throat with a knife. Then Achilles gave a loud cry. His mother heard it as she sat in the depths of the sea beside her old father, and she screamed. All the goddesses, daughters of Nereus, who lived at the bottom of the sea, came gathering around her. There were Glauce, Thalia and Cymodoce, Nesaia, Speo, Thoe and dark-eyed Halie, Cymothoe, Actaea and Limnorea, Melite, Iaera, Amphithoe and Agave, Doto and Proto, Pherusa and Dynamene, Dexamene, Amphinome and Callianeira, Doris, Panope, and the famous sea-nymph Galatea, Nemertes, Apseudes and Callianassa. There were also Clymene, Ianeira and Ianassa, Maera, Oreithuia and Amatheia of the lovely locks, with other Nereids who live in the depths of the sea. Their crowd filled the crystal cave, and they all beat their breasts while Thetis led them in their lament.

“Listen,” she cried, “sisters, daughters of Nereus, so that you may hear how heavy my sorrows are. Alas, woe is me, that I have borne the most glorious of sons. I bore him handsome and strong, a hero among heroes, and he shot up like a sapling. I tended him like a plant in a good garden and sent him with his ships to Ilium to fight the Trojans, but I shall never welcome him back to the house of Peleus. As long as he lives to look on the light of the sun, he is in heaviness, and though I go to him, I cannot help him. Still, I will go, to see my dear son and learn what sorrow has come to him, though he is still holding back from battle.”

She left the cave as she spoke, and the others followed her, weeping, and the waves opened a path before them. They came to the rich plain of Troy and rose up out of the sea in a long line onto the sand, at the place where the ships of the Myrmidons were drawn up in close order around the tents of Achilles. His mother went up to him as he lay groaning. She laid her hand on his head and spoke piteously. “My son,” she said, “why are you weeping like this? What sorrow has come to you now? Tell me; do not hide it from me. Surely Zeus has granted the prayer you made to him, when you lifted up your hands and begged that the Achaeans should all be penned in at their ships and bitterly regret that you were no longer with them.”

Achilles groaned and answered, “Mother, Olympian Zeus has indeed granted my prayer, but what good is that to me, now that my dear comrade Patroclus has fallen—the man I valued above all the others and loved as dearly as my own life? I have lost him. Hector killed him and then stripped off the wondrous armor, so glorious to see, that the gods gave to Peleus on the day they laid you in the bed of a mortal man. I wish you were still living among the immortal sea-nymphs, and that Peleus had taken some mortal woman as his bride. As it is, you will have endless grief for the death of a son you can never welcome home. No, I will not live or go about among mankind unless Hector falls by my spear and so pays me for killing Patroclus son of Menoetius.”
Thetis wept and answered, “Then, my son, your own end is near—for your death awaits you very soon after Hector’s.”

Then Achilles said in his great grief, “I would die here and now, since I could not save my comrade. He has fallen far from home, and in his hour of need my hand was not there to help him. What is left for me? I shall not return to my own land. I have been no rescue to Patroclus or to my other comrades, so many of whom have been slain by mighty Hector. I sit here by my ships, a useless burden on the earth—I, who in battle have no equal among the Achaeans, though in council there are better men than I. So let strife perish from among gods and men, and anger too, which can harden even a righteous man’s heart. It rises in a man’s soul like smoke, and the taste of it is sweeter than drops of honey. That is how Agamemnon has angered me. And yet—so be it, for it is over. I will force my soul into submission, as I must. I will go and hunt down Hector, who has killed the man I loved so dearly, and then I will meet my doom whenever Zeus and the other gods are pleased to send it. Even Heracles, the best beloved of Zeus—even he could not escape death, but fate and Hera’s fierce anger brought him down. I too will lie dead, if a like doom awaits me. Until then I will win fame. I will make Trojan and Dardanian women wring tears from their tender cheeks with both hands in the bitterness of their great sorrow. Then they will know that the man who has held back so long will hold back no longer. Do not hold me back, then, out of the love you bear me, for you will not move me.”

Then silver-footed Thetis answered, “My son, what you say is true. It is right to save your comrades from destruction. But your armor is in the hands of the Trojans. Hector carries it in triumph on his own shoulders. I know well that his boast will not last, for his end is close at hand. But do not go into the press of battle until you see me come back here. Tomorrow at break of day I will be here, and I will bring you good armor from King Hephaestus.”

With that she left her brave son. As she turned away she said to the sea-nymphs her sisters, “Dive down into the bosom of the sea and go to the house of the old sea-god, my father. Tell him everything. As for me, I will go to the cunning workman Hephaestus on high Olympus and ask him to give my son a suit of splendid armor.”
When she had said this, they dived at once beneath the waves, and silver-footed Thetis went on her way to bring the armor for her son.

So her feet carried the goddess to Olympus. Meanwhile the Achaeans were fleeing with loud cries before murderous Hector until they reached the ships and the Hellespont. They could not drag the body of Patroclus, the servant of Ares, out of range of the weapons showered on him. Hector son of Priam, with his host and horsemen, had caught up with it again, like the flame of a fiery furnace. Three times brave Hector seized the body by the feet, straining with might and main to drag it away and calling loudly to the Trojans. Three times the two Ajaxes, clothed in valor as in a garment, beat him off the body. But he was undaunted. Now he would charge into the thick of the fight, and now he would stand still and cry aloud, but he gave no ground. As upland shepherds cannot drive a famished lion away from a carcass, so the two Ajaxes could not scare Hector son of Priam away from the body of Patroclus.

And now Hector would even have dragged the body off and won imperishable glory, if Iris, swift as the wind, had not winged her way from Olympus as a messenger to the son of Peleus, telling him to arm. She came secretly, without the knowledge of Zeus and the other gods, for Hera sent her. When she had come close to him she said, “Up, son of Peleus, mightiest of all mankind. Rescue Patroclus, over whom this fearful fight is now raging by the ships. Men are killing one another, the Danaans defending the dead body, while the Trojans try to haul it away and take it to windy Ilium. Hector is the most furious of them all. He means to cut the head from the body and fix it on the stakes of the wall. Up, then, and wait here no longer. Shrink from the thought that Patroclus may become meat for the dogs of Troy. Shame on you, if his body suffers any kind of outrage.”
And Achilles said, “Iris, which of the gods sent you to me?”
Iris answered, “It was Hera, the royal wife of Zeus. But the son of Cronus does not know I have come, and neither does any other of the immortals who live on the snowy summits of Olympus.”

Then swift Achilles answered her, “How can I go up into the battle? They have my armor. My mother forbade me to arm until I should see her come, for she promised to bring me good armor from Hephaestus. I know of no man whose arms I could put on, except the shield of Ajax son of Telamon. And he surely must be fighting in the front rank, wielding his spear around the body of dead Patroclus.”

Iris said, “We know your armor has been taken. But go as you are. Go to the deep trench and show yourself to the Trojans, so that they will fear you and stop fighting. Then the exhausted sons of the Achaeans will gain a brief breathing space, which is hard to come by in battle.”

When Iris had spoken, she left him. Achilles, dear to Zeus, rose, and Athena threw her tasseled aegis around his strong shoulders. She crowned his head with a halo of golden cloud, and from it she kindled a glow of gleaming fire. As the smoke goes up into the sky from a city under siege on an island far out at sea—all day long the men sally out from the city and fight their hardest, and at the going down of the sun the line of beacon fires blazes up, flaring high for their neighbors to see, in case they may come with their ships and help them—so the light flared from the head of Achilles as he stood by the trench, going beyond the wall. But he did not join the Achaeans, for he heeded the charge his mother had laid on him.

There he stood and shouted aloud. Athena also raised her voice from far off and spread unspeakable terror among the Trojans. A trumpet rings out when the enemy is at the gates of a city and sounds the alarm. So rang the brazen voice of the son of Aeacus, and when the Trojans heard its clarion tones they were dismayed. The horses turned back with their chariots, sensing disaster, and the drivers were awestruck at the steady flame the gray-eyed goddess had kindled above the head of the great son of Peleus.

Three times Achilles raised his loud cry as he stood by the trench, and three times the Trojans and their brave allies were thrown into confusion. Twelve of their noblest champions fell beneath the wheels of their chariots and died on their own spears. To their great joy the Achaeans then drew Patroclus out of range of the weapons and laid him on a litter. His comrades stood mourning around him, and among them swift Achilles wept bitterly as he saw his true comrade lying dead on his bier. He had sent him out into battle with horses and chariots, and he was not to welcome his return.
Then Hera sent the busy sun, unwilling as he was, down into the waters of Oceanus. He set, and the Achaeans had rest from the tug and turmoil of war.

The Trojans, coming out of the fight, unyoked their horses and gathered in assembly before preparing their supper. They stayed on their feet, and no one dared sit down, for fear had fallen on them all because Achilles had shown himself after holding back from battle so long. Polydamas son of Panthous was the first to speak, a man of judgment, who alone among them could look both before and after. He was a comrade of Hector, and they had been born on the same night. With all sincerity and goodwill he spoke to them like this:—

“Think carefully, my friends. I urge you to go back to your city now and not wait here by the ships until morning, for we are far from our walls. As long as this man was at enmity with Agamemnon, the Achaeans were easier to deal with, and I would gladly have camped by the ships, hoping to take them. But now I am in great fear of the swift son of Peleus. He is so daring that he will never wait here on the plain, where Trojans and Achaeans fight with equal valor. He will try to storm our city and carry off our women. So do as I say, and let us retreat. This is what will happen. The darkness of night will hold the son of Peleus back for a while. But if he finds us here in the morning when he sallies out in full armor, we shall come to know him in good earnest. Glad will be the man who can escape and get back to Ilium, and many a Trojan will become meat for dogs and vultures—may I never live to hear it. If we do as I say, little as we may like it, we shall have strength in counsel during the night, and the great gates with the doors that close them will protect the city. At dawn we can arm and take our stand on the walls. He will regret it then if he sallies from the ships to fight us. He will go back when he has let his horses run their fill, driven in every direction under our walls, and he will have no mind to try to force his way into the city. Nor will he ever sack it. The dogs will devour him first.”

Hector looked fiercely at him and answered, “Polydamas, I do not like your words, telling us to go back and be penned inside the city. Have you not had enough of being cooped up behind walls? In the old days the city of Priam was famous all over the world for its wealth of gold and bronze. Now our treasures have been wasted out of our houses, and many goods have been sold away to Phrygia and lovely Meonia, because the hand of Zeus has lain heavily on us. But now the son of scheming Cronus has granted me to win glory here and to hem the Achaeans in at their ships. So stop your prating in this foolish, would-be wise way among the people. You will have no man with you. It shall not be. All of you, do as I now say—take your suppers in your companies throughout the host, keep your watches, and be wakeful, every man of you. If any Trojan is uneasy about his possessions, let him gather them and hand them out among the people. Better that these men have them than the Achaeans. At daybreak we will arm and fight around the ships. Granted that Achilles has come forward again to defend them, let it be as he wishes, but it will go hard with him. I shall not shun him. I will fight him, to fall or to conquer. The god of war deals out equal measure to all, and the slayer may yet be slain.”

So Hector spoke, and the Trojans cheered him, fools that they were, because Pallas Athena had taken away their good sense. They approved of Hector’s evil counsel, and no one would listen to the wise words of Polydamas. The Trojans ate their supper throughout the host. All night long the Achaeans mourned Patroclus, and the son of Peleus led them in their lament. He laid his murderous hands on his comrade’s chest and groaned again and again. He was like a bearded lion whose young have been stolen from a dense forest by a man hunting deer. When the lion comes back he is furious, and he searches every dingle and dell for the hunter’s trail, hoping to find him, because he is mad with rage. In the same way Achilles sighed often as he spoke among the Myrmidons. “Alas! The words I used to cheer the hero Menoetius in his own house were empty. I told him I would bring his brave son home again to Opoeis, once he had sacked Ilium and taken his share of the spoils. But Zeus does not give all men what their hearts desire. The blood of both of us will redden the same soil here at Troy. I will never be welcomed home by the old knight Peleus, or by my mother Thetis either, because the earth will cover me in this very place. Even so, Patroclus, now that I am left behind you, I will not bury you until I have brought here the head and armor of mighty Hector, who killed you. Before your bier I will behead twelve noble sons of the Trojans, to avenge you. Until I have done it, you will lie as you are, beside the ships. And the fair women of Troy and Dardanus, whom we took with spear and strength of arm when we sacked men’s goodly cities, will weep over you both night and day.”

Then Achilles told his men to put a large tripod on the fire, so they could wash the clotted gore off Patroclus. They set a tripod full of bath water over a clear fire and threw sticks under it to make it blaze. The flames played around the belly of the tripod, and the water grew hot. When the water in the cauldron was boiling, they washed the body and anointed it with oil. They closed its wounds with ointment that had been kept nine years. Then they laid it on a bier, covered it from head to foot with a linen cloth, and spread a fair white robe over that. All night long the Myrmidons gathered around Achilles to mourn Patroclus.
Then Zeus spoke to Hera, his sister and wife. “Well, Queen Hera, you have got what you wanted and roused swift Achilles. Anyone would think the Achaeans were your own flesh and blood.”

Hera answered, “Dread son of Cronus, why do you say such a thing? Even a mortal man, who knows less than we do, can do what he is able for another person. And I am the foremost of all goddesses, both by birth and as the wife of you who reign in heaven. Shall I not plan harm for the Trojans if I am angry with them?”

While they talked, Thetis reached the house of Hephaestus. It was imperishable and star-bespangled, the fairest of the homes in heaven, a house of bronze built by the lame god’s own hands. She found him sweating and hard at work with his bellows. He was making twenty tripods to stand along the wall of his house, and under each one he fitted wheels of gold, so that they could go by themselves to the assemblies of the gods and come back again—marvels indeed to see. They were finished except for the ears, which were of cunning workmanship and still had to be attached. He was fixing these on now, hammering at the rivets. While he was at this work, silver-footed Thetis arrived at the house. Charis, of graceful head-dress, the wife of the far-famed lame god, saw her and came to meet her. She took Thetis by the hand and said, “Why have you come to our house, Thetis, honored and always welcome? You do not visit us often. Come inside, and let me set refreshment before you.”

The goddess led the way and told Thetis to sit on a richly decorated seat inlaid with silver, with a footstool under her feet. Then she called Hephaestus and said, “Hephaestus, come here, Thetis wants you.” The far-famed lame god answered, “Then an august and honored goddess has indeed come here. She is the one who took care of me when I was suffering from the heavy fall that came from my cruel mother’s anger, because she wanted to be rid of me for being lame. It would have gone hard with me if Eurynome, daughter of the ever-encircling waters of Oceanus, and Thetis had not taken me to their bosom. I stayed with them nine years. In their cave, with the roaring waters of Oceanus foaming ever past it, I made many beautiful works in bronze for them: brooches, spiral armlets, cups, and chains. No one knew about it, neither god nor man, except Thetis and Eurynome, who took care of me. So if Thetis has come to my house, I must repay her for saving me. Entertain her with all hospitality while I put away my bellows and all my tools.”

At this the mighty monster hobbled away from his anvil, his thin legs working hard beneath him. He set the bellows away from the fire and gathered his tools into a silver chest. Then he took a sponge and washed his face and hands, his shaggy chest and brawny neck. He put on his shirt, took up his strong staff, and limped toward the door. Golden handmaids worked for him as well. They looked like real young women, with sense and reason, voice and strength, and all the learning of the immortals. These busied themselves as the king told them, while he drew near to Thetis, seated her on a goodly seat, took her hand in his, and said, “Why have you come to our house, Thetis, honored and always welcome? You do not visit us often. Say what you want, and I will do it for you at once if I can, and if it can be done at all.”

Thetis wept and answered, “Hephaestus, is there any other goddess on Olympus whom the son of Cronus has chosen to burden with as much affliction as he has me? Of all the sea goddesses, he made me alone subject to a mortal husband, Peleus son of Aeacus. I submitted very much against my will to the embraces of a mere mortal, who now stays at home worn out with age. And that is not all. Heaven granted me a son, a hero among heroes, and he shot up like a sapling. I tended him like a plant in a goodly garden and sent him with his ships to Ilium to fight the Trojans, but I shall never welcome him back to the house of Peleus. As long as he lives to see the light of the sun, he is weighed down with grief, and though I go to him I cannot help him. King Agamemnon has made him give up the maiden whom the sons of the Achaeans had awarded him, and he wastes away with sorrow for her sake. Then the Trojans hemmed the Achaeans in at their ships’ sterns and would not let them come out. The elders of the Argives begged Achilles and offered him great treasure. He refused to bring them deliverance himself, but he put his own armor on Patroclus and sent him into the fight with many people behind him. All day long they fought by the Scaean gates, and they would have taken the city there and then, if Apollo had not given glory to Hector and killed the valiant son of Menoetius after he had done the Trojans much harm. So I am a suppliant at your knees, in case you are willing to provide my son, whose end is near, with a helmet and shield, with goodly greaves fitted with ankle-clasps, and with a breastplate. He lost his own when his true comrade fell at the hands of the Trojans, and now he lies stretched on the earth in the bitterness of his soul.”

Hephaestus answered, “Take heart, and do not be troubled about this. I wish I could hide him from death when his hour comes, as surely as I can find him armor that will amaze the eyes of everyone who sees it.”

When he had said this, he left her and went to his bellows. He turned them toward the fire and told them to do their work. Twenty bellows blew on the melting pots, sending out blasts of every kind: some fierce, to help him when he needed them, and others gentler, as Hephaestus wished while he worked. He threw tough copper into the fire, with tin, silver, and gold. He set his great anvil on its block, took his mighty hammer in one hand, and held the tongs in the other.

First he shaped the shield, great and strong, adorning it all over and binding it round with a gleaming rim in three layers. The baldric was made of silver. He made the shield in five thicknesses, and his cunning hand enriched it with many wonders.

On it he worked the earth, the heavens, and the sea. He added the full moon and the untiring sun, along with all the signs that crown the face of heaven: the Pleiads, the Hyads, huge Orion, and the Bear, which men also call the Wain. The Bear always turns in one place, facing Orion, and it alone never dips into the stream of Oceanus.

He also made two cities, fair to see and busy with the hum of men. In one there were weddings and wedding feasts. People were going about the city with brides, escorting them by torchlight from their chambers. The cry of Hymen rose loud, and the youths danced to the music of flute and lyre, while the women stood each at her house door to watch them.

Meanwhile the people were gathered in assembly, because a quarrel had broken out. Two men were wrangling over the blood-money for a man who had been killed. One said before the people that he had paid in full, and the other said he had not been paid. Each was trying to make his own case good, and the people took sides, each man backing the side he had chosen. The heralds held them back, and the elders sat on their seats of stone in a solemn circle, holding the staves the heralds had put into their hands. Then they rose, and each in his turn gave judgment. Two talents were laid down, to be given to the man whose judgment was held to be the fairest.

Around the other city two hosts lay encamped in gleaming armor. They were divided over whether to sack it, or to spare it and accept half of what it contained. But the men of the city would not yet agree, and they armed for a surprise attack. Their wives and little children kept guard on the walls, together with the men who were too old to fight. The others sallied forth with Ares and Pallas Athena at their head. Both were wrought in gold and dressed in golden raiment, great and fair in their armor, as befits gods, while the people who followed them were smaller. They came to the place where they would lay their ambush, a riverbed where livestock of every kind came from far and near to drink. There they lay hidden, in full armor. Some way off from them were two scouts, watching for the coming of sheep or cattle. These soon came, followed by two shepherds who were playing on their pipes and had not so much as a thought of danger. When the men in ambush saw this, they cut off the flocks and herds and killed the shepherds. Meanwhile the besiegers were sitting in council. When they heard the loud noise among the cattle, they sprang to their horses and rode at full speed toward it. They reached the place and set their battle line by the banks of the river, and the two hosts aimed their bronze-shod spears at one another. Strife and Riot were with them, and grim Fate, who was dragging three men after her: one with a fresh wound, one unwounded, and the third dead, whom she dragged along by the heel. Her robe was drenched in men’s blood. They went in and out among one another and fought like living people dragging away one another’s dead.

He also made a fair fallow field, large, and already plowed three times. Many men were working their plows in it, turning their oxen this way and that, furrow after furrow. Each time they turned at the headland, a man came up and gave them a cup of wine, and they went back to their furrows looking forward to reaching the headland again. The part they had plowed was dark behind them, so that the field, though made of gold, still looked as if it were being plowed—very curious to behold.

He also made a field of harvest grain, where the reapers were cutting with sharp sickles in their hands. Swathe after swathe fell to the ground in a straight line behind them, and the binders tied the swathes in bands of twisted straw. There were three binders, and behind them boys gathered the cut grain in armfuls and kept bringing it to be bound. Among them all the owner of the land stood by in silence and was glad. Under an oak the servants were getting a meal ready. They had sacrificed a great ox and were busy cutting it up, while the women were making a porridge of much white barley for the laborers’ dinner.

He also made a vineyard, golden and fair to see, with the vines loaded with grapes. The bunches overhead were black, but the vines were trained on poles of silver. Around it he ran a ditch of dark metal and fenced it with a fence of tin. Only one path led to it, and the vintagers took it when they went to gather the vintage. Youths and maidens, light-hearted and full of glee, carried the luscious fruit in plaited baskets. With them went a boy who made sweet music on his lyre and sang the Linos-song in his clear boyish voice.

He also made a herd of horned cattle. He made the cows of gold and tin, and they lowed as they came at full speed out of the yards to feed among the waving reeds that grow by the banks of the river. Four shepherds, all of them in gold, went along with the cattle, and their nine swift dogs went with them. Two terrible lions had seized a bellowing bull that was among the foremost cows. Bellow as he might, they dragged him off while the dogs and men gave chase. The lions tore through the bull’s thick hide and were gorging on his blood and bowels, but the herdsmen were afraid to do anything and only urged on their dogs. The dogs did not dare to fasten on the lions. They stood by barking and keeping out of harm’s way.
The god also made a pasture in a fair mountain dell. It held a large flock of sheep, a homestead, huts, and sheltered sheepfolds.

He also made a dancing green, like the one Daedalus once made in Cnossus for lovely Ariadne. On it danced youths and maidens whom everyone would woo, with their hands on one another’s wrists. The maidens wore robes of light linen, and the youths wore well-woven shirts that were slightly oiled. The girls were crowned with garlands, and the young men had daggers of gold hanging from silver baldrics. Sometimes they danced deftly in a ring on merry twinkling feet, like a potter sitting at his work and testing his wheel to see whether it will run. Sometimes they went in line with one another. Many people had gathered joyously around the green. A bard was there too, to sing to them and play his lyre, and two tumblers went about performing in the midst of them when the man struck up his tune.
Around the outermost rim of the shield he set the mighty stream of the river Oceanus.

When he had finished the shield, great and strong, he made a breastplate that shone brighter than fire. He made a helmet that fitted close to the brow, richly worked, with a golden plume overhanging it. He also made greaves of beaten tin.

Lastly, when the famed lame god had finished all the armor, he took it and set it before the mother of Achilles. She darted like a falcon from the snowy summits of Olympus and carried the gleaming armor away from the house of Hephaestus.

chapters.title: Book 19
paragraphs: Achilles makes peace with Agamemnon, puts on the armor that Hephaestus made for him, and goes out to fight.

Saffron-robed Dawn was rising from the streams of Oceanus to bring light to mortals and immortals when Thetis reached the ships, carrying the armor the god had given her. She found her son lying across the body of Patroclus, weeping bitterly. Many of his followers were weeping around him too. The goddess walked in among them and took his hand in hers. “My son,” she said, “however much we grieve, we must let this man lie. It was heaven’s will that he fell. Now take this rich and beautiful armor from Hephaestus. No man has ever yet carried it on his shoulders.”

As she spoke she set the armor down in front of Achilles, and it rang out loudly. Awe came over the Myrmidons, and none of them dared look straight at it. They were afraid. Achilles, though, was stirred to even greater fury, and his eyes blazed with a fierce light. He was glad to hold the splendid gift the god had made him. When he had looked at it long enough to satisfy himself, he spoke to his mother. “Mother,” he said, “the god has given me armor fit for the work of an immortal, such as no living man could have made. I will arm now. But I am very afraid that flies will settle on the son of Menoetius and breed worms in his wounds. His body is dead, and it would be disfigured and the flesh would rot.”

Silver-footed Thetis answered, “My son, do not trouble yourself about this. I will find a way to protect him from the swarms of foul flies that feed on men killed in battle. He could lie there a whole year, and his flesh will be as sound as ever, or even sounder. Now call the Achaean heroes to assembly. Give up your anger against Agamemnon. Arm at once and fight with all your strength.”
As she spoke she filled him with strength and courage. Then she dripped ambrosia and red nectar into the wounds of Patroclus, so that his body would not change.

Achilles went out along the sea shore and called the Achaean heroes with a loud cry. Even those who until now had always stayed at the ships came to the place of assembly: the pilots and helmsmen, and the stewards who looked after the ships and handed out rations. They came because Achilles had shown himself after keeping away from the fighting for so long. Two sons of Ares, Odysseus and the son of Tydeus, came limping, because their wounds still hurt. They came anyway and took seats in the front row. Last of all came Agamemnon, king of men. He was wounded too, since Coon son of Antenor had struck him with a spear in battle.

When the Achaeans had gathered, Achilles stood up and spoke. “Son of Atreus, it would have been better for both of us, when we were so furious with each other over Briseis, if Artemis’s arrow had killed her at the ships on the day I took her, after I sacked Lyrnessus. Think of it: many fewer Achaeans would have bitten the dust before the enemy while my anger lasted. It has served Hector and the Trojans well, but the Achaeans will remember our quarrel for a long time. Now let it be. It is over. If we were angry, necessity has taught us better. I put my anger away from me. I cannot keep nursing it forever. So tell the Achaeans to arm at once, so that I can go out against the Trojans and find out whether they still mean to sleep beside the ships. Anyone who escapes my spear when I swing it will be glad, I think, to rest his knees.”
So he spoke, and the Achaeans were glad that he had put his anger aside.

Then Agamemnon rose in his place, without going out into the middle of the assembly, and spoke. “Danaan heroes,” he said, “servants of Ares, it is right to listen when a man stands up to speak, and it is not proper to interrupt him. Even a practiced speaker is hard put when that happens. Who can hear or speak in an uproar? The finest orator would be thrown off by it. I will make my case to the son of Peleus, and the rest of you Achaeans, pay attention and listen well. Often the Achaeans have spoken to me about this matter and blamed me. But I was not the one who did it. Zeus, and Fate, and Erinys who walks in darkness, drove me mad on the day of the assembly, when I took from Achilles the prize that had been awarded to him. What could I do? All things are in the hand of heaven. Folly, the eldest of Zeus’s daughters, blinds men to their own destruction. She walks lightly. She does not tread on the solid earth but floats over the heads of men, making them stumble or catching them in her snare.

“There was a time when she fooled Zeus himself, who they say is the greatest of gods and men. Hera, though only a woman, tricked him on the day Alcmena was to give birth to mighty Heracles in the fair city of Thebes. He announced to the gods, ‘Hear me, all gods and goddesses, so that I may say what I have in mind. Today an Ilithuia, helper of women in labor, will bring into the world a male child who will be lord over all who live around him and are of my blood and lineage.’ Then Hera, crafty and full of guile, said, ‘You will cheat, and you will not keep your word. Swear to me, Olympian, swear a great oath that the child who falls between a woman’s feet today will be lord over all who live around him and are of your blood and lineage.’

“So she spoke, and Zeus did not suspect her. He swore the great oath, and afterward he bitterly regretted it. Hera darted down from the high peak of Olympus and hurried to Achaean Argos, where she knew the noble wife of Sthenelus son of Perseus was living. The woman was with child, in her seventh month. Hera brought that child to birth although a month was still lacking. Meanwhile she held back Alcmena’s offspring and kept the Ilithuiae from her. Then she went to tell Zeus the son of Cronus. ‘Father Zeus, lord of the lightning,’ she said, ‘I have a word for your ear. A fine child has been born today, Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus the son of Perseus. He is of your lineage, so it is right that he should rule the Argives.’

“At this Zeus was stung to the quick. In his rage he seized Folly by the hair and swore a great oath that she would never again set foot in starry heaven and Olympus, since she was the ruin of everyone. He whirled her around with a twist of his hand and flung her down from heaven, and she landed in the fields of mortal men. And he was always angry with her whenever he saw his son groaning under the cruel labors that Eurystheus laid on him. In the same way I grieved when mighty Hector was killing the Argives at their ships. All the while I kept thinking of Folly, who had ruined me. I was blind, and Zeus robbed me of my reason. Now I will make atonement, and I will add much treasure in payment. Go into battle, you and your people with you. I will give you everything Odysseus offered you yesterday in your tents. Or if you prefer, wait, though you are eager to fight at once, and my squires will bring the gifts from my ship, so that you can see whether what I give is enough.”

Achilles answered, “Son of Atreus, king of men Agamemnon, you may give such gifts as you think proper, or keep them back. That is in your own hands. Let us now draw up for battle. It is not right to stand talking about trifles, because there is a deed still to be done. Achilles will be seen again fighting among the foremost and laying low the Trojan ranks. Let every one of you keep that in mind when he fights.”

Then Odysseus spoke. “Godlike and brave Achilles, do not send the Achaeans against Ilium to fight the Trojans without food. The battle will not be short once it begins, since heaven has filled both sides with fury. Tell them first to take bread and wine by the ships, because that gives strength and staying power. No man can fight all day until the sun goes down if he has no food. However much he wants to fight, his strength will fail him before he knows it. Hunger and thirst will find him out, and his legs will grow tired under him. A man who has eaten his fill of meat and wine can fight all day. His heart beats high, and his strength will hold until he has routed all his enemies. So send the people away and tell them to prepare their meal. King Agamemnon will bring out the gifts in front of the assembly, so that everyone can see them and you can be satisfied. Also, let him swear an oath before the Argives that he has never gone up to the bed of Briseis or lain with her as men and women do. And you, too, show a gracious spirit. Let Agamemnon entertain you in his tents with a feast of reconciliation, so that you will have received what is owed you in full. As for you, son of Atreus, treat people more justly in future. It is no disgrace even for a king to make amends if he was wrong in the first place.”

King Agamemnon answered, “Son of Laertes, your words please me well, because you have spoken wisely from beginning to end. I will swear as you ask. I do it of my own free will, and I will not take the name of heaven in vain. So let Achilles wait, though he is eager to fight at once, and the rest of you wait too, until the gifts arrive from my tent and we seal the oath with a sacrifice. This is my order. Take some noble young Achaeans with you and bring from my tents the gifts I promised Achilles yesterday. Bring the women too. And let Talthybius find me a boar among the animals with the army and prepare it for sacrifice to Zeus and the sun.”

Achilles said, “Son of Atreus, king of men Agamemnon, see to these matters some other time, when there is a pause in the fighting and I am calmer. Would you have men eat while the bodies of those whom Hector son of Priam killed are still lying mangled on the plain? I say let the sons of the Achaeans fight fasting, without food, until we have avenged them. Afterward, at sundown, let them eat their fill. As for me, Patroclus lies dead in my tent, hacked and cut to pieces, with his feet toward the door, and his comrades are mourning around him. So I can think of nothing but slaughter and blood and the rattle in the throats of the dying.”

Odysseus answered, “Achilles, son of Peleus, mightiest of all the Achaeans, in battle you are better than I, and by more than a little. But in counsel I am far ahead of you, because I am older and know more. So be patient with my words. Men soon have their fill of fighting. When Zeus, who is the steward of war, weighs the outcome, it may well turn out that the straw our sickles have cut is far heavier than the grain. The Achaeans cannot mourn the dead with their bellies. Men fall thick and threefold, day after day, without end. When would we ever have a rest from our sorrow? Let us mourn our dead for one day and bury them out of sight and mind. But let those of us who are left eat and drink, so that we can arm and fight our enemies more fiercely. When that hour comes, let no man hold back waiting for a second summons. Such a summons will mean trouble for anyone found lagging behind at our ships. Let us rather charge as one man and unleash the fury of war on the Trojans.”

With these words he took the sons of Nestor, Meges son of Phyleus, Thoas, Meriones, Lycomedes son of Creontes, and Melanippus, and went to the tent of Agamemnon son of Atreus. No sooner said than done: they brought out the seven tripods Agamemnon had promised, with the twenty metal cauldrons and the twelve horses. They also brought the seven women skilled in useful arts, and Briseis made eight. Odysseus weighed out the ten talents of gold and led the way back, while the young Achaeans carried the rest of the gifts and laid them in the middle of the assembly.

Agamemnon then stood up, and Talthybius, whose voice was like a god’s, came to him with the boar. The son of Atreus drew the knife that hung by the scabbard of his mighty sword. He lifted his hands in prayer and began by cutting some bristles from the boar. The other Achaeans sat where they were, silent and orderly, to hear their king. Agamemnon looked up into the vault of heaven and prayed. “I call Zeus to witness, first and mightiest of all gods. I call also Earth and Sun and the Erinyes who dwell below and take vengeance on anyone who swears falsely. I have laid no hand on the girl Briseis, either to take her to my bed or in any other way. She has stayed in my tents untouched. If I swear falsely, may heaven bring on me every penalty it deals out to those who break their oaths.”

As he spoke he cut the boar’s throat. Talthybius then whirled it around his head and flung it into the wide sea to feed the fishes. Achilles also rose and spoke to the Argives. “Father Zeus, it is true that you blind men’s eyes and ruin them. Otherwise the son of Atreus would not have stirred me to such fierce anger, or so stubbornly taken Briseis from me against my will. Zeus must have meant many an Argive to die. Go now and eat, so that we can begin fighting.”

Achilles dissolved the assembly, and every man returned to his own ship. The Myrmidons took the presents in hand and carried them down to the ship of Achilles, where they stored them in his tents. The stable-men drove the horses off to join the rest.

Briseis, as fair as Aphrodite, saw the mangled body of Patroclus and threw herself on it. She cried aloud, tearing at her breast, her neck, and her lovely face with both hands. Beautiful as a goddess, she wept and said, “Patroclus, dearest friend, when I left this place I left you living. Now I come back, O prince, and find you dead. New sorrows keep piling on me, one after another. I saw the man my father and mother married me to cut down before our city. Three dear brothers of mine died with him on the same day. But you, Patroclus, even when Achilles killed my husband and sacked the city of noble Mynes, told me I must not weep. You said you would make Achilles marry me and take me back with him to Phthia, and we would have a wedding feast among the Myrmidons. You were always kind to me, and I will never stop grieving for you.”

She wept as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament. They seemed to cry for Patroclus, but in truth each was weeping for her own sorrows. The elders of the Achaeans gathered around Achilles and begged him to eat. He groaned and refused. “I beg you,” he said, “if any comrade will listen to me, do not tell me to eat or drink. I am weighed down with grief, and I will stay fasting until the sun goes down.”

With this he sent the other princes away. Only the two sons of Atreus remained, with Odysseus, Nestor, Idomeneus, and the knight Phoenix, and they tried to comfort him in the bitterness of his sorrow. But he would not be comforted until he had thrown himself into the jaws of battle. He sighed again and again, thinking always of Patroclus. Then he said—

“Unhappy and dearest comrade, you were the one who would have a good dinner ready for me at once, without delay, whenever the Achaeans were hurrying to fight the Trojans. Now I have meat and drink in my tents, yet I will fast for sorrow. I could know no greater grief than this. It would not be greater if I heard of the death of my father, who is now in Phthia weeping for the loss of me, his son, while I fight the Trojans in a strange land for the sake of accursed Helen. Nor would it be greater if I heard that my son was dead, the boy being brought up in Scyros, if Neoptolemus is indeed still living. Until now I felt sure that I alone was to fall here at Troy, far from Argos, and that you would go back to Phthia, bring my son home with you in your own ship, and show him all my property, my bondsmen, and the greatness of my house—for Peleus must surely be dead, or else what little life he has left is weighed down by the infirmities of age and by constant fear that he will hear the sad news of my death.”

He wept as he spoke, and the elders sighed together, each thinking of what he had left at home. The son of Cronus looked down on them with pity and presently said to Athena, “My child, you have quite abandoned your hero. Has he gone so completely out of your mind? There he sits by the ships, desolate for the loss of his dear comrade. The others have gone to their dinner, but he will neither eat nor drink. Go and drop nectar and ambrosia into his breast, so that he feels no hunger.”

With these words he urged on Athena, who was already of the same mind. She darted down from heaven through the air, like a falcon sailing on broad wings and screaming. Meanwhile the Achaeans were arming all through the host. Athena dropped nectar and ambrosia into Achilles, so that no cruel hunger would make his limbs fail, and then she went back to the house of her mighty father. The gleaming helmets, the bossed shields, the strongly plated breastplates, and the ashen spears streamed from the ships as thick as chill snowflakes shed from the hand of Zeus and driven on the keen blasts of the north wind. The sheen reached the sky. The whole land was bright with the flash of their armor, and the sound of their tramping rose from under their feet. In the midst of them all Achilles put on his armor. He gnashed his teeth, and his eyes gleamed like fire, because his grief was more than he could bear. So, full of fury against the Trojans, he put on the gift of the god, the armor that Hephaestus had made for him.

First he put on the fine greaves, fitted with ankle-clasps, and next he fastened the breastplate around his chest. He slung the silver-studded sword of bronze from his shoulders, and then took up the shield, so great and strong that it shone from afar with a splendor like the moon. Sailors at sea sometimes see the light of a fire that men have lit in their homestead high among the mountains, while wind and storm carry the sailors out to sea, far from the harbor where they want to be. In the same way the gleam of Achilles’s wondrous shield shot up into the heavens. He lifted the mighty helmet and set it on his head, and it shone like a star. The golden plumes that Hephaestus had set thick around its ridge waved all about it. Then Achilles tested himself in his armor to see whether it fitted and let his limbs move freely in it. It seemed to lift him up as though it were wings.

He also drew his father’s spear out of the spear-stand. It was so great and heavy and strong that none of the Achaeans except Achilles had the strength to wield it. This was the spear of Pelian ash from the topmost ridges of Mount Pelion, which Chiron had once given to Peleus, and it carried death for heroes. Automedon and Alcimus were busy harnessing his horses. They made the bands fast around them and put the bits in their mouths, drawing the reins back toward the chariot. Automedon sprang up behind the horses with a whip in his hand, and Achilles mounted after him in full armor, as resplendent as the sun-god Hyperion. Then in a loud voice he scolded his father’s horses. “Xanthus and Balius, famed offspring of Podarge,” he said, “this time, when we have finished fighting, be sure to bring your driver safely back to the host of the Achaeans. Do not leave him dead on the plain as you did Patroclus.”

Then swift Xanthus answered from under the yoke, for white-armed Hera had given him human speech. He bowed his head until his mane, hanging down from under the yoke-band, touched the ground. “Dread Achilles,” he said, “we will save you this time. But the day of your death is near, and we are not to blame for it. Heaven and stern fate will destroy you. It was not through any sloth or slackness of ours that the Trojans stripped Patroclus of his armor. The mighty god whom lovely Leto bore killed him as he fought among the foremost, and gave the triumph to Hector. We two can run as swiftly as Zephyrus, who they say is the fastest of all winds. Even so, it is your doom to fall by the hand of a man and a god.”

As he said this the Erinyes stopped his speech, and Achilles answered him in great sadness. “Xanthus, why do you foretell my death? You need not. I know well that I am to fall here, far from my dear father and mother. None the more shall I hold back my hand until I have given the Trojans their fill of fighting.”
With these words and a loud cry he drove his horses to the front.

chapters.title: Book 20
paragraphs: The gods hold a council and decide to watch the fight from the hill Callicolone and from the barrow of Heracles—Achilles and Aeneas begin to fight, but Poseidon interrupts them and saves Aeneas—Achilles kills many Trojans.
So the Achaeans armed by their ships around you, son of Peleus, who were hungry for battle. Across from them, the Trojans armed on the rising ground of the plain.

Meanwhile Zeus, from the top of many-delled Olympus, told Themis to gather the gods in council. She went around and summoned them to the house of Zeus. Every river came except Oceanus, and so did every one of the nymphs who haunt fair groves, the springs of rivers and the meadows of green grass. When they arrived at the house of cloud-compelling Zeus, they sat down in the arcades of polished marble that Hephaestus, with his perfect skill, had built for father Zeus.

That was how they gathered in the house of Zeus. Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, also obeyed the goddess’s call and came up out of the sea to join them. He sat among them and asked what Zeus had in mind. “Why have you called the gods to council, wielder of the lightning?” he said. “Are you weighing some matter that concerns the Trojans and Achaeans? The blaze of battle is about to be kindled between them.”

And Zeus answered, “You know my purpose, shaker of earth, and why I have called you here. I take thought for them even in their destruction. I myself will stay seated on Mt. Olympus and watch in peace. The rest of you, go among the Trojans and Achaeans and help whichever side you are inclined to. If Achilles fights the Trojans unhindered, they will not hold against him. They have always trembled at the sight of him, and now that he is roused to such fury over his comrade, he will overturn fate itself and storm their city.”

So Zeus spoke and gave the word for war, and the gods took their separate sides and went into battle. Hera, Pallas Athena, earth-encircling Poseidon, and Hermes, bringer of good luck and excellent in all cunning—all these joined the host that came from the ships. Hephaestus came with them in all his glory, limping, but moving his thin legs vigorously under him. Ares of the gleaming helmet joined the Trojans, and with him Apollo of the unshorn locks, the archer goddess Artemis, Leto, Xanthus, and laughter-loving Aphrodite.

As long as the gods kept away from the mortal warriors, the Achaeans were triumphant, because Achilles, who had refused to fight for so long, was now with them. Every Trojan’s limbs failed him for fear when he saw the swift son of Peleus, glorious in his armor and looking like Ares himself. But when the Olympians came to join the men, strong Strife, rouser of hosts, rose up at once, and Athena raised her loud voice, standing now by the deep trench outside the wall and now shouting with all her might on the shore of the sounding sea. On the other side Ares bellowed too, dark as a black thunder cloud, calling to the Trojans at the top of his voice, now from the acropolis and now running up the bank of the river Simois until he came to the hill Callicolone.

That was how the gods spurred both hosts to fight, and stirred up fierce quarrels among themselves too. The father of gods and men thundered from heaven above, while from below Poseidon shook the vast earth and made the high hills tremble. The spurs and crests of many-fountained Ida quaked, and so did the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans. Hades, king of the realms below, was struck with fear. He sprang from his throne in panic and cried aloud in terror that Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, would crack the ground over his head and lay his moldy mansions bare to mortals and immortals alike—mansions so ghastly grim that even the gods shudder to think of them. Such was the uproar as the gods came together in battle. Apollo with his arrows took his stand facing King Poseidon, and Athena took hers against the god of war. The archer goddess Artemis, sister of far-darting Apollo, with her golden arrows, stood to face Hera. Hermes, the lusty bringer of good luck, faced Leto. And the mighty eddying river, which men call Scamander but gods call Xanthus, set himself against Hephaestus.

The gods stood arrayed against one another like this. Achilles, though, wanted most of all to meet Hector son of Priam, since Hector’s blood was what he longed to feed the stubborn lord of battle. Apollo meanwhile pushed Aeneas toward the son of Peleus and put courage into his heart. He took the voice of Lycaon son of Priam, and in that likeness he said to Aeneas, “Aeneas, counselor of the Trojans, what has become of the brave words you boasted over your wine before the Trojan princes, that you would fight Achilles son of Peleus in single combat?”

And Aeneas answered, “Why do you tell me to fight the proud son of Peleus, when I have no mind to do it? If I faced him now, it would not be the first time. His spear has already driven me in flight from Ida, when he raided our cattle and sacked Lyrnessus and Pedasus. Zeus saved me then by giving me the strength to run; otherwise I would have fallen to Achilles and Athena, who went before him to protect him and urged him to attack the Lelegae and Trojans. No man can fight Achilles, because one of the gods is always with him as his guardian angel. Even without that, his weapon flies straight and never fails to pierce the flesh of the man it is aimed at. If heaven would let me fight him on even terms, he would not beat me easily, though he boasts that he is made of bronze.”

Then King Apollo, son of Zeus, said, “No, hero, pray to the ever-living gods. Men say you were born of Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite, whereas Achilles is the son of a goddess of lower rank. Aphrodite is the child of Zeus, while Thetis is only the daughter of the old man of the sea. So bring your spear against him, and do not let his taunts and threats scare you.”

As he spoke he put courage into the heart of the shepherd of his people, and Aeneas strode in full armor among the foremost fighters. The son of Anchises did not escape the notice of white-armed Hera as he went out into the throng to meet Achilles. She called the gods around her and said, “You two, Poseidon and Athena, look to this and consider how it should go. Phoebus Apollo has been sending Aeneas, clad in full armor, to fight Achilles. Shall we turn him back at once, or shall one of us stand by Achilles and give him strength, so that his heart does not fail and he learns that the chiefs of the immortals are on his side, while the others who have all along been defending the Trojans are vain helpers? Let us all come down from Olympus and join the fight, so that he takes no harm from the Trojans today. Afterward let him suffer whatever fate was spun out for him when he was begotten and his mother bore him. If Achilles is not assured by the voice of a god, he may come to fear presently, when one of us meets him in battle, for the gods are terrible when they are seen face to face.”

Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, answered her, “Hera, restrain your fury. It is not right. I do not favor forcing the other gods to fight us, for the advantage is already too much on our side. Let us take our places on some hill out of the beaten track and let mortals fight it out among themselves. If Ares or Phoebus Apollo begins fighting, or holds Achilles in check so that he cannot fight, then we too will raise the battle cry at once. In that case they will soon leave the field and go back beaten to Olympus, to the other gods.”

With these words the dark-haired god led the way to the high earth barrow of Heracles. It was built around solid masonry, and the Trojans and Pallas Athena had made it as a place for him to flee to when the sea monster was chasing him from the shore onto the plain. Poseidon and those with him sat down here, wrapped in a thick cloud of darkness. The other gods seated themselves on the brow of Callicolone, around you, Phoebus, and Ares, the waster of cities.

So the gods sat apart and made their plans. Neither side was willing to begin the battle, and Zeus on his high seat commanded them all. Meanwhile the whole plain was alive with men and horses and blazing with the gleam of armor. The earth rang under the tramp of their feet as they rushed toward each other, and two champions, by far the foremost of them all, met between the hosts to fight—Aeneas son of Anchises, and noble Achilles.

Aeneas was the first to stride forward in attack, his stout helmet tossing defiance as he came on. He held his strong shield before his breast and brandished his bronze spear. The son of Peleus sprang out from the other side to meet him, like a fierce lion that the whole countryside has gathered to hunt and kill—at first it suspects no harm, but when some daring youth has struck it with a spear, it crouches with open mouth, its jaws foam, it roars with fury, it lashes its tail from side to side about its ribs and loins, and it glares as it springs straight ahead, to find out whether it will slay or be slain among the foremost of its foes—with such fury Achilles burned to spring upon Aeneas.

When they were close to each other, Achilles spoke first. “Aeneas,” he said, “why do you come out in front of the host to fight me? Do you hope to reign over the Trojans in Priam’s seat? Even if you kill me, Priam will not hand his kingdom over to you. He is a man of sound judgment, and he has sons of his own. Or have the Trojans set aside for you an estate of surpassing richness, fair with orchard lawns and cornfields, in case you should slay me? You will hardly manage that. I have routed you once already. Have you forgotten how I chased you, alone, away from your herds, headlong down the slopes of Ida? You did not turn to look behind you. You took refuge in Lyrnessus, but I attacked the city, and with the help of Athena and father Zeus I sacked it and carried its women off into captivity. Zeus and the other gods rescued you, though. You think they will protect you now, but they will not. So I tell you, go back into the host and do not face me, or you will regret it. Even a fool may be wise after the event.”

Then Aeneas answered, “Son of Peleus, do not think your words can scare me as if I were a child. I too can brag and talk rudely, if I choose. We each know the other’s race and parentage as matters of common fame, though you have never seen my parents, nor I yours. Men say you are the son of noble Peleus, and that your mother is Thetis, fair-haired daughter of the sea. I have noble Anchises for my father and Aphrodite for my mother. The parents of one of us will mourn a son today, for when the fight is over we will be parted by more than silly talk. Learn my lineage, then, if you wish—and many people know it.

“In the beginning Dardanus was the son of Zeus, and he founded Dardania, for Ilium was not yet established on the plain for men to live in, and her people still lived on the spurs of many-fountained Ida. Dardanus had a son, King Erichthonius, who was the wealthiest of all living men. He had three thousand mares that fed by the water meadows, they and their foals with them. Boreas fell in love with them as they were feeding and covered them in the likeness of a dark-maned stallion. They conceived and bore him twelve filly foals. When these sped over the rich plain, they could bound over the ripe ears of corn without breaking them; and when they played on the broad back of Ocean, they could gallop on the crest of a breaker. Erichthonius fathered Tros, king of the Trojans, and Tros had three noble sons, Ilus, Assaracus, and Ganymede, who was the most beautiful of mortal men. For his beauty’s sake the gods carried him off to be Zeus’s cup-bearer, so that he might live among the immortals. Ilus fathered Laomedon, and Laomedon fathered Tithonus, Priam, Lampus, Clytius, and Hiketaon of the stock of Ares. Assaracus was father to Capys, and Capys to Anchises, who was my father, while Hector is the son of Priam.

“That is my blood and lineage. As for valor, Zeus gives it or takes it as he wills, for he is lord of all. And now let us have no more of this prating in the middle of battle, as if we were children. We could fling taunts at each other without end; a hundred-oared galley would not hold them all. The tongue can run anywhere and talk in any way; it can go here and there, and whatever a man says, he will be contradicted. What use is it for us to bandy hard words like women who fall out with one another, go out and wrangle in the streets, half truth and half lies, as rage inspires them? No words of yours will turn me now that I am eager to fight—so let us test each other with our spears.”

As he spoke he drove his spear at the great and terrible shield of Achilles, which rang out as the point struck it. The son of Peleus held the shield out before him with his strong hand, and he was afraid, because he thought Aeneas’s spear would go through it easily. He did not reflect that the god’s glorious gifts were little likely to give way before the blows of mortal men. And in fact Aeneas’s spear did not pierce the shield, for the layer of gold, the god’s gift, stopped the point. It went through two layers, but the god had made the shield in five: two of bronze, the two innermost of tin, and one of gold. The spear was stopped in that one.

Next it was Achilles’s turn to throw. His spear struck the round shield of Aeneas right at the rim, where the bronze was thinnest, and the spear of Pelian ash went clean through. The shield rang under the blow. Aeneas was afraid. He crouched backward and held the shield out away from his body. The spear flew over his back and stuck quivering in the ground, after piercing both rings of the shield that sheltered him. Aeneas had avoided it, but he stood rooted, blinded by fear and grief, because the weapon had come so close. Then Achilles sprang at him in fury, with a deadly cry and his sharp sword drawn. Aeneas picked up a great stone, so huge that two men of today could not have lifted it, though Aeneas swung it easily by himself.

Aeneas would have hit Achilles with that stone as he rushed in, on the helmet or on the shield that covered him, and Achilles would have closed with him and finished him with his sword. But Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, saw it quickly and at once spoke to the immortals. “Alas, I am sorry for great Aeneas. He will soon go down to the house of Hades, beaten by the son of Peleus, because he was a fool to listen to the counsel of Apollo. Apollo will never save him from destruction. Why should this man suffer for nothing, though he is guiltless, in a quarrel that is not his? He has always offered pleasing sacrifices to the gods who live in heaven. Let us snatch him from the jaws of death, in case the son of Cronus is angry if Achilles kills him. Besides, it is fated that he escape, so that the race of Dardanus does not perish utterly, without seed or sign. Zeus loved Dardanus above all the sons born to him of mortal women. Zeus has now come to hate the blood of Priam, so Aeneas shall reign over the Trojans, he and his children’s children who will be born after him.”

Hera answered, “Earth-shaker, decide this matter yourself. Consider whether to save Aeneas, or to let him fall, brave as he is, at the hands of Achilles son of Peleus. Pallas Athena and I have sworn many times before all the immortals that we would never protect the Trojans from destruction, not even when all Troy is burning in the fire the Achaeans will light.”

When earth-encircling Poseidon heard this, he went into the battle through the clash of spears and reached the place where Achilles and Aeneas were. At once he poured a darkness over the eyes of the son of Peleus. He pulled the bronze-headed ash spear out of the shield of Aeneas and laid it at the feet of Achilles. Then he lifted Aeneas high off the ground and hurried him away. Aeneas soared over the heads of many ranks of warriors, both horse and foot, speeding along on the god’s hand, until he reached the far edge of the battle, where the Cauconians were arming for the fight. Poseidon, shaker of the earth, came up to him there and said, “Aeneas, what god has pushed you into this folly of fighting the son of Peleus? He is a mightier man of valor than you, and dearer to heaven. Give way to him whenever you meet him, or you will go down to the house of Hades even though fate wills otherwise. But once Achilles is dead, you can fight among the foremost without fear, for no other Achaean will kill you.”

When the god had given these instructions he left him, and at once lifted the darkness from the eyes of Achilles. Achilles opened them wide and said in great anger, “Alas! What marvel is this I see? My spear lies here on the ground, but I cannot see the man I meant to kill when I threw it. So Aeneas also must be under heaven’s protection, though I thought his boasting was empty. Let him go hang. After so narrow an escape from being killed, he will not want to fight me again. Now I will give my orders to the Danaans and attack some other Trojans.”

He sprang forward along the line and urged his men on. “Do not let the Trojans keep you at arm’s length, Achaeans,” he cried. “Go at them and fight them man against man. However valiant I am, I cannot chase so many and fight them all. Even Ares, who is immortal, or Athena would shrink from plunging into the jaws of such a fight and laying about them. Still, as far as I am able, I will show no slackness of hand or foot and no lack of endurance, not for a moment. I will break their ranks completely, and woe to any Trojan who comes within reach of my spear.”

So he urged them on. Meanwhile Hector called to the Trojans and declared that he would fight Achilles. “Do not be afraid, proud Trojans, to face the son of Peleus,” he said. “I could fight gods myself if the battle were only a matter of words, but they would be too strong for me if we had to use spears. It will be the same with Achilles: his deeds will fall somewhat short of his word. He will do part of it, and the rest he will cut short. I will go up against him even if his hands are like fire—even if his hands are fire and his strength is iron.”

Urged on like this, the Trojans raised their spears against the Achaeans and gave the cry of battle as they threw themselves into the middle of their ranks. But Phoebus Apollo came up to Hector and said, “Hector, you must not challenge Achilles to single combat. Watch for him while you stay under cover of the others, away from the thick of the fight. Otherwise he will hit you with a spear or cut you down at close quarters.”

So he spoke, and Hector drew back into the crowd, afraid at what the god had said to him. Achilles then sprang on the Trojans with a terrible cry, clothed in valor as with a garment. First he killed Iphition son of Otrynteus, a leader of many people. A naiad nymph had borne him to Otrynteus, waster of cities, in the land of Hyde under the snowy heights of Mt. Tmolus. Achilles struck him full on the head as he came at him and split it clean in two. Iphition fell heavily to the ground, and Achilles boasted over him: “You lie low, son of Otrynteus, mighty hero. Your death is here, but your lineage is by the Gygaean lake, where your father’s estate lies, by the fish-rich Hyllus and the eddying waters of Hermus.”

So he boasted, but darkness closed Iphition’s eyes. The chariots of the Achaeans cut him to pieces as their wheels passed over him in the front of the battle. After him Achilles killed Demoleon, a valiant man of war and son of Antenor, striking him on the temple through his bronze-cheeked helmet. The helmet did not stop the spear. It drove on through, crushing the bone, so that the brain inside was scattered in all directions, and his lust for fighting was over. Then Achilles struck Hippodamas in the midriff as he leaped down from his chariot in front of him and tried to escape. Hippodamas breathed his last, bellowing as a bull bellows when young men drag him to be sacrificed to the King of Helice, and the earth-shaker’s heart is glad. Just so he bellowed as he lay dying. Achilles next went after Polydorus son of Priam. His father had always forbidden him to fight, because he was the youngest of his sons, the one Priam loved best, and the fastest runner. In his folly, showing off how swift his feet were, Polydorus was rushing about among the front ranks until he lost his life. Achilles struck him in the middle of the back as he darted past, just where the golden fastenings of his belt were and the two plates of the double breastplate overlapped. The spear point pierced him through and came out by the navel. He fell groaning to his knees, and a cloud of darkness overshadowed him as he sank down holding his entrails in his hands.

When Hector saw his brother Polydorus sinking to the ground with his entrails in his hands, a mist came over his eyes. He could no longer bear to keep his distance. He poised his spear and charged at Achilles like a flame of fire. Achilles saw him and bounded forward, boasting, “Here is the man who has wounded my heart most deeply and killed my beloved comrade. We two will not cower before each other much longer on the highways of war.”

Achilles looked fiercely at Hector and said, “Come closer, so that you meet your doom the sooner.” Hector was not afraid of him and answered, “Son of Peleus, do not think your words can frighten me as if I were a child. I too can brag and talk rudely when I choose. I know you are a mighty warrior, far mightier than I. Nevertheless the outcome lies in the lap of heaven, and worse man though I am, I may yet kill you with my spear, for it too has proved sharp before now.”

He hurled his spear as he spoke, but Athena breathed on it. Though she breathed very lightly, she turned it back away from Achilles, so that it returned to Hector and lay at his feet in front of him. Achilles sprang at him furiously with a loud cry, bent on killing him, but Apollo snatched Hector away easily, as a god can, and hid him in a thick darkness. Three times Achilles sprang at him with spear in hand, and three times he wasted his blow on the air. When he rushed forward a fourth time like a god, he shouted aloud, “Hound, you have escaped death again, though it came very near you this time. Phoebus Apollo, to whom you seem to pray before you go into battle, has saved you once more. But if I too have any friend among the gods, I will surely make an end of you when I meet you another time. For now I will chase down other Trojans.”

Then he struck Dryops with his spear in the middle of the neck, and Dryops fell headlong at his feet. Achilles left him lying there and stopped Demouchus son of Philetor, a brave man of great stature, by hitting him in the knee with a spear. Then he struck him with his sword and killed him. After this he sprang on Laogonus and Dardanus, sons of Bias, and threw them from their chariot, one with a blow from a thrown spear, the other cut down in hand-to-hand fighting. There was also Tros the son of Alastor. He came up to Achilles and clasped his knees, hoping that Achilles would spare him and let him go rather than kill him, because they were the same age. The fool might have known he would not prevail, for Achilles was in no mood for pity or mercy but in grim earnest. So when Tros took hold of his knees and tried to get a hearing for his prayers, Achilles drove his sword into his liver. The liver came rolling out, and Tros’s chest was covered with the black blood that welled from the wound. So death closed his eyes as he lay lifeless.

Achilles next went up to Mulius and struck him on the ear with a spear, and the bronze spearhead came out at the other ear. He struck Echeclus son of Agenor on the head with his sword, and the blade grew warm with blood, while death and stern fate closed the eyes of Echeclus. Next in order the bronze point of his spear wounded Deucalion in the forearm, where the sinews of the elbow join. Deucalion waited for the attack of Achilles with his arm hanging down and death staring him in the face. Achilles cut off his head with a sword blow and flung it, helmet and all, away from him, and the marrow came oozing out of the backbone as Deucalion lay there. Then he went after Rhigmus, noble son of Peires, who had come from fertile Thrace. He struck him through the middle with a spear that lodged in his belly, and Rhigmus fell headlong from his chariot. He also speared Areithous, the squire of Rhigmus, in the back as he was turning his horses to flee, and thrust him from his chariot, while the horses panicked.

Like a fire raging in a mountain glen after long drought, when the dense forest is ablaze and the wind carries great tongues of flame in every direction—so furiously did Achilles rage, wielding his spear like a god and chasing those he meant to kill, until the dark earth ran with blood. Or like a man who yokes broad-browed oxen to tread barley on a threshing floor, and it is soon crushed small under the feet of the lowing cattle—so the horses of Achilles trampled the shields and bodies of the slain. The axle underneath and the railing around the car were spattered with clots of blood thrown up by the horses’ hoofs and by the rims of the wheels. But the son of Peleus pressed on to win still more glory, and his hands were smeared with gore.

chapters.title: Book 21
paragraphs: Achilles fights with the river Scamander—The gods fight one another—Achilles drives the Trojans back inside their gates.

When they reached the ford of the full-flowing river Xanthus, who was begotten of immortal Zeus, Achilles split the Trojan force in two. He chased one half across the plain toward the city, along the same road the Achaeans had fled in panic the day before, when Hector was in full triumph. The Trojans now fled along it in a headlong rush, and Hera sent a thick mist down in front of them to hold them back. The other half were hemmed in by the deep, silver-eddying stream and fell into it with a great uproar. The waters roared and the banks echoed as the men swam this way and that among the whirling eddies, crying out loudly. As locusts fly to a river before the blast of a grass fire—the flame comes on and on until at last it overtakes them and they huddle together in the water—so the eddying stream of Xanthus was filled with the noise of men and horses, all struggling in confusion before Achilles.

At once the hero leaned his spear against a tamarisk bush and left it on the bank. Armed with his sword alone, he plunged into the river like a god. His purpose was grim, and he hewed the Trojans down on every side. They groaned horribly as they died under the sword, and the river ran red with blood. As fish flee in fear from a huge dolphin and fill every nook and corner of some fair harbor—for the dolphin is sure to eat all it can catch—so the Trojans cowered under the banks of the mighty river. When Achilles’s arms grew tired of killing, he drew twelve youths alive out of the water, to sacrifice in revenge for Patroclus son of Menoetius. He pulled them out like dazed fawns, tied their hands behind them with the belts of their own shirts, and handed them over to his men to take back to the ships. Then he sprang into the river again, thirsting for still more blood.

There he found Lycaon, son of Priam, of the seed of Dardanus, as Lycaon was escaping from the water. Achilles had once taken him prisoner. He had come on him by night in his father’s vineyard, where Lycaon was cutting young shoots from a wild fig tree to make the wicker sides of a chariot. Achilles caught him then to his sorrow, unawares, and sent him by sea to Lemnos, where the son of Jason bought him. But a guest-friend, Eetion of Imbros, paid a great sum to free him and sent him to Arisbe. From there he escaped and came back to his father’s house. After returning from Lemnos he spent eleven days happily with his friends. On the twelfth, heaven delivered him into the hands of Achilles again, who was to send him to the house of Hades, sorely against his will. When Achilles caught sight of him he was unarmed, with no helmet or shield, and no spear either. He had thrown all his armor on the bank, and he was sweating from his struggle to get out of the river, so that his strength was now failing him.
