“What marvel is this I see?” Achilles said to himself in his surprise. “If this man can come back alive after being sold off to Lemnos, then the Trojans I have killed will rise again from the world below. The waters of the gray sea did not hold him, though they hold many another whether he wants it or not. This time let him taste my spear. I want to know for certain whether mother earth, who can keep even a strong man down, will be able to hold him, or whether he will return from there too.”

So Achilles paused and pondered. Lycaon came up to him dazed, trying hard to embrace his knees, for he wanted to live, not die. Achilles thrust at him with his spear, meaning to kill him, but Lycaon ran up crouching and caught his knees. The spear passed over his back and stuck in the ground, though it hungered for blood. With one hand Lycaon clasped Achilles’s knees as he begged, and with the other he gripped the spear and would not let it go. Then he said, “Achilles, have mercy on me and spare me, for I am your suppliant. It was in your tents that I first broke bread, on the day you took me prisoner in the vineyard. After that you sold me away to Lemnos, far from my father and my friends, and I brought you the price of a hundred oxen. I have paid three times as much to gain my freedom. It is only twelve days since I came to Ilium after much suffering, and now cruel fate has thrown me into your hands again. Father Zeus must surely hate me, to give me over to you a second time. My mother Laothoe bore me for a short life, she the daughter of aged Altes—of Altes, who rules the warlike Lelegae and holds steep Pedasus on the river Satnioeis. Priam married his daughter along with many other women, and two sons were born of her, and you will have slain them both. Your spear killed noble Polydorus as he fought in the front ranks, and now evil will come upon me here, for I fear I shall not escape you, since heaven has delivered me to you. One thing more I say, so take it to heart: spare me, for I am not of the same womb as Hector, who killed your brave and noble comrade.”

With such words the princely son of Priam begged Achilles, but Achilles answered him sternly. “Idiot,” he said, “do not talk to me of ransom. Until Patroclus fell, I preferred to spare the Trojans, and I sold many of those I took alive across the sea. Now not one man will live whom heaven delivers into my hands before the city of Ilium—and of all the Trojans, it will go hardest with the sons of Priam. So, my friend, you too will die. Why do you whine like this? Patroclus fell, and he was a better man than you are. I too—do you not see how great and handsome I am? I am the son of a noble father and have a goddess for my mother, yet the hands of doom and death overshadow me just the same. The day will come, at dawn or dusk or noon, when someone will take my life in battle too, either with his spear or with an arrow shot from his bow.”

So he spoke, and Lycaon’s heart sank within him. He let go of the spear and held out both hands in front of him. But Achilles drew his keen blade and struck him on the neck by the collar-bone. He drove the two-edged sword into him up to the hilt, and Lycaon fell at full length on the ground, the dark blood welling out of him until the earth was soaked. Then Achilles took him by the foot and flung him into the river to drift downstream, and boasted over him, saying, “Lie there among the fishes. They will lick the blood from your wound and gloat over it. Your mother will not lay you on a bier and mourn you, but the eddies of Scamander will carry you into the broad bosom of the sea. There the fishes will feed on the fat of Lycaon as they dart beneath the dark ripple of the waters. So may all of you perish until we reach the citadel of strong Ilium—you in flight, and I following after to destroy you. The river with his broad silver stream will do you no good, for all the bulls you offered him and all the horses you flung living into his waters. You will perish just as miserably, until not one of you is left who has not paid in full for the death of Patroclus and for the havoc you wrought among the Achaeans, whom you killed while I held aloof from battle.”

So Achilles spoke, but the river grew angrier and angrier, and wondered within himself how he could stop Achilles’s hand and save the Trojans from disaster. Meanwhile the son of Peleus, spear in hand, sprang at Asteropaeus son of Pelegon to kill him. Asteropaeus was the son of the broad river Axius and of Periboea, eldest daughter of Acessamenus, for the river had lain with her. He stood up out of the water to face Achilles with a spear in each hand, and Xanthus filled him with courage, being angry at the death of the youths whom Achilles was slaughtering ruthlessly in his waters. When they were close to each other, Achilles spoke first. “Who are you and where are you from,” he said, “that you dare to face me? Woe to the parents whose son stands up against me.” The son of Pelegon answered, “Great son of Peleus, why do you ask my lineage? I come from the fertile land of far Paeonia and am captain of the Paeonians, and it is now eleven days since I came to Ilium. I am of the blood of the river Axius—Axius, the fairest of all rivers that run. He fathered the famed warrior Pelegon, whose son men call me. Now let us fight, Achilles.”

So he defied him, and Achilles raised his spear of Pelian ash. Asteropaeus missed with both his spears, for he could use both hands alike. With one spear he struck Achilles’s shield but did not pierce it, because the layer of gold, the gift of the god, stopped the point. With the other he grazed the elbow of Achilles’s right arm and drew dark blood, but the spear itself flew past and stuck in the ground, cheated of its bloody banquet. Then Achilles, eager to kill him, hurled his spear at Asteropaeus. He failed to hit him and struck the steep bank of the river, driving the spear half its length into the earth. The son of Peleus drew his sword and sprang at him in fury. Asteropaeus tried in vain to pull Achilles’s spear out of the bank by main force. Three times he tugged at it with all his might, and three times he had to give up. The fourth time he tried to bend and break it, but before he could, Achilles struck him with his sword and killed him. He hit him in the belly near the navel, so that all his bowels came gushing out on the ground, and the darkness of death came over him as he lay gasping. Then Achilles set his foot on his chest, stripped off his armor, and boasted over him, saying, “Lie there—born of a river though you are, it is hard for you to fight the offspring of the son of Cronus. You declare you are sprung from the blood of a broad river, but I am of the seed of mighty Zeus. My father is Peleus son of Aeacus, ruler of the many Myrmidons, and Aeacus was the son of Zeus. As Zeus is mightier than any river that flows into the sea, so his children are stronger than the children of any river whatever. You have a great river close by, if he can be of any use to you, but there is no fighting against Zeus the son of Cronus. Not even King Achelous can compare with him, nor the mighty stream of deep-flowing Oceanus, from whom all rivers and seas, with all springs and deep wells, proceed. Even Oceanus fears the lightnings of great Zeus and his thunder, which comes crashing out of heaven.”

With this he pulled his bronze spear out of the bank. Having killed Asteropaeus, he left him lying on the sand, with the dark water flowing over him and the eels and fishes busy nibbling and gnawing the fat around his kidneys. Then he went after the Paeonians, who were fleeing in panic along the bank of the river when they saw their leader slain by the son of Peleus. There he killed Thersilochus, Mydon, Astypylus, Mnesus, Thrasius, Oeneus and Ophelestes, and he would have killed still more, if the river had not taken human form in anger and spoken to him from the deep waters. “Achilles,” he said, “you excel all in strength, and you excel all in wickedness too, for the gods are always with you to protect you. If the son of Cronus has granted you to destroy all the Trojans, at least drive them out of my stream and do your grim work on land. My fair waters are now filled with corpses, and I cannot find any channel to pour myself into the sea, for I am choked with dead, and still you go on killing without mercy. I am in despair, so, O captain of your host, trouble me no further.”

Achilles answered, “So be it, Scamander, descended from Zeus. But I will never stop dealing out death among the Trojans until I have penned them up in their city and tested myself against Hector face to face, to learn whether he is to defeat me or I him.”

As he spoke he fell on the Trojans with a fury like that of the gods. But the river said to Apollo, “Surely, son of Zeus, lord of the silver bow, you are not obeying the commands of Zeus? He strictly charged you to stand by the Trojans and defend them until twilight fades and darkness covers the earth.”

Achilles meanwhile leaped from the bank into midstream. The river heaved up a high wave and went for him. Swelling into a torrent, he swept off the many dead whom Achilles had killed and left lying in his waters, and threw them out onto the land, bellowing like a bull. The living he saved, hiding them in his mighty eddies. A great, terrible wave piled up around Achilles and fell on him, beating against his shield until he could not keep his feet. He grabbed a great elm tree, but it came up by the roots and tore the bank away with it. Its thick branches dammed the stream and bridged it from side to side. Achilles struggled out of the water and ran at full speed over the plain, because he was afraid.

But the mighty god did not stop pursuing him. He sprang on him with a dark-crested wave, to stop his hands and save the Trojans from destruction. The son of Peleus darted away a spear’s throw from him, swift as the swoop of a black hunter-eagle, the strongest and swiftest of all birds, and his armor rang loudly about his breast. He fled on in front, and the river came tearing after him with a loud roar. As a man who wants to water his garden leads a stream from some fountain over his plants and all his ground—spade in hand, he clears away the dams to free the channels, and the little stones roll round and round with the water as it goes merrily down the bank, faster than the man can follow—so the river kept catching up with Achilles, although he was a swift runner, for the gods are stronger than men. Each time he tried to stand his ground and see whether all the gods in heaven were in league against him, the mighty wave came beating down on his shoulders, and he had to keep fleeing on and on in great dismay. The angry flood was tiring him out as it flowed past him and ate the ground from under his feet.

Then the son of Peleus raised his voice to heaven. “Father Zeus,” he said, “is there none of the gods who will pity me and save me from the river? I do not care what happens to me afterward. I blame none of the other dwellers on Olympus as severely as my dear mother, who has deceived and tricked me. She told me I would fall under the walls of Troy to the flying arrows of Apollo. I wish Hector, the best man among the Trojans, would kill me there. Then I would fall a hero by the hand of a hero. Instead it now seems I will come to a most pitiable end, trapped in this river like some swineherd’s boy, who is carried down a torrent while trying to cross it during a storm.”

As soon as he had spoken, Poseidon and Athena came up to him in the likeness of two men, and took him by the hand to reassure him. Poseidon spoke first. “Son of Peleus,” he said, “do not be so terribly afraid. We are two gods, come with the approval of Zeus to help you, I and Pallas Athena. It is not your fate to perish in this river. He will soon go down, as you will see. And we strongly advise you, if you will be guided by us, not to stop fighting until you have penned the Trojan host inside the famed walls of Ilium—as many of them as escape. Then kill Hector and go back to the ships, for we will grant you a triumph over him.”

When they had said this they went back to the other immortals, but Achilles pressed on over the plain, encouraged by the charge the gods had given him. Everything was now covered with the flood, and much fine armor from the slain youths was floating about, along with many corpses. But he forced his way against the stream, speeding straight on, and the broad waters could not stop him, for Athena had given him great strength. Nevertheless Scamander did not slacken his pursuit, but became still more furious with the son of Peleus. He lifted his waters into a high crest and cried out to Simois, “Dear brother, let the two of us join together to save this man, or he will sack the mighty city of King Priam, and the Trojans will not hold out against him. Help me at once. Fill your streams with water from their sources, rouse all your torrents to fury, raise your wave on high, and let snags and stones come thundering down you, so that we may make an end of this savage creature, who is now lording it as though he were a god. Nothing will help him any longer, not his strength nor his good looks nor his fine armor, which indeed will soon be lying low in the deep waters, covered with mud. I will wrap him in sand and pour tons of shingle around him, so that the Achaeans will not know how to gather his bones, for the silt in which I will have hidden him. When they hold his funeral, they will not need to build a barrow.”

With that, the river raised his roaring flood high against Achilles. It seethed with foam, blood and the bodies of the dead. The dark waters of the river stood upright and would have overwhelmed the son of Peleus, but Hera was afraid that Achilles would be swept away in the great torrent, and she cried out loudly to her son Hephaestus. “Crook-foot,” she called, “my child, get up and act! I think it is you Xanthus wants to fight. Help us at once and light a fierce fire. Meanwhile I will bring the west wind and the white south wind up from the sea in a mighty hurricane. It will carry the flames against the heads and armor of the Trojans and burn them up. You, for your part, go along the banks of Xanthus, burning his trees and wrapping him in fire. Do not let him turn you back, whether he speaks kindly or harshly. Do not ease off until I shout to you. Then you may stop your flames.”

Hephaestus lit a fierce fire. It started on the plain and burned the many dead whom Achilles had killed, whose bodies lay scattered everywhere. This dried the plain and held back the flood. When the north wind blows on an orchard soaked by autumn rain, it dries the ground quickly and the owner is glad. In the same way the whole plain dried and the dead bodies were consumed. Then Hephaestus turned his tongues of fire on the river. He burned the elms, the willows and the tamarisks, and the lotus too, along with the rushes and the marsh plants that grew thickly on the riverbanks. The eels and fishes that dart about everywhere in the water were badly tormented by the flames that cunning Hephaestus had lit. The river himself was scalded, and he spoke out: “Hephaestus, no god can stand against you. I cannot fight you when you blaze at me like this. Stop struggling with me. Let Achilles drive the Trojans out of their city right now. What do I have to do with quarrels and with helping people?”

He spoke while boiling, and all his waters were seething. A cauldron over a big fire boils when it melts the lard of a fattened hog, and the lard keeps bubbling up all over as the dry sticks blaze beneath it. In the same way the fair waters of Xanthus were heated by the fire until they boiled. He could flow no longer and halted his stream, so tormented was he by the blasts of fire that cunning Hephaestus had raised. Then he turned to Hera and begged her: “Hera, why does your son trouble my stream with such special fury? I am not as much to blame as all the others who have been helping the Trojans. Since you wish it, I will stop, and let your son stop too. I also swear that I will never again do anything to save the Trojans from destruction, not even when all Troy is burning in the flames the Achaeans will light.”
As soon as Hera heard this, she said to her son Hephaestus, “Son Hephaestus, hold back your flames now. We should not use such violence against a god for the sake of mortals.”
When she had said this, Hephaestus put out his flames, and the river went back into his own fair bed.

Xanthus was beaten, so these two stopped fighting, since Hera held them back, though she was still angry. But a furious quarrel broke out among the other gods, whose minds were divided. They fell on one another with a mighty uproar. The earth groaned, and the wide heavens rang as if with a blast of trumpets. Zeus heard it as he sat on Olympus, and he laughed with joy to see the gods coming to blows. They did not wait long to begin. Ares, piercer of shields, opened the battle. He sprang at Athena with his sword in his hand and insulted her. “Why, you vixen,” he said, “have you set the gods against each other again, out of the pride and arrogance of your heart? Have you forgotten how you made Diomedes son of Tydeus wound me, and how you yourself took his spear for all to see and drove it into me, hurting my fair body? Now you will pay for what you did to me then.”

As he spoke, he struck her on the terrible tasselled aegis, which is so terrible that not even the lightning of Zeus can pierce it. Murderous Ares struck it there with his great spear. She stepped back and seized a stone with her strong hand. It was lying on the plain, great and rugged and black, and men long ago had set it up as the boundary of a field. With it she struck Ares on the neck and brought him down. He covered nine roods as he fell, and his hair was filthy with dust, while his armor clattered around him. But Athena laughed and boasted over him. “Idiot,” she said, “have you still not learned how much stronger I am than you? You keep matching yourself against me. This is how your mother’s curses now come home to roost on you. She is angry and wants to harm you, because you have deserted the Achaeans and are helping the Trojans.”

She then turned her two piercing eyes elsewhere. Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, took Ares by the hand and led him away, and he groaned the whole time, for it was only with great difficulty that he had come to himself again. Queen Hera saw her and said to Athena, “Look, tireless daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus. That vixen Aphrodite is leading Ares out of the battle through the crowd again. Go after her at once.”

So she spoke. Athena hurried after Aphrodite eagerly and rushed at her, striking her on the chest with her strong hand. Aphrodite fell fainting to the ground, and the two of them lay there stretched out at full length. Then Athena boasted over her: “I wish that everyone who helps the Trojans against the Argives would prove as bold and stubborn as Aphrodite was when she met me while helping Ares. If that were so, we would have ended the war long ago by sacking the strong city of Ilium.”

Hera smiled as she listened. Meanwhile King Poseidon turned to Apollo and said, “Phoebus, why are we keeping away from each other? It is not right, now that the others have begun to fight. It will be shameful for us to go back to the bronze-floored house of Zeus on Olympus without having fought each other. So come on. You are the younger of us two, and I should not attack you first, for I am older and have more experience. Idiot, you have no sense. You forget how much we two alone of all the gods suffered around Ilium, when we came from the house of Zeus and worked a whole year for Laomedon at a fixed wage, and he gave us our orders. I built the Trojans the wall around their city, so wide and fair that it could not be taken. And you, Phoebus, herded his cattle in the valleys of many-valleyed Ida. But when the glad seasons brought round the time for payment, mighty Laomedon robbed us of all our wages and sent us away with nothing but abuse. He threatened to bind us hand and foot and sell us to some distant island. He also tried to cut off the ears of both of us. So we left in a rage, furious about the payment he had promised and then kept back. Even so, you now favor his people, and you will not join us in bringing total ruin on the proud Trojans, with their wives and children.”

King Apollo answered, “Lord of the earthquake, you would think little of me if I fought you over a pack of miserable mortals. They are like leaves in summer: they come out and eat the fruit of the field, and before long they drop lifeless to the ground. Let us end this fight right now and leave them to settle it among themselves.”

He turned away as he spoke, because he would not lay a hand on his own father’s brother. But his sister Artemis, the huntress, patroness of wild beasts, was very angry with him. She said, “So you would run, Far-Darter, and hand victory to Poseidon, with a cheap boast on top of it. Baby, why do you keep your bow idle like this? Never let me hear you bragging in my father’s house again, as you have often done in front of the immortals, that you would stand up and fight Poseidon.”

Apollo gave her no answer, but the august queen of Zeus was angry and scolded her bitterly. “Bold vixen,” she cried, “how dare you cross me like this? With all your bow, you will find it hard to stand against me. Zeus made you a lion among women and lets you kill them whenever you choose. You would do better to chase wild beasts and deer on the mountains than to fight those who are stronger than you. If you want to try war, go ahead, and learn by pitting yourself against me how much stronger I am than you.”

As she spoke, she caught both of Artemis’s wrists in her left hand. With her right she took the bow from the goddess’s shoulders, and laughing, she beat her about the ears with it while Artemis wriggled and writhed under the blows. Her swift arrows spilled onto the ground. She fled weeping from under Hera’s hand, like a dove that flies from a falcon to the cleft of a hollow rock, when it is her good luck to escape. In the same way she fled away weeping and left her bow and arrows behind.

Then the slayer of Argus, guide and guardian, said to Leto, “Leto, I will not fight you. It is bad to come to blows with any of the wives of Zeus. So boast as much as you like among the immortals that you beat me in fair fight.”

Leto then gathered up the bow and arrows of Artemis, which had fallen in the whirling dust. When she had them, she hurried after her daughter. Artemis had by now reached the bronze-floored house of Zeus on Olympus. She sat down in tears on her father’s knees, and her ambrosial robe trembled all around her. The son of Cronus drew her to him and laughed pleasantly as he began to question her. “Which of the heavenly beings, my dear child, has treated you so cruelly, as though you had misbehaved in front of everybody?” The fair-crowned goddess of the chase answered, “It was your wife Hera, father, who has been beating me. She is always the cause when there is any quarreling among the immortals.”

So they talked. Meanwhile Phoebus Apollo entered the strong city of Ilium. He was uneasy that the wall might not hold out and that the Danaans would take the city then and there, before its time had come. The rest of the ever-living gods went back to Olympus, some angry and some triumphant, and took their seats beside Zeus, lord of the storm cloud. Achilles kept dealing out death to the Trojans and to their horses alike. When smoke rises to heaven from a burning city that the anger of the gods has set alight, there is toil for all and sorrow for not a few. In the same way Achilles brought toil and sorrow on the Trojans.

Old King Priam stood on a high tower of the wall and looked down at huge Achilles, as the Trojans fled in panic before him and there was no one to help them. Presently he came down from the tower. Groaning many times, he went along the wall to give orders to the brave guards of the gate. “Keep the gates wide open,” he said, “until the people come flying into the city. Achilles is close behind and is driving them before him in a rout. I see we are in great danger. As soon as our people are inside and safe, shut the strong gates. I fear that terrible man will come bounding in along with the others.”

As he spoke, they drew back the bolts and opened the gates, and once they were open, they were a haven of refuge for the Trojans. Apollo then ran out of the city at full speed to meet them and protect them. The Trojans made straight for the city and the high wall, parched with thirst and grimy with dust, and Achilles came furiously behind them, wielding his spear. He was like a man possessed and was thirsting for glory.

Then the sons of the Achaeans would have taken the lofty gates of Troy, if Apollo had not spurred on Agenor, the valiant and noble son of Antenor. He put courage into Agenor’s heart and stood by his side to guard him, leaning against a beech tree and wrapped in thick darkness. When Agenor saw Achilles, he stood still, and his heart was clouded with worry. “Alas,” he said to himself in his dismay, “if I run from mighty Achilles and go where all the others are being driven in a rout, he will catch me anyway and kill me as a coward. What if I let Achilles drive the others ahead of him, and then run from the wall across the plain behind Ilium, until I reach the foothills of Ida and can hide in the underbrush there? Then I could wash the sweat off in the river and come back to Ilium in the evening. But why am I talking to myself like this? He would probably see me hurrying from the city over the plain, and chase me until he caught me. I would have no chance against him, for he is the mightiest of all men. What if I go out and meet him in front of the city instead? His flesh too, I think, can be pierced by pointed bronze. There is one life in all of us, and men say he is only mortal, despite the triumph that Zeus son of Cronus grants him.”

So saying, he stood on guard and waited for Achilles, for he was now eager to fight him. A leopardess bounds out of a thick thicket to attack a hunter. She knows no fear and is not dismayed by the baying of the hounds. Even if the man is too quick for her and wounds her with a thrust or a throw of his spear, she will not give in, though the spear has pierced her, until she has either caught him in her grip or been killed outright. In the same way noble Agenor son of Antenor refused to run until he had tried Achilles. He aimed his spear at him, holding his round shield in front of him, and shouted in a loud voice. “Truly,” he said, “noble Achilles, you think you will sack the city of the proud Trojans today. Fool, there will be trouble enough before that happens. There are many brave men of us still inside who will stand in front of our dear parents, our wives and our children, to defend Ilium. Here, huge and mighty warrior though you are, here you will die.”

As he spoke, his strong hand hurled the javelin, and the spear struck Achilles on the leg below the knee. The greave of newly worked tin rang loudly, but the spear bounced off the body it had struck and did not pierce it, for the gift of the god held it back. Achilles in his turn attacked noble Agenor, but Apollo would not grant him the glory. He snatched Agenor away and hid him in a thick mist, sending him out of the battle unharmed. Then he cleverly drew the son of Peleus away from pursuing the army. He took on the likeness of Agenor and stood in front of Achilles, who ran toward him to chase him. Achilles pursued him over the grain fields of the plain, turning him toward the deep waters of the river Scamander. Apollo ran only a little way ahead and tricked Achilles, making him think the whole time that he was about to overtake him. Meanwhile the rabble of routed Trojans was glad to crowd into the city until it was packed with them. They no longer dared to wait for one another outside the walls, to learn who had escaped and who had fallen in the fight. All whose feet and knees could still carry them poured into the town in a heap.

chapters.title: Book 22
paragraphs: The death of Hector.

The Trojans in the city, scared like fawns, wiped the sweat from their bodies and drank to quench their thirst, leaning against the fine battlements. Meanwhile the Achaeans came up close to the walls with their shields slung over their shoulders. But harsh fate held Hector where he was, in front of Ilium and the Scaean gates. Then Phoebus Apollo spoke to the son of Peleus. “Son of Peleus, why do you chase me? You are only a man, and I am immortal. Have you still not realized that it is a god you are pursuing so furiously? You did not bother the Trojans you had routed, and now they are inside their walls, while you have been lured away from them to this spot. You cannot kill me, because death has no hold on me.”

Achilles was furious. “You have cheated me, Far-Darter, most malicious of all the gods,” he said. “You have drawn me away from the wall, where many a man would have bitten the dust before he got inside Ilium. You have robbed me of great glory, and you have saved the Trojans at no risk to yourself, since you have nothing to fear. If it were in my power, I would certainly take my revenge on you.”

With that, Achilles headed for the city with deadly purpose. A winning horse in a chariot race strains every nerve as it flies over the plain, and just as fast and fiercely the legs of Achilles carried him forward. King Priam was the first to see him racing across the plain. He shone like the star men call Orion’s Hound, which blazes at harvest time more brightly than any other star of the night. It is the brightest of them all, yet it is a bad omen for mortals, because it brings fire and fever with it. In the same way the armor on the chest of Achilles gleamed as he rushed on. Priam cried out and beat his head with his raised hands. He shouted to his dear son, begging him to come back, but Hector stayed in front of the gates, because his heart was set on fighting Achilles. The old man stretched out his arms toward him and pleaded with him, for pity’s sake, to come inside the walls. “Hector,” he cried, “my son, do not wait to face this man alone and without support, or you will meet your death at the hands of the son of Peleus, who is stronger than you. He is a monster! I wish the gods loved him no more than I do. Then dogs and vultures would soon devour him as he lay stretched out on the ground, and a load of grief would be lifted from my heart. He has taken many brave sons from me, either killing them or selling them away to islands beyond the sea. Even now I miss two sons among the Trojans who have crowded into the city, Lycaon and Polydorus, whom Laothoe, peeress among women, bore me. If they are still alive in the hands of the Achaeans, we will ransom them with gold and bronze, which we have in store, because the old man Altes gave his daughter a rich dowry. But if they are already dead and in the house of Hades, it will be a sorrow to the two of us who were their parents. Other people’s grief will be shorter-lived, unless you too die at the hands of Achilles. So come inside the city, my son, to guard the Trojan men and Trojan women. Otherwise you will lose your own life and hand the son of Peleus a great triumph. Have pity also on your unhappy father while he still has life—on me, whom the son of Cronus will destroy with a terrible doom on the threshold of old age, after I have seen my sons slain, my daughters dragged away as captives, my bridal chambers plundered, little children dashed to the ground in the rage of battle, and my sons’ wives hauled off by the cruel hands of the Achaeans. In the end fierce hounds will tear me to pieces at my own gates, after someone has beaten the life out of my body with sword or spear—hounds I raised myself and fed at my own table to guard my gates, but they will lap up my blood and then lie crazed at my doors. When a young man falls in battle by the sword, he may lie where he is, and there is nothing shameful in it. Whatever is seen, all is honorable in death. But when an old man is killed, nothing in the world is more pitiable than dogs defiling his gray hair and beard and all that men hide for shame.”

The old man tore his gray hair as he spoke, but he did not move the heart of Hector. His mother, close by, wept and wailed aloud. She bared her bosom and pointed to the breast that had nursed him. “Hector,” she cried, weeping bitterly, “Hector, my son, do not scorn this breast, but have pity on me too. If I ever gave you comfort from my own bosom, remember it now, dear son. Come inside the wall to protect us from this man, and do not stand outside to meet him. If the wretch kills you, neither I nor your richly dowered wife will ever weep, dear offshoot of myself, over the bed where you lie, because dogs will devour you at the ships of the Achaeans.”

In this way the two of them pleaded with their son through many tears, but they did not move the heart of Hector. He held his ground and waited for huge Achilles as he came nearer. A serpent in its den in the mountains, full fed on deadly poisons, waits for a man to approach. It is filled with fury, and its eyes glare terribly as it coils and writhes around its den. In the same way Hector leaned his shield against a tower that jutted out from the wall and stood where he was, undaunted.

“Alas,” he said to himself, with a heavy heart, “if I go inside the gates, Polydamas will be the first to heap reproach on me. He was the one who urged me to lead the Trojans back to the city on that awful night when Achilles came out against us again. I would not listen, though it would have been far better if I had. Now my folly has destroyed the army, and I dare not look Trojan men and Trojan women in the face, for fear that a worse man might say, ‘Hector has ruined us by his self-confidence.’ Surely it would be better for me to go back after fighting Achilles and killing him, or else to die gloriously here in front of the city. But what if I were to lay down my shield and helmet, lean my spear against the wall, and walk straight up to noble Achilles? What if I promised to give up Helen, who was the source of all this war, and all the treasure that Paris brought to Troy in his ships, and even to let the Achaeans divide half of everything the city holds? I might make the Trojans, through their princes, swear a solemn oath that they would hide nothing, and would split everything inside the city into two shares. But why argue with myself like this? If I went up to him, he would show me no mercy at all. Once I had taken off my armor, he would kill me on the spot as easily as if I were a woman. There is no talking with him from behind some rock or oak tree, the way young men and maidens chatter with one another. It is better to fight him at once, and find out which of us Zeus will grant victory.”

So he stood and pondered, but Achilles came up to him like Ares himself, plumed lord of battle. From his right shoulder he brandished his terrible spear of Pelian ash, and the bronze flashed around him like fire or the rays of the rising sun. Fear seized Hector when he saw him. He did not dare stay where he was. He fled in dismay from the gates, and Achilles darted after him at top speed. A mountain falcon, swiftest of all birds, swoops down on a cowering dove. The dove flies ahead of him, but the falcon follows close behind with a shrill scream, determined to have her. In the same way Achilles ran straight at Hector with all his might, while Hector fled under the Trojan wall as fast as his legs could carry him.

They flew along the wagon road that ran close beneath the wall, past the lookout station and past the weather-beaten wild fig tree, until they came to two fair springs that feed the river Scamander. One of the two springs is warm, and steam rises from it like smoke from a burning fire. The other is as cold as hail or snow or ice on water, even in summer. Close to the springs are the fine stone washing troughs, where the wives and fair daughters of the Trojans used to wash their clothes in peacetime, before the Achaeans came. The two men flew past these, one in front and the other chasing behind. The man fleeing was good, but the man pursuing was far better. They ran swiftly indeed, because the prize was no ordinary beast for sacrifice or bullock’s hide, such as people race for in a common foot race. They were running for the life of Hector. Horses in a chariot race speed around the turning posts when they run for some great prize, a tripod or a woman, at the games in honor of a dead hero. In the same way these two ran at full speed three times around the city of Priam. All the gods watched them, and the father of gods and men was the first to speak.

“Alas,” he said, “I see a man who is dear to me being chased around the walls of Troy. My heart is full of pity for Hector, who has burned the thigh bones of many a heifer in my honor, sometimes on the crests of many-valleyed Ida and sometimes on the citadel of Troy. Now I see noble Achilles chasing him around the city of Priam. What do you say? Think it over among yourselves and decide whether we should save him now, or let him fall, brave as he is, to Achilles, son of Peleus.”

Then Athena said, “Father, wielder of the lightning, lord of the cloud and storm, what are you saying? Would you pull this mortal out of the jaws of death, when his doom was decreed long ago? Do as you like, but the rest of us will not agree with you.”
Zeus answered, “My child, Trito-born, take heart. I was not speaking in full earnest, and I will let you have your way. Do as you are minded, without hindrance.”
So he urged on Athena, who was already eager, and she darted down from the topmost summits of Olympus.

Achilles was still chasing Hector, like a hound chasing a fawn that it has started from its covert on the mountains, hunting it through glade and thicket. The fawn may try to elude him by crouching under a bush, but the hound scents her out and follows until he catches her. In the same way Hector could not escape the swift son of Peleus. Whenever he made a dash toward the Dardanian gates and the walls, so that his people might help him by showering weapons down from above, Achilles would gain on him and head him back toward the plain, always keeping himself on the city side. A man in a dream cannot lay hands on someone he is chasing, and the one cannot escape nor the other overtake. In the same way Achilles could not catch Hector, and Hector could not break away from Achilles. Even so, Hector might still have escaped death, if the time had not come when Apollo, who until now had kept up his strength and quickened his running, was to stay by him no longer. Achilles signaled to the Achaean host, shaking his head to show that no man was to throw a dart at Hector, in case someone else won the glory of hitting him and he himself came in second. Then, as they reached the fountains for the fourth time, the father of all balanced his golden scales and put a doom in each of them, one for Achilles and the other for Hector. He held the scales by the middle, and the doom of Hector sank down deep into the house of Hades. Then Phoebus Apollo left him. Athena went close up to the son of Peleus and said, “Noble Achilles, favored of heaven, the two of us will surely bring back a triumph to the Achaeans at the ships by killing Hector, for all his lust for battle. Whatever Apollo does, groveling before his father, aegis-bearing Zeus, Hector cannot escape us any longer. Stay here and catch your breath, while I go up to him and persuade him to make a stand and fight you.”

So spoke Athena. Achilles gladly obeyed and stood still, leaning on his ashen spear with its bronze point. Athena left him and went after Hector, in the form and with the voice of Deiphobus. She came close up to him and said, “Dear brother, I see Achilles is pressing you hard, chasing you at full speed around the city of Priam. Let us wait for his attack and stand on our defense.”

Hector answered, “Deiphobus, of all my brothers, the children of Hecuba and Priam, you have always been dearest to me. From now on I will value you even more, because you have ventured outside the wall for my sake, when all the others stay inside.”

Then Athena said, “Dear brother, my father and mother went down on their knees and begged me, as did all my comrades, to stay inside, so great is the fear that has fallen on them all. But I was in agony of grief when I saw you. So now let the two of us make a stand and fight, and let us not hold back our spears, so that we may learn whether Achilles will kill us and carry off our spoils to the ships, or whether he will fall before you.”

So Athena deceived him with her cunning. When the two were close to one another, great Hector spoke first. “I will no longer run from you, son of Peleus,” he said, “as I have been doing. Three times I have fled around the mighty city of Priam without daring to withstand you. Now I am ready to face you, to slay or be slain. Let us give pledges to one another by our gods, who are the fittest witnesses and guardians of all covenants. Let it be agreed between us that if Zeus grants me the longer stay and I take your life, I will not treat your dead body in any unseemly way. When I have stripped you of your armor, I will give your body back to the Achaeans. You must do the same.”

Achilles glared at him and answered, “Fool, do not babble to me about covenants. There can be no covenants between men and lions. Wolves and lambs can never be of one mind, but hate each other out and out. So there can be no understanding between you and me, and no covenants between us, until one or the other falls and gluts grim Ares with his life’s blood. Put forth all your strength. You need now to prove yourself a bold soldier and man of war. You have no more chance. Pallas Athena will vanquish you by my spear at once, and you will pay me in full for the grief you caused me by killing my comrades in battle.”

With these words he balanced his spear and threw it. Hector saw it coming and avoided it. He kept his eye on it and crouched, so that it flew over his head and stuck in the ground beyond. Athena snatched it up and gave it back to Achilles, and Hector never saw her. Then Hector said to the son of Peleus, “You missed, Achilles, peer of the gods. Zeus has not yet shown you the hour of my doom, though you were sure he had. You were a false-tongued liar to think I would forget my courage and cower before you. You will not drive your spear into the back of a man running away. If heaven gives you the power, drive it into me as I come straight at you. And now, for your part, dodge my spear if you can. I wish you would take the whole of it into your body. If you were dead, the Trojans would find the war easier, since you are the one who has harmed them most.”

With these words he balanced his spear and threw it. His aim was true, and he hit the middle of Achilles’s shield, but the spear bounced off and did not pierce it. Hector was angry that the weapon had left his hand for nothing. He stood there at a loss, because he had no second spear. He called out loudly to Deiphobus and asked him for one, but no one was there. Then he understood, and said to himself, “Alas! The gods have lured me on to my death. I thought the hero Deiphobus was at my side, but he is inside the wall, and Athena has tricked me. Death is very near now, and there is no way out of it. Zeus and his son Apollo, who strikes from afar, have willed it so, though until now they were always ready to protect me. My doom has caught up with me. Still, let me not die without glory or without a fight. Let me first do some great thing that men will tell of in times to come.”

With that he drew the keen sword that hung so great and strong at his side. He gathered himself and sprang at Achilles like a soaring eagle that swoops down from the clouds on a lamb or a timid hare. In the same way Hector brandished his sword and sprang. Achilles, mad with rage, rushed to meet him. His wondrous shield covered his chest, and his gleaming helmet, made of four layers of metal, nodded fiercely forward. The thick golden plumes that Hephaestus had set on the helmet’s crest floated around it. The evening star shines brighter than any other star through the stillness of night, and just so did the spear gleam in Achilles’s right hand, carrying death for noble Hector. Achilles looked over Hector’s fair flesh again and again, searching for the best place to wound it. But all of it was covered by the fine armor Hector had taken from Patroclus after killing him, except the throat, where the collar-bones separate the neck from the shoulders. This is a most deadly place, and here Achilles struck him as he came on. The point of the spear went straight through the fleshy part of the neck, but it did not cut the windpipe, so Hector could still speak. He fell headlong, and Achilles boasted over him, saying, “Hector, you thought you would come out of it unharmed when you stripped Patroclus, and you gave no thought to me, who was not with him. Fool! I was still left behind at the ships, his comrade and far mightier than he, and now I have laid you low. The Achaeans will give him all the funeral rites he is due, while dogs and vultures will do as they please with you.”

Hector spoke as his life ebbed away. “By your life and your knees and your parents, I beg you: do not let dogs devour me at the ships of the Achaeans. My father and mother will offer you a rich treasure of gold and bronze. Take it, and send my body home, so that the Trojans and their wives can give me the fire that is my due when I am dead.”

Achilles glared at him and answered, “Dog, do not talk to me of knees or parents. I wish I could be as sure of having the strength to cut your flesh into pieces and eat it raw, for the harm you have done me, as I am that nothing will save you from the dogs. It will not happen, though they bring ten or twenty times the ransom and weigh it out for me on the spot, with a promise of more to come. Even if Priam son of Dardanus tells them to offer me your weight in gold, your mother will still never lay you out and mourn the son she bore. Dogs and vultures will eat you up completely.”

With his dying breath Hector said, “I know you for what you are. I was sure I would not move you, for your heart is hard as iron. Take care that I do not bring the anger of heaven on you, on the day when Paris and Phoebus Apollo kill you at the Scaean gates, valiant though you are.”

When he had said this, the shrouds of death closed around him. His soul left his body and flew down to the house of Hades, lamenting its sad fate, that it must leave youth and strength behind. But Achilles spoke to the dead body. “Die! For my part, I will accept my own fate whenever Zeus and the other gods choose to send it.”

As he spoke he drew his spear out of the body and laid it to one side. Then he stripped the blood-stained armor from Hector’s shoulders, while the other Achaeans came running up to look at his wondrous strength and beauty. No one came near him without giving him a fresh wound. One would turn to his neighbor and say, “Hector is easier to handle now than when he was flinging fire on our ships.” And as he said it, he would thrust his spear into him again.

When Achilles had finished stripping Hector of his armor, he stood among the Argives and said, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, heaven has granted us victory over this man, who has done us more harm than all the others together. Now consider whether we should attack the city in force and find out what the Trojans have in mind. We would learn whether they will abandon their city now that Hector has fallen, or hold out even though he is no longer alive. But why do I argue this way with myself, when Patroclus is still lying at the ships, unburied and unmourned? I can never forget him as long as I live and my strength does not fail. Men forget their dead once they are in the house of Hades, but even there I will not forget the comrade I have lost. So now, Achaean youths, let us sing the song of victory and go back to the ships, taking this man with us. We have won a mighty triumph and killed noble Hector, to whom the Trojans prayed throughout their city as though he were a god.”

With that he treated Hector’s body shamefully. He pierced the sinews at the back of both feet, from heel to ankle, and ran thongs of ox-hide through the slits he had made. In this way he tied the body to his chariot and let the head trail along the ground. Then he put the fine armor on the chariot and climbed up himself, and he lashed the horses on. They flew forward willingly. Dust rose from Hector as he was dragged along, and his dark hair flew out in all directions. His head, once so handsome, lay low on the earth, for Zeus had now handed him over to his foes to be outraged in his own land.

So the head of Hector was dishonored in the dust. His mother tore her hair and flung her veil away with a loud cry when she saw her son. His father groaned piteously, and all through the city the people began to weep and wail. It was as if the whole of frowning Ilium were smoldering in fire. The people could hardly hold Priam back, so hot was his haste to rush out of the city gates. He groveled in the mire and begged them, calling each one by name. “Let me be, my friends,” he cried, “and for all your sorrow, allow me to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans. Let me plead with this cruel and terrible man. Perhaps he will respect the feelings of his fellow men and have pity on my old age. His own father is just such another as I am—Peleus, who bred him and raised him to be the bane of us Trojans, and of me more than of all others. He has killed many a son of mine in the flower of his youth. Yet however I grieve for those, I grieve for one—Hector—more than for them all, and the bitterness of my sorrow will bring me down to the house of Hades. I wish he had died in my arms. Then both his ill-starred mother who bore him and I would have had the comfort of weeping and mourning over him.”

So he spoke with many tears, and all the people of the city joined in his lament. Then Hecuba started the cry of wailing among the Trojans. “Alas, my son,” she cried, “what do I have left to live for, now that you are gone? Night and day I took glory in you throughout the city. You were a tower of strength to everyone in Troy, and men and women alike hailed you as a god. While you lived you were their pride, but now death and destruction have come upon you.”

Hector’s wife had heard nothing yet, because no one had come to tell her that her husband had stayed outside the gates. She was at her loom in an inner room of the house, weaving a double purple web and embroidering it with many flowers. She had told her maids to set a large tripod on the fire, so that a warm bath would be ready for Hector when he came out of battle. Poor woman, she did not know that he was now far beyond the reach of baths, and that Athena had laid him low by the hands of Achilles. Then she heard the crying from the direction of the wall, and she trembled in every limb. The shuttle fell from her hands, and she spoke again to her waiting-women. “Two of you come with me,” she said, “so that I can learn what has happened. I heard the voice of my husband’s honored mother. My own heart is pounding as though it would jump into my mouth, and my legs will not carry me. Some great misfortune must be near for Priam’s children. I hope I never live to hear it, but I am terribly afraid that Achilles has cut off brave Hector’s retreat and chased him onto the plain, where he was alone. I fear he may have put an end to the reckless daring that possessed my husband. He would never stay with the body of his men. He would dash far out in front, foremost of them all in courage.”

Her heart beat fast, and as she spoke she flew from the house like a madwoman, with her waiting-women following behind. She reached the battlements and the crowd of people, and stood looking out from the wall. She saw Hector being carried away in front of the city, the horses dragging him over the ground toward the ships of the Achaeans, without heed or care. Her eyes were shrouded as if with the darkness of night, and she fell backward in a faint. She tore the headdress from her head and flung it away—the frontlet, the net with its plaited band, and the veil that golden Aphrodite had given her on the day Hector took her from the house of Eetion, after giving countless gifts of courtship for her sake. Her husband’s sisters and his brothers’ wives crowded around her and held her up, for in her distraction she wanted to die. When she breathed again and came to herself, she sobbed and lamented among the Trojan women, saying, “Woe is me, Hector! Woe indeed, that we were born to share one lot, you at Troy in the house of Priam, and I at Thebes under the wooded mountain of Placus in the house of Eetion, who raised me when I was a child. Ill-starred father of an ill-starred daughter! I wish he had never begotten me. You are going now into the house of Hades, under the secret places of the earth, and you leave me behind as a sorrowing widow in your house. Our child, whose unhappy parents we are, is still a mere infant. Now that you are gone, Hector, you can do nothing for him, nor he for you. Even if he escapes the horrors of this woeful war with the Achaeans, his life from now on will be one of labor and sorrow, for others will seize his lands. The day that robs a child of his parents cuts him off from his own kind. His head is bowed and his cheeks are wet with tears, and he will go about destitute among his father’s friends, plucking one by the cloak and another by the shirt. One or another of them may pity him enough to hold a cup out to him for a moment and let him wet his lips, but he must not drink enough to wet the roof of his mouth. Then a boy whose parents are alive will drive him from the table with blows and angry words. ‘Out with you,’ he will say, ‘you have no father here.’ And the child will go crying back to his widowed mother—he, Astyanax, who once would sit on his father’s knees and have nothing set before him but the daintiest and choicest morsels. When he had played until he was tired and fell asleep, he would lie in a bed, in the arms of his nurse, on a soft couch, knowing neither want nor care. Now that he has lost his father, his lot will be full of hardship—he, whom the Trojans call Astyanax because you, Hector, were the only defense of their gates and battlements. Now the wriggling, writhing worms will eat you at the ships, far from your parents, when the dogs have gorged themselves on you. You will lie naked, though in your house you have fine and goodly clothes made by the hands of women. I will burn them now. They are of no use to you, since you can never wear them again, and by this you will have respect shown to you by the Trojans, both men and women.”
So she cried aloud amid her tears, and the women joined in her lament.

chapters.title: Book 23
paragraphs: Patroclus is buried, and games are held at his funeral.

So the Trojans mourned throughout their city. The Achaeans reached the Hellespont and each man went back to his own ship. But Achilles would not let the Myrmidons scatter. He spoke to his brave comrades: “Myrmidons, famed horsemen and my own trusted friends, we will not unyoke yet. Let us drive our horses and chariots up to the body and mourn Patroclus, as the dead are owed. When we have had our fill of lamenting, we will unyoke the horses and all eat our supper here.”

They all broke into a wail, and Achilles led their lament. Three times they drove their chariots around the body in sorrow, and Thetis stirred a deeper longing to weep in every one of them. The sand of the shore and the men’s armor were wet with tears, so great a source of fear was the man they had lost. The son of Peleus mourned above them all. He laid his blood-stained hand on his friend’s chest and cried out: “Farewell, Patroclus, even in the house of Hades. Now I will do everything I promised you earlier. I will drag Hector here and let the dogs eat him raw. And before your pyre I will kill twelve noble sons of the Trojans, to avenge you.”

With these words he treated the body of noble Hector shamefully, stretching it out in the dust beside the bier of Patroclus. Then the others took off their armor, unhitched the horses from their chariots, and sat down in a great crowd beside the ship of the swift descendant of Aeacus. He gave them a rich funeral feast. They slaughtered and cut up many fine oxen, and many sheep and bleating goats. They also singed many fat, well-fed tusked boars and set them to roast in the flames of Hephaestus. Streams of blood ran all around the place where the body lay.

Then the Achaean princes brought the son of Peleus to Agamemnon. They could hardly persuade him to come, so angry was he over the death of his comrade. When they reached Agamemnon’s tent, they told the attendants to set a large tripod over the fire, hoping to persuade the son of Peleus to wash the clotted gore off his body. He sternly refused, and swore a solemn oath: “No, by King Zeus, first and greatest of all the gods, it is not right for water to touch my body until I have laid Patroclus on the fire, raised a mound for him, and cut my hair. As long as I live, no second sorrow like this will come near me. For now, let us carry out everything this sad feast requires. But at daybreak, King Agamemnon, order your men to bring wood and to supply everything else the dead man needs to enter the realm of darkness. The fire will then burn him out of our sight sooner, and the people can go back to their own work.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said. They hurried to prepare the meal and ate, and every man had his full share, so that all were satisfied. When they had eaten and drunk enough, the others went to rest, each in his own tent. But the son of Peleus lay grieving among his Myrmidons on the shore of the sounding sea, in an open place where the waves came rolling in one after another. A very deep sleep took hold of him there and eased the weight of his sorrows, for his limbs were tired from chasing Hector around windy Ilium. Then the sad spirit of Patroclus came up to him. It looked just as he had in life, with the same height, the same voice, the same light in his beaming eyes, and it wore the same clothes as he had worn alive. The spirit hovered over his head and said—

“You are asleep, Achilles, and you have forgotten me. You loved me when I was alive, but now that I am dead you give me no more thought. Bury me as quickly as you can, so that I may pass through the gates of Hades. The ghosts, the empty shadows of men who can work no more, drive me away from them. They will not yet let me join those on the far side of the river, and I wander alone by the wide gates of the house of Hades. Give me your hand, I beg you, because once you have given me my due of fire, I will never again come back out of the house of Hades. Never again will we sit apart from the living and make plans together. The cruel fate that was mine from birth has opened its wide jaws around me. And you too, Achilles, equal of the gods, are doomed to die beneath the wall of the noble Trojans.

“I will make one more request of you, if you will grant it. Do not let my bones be laid apart from yours, Achilles, but together with them. We grew up together in your own home, ever since Menoetius brought me to you as a child from Opoeis, because in a bitter quarrel I had killed the son of Amphidamas. I did not mean to. It happened in a childish fight over dice. The horseman Peleus took me into his house, treated me kindly, and made me your squire. So let our bones lie in one single urn, the golden two-handled vase your mother gave you.”

Achilles answered: “Why have you come here, dear friend, to give me these orders? I will do everything you ask, of my own accord. Come closer. Let us put our arms around each other once more and find some sad comfort in sharing our sorrow.”

He stretched out his arms toward the spirit as he spoke and tried to hold it, but there was nothing there. The spirit vanished like vapor, gibbering and whining, into the earth. Achilles sprang to his feet and struck his hands together. He cried out in grief: “It is true, then. Even in the house of Hades there are ghosts and phantoms with no life in them. All night long the sad spirit of Patroclus has hovered over my head, moaning pitifully, telling me what I must do for him, and looking amazingly like himself.”

So he spoke, and his words set them all weeping and mourning over the poor silent dead, until rosy-fingered morning appeared. Then King Agamemnon sent men and mules from every part of the camp to fetch wood, with Meriones, squire to Idomeneus, in charge of them. They set out with woodcutters’ axes and strong ropes in their hands, and the mules went ahead of them. They traveled up hill and down valley, by straight roads and winding ones. When they reached the heights of many-fountained Ida, they set their axes to the roots of many tall, branching oaks, which crashed down with a roar as they were felled. The men split the trees and tied the pieces behind the mules. The mules made their way back across the thick brushwood to the plain as best they could. Everyone who had been cutting wood carried logs, since Meriones, squire to Idomeneus, had ordered it. They threw them down in a line on the shore, at the place where Achilles meant to build a mighty monument for Patroclus and for himself.

When they had thrown down their great logs over the whole ground, they all stayed where they were. Achilles then ordered his brave Myrmidons to put on their armor and yoke their horses. They got up, put on their armor, and each mounted his chariot, the fighters and their charioteers together. The chariots went in front, and the men on foot followed behind like a cloud, tens of thousands strong. In the middle of them his comrades carried Patroclus. They covered him with locks of their hair, which they cut off and threw on his body. Achilles came last, his head bowed in sorrow, because he was taking such a noble comrade to the house of Hades.

When they came to the place Achilles had named, they set the body down and piled up the wood. Then Achilles thought of something else. He walked a little way from the pyre and cut off the yellow lock of hair he had let grow for the river Spercheius. He gazed sadly out over the dark sea and said: “Spercheius, my father Peleus vowed to you in vain that when I came home to my beloved native land, I would cut off this lock and offer you a holy great sacrifice. I was to sacrifice fifty she-goats to you there at your springs, where your grove is, and your altar fragrant with burnt offerings. That is what my father vowed, but you have not granted his prayer. Now I will never see my home again, so I give this lock to the hero Patroclus to keep.”

With these words he placed the lock in the hands of his dear comrade, and everyone standing there was filled with longing and sorrow. The sun would have set on their weeping if Achilles had not spoken to Agamemnon: “Son of Atreus, it is you the people will listen to. There is a time to mourn and a time to stop mourning. Tell the people to leave the pyre now and go get their dinners. We, who held the dead man dearest, will see to what is needed here, and let the other princes stay with me too.”

When King Agamemnon heard this, he sent the people away to their ships. But those who were with the dead man piled up wood and built a pyre a hundred feet square, and sadly laid the body on top of it. In front of the pyre they skinned and dressed many fat sheep and oxen. Achilles took fat from all of them and wrapped the body in it from head to foot, then heaped the skinned carcasses around it. Against the bier he leaned two-handled jars of honey and oils. He threw four proud horses onto the pyre, groaning as he did so. The dead hero had kept house-dogs, and Achilles killed two of them and threw them onto the pyre. He also put twelve brave sons of noble Trojans to the sword and laid them with the rest, for he was full of bitterness and fury. Then he gave everything to the unstoppable, devouring power of the fire. He groaned aloud and called his dead comrade by name: “Farewell, Patroclus, even in the house of Hades. I am now doing everything I promised you. The flames will consume twelve brave sons of noble Trojans together with you. But the flesh of Hector son of Priam will be eaten by dogs, not by fire.”

So he boasted, but the dogs did not come near the body of Hector. Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite kept them away from him night and day. She rubbed him with ambrosial oil of roses so that his flesh would not be torn as Achilles dragged him around. Phoebus Apollo also sent a dark cloud down from heaven to earth. It shaded the whole place where Hector lay, so that the heat of the sun would not dry out his body.

Now the pyre around dead Patroclus would not catch fire. So Achilles thought of something else. He went apart and prayed to the two winds, Boreas and Zephyrus, promising them fine offerings. He poured them many drink offerings from a golden cup and begged them to come and help, so that the wood would quickly catch and the dead bodies be consumed. Swift Iris heard his prayer and set off to fetch the winds. They were holding a great feast in the house of boisterous Zephyrus. Iris came running up to the stone threshold of the house and stood there. As soon as the winds saw her, they all rose and came toward her, each calling her to sit beside him, but Iris would not sit down. “I cannot stay,” she said. “I must go back to the streams of Oceanus and the land of the Ethiopians, who are offering great sacrifices to the immortals, and I want my share. But Achilles is praying that Boreas and shrill Zephyrus will come to him, and he promises them fine offerings. He wants you to blow on the pyre of Patroclus, for whom all the Achaeans are mourning.”

With this she left them, and the two winds rose with a cry that tore the air and swept the clouds ahead of them. They blew on and on until they came to the sea, and the waves rose high beneath them. When they reached Troy, they fell on the pyre, and the mighty flames roared under the blast. All night long the winds blew hard and beat on the fire. All night long Achilles held his double cup, drawing wine from a golden mixing-bowl and calling on the spirit of dead Patroclus as he poured it on the ground, until the earth was soaked. A father mourns as he burns the bones of his bridegroom son, whose death has broken the hearts of his parents. In the same way Achilles mourned as he burned the body of his comrade, pacing around the bier with pitiful groaning and lamentation.

At last the Morning Star began to announce the light that saffron-mantled Dawn would soon spread over the sea. The flames sank and the fire began to die. The winds then went home across the Thracian sea, which roared and boiled as they swept over it. The son of Peleus turned away from the pyre and lay down, worn out with toil, until he fell into a sweet sleep. Soon the men around the son of Atreus came toward him together, and the noise and tramp of their coming woke him. He sat upright and said: “Son of Atreus, and all you other princes of the Achaeans, first pour red wine on the fire everywhere and put it out. Then let us gather the bones of Patroclus son of Menoetius, picking them out with care. They are easy to find, because they lie in the middle of the pyre, while everything else, men and horses alike, was thrown in a heap and burned at the outer edge. We will lay the bones in a golden urn, in two layers of fat, to be kept until I myself go down into the house of Hades. As for the mound, do not labor to raise a great one now, only a reasonable one. Afterwards, let those Achaeans who are left at the ships when I am gone build it broad and high.”

So he spoke, and they obeyed the son of Peleus. First they poured red wine on the thick layer of ashes and put out the fire. With many tears they picked out the whitened bones of their beloved comrade and laid them in a golden urn in two layers of fat. They covered the urn with a linen cloth and took it inside the tent. They marked out the circle for the mound, laid a foundation for it around the pyre, and at once heaped up the earth. When they had raised the mound, they were going away, but Achilles kept the people there and made them sit in assembly. He brought prizes from the ships: cauldrons, tripods, horses and mules, noble oxen, women with fair girdles, and dark iron.

The first prize he offered, for the chariot races, was a woman skilled in all useful crafts, and a three-legged cauldron with ears for handles that would hold twenty-two measures. This was for the man who came in first. For the second there was an unbroken six-year-old mare, in foal to a he-ass. The third was to have a fine cauldron that had never been on the fire. It was still as bright as when it left the maker, and would hold four measures. The fourth prize was two talents of gold, and the fifth a two-handled urn not yet blackened by smoke. Then he stood up and spoke among the Argives, saying—

“Son of Atreus, and all you other Achaeans, these are the prizes waiting for the winners of the chariot races. At any other time I would carry off the first prize and take it to my own tent. You know how far my horses surpass all others, for they are immortal. Poseidon gave them to my father Peleus, and he in turn gave them to me. But I will stay out of the race, I and my horses, which have lost their brave and kind driver. Many a time he washed them in clear water and rubbed oil into their manes. See how they stand here weeping, with their manes trailing on the ground in their extreme sorrow. But the rest of you, take your places throughout the host, whoever has confidence in his horses and in the strength of his chariot.”

So the son of Peleus spoke, and the chariot drivers stirred themselves. First of all, Eumelus, king of men, son of Admetus, got up, a man excellent at horsemanship. Next to him rose mighty Diomedes son of Tydeus. He yoked the Trojan horses he had taken from Aeneas when Apollo carried Aeneas out of the fight. After him yellow-haired Menelaus son of Atreus rose and yoked his swift horses, Agamemnon’s mare Aethe and his own horse Podargus. Echepolus son of Anchises had given the mare to Agamemnon so that he would not have to follow him to Ilium, but could stay at home and take his ease. Zeus had given Echepolus great wealth, and he lived in spacious Sicyon. Menelaus put this mare under the yoke, all eager for the race.

Antilochus, son of noble Nestor son of Neleus, was the fourth to get his horses ready. They had been bred in Pylos. His father came up to him with some good advice, though Antilochus had little need of it. “Antilochus,” said Nestor, “you are young, but Zeus and Poseidon have loved you well and made you an excellent horseman. So I do not need to teach you much. You are skilled at wheeling your horses around the post. But the horses themselves are very slow, and I fear that is what will ruin your chances. The other drivers know less than you do, but their horses are swifter. So, my dear son, find some clever trick to make sure the prize does not slip through your fingers. A woodman gets more done by skill than by brute strength. By skill the pilot steers his storm-tossed ship over the sea. By skill, in the same way, one driver beats another. Take a man who goes wide, turning this way and that, while a man who knows what he is doing may have worse horses but will keep them well in hand when he sees the doubling-post. He knows the exact moment to pull the rein, and he keeps his eye on the man in front of him. I will give you a sure sign that you cannot miss. There is the stump of a dead tree, oak or pine, standing about six feet above the ground. Rain has not yet rotted it away. It stands at the fork of the road, with a white stone set on each side of it, and there is a clear course all around it. It may be a monument to someone long dead, or it may have served as a doubling-post in days gone by. Now Achilles has chosen it as the mark the chariots must turn around. Hug it as close as you can. As you stand in your chariot, lean a little to the left. Urge on your right-hand horse with voice and lash and give him a loose rein, but let the left-hand horse keep so close that the hub of your wheel almost grazes the post. Watch out for the stone, though, or you will wound your horses and smash your chariot to pieces. That would be sport for others but ruin for you. So, my dear son, take care what you are doing. If you are first around the post, no one can pass you later, not even if you had Adrestus’s horse Arion behind you, a horse of divine race, or the horses of Laomedon, the noblest in this country.”

When Nestor had finished advising his son, he sat down in his place. Fifth in order, Meriones got his horses ready. Then they all mounted their chariots and drew lots. Achilles shook the helmet. The lot of Antilochus son of Nestor fell out first, then that of King Eumelus, then those of Menelaus son of Atreus and of Meriones. The last place went by lot to Diomedes son of Tydeus, who was the best man of them all. They took their places in a line. Achilles pointed out the doubling-post they were to turn around, some way off on the plain. There he stationed his father’s follower Phoenix as umpire, to watch the running and report it truthfully.

All at the same instant they lashed their horses, struck them with the reins, and shouted at them with all their might. The horses flew at full speed over the plain, away from the ships. The dust rose from under them like a cloud or a whirlwind, and their manes streamed in the wind. One moment the chariots seemed to touch the ground, and the next they bounded into the air. The drivers stood upright, and their hearts beat fast and fierce with the lust for victory. Each man kept calling to his horses, and the horses raced across the plain through the clouds of dust they raised.

On the last part of the course, as they headed back toward the sea, the pace was strained to the utmost and it became clear what each could do. The horses of the descendant of Pheres took the lead, and close behind them came the Trojan stallions of Diomedes. They looked as if they were about to climb into Eumelus’s chariot. He could feel their warm breath on his back and on his broad shoulders, because their heads were so close to him as they flew along. Diomedes would now have passed him, or the race would have been a dead heat, but Phoebus Apollo, out of spite, made him drop his whip. Tears of anger fell from his eyes as he watched the mares go faster than ever, while his own horses lost ground because he had no whip. Athena saw the trick Apollo had played on the son of Tydeus. She brought him his whip and put spirit into his horses. Then, in a rage, she went after the son of Admetus and broke his yoke. The mares ran off, one to one side of the course and one to the other, and the pole broke against the ground. Eumelus was thrown from his chariot beside the wheel. His elbows, mouth and nostrils were all torn, and his forehead was bruised above the eyebrows. His eyes filled with tears, and he could not speak. But the son of Tydeus turned his horses aside and shot far ahead, for Athena had put fresh strength into them and given Diomedes himself glory.

Menelaus son of Atreus came next behind Diomedes, but Antilochus called out to his father’s horses. “On with you both,” he cried, “and do your very best. I am not telling you to beat the horses of the son of Tydeus. Athena has put speed into them and covered Diomedes with glory. But you must catch the horses of the son of Atreus and not be left behind, or Aethe, who is so swift, will taunt you. Why are you lagging, my good fellows? I tell you, and it will surely happen: Nestor will not keep either of you. He will put both of you to the sword if we win any worse a prize because of your carelessness. Fly after them at your utmost speed. I will find a way to pass them in a narrow part of the road, and it will not fail me.”

The horses feared their master’s rebuke and for a short while went faster. Soon Antilochus saw a narrow place where the road had sunk. The winter’s rain had collected there and worn the road away, so the whole place was deepened and the ground was broken. Menelaus was making for it so as to get there first, for fear of a collision. But Antilochus turned his horses out of the way and followed him a little to one side. The son of Atreus was afraid and shouted, “Antilochus, you are driving recklessly. Rein in your horses. The road is too narrow here, and it will be wider soon, so you can pass me then. If you foul my chariot you may bring us both to grief.”

But Antilochus plied his whip and drove faster, as though he had not heard. They went side by side for about as far as a young man can throw a disc from his shoulder when he is testing his strength. Then Menelaus’s mares fell behind, for he stopped driving them hard, afraid that the horses would collide and upset the chariots. In pressing on after victory, they might both have tumbled headlong to the ground. Menelaus then scolded Antilochus. “No man alive is a greater trickster than you,” he said. “Go, and bad luck go with you. The Achaeans are wrong to say you have understanding. Whatever happens, you will not carry off the prize without my sworn protest.”
Then he called to his horses. “Keep up your pace and do not slacken,” he said to them. “The other horses will tire sooner than you, for neither of them is young.”
The horses feared their master’s rebuke and went faster, so that they were soon nearly level with the others.

Meanwhile the Achaeans, sitting in their seats, were watching how the horses went as they raced over the plain through clouds of their own dust. Idomeneus captain of the Cretans was the first to make out the running. He was not in the thick of the crowd but stood on the highest part of the ground. The driver was a long way off, but Idomeneus could hear him shouting, and he could see the foremost horse quite plainly. It was a chestnut with a round white star on its forehead, like the moon. He stood up and said among the Argives, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, can you see the running as well as I can? There seems to be a different pair in front now, and a different driver. The ones that led at the start must have been disabled out on the plain. I saw them at first making their way around the doubling-post, but now I search the plain of Troy and cannot find them. Perhaps the reins fell from the driver’s hand at the doubling-post, so that he lost control of his horses and could not turn. I suppose he was thrown out there and broke his chariot, while his mares left the course and bolted in a panic. Come up and look for yourselves. I cannot be sure, but the driver seems to be an Aetolian by descent, a ruler over the Argives: brave Diomedes, the son of Tydeus.”

Ajax the son of Oileus answered him rudely. “Idomeneus,” he said, “why are you in such a hurry to tell us all about it, when the mares are still so far out on the plain?
