You are not the youngest man here, and your eyes are not the sharpest, but you are always laying down the law. You have no right to, for there are better men here than you. Eumelus’s horses are in front now, as they always have been, and he is on the chariot holding the reins.”

The captain of the Cretans flared up. “Ajax,” he answered, “you are a fine hand at abuse, but you have no judgment, and plenty else is missing in you too, because your temper is vile. I will bet you a tripod or a cauldron, and let Agamemnon son of Atreus decide whose horses are first. You will find out, and it will cost you.”

Ajax son of Oileus was ready to give him an angry answer, and there would have been more brawling between them, but Achilles rose in his place and said, “Stop your railing, Ajax and Idomeneus. It is not seemly. You would be scandalized if you saw anyone else behave this way. Sit down and keep your eyes on the horses. They are speeding toward the winning-post and will be here directly. Then you will both know whose horses are first and whose come after.”

While he was still speaking, the son of Tydeus came driving in, plying his whip hard from the shoulder, with his horses stepping high as they flew over the course. Sand and grit rained thick on the driver. The chariot, inlaid with gold and tin, ran close behind his swift horses, and the fine dust held hardly any trace of wheel-marks as the horses came flying in at their utmost speed. Diomedes stopped them in the middle of the crowd, and sweat fell in streams from their manes and chests to the ground. At once he sprang down from his goodly chariot and leaned his whip against the yoke. Brave Sthenelus lost no time. He promptly brought on the prize and gave the woman and the ear-handled cauldron to his comrades to take away. Then he unyoked the horses.

Antilochus of the race of Neleus came in next. He had got past Menelaus by a trick, not by the swiftness of his horses. Even so, Menelaus finished right behind him, as close as a wheel is to the horse that pulls a chariot and its master. The end hairs of a horse’s tail brush the tire of the wheel, and while the chariot is moving there is hardly any gap between wheel and horse. That was how near Menelaus came to Antilochus, though at first he had been a full disc’s throw behind. He had closed the gap quickly, because Agamemnon’s mare Aethe pulled harder and harder. Had the course been longer, Menelaus would have passed him, and it would not even have been a dead heat. Idomeneus’s brave squire Meriones was about a spear’s cast behind Menelaus. His horses were the slowest of all, and he was the worst driver. The son of Admetus came last of them all, dragging his chariot and driving his horses on ahead of him. Achilles saw him and felt sorry. He stood up among the Argives and said, “The best man is coming in last. Let us give him a prize, since that is only reasonable. He shall have the second, but the first must go to the son of Tydeus.”

So he spoke, and the others all applauded and were ready to do as he said. But Nestor’s son Antilochus stood up and claimed his rights from the son of Peleus. “Achilles,” he said, “I will take it very badly if you do this. You would rob me of my prize because you think Eumelus and his chariot and horses were thrown out, and he himself too, good man that he is. He should have prayed properly to the immortals. If he had, he would not have come in last. If you feel sorry for him and choose to, you have plenty of gold in your tents, and bronze, sheep, cattle and horses. Take something from that store, if you want the Achaeans to speak well of you, and give him a better prize even than the one you have just offered. But I will not give up the mare, and let any man who wants to fight me for her come on.”
Achilles smiled when he heard this. He was pleased with Antilochus, who was one of his dearest comrades. So he said—

“Antilochus,” he said, “you want me to find Eumelus another prize, and I will. I will give him the bronze breastplate that I took from Asteropaeus, with a rim of tin running all the way around it. It will be worth a great deal of money to him.”
Achilles told his comrade Automedon to fetch the breastplate from his tent, and Automedon went and brought it. Then Achilles handed it to Eumelus, who took it gladly.

But Menelaus got up in a rage, furiously angry with Antilochus. An attendant put his staff in his hands and told the Argives to be silent. Then the hero addressed them. “Antilochus,” he said, “what is this from you, who have been blameless until now? You have made me cut a poor figure. You blocked my horses by flinging your own in front of them, though yours are much worse than mine. So, princes and counselors of the Argives, judge between us and show no favor, or one of the Achaeans may say, ‘Menelaus has got the mare through lying and corruption. His horses were far inferior to Antilochus’s, but he has greater weight and influence.’ No, I will settle the matter myself, and no man will blame me, for I will do what is just. Come here, Antilochus, and stand in front of your chariot and horses, whip in hand, as our custom is. Lay your hand on your horses and swear by earth-encircling Poseidon that you did not get in the way of my horses on purpose and by guile.”

And Antilochus answered, “Forgive me, King Menelaus. I am much younger than you, and you stand higher than I do and are the better man of the two. You know how easily young men are led into indiscretion. Their tempers are more hasty and they have less judgment. So make allowances and bear with me. Of my own accord I will give up the mare I have won. And if you claim any further property from my own possessions, I would rather yield it to you at once than fall from your good graces from now on and do wrong in the sight of heaven.”

The son of Nestor then took the mare and gave her over to Menelaus, and his anger was appeased. As dew falls upon a field of ripening corn when the lands are bristling with the harvest, so, O Menelaus, was your heart made glad within you. He turned to Antilochus and said, “Now, Antilochus, angry though I have been, I can give way to you of my own free will. You have never been headstrong or ill-disposed before, but this time your youth got the better of your judgment. Be careful in future how you outwit your betters. No one else could have brought me around so easily, but your good father, your brother, and you yourself have all gone to infinite trouble on my behalf. So I yield to your entreaty and will give up the mare to you, though she is mine by right. Then the people will see that I am neither harsh nor vindictive.”

With that he handed the mare to Noemon, the comrade of Antilochus, and took the cauldron for himself. Meriones had come in fourth, and he carried off the two talents of gold. The fifth prize, the two-handled urn, was still unclaimed, so Achilles gave it to Nestor. He went up to the old man among the gathered Argives and said, “Take this, my good old friend, as an heirloom and a memorial of the funeral of Patroclus, for you will not see him again among the Argives. I give you this prize though you cannot win one. You can no longer wrestle or fight, you cannot enter the javelin match or the foot races, because age has laid its heavy hand on you.”

With these words he gave the urn to Nestor, who took it gladly and answered, “My son, everything you have said is true. My legs and feet have no strength now, and I cannot strike out with my arms from either shoulder. I wish I were young and strong again, as I was when the Epeans buried King Amarynceus in Buprasium and his sons set out prizes in his honor. In those games nobody could match me, not among the Epeans, not among the Pylians themselves, and not among the Aetolians. In boxing I beat Clytomedes son of Enops. In wrestling I beat Ancaeus of Pleuron, who had stepped forward to face me. Iphiclus was a good runner, but I outran him, and with the spear I threw farther than Phyleus or Polydorus. Only in the chariot race did the two sons of Actor get the better of me. They crowded their horses in front of mine, because they were angry at how the victory had gone and that most of the prizes were left lying where they had been set out. They were twins, and one of them kept hold of the reins, and kept hold of the reins, while the other worked the whip. That is what I was then. Now I must leave such things to younger men and bow to the weight of my years, though in those days I stood out among heroes. Now, sir, go on with the funeral contests for your comrade. I accept this urn gladly, and my heart is glad that you have not forgotten me. You always remember my goodwill toward you and the respect the Achaeans owe me. May heaven reward you richly for it.”

When the son of Peleus had heard all of Nestor’s thanks, he went through the crowd of Achaeans and set out prizes for the painful art of boxing. He led out a strong mule and tied it up in the middle of the crowd. She was a she-mule, six years old and never yet broken, which is the hardest age of all to break them. This was for the winner. For the loser he put up a double cup. Then he stood and spoke among the Argives. “Son of Atreus, and all you other Achaeans, I call on our two best boxers to fight hard for these prizes. The one to whom Apollo grants the greater endurance, and whom the Achaeans declare the winner, will take the mule back to his own tent. The one who is beaten will have the double cup.”

As he spoke, a brave and tall champion stood up, Epeus son of Panopeus, a skilled boxer. He laid his hand on the mule and said, “Let the man who wants the cup come here, because nobody but me will take the mule. I am the best boxer of everyone present, and no one can beat me. Is it not enough that I fall short of you in actual fighting? A man cannot be good at everything. I tell you plainly, and it will come true. If anyone boxes with me, I will bruise his body and break his bones. So let his friends stay here together, ready to carry him away when I am finished with him.”

They all kept silent, and only one man stood up, Euryalus son of Mecisteus, who was the son of Talaus. Mecisteus once went to Thebes, after the fall of Oedipus, to attend his funeral, and there he beat all the people of Cadmus. The son of Tydeus acted as second to Euryalus, urging him on and hoping with all his heart that he would win. First he tied a waistband around him, then gave him thongs of ox-hide, well cut. Now that the two men were belted, they went into the middle of the ring and at once set to. They punished each other badly, swinging their heavy fists. Their jaws made a horrible crashing sound, and sweat ran from every pore of their skin. Then Epeus attacked and struck Euryalus on the jaw while he was looking around. Euryalus could not stay on his feet. His legs gave way under him in an instant. He leaped up, the way a fish leaps into the air near a shore covered in sea-wrack when Boreas ruffles the top of the waves, and then drops back into deep water. But noble Epeus took hold of him and raised him up. His comrades came around him and led him out of the ring. He walked unsteadily with his head hanging to one side, spitting great clots of gore. They sat him down in a faint and then went to fetch the double cup.

Next the son of Peleus brought out the prizes for the third contest and showed them to the Argives. These were for the painful art of wrestling. The winner would get a great tripod, ready to set on the fire, which the Achaeans valued at twelve oxen. For the loser he brought out a woman skilled in all kinds of work, whom they valued at four oxen. He stood and said among the Argives, “Come forward, you who will try this contest.”

At once great Ajax son of Telamon stood up, and crafty Odysseus, full of wiles, stood up too. The two tied on their belts and went into the middle of the ring. They locked their strong hands on each other like the rafters a master builder fits together for the roof of a high house, to keep out the wind. Their backbones cracked as they tugged at each other with their mighty arms, and sweat poured off them. Many bloody welts rose on their sides and shoulders, but they kept struggling with all their might for the victory and the tripod. Odysseus could not throw Ajax, and Ajax could not throw him. Odysseus was too strong for him. But when the Achaeans began to tire of watching, Ajax said to Odysseus, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, either you lift me or I lift you, and let Zeus decide between us.”

With those words he lifted Odysseus off the ground, but Odysseus did not forget his cunning. He struck Ajax in the hollow at the back of the knee, so that Ajax lost his footing and fell on his back, with Odysseus lying on his chest. Everyone who saw it was amazed. Then Odysseus in turn lifted Ajax. He moved him a little off the ground but could not lift him clear. His own knee gave way, and the two fell side by side on the ground, covered in dust. They sprang up again and were about to wrestle a third time, but Achilles rose and held them back. “Do not wear each other down with any more of this cruel suffering,” he said. “The victory belongs to both of you equally. Each of you take an equal prize, and let the other Achaeans compete now.”
So he spoke, and they did as he said. They wiped the dust from their bodies and put their shirts on again.

Then the son of Peleus set out prizes for speed in running. The first was a mixing-bowl of pure silver, beautifully made. It held six measures, and it was far lovelier than any other in the whole world. Skilled craftsmen of Sidon had made it, and Phoenicians had carried it across the sea and brought it into port, where they presented it to Thoas. Eueneus son of Jason had given it to Patroclus as ransom for Priam’s son Lycaon. Now Achilles offered it in honor of his comrade as a prize for the swiftest runner. For the second prize he put up a large ox, well fattened, and for the last there was to be half a talent of gold. Then he stood and said among the Argives, “Come forward, you who will try this contest.”

At once swift Ajax son of Oileus stood up, together with cunning Odysseus and Nestor’s son Antilochus, the fastest runner of all the young men of his time. They stood side by side, and Achilles pointed out the goal. The course was marked out for them from the starting-post. The son of Oileus took the lead at once, and Odysseus ran right behind him, as close as the shuttle is to a woman’s breast when she throws the woof across the warp and holds it tight against her. That was how close Odysseus ran behind him. He stepped in Ajax’s footprints before the dust could settle in them, and Ajax felt his breath on the back of his head as he ran swiftly on. The Achaeans all shouted applause as they saw him straining his utmost, and they cheered him as he shot past. But when they were nearing the end of the course, Odysseus prayed silently to Athena. “Hear me, goddess,” he cried, “and help my feet.” So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him. She made his hands and feet feel light. The runners were just about to pounce on the prize when Ajax slipped, because Athena bore him a grudge. He slid on some offal left there from the cattle Achilles had slaughtered in honor of Patroclus, and his mouth and nostrils filled with cow dung. So Odysseus carried off the mixing-bowl, since he got ahead of Ajax and came in first. Ajax took the ox. He stood holding one of its horns and spitting the dung out of his mouth. Then he said to the Argives, “Alas, the goddess has spoiled my running. She watches over Odysseus and stands by him as though she were his own mother.” So he spoke, and they all laughed heartily.

Antilochus took the last prize, smiling as he said to the bystanders, “You can all see, my friends, that the gods again show respect for seniority. Ajax is a little older than I am. As for Odysseus, he belongs to an earlier generation, but he is hale despite his years, and none of the Achaeans can race against him except Achilles.”

He said this to pay a compliment to the son of Peleus, and Achilles answered, “Antilochus, your praise of me will not be wasted. I will give you an extra half talent of gold.” He then gave Antilochus the half talent, and Antilochus took it gladly.

Then the son of Peleus brought out the spear, helmet and shield that Sarpedon had carried and Patroclus had taken from him. He stood and said among the Argives, “I call on two champions to put on their armor, take up their sharp blades, and test each other before the whole crowd. Whichever of them first wounds the other’s flesh, cuts through his armor, and draws blood, to him I will give this fine Thracian sword inlaid with silver, which I took from Asteropaeus. The armor they will both keep together, and I will give each of them a hearty meal in my own tent.”

At once great Ajax son of Telamon stood up, and mighty Diomedes son of Tydeus with him. Each put on his armor on his own side of the ring, then both walked to the middle, eager to fight, with fire flashing from their eyes. The Achaeans watched in amazement. When the two came close to each other, three times they sprang forward and three times tried to strike in close combat. Ajax pierced Diomedes’s round shield but drew no blood, because the cuirass under the shield protected him. Then the son of Tydeus, over the top of his huge shield, kept aiming the point of his spear at Ajax’s neck. The Achaeans feared for Ajax’s safety and told them to stop fighting and share the prize. Achilles then gave the great sword to the son of Tydeus, with its scabbard and the leather belt to hang it from.

Next Achilles set out the massive iron quoit that mighty Eetion used to hurl, until Achilles killed him and carried it off in his ships with the rest of his spoils. He stood and said among the Argives, “Come forward, you who want to try this contest. The man who wins it will have a store of iron to last him five years as they roll around. If his fair fields lie far from a town, his shepherd or plowman will not need to make a trip to buy iron, because he will have a stock of it on his own land.”

Then two mighty men stood up, Polypoetes and Leonteus, and with them Ajax son of Telamon and noble Epeus. They stood in a line, one after another. Epeus took the quoit first, whirled it, and flung it, and all the Achaeans burst out laughing. After him Leonteus of the race of Ares threw. Ajax son of Telamon threw third and sent the quoit beyond any mark made so far. But when mighty Polypoetes took the quoit, he hurled it like a stockman’s stick, which a herdsman sends spinning among his cattle as he drives them. His throw went that far beyond the others. All who saw it roared their applause, and his comrades carried the prize away for him and put it on board his ship.

Achilles next offered a prize of iron for archery: ten double-edged axes and ten with a single edge. He set up a ship’s mast some way off on the sands and tied a pigeon to it by the foot with a fine string. This was what they were to aim at. “Whoever hits the pigeon,” he said, “will have all the axes and take them away with him. Whoever hits the string but misses the bird has made a worse shot, and he will have the single-edged axes.”

Then King Teucer stood up, and Meriones, the stalwart squire of Idomeneus, stood up too. They cast lots in a bronze helmet, and the lot of Teucer fell first. He let fly his arrow at once, but he had not promised King Apollo a sacrifice of firstling lambs, and he missed the bird, because Apollo spoiled his aim. He did hit the string that held the bird, near its foot. The arrow cut the string clean through, so that it hung down toward the ground, and the bird flew up into the sky. The Achaeans shouted applause. Meriones had his arrow ready while Teucer was aiming. He snatched the bow out of Teucer’s hand and at once promised Apollo, lord of the bow, a sacrifice of firstling lambs. Then he caught sight of the pigeon high up under the clouds, circling upward, and hit her in the middle of the wing. The arrow went clean through the wing and stuck in the ground at Meriones’ feet. The bird perched on the ship’s mast with her head hanging and all her feathers drooping. The life went out of her, and she fell heavily from the mast. So Meriones took all ten double-edged axes, and Teucer carried the single-edged ones off to his ships.

Then the son of Peleus brought in a spear and a cauldron that had never been on the fire. It was worth an ox and was decorated with a pattern of flowers. Those who throw the javelin stood up: the son of Atreus, king of men Agamemnon, and Meriones, stalwart squire of Idomeneus. But Achilles spoke. “Son of Atreus, we know how far you surpass everyone else, both in power and in throwing the javelin. Take the cauldron back with you to your ships. If you are willing, let us give the spear to Meriones. That at least is what I would wish myself.”
King Agamemnon agreed. He gave the bronze spear to Meriones, and handed the fine cauldron to his esquire Talthybius.

chapters.title: Book 24
paragraphs: Priam ransoms the body of Hector—Hector’s funeral.

The assembly broke up, and the people scattered, each man to his own ship. There they prepared their supper and turned their thoughts to the welcome gift of sleep. But Achilles kept weeping for his dear comrade, and sleep, to whom all things submit, would not take hold of him. He tossed from one side to the other, longing for the strength and manliness of Patroclus. He remembered everything they had done together and everything they had endured, in battle and on the waves of the wearying sea. As he dwelt on these memories he wept bitterly. He lay first on his side, then on his back, then face down, until at last he got up and went out like a man out of his mind to wander along the shore. When he saw dawn breaking over the beach and the sea, he harnessed his horses to his chariot and tied the body of Hector behind it to drag it along. Three times he dragged it around the tomb of the son of Menoetius. Then he went back into his tent and left the body lying on the ground, stretched out full length and face down. But Apollo would not allow it to be disfigured. He pitied the man, dead though he was, and so he kept covering him with his golden aegis, so that Hector would come to no harm while Achilles dragged him.

In this way Achilles, in his fury, shamefully dishonored Hector. The blessed gods looked down from heaven in pity, and they urged Hermes, slayer of Argus, to steal the body. All of them agreed except Hera, Poseidon, and Zeus’s gray-eyed daughter. They held on to the hatred they had always felt for Ilium, for Priam and his people. They had never forgiven the wrong Paris did them, when the goddesses came to him in his sheepyards and he scorned them, favoring instead the one who offered him a wanton woman, to his ruin.

When the morning of the twelfth day came, Phoebus Apollo spoke among the immortals. “You gods should be ashamed of yourselves. You are cruel and hard-hearted. Did Hector not burn thigh-bones of heifers and unblemished goats for you? Yet now you do not dare to rescue even his dead body, so that his wife could look on it, with his mother and his child, his father Priam, and his people, who would burn him at once and give him his proper funeral rites. So all of you would rather take the side of raging Achilles, who knows neither right nor pity? He is like a savage lion that, proud of its great strength and daring, springs on men’s flocks and gorges itself on them. In the same way Achilles has thrown away all pity, and all that conscience which does a man great harm and great good if he heeds it. A man may lose someone far dearer than Achilles has lost—a son, perhaps, or a brother born from his own mother’s womb. Yet when he has mourned and wept for him, he lets him rest, for it takes a great deal of sorrow to kill a man. But Achilles, now that he has killed noble Hector, drags him behind his chariot around the tomb of his comrade. It would be more honorable of him, and better for him, not to do this. Brave though he is, we gods may take offense when he vents his fury on dead clay.”

Hera answered angrily. “That would be fine, lord of the silver bow,” she cried, “if you would give Hector and Achilles equal honor. But Hector was mortal and nursed at a woman’s breast, while Achilles is the child of a goddess, one I raised and brought up myself. I gave her in marriage to Peleus, who is exceedingly dear to the immortals. All of you gods came to her wedding. You feasted there with them yourself, and you brought your lyre—you who have always been false, and fond of bad company.”

Then Zeus said, “Hera, do not be so bitter. Their honor will not be equal. But of all who live in Ilium, Hector was the dearest to the gods, and to me as well, because his offerings never failed me. My altar was never short of its dues, or of the drink-offerings and the savor of sacrifice, which we claim as our right. So I will allow mighty Hector’s body to be stolen. But this can hardly be done without Achilles finding out, for his mother stays beside him night and day. Let one of you send Thetis to me, and I will give her my counsel: Achilles is to accept a ransom from Priam and give up the body.”

At this Iris, swift as the wind, went off to deliver Zeus’s message. She plunged down into the dark sea midway between Samos and rocky Imbrus. The water hissed as it closed over her, and she sank to the bottom like the lead on an ox-horn line, which speeds down to bring death to fishes. She found Thetis sitting in a great cave, with the other sea-goddesses gathered around her. In the midst of them she sat weeping for her noble son, who was to fall far from his own land, on the rich plains of Troy. Iris went up to her and said, “Rise, Thetis. Zeus, whose counsels never fail, calls you to him.” Thetis answered, “Why does the mighty god call me? I am in great grief, and I shrink from moving among the immortals. Still, I will go, and whatever word he speaks will not be spoken in vain.”

The goddess took her dark veil, the most somber robe there is, and set out, with swift Iris leading the way. The waves of the sea parted to make a path for them. When they reached the shore they flew up into the heavens, where they found the all-seeing son of Cronus with the blessed gods who live forever gathered around him. Athena gave up her seat to Thetis, and she sat down beside father Zeus. Hera then put a fair golden cup in her hand and spoke words of comfort to her. Thetis drank and handed the cup back, and the father of gods and men was the first to speak.

“So, goddess,” he said, “despite all your sorrow, and the grief that I know well fills your heart always, you have come here to Olympus. I will tell you why I sent for you. For nine days now the immortals have been quarreling over Achilles, the waster of cities, and the body of Hector. The gods wanted Hermes, slayer of Argus, to steal the body. But to further our peace and friendship from now on, I will grant your son an honor, which I will now tell you. Go to the army and lay these commands on him. Tell him that the gods are angry with him, and that I am angrier than all of them, because he keeps Hector at the ships and will not give him up. Perhaps he will fear me and let the body go. At the same time I will send Iris to great Priam, to tell him to go to the ships of the Achaeans and ransom his son, bringing gifts for Achilles that will satisfy him.”

Silver-footed Thetis did as the god had told her. At once she darted down from the topmost summits of Olympus. She went to her son’s tents and found him grieving bitterly, while his faithful comrades around him were busy preparing their morning meal, for which they had killed a great woolly sheep. His mother sat down beside him and stroked him with her hand. “My son,” she said, “how long will you go on grieving and moaning like this? You are gnawing at your own heart, and you think neither of food nor of a woman’s embrace. Yet these things too are good, for you have not long to live, and death and strong-handed fate are already close beside you. Now listen to what I say, for I come as a messenger from Zeus. He says that the gods are angry with you, and that he is angrier than all of them, because you keep Hector at the ships and will not give him up. So let him go, and accept a ransom for his body.”
Achilles answered, “So be it. If Olympian Zeus of his own will commands this, then let the man who brings the ransom carry the body away.”

So mother and son spoke together at the ships, at long length. Meanwhile the son of Cronus sent Iris to the strong city of Ilium. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “from the mansions of Olympus, and tell King Priam in Ilium to go to the ships of the Achaeans and free the body of his dear son. He is to take gifts with him that will satisfy Achilles. He is to go alone, with no other Trojan, except some honored servant who can drive his mules and wagon and bring back the body of the man whom noble Achilles has killed. Let him have no thought or fear of death in his heart, for we will send the slayer of Argus to escort him and bring him into Achilles’s tent. Achilles will not kill him or let anyone else do it. He will be careful in his conduct and do no wrong, and he will treat a suppliant with all honorable courtesy.”

At this Iris, swift as the wind, sped off to deliver her message. She came to Priam’s house and found weeping and lamentation inside. His sons sat around their father in the outer courtyard, their clothes wet with tears. The old man sat among them wrapped tightly in his mantle, his head and neck covered with the filth he had clutched up as he lay groveling in the mire. His daughters and his sons’ wives went wailing through the house, thinking of the many brave men who lay dead, killed by the Argives. The messenger of Zeus stood beside Priam and spoke gently to him, but fear came over him as she did. “Take heart, Priam, offspring of Dardanus,” she said. “Take heart and do not be afraid. I bring no evil news; I mean well toward you. I come as a messenger from Zeus, who is far away but cares for you and pities you. The lord of Olympus tells you to go and ransom noble Hector, taking gifts that will satisfy Achilles. You are to go alone, with no Trojan, except some honored servant who can drive your mules and wagon and bring back to the city the body of the man whom noble Achilles has killed. You are to have no thought or fear of death, for Zeus will send the slayer of Argus to escort you. When he has brought you into Achilles’s tent, Achilles will not kill you or let anyone else do it. He will be careful in his conduct and do no wrong, and he will treat a suppliant with all honorable courtesy.”

When she had spoken, Iris went on her way. Priam told his sons to get a mule-wagon ready and to fasten the wagon body firmly on top of its frame. Then he went down into his fragrant storeroom, high-vaulted and made of cedar, where his many treasures were kept, and called his wife Hecuba. “Wife,” he said, “a messenger has come to me from Olympus and has told me to go to the ships of the Achaeans and ransom my dear son, taking gifts that will satisfy Achilles. What do you think of this? For my own part, I am strongly drawn to go through the camps of the Achaeans and to their ships.”

His wife cried out when she heard him. “Alas,” she said, “what has become of the good judgment for which you have always been famous, among strangers and your own people? How can you dare to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans and look in the face of the man who has killed so many of your brave sons? You must have a heart of iron. If that cruel savage sees you and lays hands on you, he will show neither respect nor pity. Let us weep for Hector from afar, here in our own house. When I gave birth to him, the threads of overruling fate were spun for him so that dogs would eat his flesh far from his parents, in the house of that terrible man. I would gladly fasten on his liver and devour it. That is how I would avenge my son, who showed no cowardice when Achilles killed him, and thought neither of flight nor of avoiding battle as he stood defending the Trojan men and Trojan women.”

Then Priam said, “I will go. Do not try to stop me, and do not be a bird of ill omen in my house, for you will not move me. If some mortal man had sent me—a prophet or a priest who reads the future from sacrifice—I would have thought him false and paid him no heed. But now I have heard the goddess and seen her face to face. So I will go, and her word will not be spoken in vain. If it is my fate to die at the ships of the Achaeans, so I would have it. Let Achilles kill me, if only I can first take my son in my arms and mourn him until my heart is comforted.”

With these words he lifted the lids of his chests and took out twelve fine robes. He also took twelve single-fold cloaks, twelve rugs, twelve fair mantles, and the same number of shirts. He weighed out ten talents of gold, and brought two burnished tripods, four cauldrons, and a very beautiful cup that the Thracians had given him when he went to them on an embassy. It was very precious, but he did not begrudge even this, so eager was he to ransom his son’s body. Then he drove all the Trojans out of the courtyard, scolding them angrily. “Get out,” he cried, “you shame and disgrace to me. Have you no grief in your own homes, that you come to pester me here? Do you think it a small thing that the son of Cronus has sent this sorrow on me, the loss of the bravest of my sons? No, you will find it out yourselves, for now that he is gone the Achaeans will have an easier time killing you. As for me, let me go down into the house of Hades before my eyes see the sacking and wasting of the city.”

He drove the men away with his staff, and they left as the old man hurried them. Then he called to his sons, scolding Helenus, Paris, noble Agathon, Pammon, Antiphonus, Polites of the loud battle cry, Deiphobus, Hippothous, and Dius. These nine the old man called to him. “Come to me at once,” he cried, “you worthless sons who shame me. I wish you had all been killed at the ships instead of Hector. Miserable man that I am, I had the bravest sons in all Troy—noble Nestor, Troilus the dauntless charioteer, and Hector, who was a god among men, so that one would have thought him the son of an immortal. Yet not one of them is left. Ares has killed them, and the ones I am ashamed of are all that remain to me. Liars, and light on your feet, heroes of the dance, robbers of lambs and kids from your own people, why do you not get a wagon ready for me at once and load all these things on it, so that I can set out on my way?”

So he spoke, and they feared their father’s rebuke. They brought out a strong mule-wagon, newly made, and fastened the wagon body on its frame. They took the mule-yoke down from its peg, a boxwood yoke with a knob on top and rings for the reins to pass through. Then they brought out a yoke-band eleven cubits long to bind the yoke to the pole. They tied it on at the far end of the pole and put the ring over the upright pin, fastening it with three turns of the band on each side of the knob and bending the thong of the yoke beneath it. When this was done, they brought the rich ransom for Hector’s body out of the storeroom and set it all in order on the wagon. Then they yoked the strong harness-mules that the Mysians had once given Priam as a fine present. For Priam himself they yoked horses that the old king had bred and kept for his own use.

Priam and his servant carefully saw to the yoking of their vehicles at the palace. Then Hecuba came up to them, heavy with sorrow, carrying a golden goblet of wine in her right hand so that they could pour a drink-offering before leaving. She stopped in front of the horses and said, “Take this and pour a drink-offering to father Zeus. You are determined to go to the ships against my wishes, so pray that you return safely from the hands of your enemies. Pray to the son of Cronus, lord of the whirlwind, who sits on Ida and looks down over all Troy. Ask him to send his swift messenger to your right, the bird of omen that is strongest and dearest to him of all birds, so that you see it with your own eyes and can trust it as you set out for the ships of the Danaans. If all-seeing Zeus will not send you this messenger, then however set on going you may be, I would not have you approach the ships of the Argives.”
Priam answered, “Wife, I will do as you ask. It is good to lift hands in prayer to Zeus, in the hope that he may have mercy on me.”

With this the old man told the serving-woman to pour pure water over his hands. She came with the water in a bowl, and he washed his hands and took the cup from his wife. Standing in the middle of the courtyard with his eyes turned to heaven, he poured the drink-offering and prayed. “Father Zeus,” he said, “you who rule from Ida, most glorious and most great, let me find a kind and compassionate welcome in the tents of Achilles. Send your swift messenger to my right, the bird of omen that is strongest and dearest to you of all birds, so that I see it with my own eyes and can trust it as I set out for the ships of the Danaans.”

So he prayed, and Zeus, lord of counsel, heard his prayer. At once he sent an eagle, the most unerring portent of all flying birds, the dusky hunter that men also call the Black Eagle. Its wings spread out on either side as wide as the well-made, well-bolted door of a rich man’s chamber. It came flying over the city on their right, and when they saw it they were glad, and their hearts took comfort. The old man hurried to mount his chariot and drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court. In front went the mules pulling the four-wheeled wagon, driven by wise Idaeus. Behind them came the horses, which the old man lashed with his whip and drove quickly through the city, while his friends followed, wailing and lamenting for him as though he were on his way to death. As soon as they had come down from the city and reached the plain, his sons and sons-in-law, who had followed him, turned back to Ilium.

But Priam and Idaeus, as they came into view on the plain, did not escape the notice of all-seeing Zeus, who looked down at the old man and pitied him. He spoke to his son Hermes. “Hermes,” he said, “you are the one who most likes to escort men on their way, and you listen to whomever you choose. Go, and guide Priam to the ships of the Achaeans in such a way that none of the other Danaans will see him or notice him until he reaches the son of Peleus.”

So he spoke, and Hermes, guide and guardian, slayer of Argus, did as he was told. At once he tied on his glittering golden sandals, with which he could fly like the wind over land and sea. He took the wand with which he closes men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them whenever he pleases, and flew with it in his hand until he came to Troy and the Hellespont. To look at, he was like a young man of noble birth in the prime of his youth and beauty, with the first down just coming on his face.

Now when Priam and Idaeus had driven past the great tomb of Ilus, they halted their mules and horses to let them drink in the river, for the shades of night were falling. Then Idaeus saw Hermes standing near them and said to Priam, “Take care, descendant of Dardanus. This is a matter that needs thought. I see a man who I think will attack us at any moment. Let us flee with our horses, or at least embrace his knees and beg him to have compassion on us.”

When the old man heard this, his heart failed him and he was in great fear. He stayed where he was as if dazed, and the hair stood on end all over his body. But the bringer of good luck came up, took him by the hand, and said, “Where, father, are you driving your mules and horses like this, in the dead of night, when other men are asleep? Are you not afraid of the fierce Achaeans, so cruel and relentless, who are close by? If one of them saw you carrying so much treasure through the darkness of the fleeting night, what would become of you? You are no longer young, and the man with you is too old to protect you from those who would attack you. As for me, I will do you no harm, and I will defend you against anyone else, for you remind me of my own father.”

Priam answered, “It is just as you say, my dear son. Still, some god has held his hand over me, since he has sent such a traveler as you to meet me at such a good moment. You are so handsome in looks and figure, and your judgment is so sound, that you must come from blessed parents.”

Then the slayer of Argus, guide and guardian, said, “Sir, everything you have said is right. But tell me, and tell me truly: are you sending this rich treasure to a foreign people, where it may be safe? Or are you all abandoning strong Ilium in dismay now that your son has fallen, who was the bravest man among you and never lacked courage in battle with the Achaeans?”
Priam asked, “Who are you, my friend, and who are your parents? How is it that you speak so truly of the fate of my unhappy son?”

The slayer of Argus, guide and guardian, answered him. “Sir, you are testing me when you question me about noble Hector. Many a time I have seen him in battle, driving the Argives to their ships and putting them to the sword. We stood still and marveled, because Achilles, in his anger with the son of Atreus, did not let us fight. I am his squire, and I came with him in the same ship. I am a Myrmidon, and my father’s name is Polyctor. He is a rich man and about as old as you are. He has six sons besides me, and I am the seventh. We cast lots, and it fell to me to sail here with Achilles. I have now come from the ships onto the plain, because at daybreak the Achaeans will set up their battle lines around the city. They are restless from doing nothing and so eager that their princes cannot hold them back.”
Priam replied, “If you really are a squire of Achilles son of Peleus, tell me the whole truth. Is my son still beside the ships? Or has Achilles hacked him limb from limb and thrown him to his dogs?”

“Sir,” said the slayer of Argus, who was his guide and guardian, “no dogs or vultures have eaten him. He is simply lying at the tents, by Achilles’s ship. Twelve days have now passed while he lay there, and his flesh has not wasted away, nor have the worms eaten him, though they feed on men killed in war. Each daybreak Achilles drags him cruelly around the tomb of his dear comrade, but this does no harm to the body. You should come and see for yourself how he lies there fresh as dew, with the blood washed off, and every one of his wounds closed, though many men drove their spears into him. That is how well the blessed gods have looked after your brave son, because he was dear to them beyond measure.”

The old man was comforted by this. He said, “My son, it is a good thing to have given the immortals their due offerings. As surely as he was my son, he never forgot the gods who hold Olympus, and now they repay him for it even in death. So accept this fine cup from me. Protect me, and with the help of the gods lead me until I reach the tent of the son of Peleus.”

The slayer of Argus, his guide and guardian, answered, “Sir, you are testing me and taking advantage of my youth, but you will not persuade me. You are offering me gifts behind the back of Achilles, whom I fear. I think it a great wrong to cheat him, in case something bad happens to me for it. But as your guide I would go with you all the way to Argos itself, and I would guard you so carefully, by sea or by land, that nobody would attack you out of contempt for the one who was with you.”

The bringer of good luck then jumped onto the chariot. He took the whip and reins and put new spirit into the mules and horses. When they reached the trench and the wall in front of the ships, the guards there had just been eating their suppers. The slayer of Argus put them all into a deep sleep. He then pulled back the bolts to open the gates, and brought Priam inside, along with the treasure on his wagon. Before long they came to the tall dwelling of the son of Peleus. The Myrmidons had cut pine for it and built it for their king. When it was built, they had roofed it with coarse tussock grass mown from the plain, and all around it they had made a large courtyard, fenced with stakes set close together. The gate was held shut by a single bolt of pine. It took three men to push it into place and three to pull it back and open the gate, but Achilles could draw it by himself. Hermes opened the gate for the old man and brought in the treasure that Priam was taking for the son of Peleus. Then he jumped down from the chariot to the ground and said, “Sir, I am the immortal Hermes. I came with you because my father sent me to escort you. Now I will leave you, and I will not go into the presence of Achilles. It might anger him if a god were seen helping mortals so openly. Go in yourself and clasp the knees of the son of Peleus. Beg him in the name of his father, his lovely mother and his son, and you may move him.”

With these words Hermes returned to high Olympus. Priam jumped down from his chariot to the ground and left Idaeus where he was, to look after the mules and horses. The old man walked straight into the house where Achilles, beloved of the gods, was sitting. He found him there, with his men sitting apart from him. Only two of them, the hero Automedon and Alcimus of the race of Ares, were busy attending to him. He had only just finished eating and drinking, and the table was still in place. King Priam came in without being noticed, went right up to Achilles, and clasped his knees. He kissed those dreadful, murderous hands that had killed so many of his sons.

When a cruel blow of fate has made a man kill someone in his own country, and he has to flee to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, everyone who sees him is amazed. Achilles was amazed in just that way when he saw Priam. The others looked at one another in amazement too. Then Priam begged Achilles, saying, “Think of your father, Achilles, you who are like the gods. He is as old as I am, standing on the sad threshold of old age. Perhaps his neighbors are harassing him, and there is no one to keep war and ruin away from him. Yet when he hears that you are still alive, he is glad, and every day he hopes to see his dear son come home to him from Troy. But I am a wretched man. I had the bravest sons in all Troy, and not one of them is left. I had fifty sons when the Achaeans came here. Nineteen of them came from a single womb, and the others were borne to me by the women of my household. Fierce Ares has laid most of them low. Hector was the only one left, the guardian of our city and of ourselves, and you killed him not long ago. That is why I have now come to the ships of the Achaeans, to ransom his body from you with a great ransom. Fear the anger of heaven, Achilles. Think of your own father and pity me. I am more pitiable than he, because I have steeled myself as no man on earth has ever done before me. I have raised to my lips the hand of the man who killed my son.”

So Priam spoke, and Achilles ached with longing as he thought of his father. He took the old man’s hand and gently pushed him back. The two of them wept bitterly. Priam lay at Achilles’s feet and wept for Hector, and Achilles wept sometimes for his father and sometimes for Patroclus, until the house was full of their crying. But when Achilles had had enough of grief and the bitterness of his sorrow had left him, he rose from his seat. In pity for the old man’s white hair and beard, he lifted him up by the hand. Then he said, “Unhappy man, you have dared a great deal. How could you come alone to the ships of the Achaeans, into the presence of the man who has killed so many of your brave sons? Your courage must be iron. Sit down on this seat now. Whatever our grief, we will let our sorrows lie quiet in our hearts, because weeping gets us nowhere. The immortals feel no care, yet the lot they spin for men is full of sorrow. On the floor of Zeus’s palace stand two urns, one filled with evil gifts and the other with good ones. The man for whom Zeus, the lord of thunder, mixes the gifts he sends will meet with good fortune at one time and evil at another. But the man to whom Zeus sends only evil gifts will be pointed at with scorn. Hunger will hound him to the ends of the world, and he will wander the face of the earth, honored by neither gods nor men. That is what happened to Peleus. From his birth the gods gave him every good thing. He ruled the Myrmidons and surpassed all men in prosperity and wealth, and though he was mortal, they gave him a goddess for his wife. But heaven sent him misfortune too. No line of royal children was born to him in his house. He has one son only, who is doomed to die before his time. I cannot look after him now that he is growing old, because I must stay here at Troy to bring ruin to you and your children. And you also, Priam, I have heard were happy once. They say that in wealth and in number of children you surpassed everyone in Lesbos, the realm of Makar to the north, in Phrygia farther inland, and among the people along the great Hellespont. But since the day the dwellers in heaven brought this evil on you, there has been war and slaughter around your city without end. Bear up under it, and let your sorrow have some pauses. You will gain nothing by mourning your brave son. You cannot raise him from the dead, and before you do, you will suffer yet another sorrow.”

Priam answered, “O king, do not tell me to sit while Hector is still lying uncared for in your tents. Accept the great ransom I have brought you, and give him to me at once so that I can look at him. May you enjoy the ransom and reach your own land safely, since you have let me live and see the light of the sun.”

Achilles looked at him sternly and said, “Do not provoke me any more, sir. I myself intend to give up Hector’s body. My mother, the daughter of the old man of the sea, came to me from Zeus to tell me to hand it over to you. And I know well, Priam, and you cannot hide it from me, that some god brought you to the ships of the Achaeans. No man, however strong and in his prime, would dare to come into our camp otherwise. He could not get past our guards unseen, and he could not draw the bolt of my gates so easily. So do not stir me up further, or I may sin against the word of Zeus and refuse to receive you in my tents, suppliant though you are.”

The old man was afraid of him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang out through the door of his house like a lion. He did not go alone. His two squires, Automedon and Alcimus, went with him. Now that Patroclus was dead, he valued these two above all his other comrades. They unyoked the horses and mules, and told Priam’s herald and attendant to sit inside the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body down from the wagon, but left two mantles and a fine shirt for Achilles to wrap the body in when it was given back to be taken home. Then Achilles called to his servants and told them to wash the body and anoint it. First he took it to a place where Priam could not see it. He was afraid that Priam, seeing it, might break out in the bitterness of his grief and enrage him, so that he would kill the old man and sin against the word of Zeus. When the servants had washed and anointed the body and wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it onto a bier, and he and his men laid it on the wagon. As he did so he cried aloud and called on his dear comrade by name. “Do not be angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I gave Hector back to his father for a ransom. It was not an unworthy one, and I will share it with you fairly.”

Achilles then went back into the tent and sat down again in the richly inlaid seat he had risen from. It stood by the wall at right angles to the one Priam was sitting against. “Sir,” he said, “your son is laid on his bier and ransomed as you wished. You will see him when you take him away at daybreak. For now, let us get our supper ready. Even lovely Niobe had to think about eating, though her twelve children, six daughters and six strong sons, had all been killed in her house. Apollo killed the sons with arrows from his silver bow, as a punishment to Niobe, and Artemis killed the daughters, because Niobe had boasted against Leto. She said that Leto had borne only two children, while she herself had borne many. So the two killed the many. For nine days they lay in their blood and there was no one to bury them, because the son of Cronus had turned the people to stone. On the tenth day the gods of heaven buried them themselves, and then Niobe, worn out with weeping, ate. They say that somewhere among the rocks on the mountain pastures of Sipylus, where the nymphs who haunt the river Achelous have their home, she lives on as stone, and still nurses the sorrows the gods sent her. So, noble sir, let the two of us eat now. You can weep for your dear son later, when you carry him back to Ilium, and he will cost you many tears.”

With this Achilles sprang up from his seat and killed a sheep with silvery white wool. His followers skinned it and prepared it in the proper way. They cut the meat carefully into smaller pieces, put them on spits, and drew them off again when they were well roasted. Automedon brought bread in fair baskets and served it around the table, while Achilles dealt out the meat, and they reached for the good things set before them. When they had had enough to eat and drink, Priam, descendant of Dardanus, looked in wonder at the strength and beauty of Achilles, who was like a god to see. Achilles in turn wondered at Priam as he listened to him and looked at his noble presence. When they had looked their fill at each other, Priam spoke first. “Now, O king,” he said, “take me to my bed, so that we may lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep. My eyes have not closed once since the day your hands took my son’s life. I have wallowed without stopping in the mud of my stable yard, moaning and brooding over my countless sorrows. Now I have also eaten bread and drunk wine. Until now I had tasted nothing.”

As he spoke, Achilles told his men and the women servants to set up beds in the room in the gatehouse. They were to make them with good red rugs, spread coverlets on top, and put woolen cloaks there for Priam and Idaeus to wear. So the maids went out with a torch and got the two beds ready in great haste. Then Achilles said to Priam, half laughing, “Dear sir, you must sleep outside. One of the counselors who regularly come to advise with me might see you here in the darkness of the fleeting night and tell Agamemnon. That could delay the handing over of the body. Now tell me, and tell me truly, how many days do you want for the funeral rites of noble Hector? Tell me, so that I can keep away from fighting and hold back the army.”

Priam answered, “Since you are letting me bury my noble son with all the proper rites, Achilles, do as I ask and I will be grateful. You know how we are shut up inside our city. It is a long way for us to fetch wood from the mountain, and the people are afraid. So we will mourn Hector in my house for nine days. On the tenth day we will bury him, and there will be a public feast in his honor. On the eleventh we will build a mound over his ashes, and on the twelfth, if we must, we will fight.”
Achilles answered, “King Priam, everything will be as you have said. I will hold back our fighting for as long as you have named.”

As he spoke he laid his hand on the old man’s right wrist, as a sign that he should have no fear. So Priam and his attendant slept there in the forecourt, their minds full of thought. Achilles lay in an inner room of the house, with fair Briseis beside him.

Now gods and mortals alike lay fast asleep through the whole night. Only Hermes, the bringer of good luck, could not be taken by sleep. He was thinking the whole time how to get King Priam away from the ships without being seen by the strong force of sentries. He hovered over Priam’s head and said, “Sir, now that Achilles has spared your life, you seem to have no fear of sleeping among your enemies. You have paid a great ransom and received the body of your son. If you were alive and a prisoner, the sons you left at home would have to give three times as much to free you. And so it would be if Agamemnon and the other Achaeans found out you were here.”

When the old man heard this, he was afraid and woke his servant. Hermes yoked their horses and mules and drove them quickly through the army, so that no one saw them. When they came to the ford of eddying Xanthus, begotten of immortal Zeus, Hermes went back to high Olympus, and saffron-robed Dawn began to break over all the land. Priam and Idaeus drove on toward the city, crying out and groaning, and the mules drew the body of Hector. No one, man or woman, saw them until Cassandra, as fair as golden Aphrodite, standing on Pergamus, caught sight of her dear father in his chariot, with his servant, who was the city’s herald, beside him. Then she saw the man lying on the bier behind the mules. With a loud cry she went about the city, saying, “Come here, Trojans, men and women, and look at Hector. If you ever rejoiced to see him coming home from battle while he was alive, look now at the man who was the glory of our city and of all our people.”

At this, not a man or woman was left in the city, so great a sorrow came over them. Close to the gates they met Priam as he was bringing in the body. Hector’s wife and his mother were the first to mourn him. They rushed toward the wagon and laid their hands on his head, while the crowd stood weeping around them. They would have stayed before the gates weeping and lamenting all day until the sun went down, if Priam had not spoken to them from the chariot. He said, “Make way for the mules to pass. Afterward, when I have taken the body home, you may weep as much as you like.”

At this the people stood aside and made way for the wagon. When they had carried the body into the house, they laid it on a bed and seated singers around it to lead the dirge. Then the women joined in with the sad music of their lament. Andromache led their wailing, foremost of them all, holding the head of mighty Hector in her arms. “Husband,” she cried, “you have died young and left me a widow in your house. The child we ill-starred parents have is still only a boy, and I fear he may not reach manhood. Before he can, our city will be destroyed and overthrown, because you who watched over it are gone, you who saved it and guarded our wives and children. Our women will be carried off to the ships as captives, and I with them. And you, my child, who will be with me, will be put to some unseemly tasks, working for a cruel master. Or perhaps some Achaean will hurl you from our walls to a miserable death, to avenge a brother, son or father whom Hector killed. Many of them have bitten the dust at his hands, because your father’s hand in battle was no light one. That is why the people mourn him. Hector, you have left unspeakable sorrow to your parents, and my own grief is greatest of all. You did not stretch out your arms to embrace me as you lay dying, and you said no words to me that I could have kept in my mind as I weep night and day for evermore.”

She wept bitterly as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament. Hecuba in her turn took up the cry of woe. “Hector,” she cried, “you are the dearest to me of all my children. As long as you were alive the gods loved you well, and even in death they have not forgotten you entirely. When Achilles took any other son of mine, he would sell him across the seas, to Samos, Imbrus or rugged Lemnos. And when he had killed you too with his sword, he dragged you many times around the tomb of his comrade, though that could not bring his comrade back to life. Yet here you lie, fresh as dew and beautiful as someone Apollo has killed with his painless arrows.”

So she too spoke through her tears, with bitter moaning. Then Helen took up the lament for the third time. “Hector,” she said, “you are the dearest to me of all my brothers-in-law. I am the wife of Paris, who brought me here to Troy, and I wish I had died before he did that. Twenty years have now passed since I left my home and came from over the sea, and in all that time I have never heard one insulting or unkind word from you. When someone else scolded me, one of your brothers or sisters or your brothers’ wives, or my mother-in-law (Priam was as kind to me as if he were my own father), you would stop them and correct them with gentle, kindly words. So my tears flow both for you and for my unhappy self. There is no one else in Troy who is kind to me. Everyone shrinks and shudders as they go by me.”

She wept as she spoke, and the vast crowd gathered around her joined in her lament. Then King Priam spoke to them. He said, “Bring wood to the city, Trojans, and do not fear any cunning ambush by the Argives. When Achilles sent me away from the ships, he gave me his word that they would not attack us until the morning of the twelfth day.”

At once they yoked their oxen and mules and gathered in front of the city. For nine days they brought in great heaps of wood. On the morning of the tenth day, with many tears, they carried brave Hector out, laid his dead body on top of the pile, and set fire to it. Then, when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared on the eleventh day, the people gathered again around the pyre of mighty Hector. When they were all there, they first put out the fire with wine wherever it was still burning. Then his brothers and comrades, with many bitter tears, gathered his white bones. They wrapped them in soft purple robes and laid them in a golden urn, which they placed in a grave and covered with large stones set close together. Then they hurriedly built a barrow over it, posting guards on every side in case the Achaeans attacked before they had finished. When they had heaped up the barrow, they went back into the city. They all assembled and held a grand feast in the house of Priam their king.
That is how they celebrated the funeral of Hector, tamer of horses.
